Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a variation of G1037; depthless, i.e. (specially) (infernal) "abyss":--deep, (bottomless) pit.
BiblicalUsage: The abyss is the bottomless deep — the pit without a floor. The demons beg Jesus not to send them 'into the deep'; Paul asks who will descend 'into the deep' to bring Christ up; a star falls and opens 'the bottomless pit'; and an angel comes down with the key of the bottomless pit to bind Satan for a thousand years.
TheologicalSignificance: The deep is where demons fear to go and where Satan will be shut — and the key is held by an angel, not by the devil. I believe the abyss shows me that evil has a bottom, even if it looks bottomless, and that God holds the key to every prison, including the ones I fear most.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals the Gerasene Demoniac; The Thousand Years
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asa, the name of a king and of a Levite
BiblicalUsage: Asa is the third king of Judah, son of Abijam, who reigns forty-one years. He does ‘that which was good and right in the eyes of the LORD’, removes the idols and the high places, defeats Zerah the Ethiopian with a million men, and then, in his later years, trusts Syria instead of God and dies diseased in his feet.
TheologicalSignificance: Asa starts well and ends badly — a king who trusted God against a million men and would not trust Him against a sore foot. I believe his story is the warning I need most: a good beginning does not guarantee a good ending, and the God who gave me the victory at the start is the same God I need at the end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to squeeze out juice; figuratively, to trample
BiblicalUsage: This verb for treading down — pressing, crushing underfoot — occurs once, in Malachi 4:3: 'And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do this, saith the LORD of hosts.' It is the last promise of the Old Testament's last prophet.
TheologicalSignificance: The Old Testament ends with the righteous treading the wicked to ashes — a hard promise, and a just one — and I believe it is the hope of everyone who has watched the wicked prosper.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a storehouse (only in the plural)
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for a storehouse or barn — the place where the harvest is kept. God promises to command the blessing ‘upon thee in thy storehouses’; and the proverb says ‘so shall thy barns be filled with plenty’ when you honour the LORD with your substance.
TheologicalSignificance: The storehouse is where God’s blessing is kept, and the promise is plain — honour Him with what fills it, and He will fill it again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asaph, the name of three Israelites, and of the family of the first
BiblicalUsage: Asaph is the chief musician of David’s tabernacle — a Levite set over the songs, the cymbals, and the psalms. His name heads twelve psalms, from the great Psalm 73 to the laments of 74 through 83; his sons sing at the return from exile.
TheologicalSignificance: Asaph sings the hardest psalms in the book — 'my feet were almost gone' when he envied the wicked — and he sings his way back to God. I believe that is why his name heads so many psalms: worship is not only for the certain, it is for the doubting too, and the way back is through the sanctuary, not around it.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gather for any purpose; hence, to receive, take away, i.e. remove (destroy, leave behind, put up, restore, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: This is the everyday verb for gathering — to collect, to take in, to take away. Rachel says 'God hath taken away my reproach' when Joseph is born; Moses tells Pharaoh to 'gather thy cattle' before the hail; and the people 'gathered the quails' all day and all night in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: The same word gathers a reproach away, gathers cattle from the field, and gathers quails for a hungry camp — God gathers and God takes away. I believe the word is a small picture of His providence: He gathers what we need, and He takes away what shames us, and both are His work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to yoke or hitch; by analogy, to fasten in any sense, to join battle
BiblicalUsage: This verb for binding — to tie, to yoke, to fasten — runs through the whole story. Joseph 'bound' Simeon before his brothers' eyes; a vow 'binds' the soul that makes it; the men of Judah 'bound' Samson with new ropes; and Elijah tells Ahab to harness — 'prepare' — his chariot before the rain.
TheologicalSignificance: Binding is sometimes judgment and sometimes duty: Simeon bound, Samson bound, a soul bound by its vow. I believe the word shows me that what I bind myself to matters — a vow is a chain I put on willingly, and God holds me to the words I speak.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Assir, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Assir is the name of two Israelites: a son of Korah, named in the genealogy of Levi, and a son of Jeconiah, named in the line of David after the exile — 'the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son.' One sits in the priestly line, the other in the royal line after the captivity.
TheologicalSignificance: Two men, one name, and both sit in the lines that matter most — Levi and David, priest and king, before and after the exile. I believe the name Assir is a quiet sign that God keeps both lines alive through the captivity: the priesthood and the promise survive together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {bound, i.e. a captive}
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for a prisoner — one bound, one shut up. Joseph is put 'into the prison, a place where the king's prisoners were bound'; Isaiah promises the Servant will 'bring out the prisoners from the prison'; and Lamentations says God does not delight in crushing 'all the prisoners of the earth' under His feet.
TheologicalSignificance: Joseph the prisoner becomes the keeper of the prisoners, and Isaiah promises a Servant who will open the prison doors. I believe the word runs straight to Christ: the prisoners of the earth are not forgotten by God, and the One who was bound sets the bound free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asenath, the wife of Joseph
BiblicalUsage: Asenath is the daughter of Potipherah, priest of On, whom Pharaoh gives to Joseph as wife. She bears him Manasseh and Ephraim 'before the years of famine came', and her sons are named in the genealogy of the tribes when Jacob's family goes down into Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: An Egyptian priest's daughter becomes the mother of two tribes of Israel — and the Bible tells it without apology. I believe Asenath is a reminder that God's family grows in surprising ways: the sons of Joseph and an Egyptian woman stand in the inheritance, and grace does not check a birth certificate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a collection of people (only adverbial)
BiblicalUsage: This noun for a gathering or collection occurs once, in Isaiah 24:22: 'they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison, and after many days shall they be visited.' It is the herding of the proud kings and powers into a pit, like captives rounded up after a battle.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse gathers the kings of the earth like prisoners into a pit — and then says ‘after many days shall they be visited’ — and I believe the gathering is God’s judgment and the visit is His reckoning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achab, the name of a king of Israel and of a prophet at Babylon
BiblicalUsage: Ahab is the seventh king of Israel, son of Omri, who reigns twenty-two years in Samaria — and the Bible’s verdict is that he ‘did evil in the sight of the LORD above all that were before him.’ He marries Jezebel, builds Baal a temple, hunts Elijah, and seizes Naboth’s vineyard — and dies by a random arrow at Ramoth-gilead.
TheologicalSignificance: Ahab had a prophet at his door for twenty years and still chose Jezebel's gods — and the dogs licked his blood in the very vineyard he stole. I believe Ahab is the clearest warning in Kings: a man can hear God's word again and again and still die in his sin, and the word he ignored is the word that judges him.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Naboth's Vineyard
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a brother (used in the widest sense of literal relationship and metaphorical affinity or resemblance)}
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word for brother occurs once, in Ezra 7:18, in the king's letter to Ezra: 'whatsoever shall seem good to thee, and to thy brethren, to do with the rest of the silver and the gold, that do after the will of your God.' It names Ezra's fellow workers — the brethren who share his charge over the temple funds.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, one word — ‘thy brethren’ — and it is about shared stewardship, which is how God’s work is meant to be carried: together, by brethren, according to the will of God.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Oh! (expressive of grief or surprise)
BiblicalUsage: Ach is a cry, not a word with a definition you can pin down — it appears only twice, both times in Ezekiel, both times as "Alas" or "Ah!" In Ezekiel 6:11 the prophet is told to stamp his foot and cry it over Israel's abominations; in Ezekiel 21:15 it breaks out over the glittering sword drawn for judgment. It is the sound a man makes when words run out.
TheologicalSignificance: A gasp carries no doctrine, and the weight here sits in Ezekiel's grief over the judgment he had to announce, not in the cry itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achasbai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Achasbai — Ahasbai in the King James text — is named exactly once, as the father of Eliphelet, one of David's mighty men. Beyond this verse the Bible tells no more of him, and his son's story is told on Eliphelet's People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: A single name in a list carries no doctrine of its own. What it quietly shows is that God keeps a record — the faithful are named, and so are the fathers who raised them.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to unify, i.e. (figuratively) collect (one's thoughts)
BiblicalUsage: Achad occurs once in the whole Bible, in the song of the sword: "Go thee one way or other, either on the right hand, or on the left, whithersoever thy face is set." The sword is commanded to converge, to make one choice and strike. A word used once, for a blade that will not be turned aside.
TheologicalSignificance: One occurrence of a rare verb proves nothing on its own, and the force of the verse lies in God's settled judgment, not in the word for converging.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Achaia (i.e. Greece), a country of Europe:--Achaia.
BiblicalUsage: Achaia was the Roman province covering southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital, and Paul was hauled before Gallio its deputy, while its churches sent a gift to the poor saints in Jerusalem. As a place, Achaia is covered in the Biblical Places collection rather than in a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: Achaia is geography, not doctrine, and I will not dress it up as more. What matters is what happened there: ordinary believers in a Roman province gave generously to strangers, and Paul boasted of their readiness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G882; an Achaian; Achaicus, a Christian:--Achaicus.
BiblicalUsage: Achaicus is named once, in Paul's closing greetings, when he came with Stephanas and Fortunatus and his visit supplied what the Corinthian church itself could not.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no great theology in a name on a greeting list. But I believe it still preaches: the encouragement of a faithful brother's presence is real ministry, and Paul was glad for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: would that!
BiblicalUsage: Achalay is the Hebrew for 'would that' — a wish spoken aloud. It appears twice: a captive Israelite girl telling her mistress she wished her lord were with the prophet in Samaria, and the psalmist longing for his ways to be directed to keep God's statutes. One wish heals a leper; the other longs for obedience.
TheologicalSignificance: A wish is a small thing in itself, and what matters here is what the two wishes ask for — healing for a stranger and obedience for the psalmist.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, the hind part; generally used as an adverb or conjunction, after (in various senses)
BiblicalUsage: Achar is the plain Hebrew word for "after" — after in time, after in place, after in loyalty. Adam lived "after he had begotten Seth"; Sarah laughed, "after I am waxed old shall I have pleasure"; and a generation arose that "went a whoring after other gods." It does the quiet work of sequence in hundreds of verses.
TheologicalSignificance: A word as common as 'after' carries no theology of its own, and the teaching sits in the story that follows it, not in the preposition.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to loiter (i.e. be behind); by implication to procrastinate
BiblicalUsage: To loiter, to delay, to tarry — that is achar as a verb. Eliezer pleads, "Hinder me not"; Sisera's mother asks why his chariot tarries; Amasa "tarried longer than the set time" and it cost him his life; and Habakkuk is told the vision "will not tarry." The word shows up wherever waiting turns into danger.
TheologicalSignificance: Delay is a plain human fault, and the pattern in these verses is what preaches — men who tarry come to grief, while God's promise never tarries.
RelatedPeople: Eliezer of Damascus; Amasa, Son of Ithra; Habakkuk
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Acharchel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Acharchel — Aharhel in the King James text — appears once, in a genealogy, as one of the families of Harum in Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching to draw from a name in a list, and I will not invent one. The list itself is the point: God kept the families, and the Chronicler kept the names.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G5483; thankless, i.e. ungrateful:--unthankful.
BiblicalUsage: Unthankful — the word appears twice. Jesus says God "is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil," and calls us to love our enemies the same way; Paul lists "unthankful" among the marks of men in the last days, lovers of themselves and disobedient to parents. The same word describes the people God is kind to and the people who have forgotten Him.
TheologicalSignificance: Ingratitude is not a small fault in Scripture; it is the mark of a heart turned away from its Giver. I hold that thankfulness is one of the plainest tests of whether we remember who gave us everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: later
BiblicalUsage: Achariyth is the Aramaic word for the latter days, and it appears only once — in Daniel's answer to Nebuchadnezzar: "there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days." One word, one verse, and it opens the whole prophetic future.
TheologicalSignificance: One Aramaic word for the latter days is a small peg to hang much on, and the verse itself does the work, showing a God who reveals what is to come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hinder; generally, late or last; specifically (as facing the east) western
BiblicalUsage: Acharown means last, latter, hindmost — and, facing east, western. Jacob put Rachel and Joseph hindermost; Job confessed his Redeemer "shall stand at the latter day upon the earth"; the Lord declares, "I am the first, and I am the last"; and Haggai promises, "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former." One word stretches from the back of a caravan to the end of the age.
TheologicalSignificance: When God calls Himself the last, He is claiming the end of the story as His own. I hold that as a firm anchor: the God who was first will also be last, and nothing after Him can undo what He has done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a satrap or governor of a main province (of Persia)}
BiblicalUsage: A satrap was a governor of a Persian province — the king's lieutenants in Ezra and Esther, the princes summoned to Nebuchadnezzar's golden image, and the hundred and twenty princes set over Darius's kingdom. The word belongs to empire: administration, decrees, and the machinery of foreign rule over God's people.
TheologicalSignificance: A satrap is only a Persian governor's title, and any weight in the word comes from the scenes around it, where earthly rulers meet the God who outranks them.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

The word belongs to empire: administration, decrees, and the machinery of foreign rule over God's people.

Definition: a mule
BiblicalUsage: The achashtaran were the swift mounts of the Persian royal post — mules and camels, and young dromedaries, carrying Mordecai's counter-decree to every province. The posts "went out, being hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment." The word is the hurry of good news racing against a death sentence.
TheologicalSignificance: A mule's name carries no doctrine, and the hurry in the verses is the point — good news racing the king's own couriers to undo a death sentence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an achastarite (i.e. courier); the designation (rather than name) of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Haahashtari — the Achashtari — is named once, as a son of Naarah in the genealogy of Judah. The verse gives his brothers' names and nothing more. He is one of the many whose whole biblical record is a single line in a family list.
TheologicalSignificance: A single name in a genealogy teaches nothing by itself, and it stands in the record only because the Chronicler kept Judah's families.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achashverosh (i.e. Ahasuerus or Artaxerxes, but in this case Xerxes), the title (rather than name) of a Persian king
BiblicalUsage: Ahasuerus — Achashverosh in the Hebrew — is the Persian king of Esther's story, reigning from India even unto Ethiopia, and the same name appears in Ezra and Daniel.
TheologicalSignificance: The name itself teaches nothing, but the throne it sat on is the stage for one of Scripture's clearest pictures of hidden providence: a pagan king, a Jewish queen, and a God who is never named yet moves every piece.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fraternity
BiblicalUsage: Achavah means brotherhood, and it appears once. Zechariah cut asunder his staff Bands, "that I might break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel." The word names the bond between the two kingdoms — and the prophet's act declares that bond broken.
TheologicalSignificance: Brotherhood is named once, when Zechariah breaks it, and the word itself is only the bond — the broken staff does the preaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H271); Achaz, an Israelite:--Achaz.
BiblicalUsage: Ahaz was king of Judah for sixteen years, and the record is blunt: he did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord, shutting the temple doors and trusting Assyria instead of God.
TheologicalSignificance: Ahaz is a warning, not a model. I hold his story up plainly: a king who would not ask God for a sign ended up asking a foreign king for help, and the help cost him everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achaz, the name of a Jewish king and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahaz was king of Judah for sixteen years, and the record is blunt: he did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord, shutting the temple doors and trusting Assyria instead of God.
TheologicalSignificance: Ahaz is a warning, not a model. I hold his story up plainly: a king who would not ask God for a sign ended up asking a foreign king for help, and the help cost him everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to seize (often with the accessory idea of holding in possession)
BiblicalUsage: To seize, to take hold — achaz is a gripping word. The ram was "caught in a thicket" when Abraham looked up; Moses was told to put out his hand and "take it by the tail" when the rod became a serpent; and Potiphar's wife "caught" Joseph by his garment. The same grip appears in deliverance, in obedience, and in temptation.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice the verb cuts both ways: God tells men to take hold, and sinners take hold of the godly. The difference is never the grip — it is what is being held, and who told the hand to close.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Moses; Joseph, Son of Jacob
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achazjah, the name of a Jewish and an Israelite king
BiblicalUsage: Two kings shared the name Ahaziah, and neither reigned long: Ahab's son ruled Israel two years before he died of his fall, and Jehoram's son ruled Judah one year before Jehu killed him.
TheologicalSignificance: Two short reigns, one lesson: when a king in trouble consults anyone but God, the answer is death. I hold both Ahaziahs up as the same warning — the throne is no shelter from the word of the Lord.
RelatedPeople: Ahaziah, King of Israel; Ahaziah, King of Judah; Elijah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achban, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahban is named once: 'she bare him Ahban, and Molid' — a son of Abishur in the genealogy of Judah, with no story, no deed, and no word spoken.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no doctrine in this name, and I will not manufacture one. He is remembered because the Chronicler remembered the families of Judah, and Judah's families mattered because the Messiah would come from them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin (compare H3137); Achim, an Israelite:--Achim.
BiblicalUsage: Achim appears once, in Matthew's genealogy: 'Sadoc begat Achim; and Achim begat Eliud,' standing between two names we know no more about than him. Beyond this verse the Bible tells no more of him.
TheologicalSignificance: The genealogy is full of men like Achim — no story, only a place in the chain. I hold that as the point: God's promise did not depend on any one man's fame.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5499; unmanufactured, i.e. inartificial:--made without (not made with) hands.
BiblicalUsage: Made without hands — the word is used three times, and every use matters. False witnesses threw it at Jesus: "I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and within three days I will build another made without hands." Paul says we have "an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens"; and that in Christ we are circumcised "with the circumcision made without hands."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the heart of the gospel in miniature: everything God truly builds, no human hand made. The temple they accused Him of threatening, the body He promises us, the cleansing He gives — all of it is God's work, not ours.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Acher, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aher is named once, in the genealogy of Benjamin, among the children of Ir and the sons of Aher — a verse scholars still debate, and the Chronicler's record is all we have.
TheologicalSignificance: No teaching hangs on this name. I leave the puzzle as it stands rather than forcing an answer the text does not give.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, hinder; generally, next, other, etc.
BiblicalUsage: Acher means other, another, next — the word for what is not this one. "Thou shalt have no other gods before me"; Noah waited "yet other seven days" before sending the dove again; Isaac's servants "digged another well." It is one of the commonest words in the Bible, doing humble work in commandments, calendars, and wells.
TheologicalSignificance: The word for 'other' is too small to build on, and its weight comes entirely from the commandment it serves — no other gods before the Lord.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Noah and the Flood
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achiam, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahiam, son of Sacar the Hararite, is named twice, both times in the lists of David's mighty men, and no single deed of his is recorded — the honour is the list itself.
TheologicalSignificance: A name on the honour roll carries no doctrine. But I believe the roll itself teaches something: God remembers the men who stood with His anointed, even when history forgets their deeds.
RelatedPeople: King David; Ahiam, Son of Sacar
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achiezer, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai, was the prince of Dan, named at the census in the wilderness and again when he brought Dan's offering on the tenth day of the dedication. Beyond these verses the Bible tells no more of him.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on this prince. He is one of the twelve whose names mark the order God set on His people — every tribe counted, every tribe placed, none forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achi, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ahi is named twice: a chief among the Gadites, and a son of Shamer among the sons of Asher — two men, one short name, both appearing only in genealogies. Beyond these verses the Bible tells no more of either man.
TheologicalSignificance: There is nothing more to say about either man, and I will not stretch a verse into a sermon. The genealogies keep their names because the tribes kept their families.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achijah, the name of nine Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Two men share this name, and both matter: Ahijah the Shilonite, the prophet who tore his garment and gave ten pieces to Jeroboam, and Ahiah son of Ahitub, the priest who wore the ephod with Saul's army.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold the prophet's torn garment as the greater of the two stories: God's word does not merely describe the future, it divides it. When Ahijah tore the cloth, the kingdom was already torn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achisamak, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahisamach is named three times, always as the father of Oholiab, the craftsman God filled with wisdom to work the tabernacle — his son's hands built God's house, and his father is remembered for it.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching in the father's name alone. But I believe the passage around it teaches plenty: God gives skill, not just zeal, for the work of His house — and He names the workmen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achichud, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahihud is named once, in a Benjaminite genealogy: Gera 'begat Uzza, and Ahihud,' a single name in a single verse inside a family list. Beyond this verse the Bible tells no more of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I will not invent a lesson from a name the Bible leaves bare. The Chronicler kept it, and that is the whole of its record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an enigma
BiblicalUsage: An enigma, a hard sentence — achiydah appears once, when the queen tells Belshazzar about Daniel: he could interpret dreams, "shew hard sentences," and dissolve doubts. The king's wise men had failed at the writing on the wall; the queen remembered the man who could untie knots no one else could.
TheologicalSignificance: One Aramaic word for a riddle is a small thing, and the gift it describes — Daniel untangling what no magician could — belongs to God, not to the noun.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achihud, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahihud, son of Shelomi, was the prince of Asher appointed to divide the land of Canaan, named once among the ten princes who stood with Eleazar and Joshua to allot the inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on this prince. His appointment is part of the order God set on the conquest: the land was not grabbed, it was divided by lot, by named men, under God's direction.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achilud, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahilud is named as the father of Jehoshaphat the recorder, the official who kept the king's records under David and again under Solomon. The name recurs in the same office lists, and as the father of Baana, one of Solomon's officers — but always as a name in a list, never a story.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching in this name. But the lists that preserve it show a kingdom with order — a king, a recorder, a history being kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achimaats, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ahimaaz, son of Zadok the priest, was the runner who begged Joab to let him carry the news of Absalom's death, outran Cushi, and arrived first with a message he could not bring himself to speak.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the runner's story is a warning about eagerness: Ahimaaz ran faster than the truth, and arrived with nothing to say. Speed is no substitute for a message, and zeal is no substitute for honesty.
RelatedPeople: King David; Absalom; Ahimaaz, Son of Zadok
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achiman, the name of an Anakite and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahiman was one of the three sons of Anak in Hebron, the giants the spies feared — and forty years later Caleb drove him out, with Sheshai and Talmai, by one old man's faith.
TheologicalSignificance: The lesson is not in the name but in the contrast: ten spies saw giants and despaired, and Caleb saw the same giants and drove them out. I hold that faith does not deny the size of the enemy — it denies him the last word.
RelatedPeople: Ahiman, Son of Anak; Caleb; Moses
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achimelek, the name of an Israelite and of a Hittite
BiblicalUsage: Ahimelech was the priest of Nob who fed David the shewbread and gave him Goliath's sword, and Saul had him killed with eighty-five priests for it — only his son Abiathar escaped.
TheologicalSignificance: Mercy to God's anointed cost Ahimelech his life, and I will not soften that. I hold his death as a shadow of a greater one: the priest who gave bread to the hungry king was murdered for it, and the King he fed would one day give His own body as bread.
RelatedPeople: King David; Ahimelech; Abiathar, Son of Ahimelech
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achimoth, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahimoth is named once, in the genealogy of the Levites: 'the sons of Elkanah; Amasai, and Ahimoth,' standing in the line of the singers and priests.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no lesson to draw from a single name in a Levite list. The list keeps him because the tribe kept its families, and the families served the house of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achinadab, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahinadab, son of Iddo, had Mahanaim — one of Solomon's twelve officers, each providing food for the king's household for one month of the year.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on this officer. He is one of the many whose work kept the kingdom fed, and whose name the record kept with the rest.
RelatedPeople: Ahinadab, Son of Iddo; King Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achinoam, the name of two Israelitesses
BiblicalUsage: Two women share this name: Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz, Saul's wife, and Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, David's wife and the mother of Amnon, carried off at Ziklag and recovered by David.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no doctrine in the name. But the two Ahinoams sit on either side of the hinge of Israel's story: Saul's house going down, David's house rising, and both women caught in the turning.
RelatedPeople: King David; Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; Ahinoam, Wife of David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achikam, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahikam, son of Shaphan, was one of the men Josiah sent to Huldah when the Book of the Law was found, and years later his hand shielded Jeremiah when the priests demanded the prophet's death.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold Ahikam up as the quiet faithful: he carried the king's question to the prophetess, and he shielded the prophet when the crowd wanted blood. Reform needs men like him — not only kings who find the book, but servants who stand by it.
RelatedPeople: Ahikam; Jeremiah; King Josiah; Gedaliah, Son of Ahikam
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achira, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahira, son of Enan, was the prince of Naphtali, named at the census in the wilderness and again on the twelfth day of the dedication, when he brought his tribe's offering.
TheologicalSignificance: No teaching hangs on this prince. He is one of the twelve whose names mark the order God set on His people in the wilderness — counted, placed, and provided for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achiram, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahiram was a son of Benjamin, named once in the second census, where the family of the Ahiramites is traced to him. Beyond this verse the Bible tells no more of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A census line is all we get for him, and I will not stretch it into a sermon. The family is remembered because the tribe was counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Achiramite or descendant (collectively) of Achiram
BiblicalUsage: The Ahiramites were the family named for Ahiram, counted among the sons of Benjamin in the second census — the word is not a man's name but a family's. The clan is traced through Ahiram, whose name stands in the same census verse.
TheologicalSignificance: A family name in a census carries no doctrine. It is one of the many threads the Bible keeps to show that Israel was not a crowd — it was families, counted by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achishachar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahishahar is named once, as the last son of Bilhan in the genealogy of Benjamin — seven brothers, one verse, no story attached to any of them.
TheologicalSignificance: A bare name is all the Bible gives me here, and I will not invent a lesson from it. The Chronicler kept the brothers together, and that is the whole of the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achishar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahishar was 'over the household' — the steward of Solomon's palace, named once in the list of the king's officials, with his office and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on a steward's name. Yet the list that holds it is a portrait of a kingdom at peace: officers, districts, and a house in order.
RelatedPeople: Ahishar, Steward of Solomon; King Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achithophel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahithophel was David's counsellor, whose advice was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God, until he went over to Absalom and, seeing his counsel rejected, went home and hanged himself.
TheologicalSignificance: Wisdom without loyalty curdles into treason — that is what I hold his story to teach. The cleverest man in the kingdom could not save himself, because he had chosen the wrong king.
RelatedPeople: King David; Absalom; Ahithophel the Gilonite
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achitub, the name of several priests
BiblicalUsage: Ahitub is named as a priestly father: Ahiah his son wore the ephod with Saul's army, and Ahimelech his son was the priest of Nob whom Saul murdered, and through him runs the line that leads to Zadok.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching in this name alone. But the line it anchors matters: from Eli's house to Zadok's, the priesthood passed through fathers and sons, and God kept the line even when kings cut it down.
RelatedPeople: Ahimelech; Ahitub, Father of Zadok; Eli
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achlab, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ahlab was a town in Asher's territory that Asher failed to drive out, and the verse records unfinished obedience — the Canaanites stayed, and dwelt among them. As a place, Ahlab is covered in the Biblical Places collection rather than in a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no doctrine in a town's name. But the verse it sits in is a warning I will not soften: half-finished obedience leaves the enemy in the land, and the enemy does not stay quiet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a gem, probably the amethyst
BiblicalUsage: The amethyst was the third stone in the third row of the high priest's breastplate — a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. Each stone stood for a tribe, carried over Aaron's heart whenever he went into the holy place. The word is a gem's name; the picture is a priest carrying a people.
TheologicalSignificance: A gemstone's name is a fact for the jeweller's shelf, and the meaning lives in the breastplate it sat in, where the priest carried the tribes over his heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achlai, the name of an Israelitess and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahlai appears twice: a son of Seshan in the genealogy of Judah, and the father of Zabad, one of David's mighty men — one name, two men.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on either Ahlai. The names are kept because the families were kept, and the families mattered because the kingdom was built from them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; dimness of sight, i.e. (probably) a cataract:--mist.
BiblicalUsage: Achlys means mist, dimness of sight — and it appears once, when Paul struck Elymas the sorcerer blind: "there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand." The man who had blinded a governor's eyes was himself blinded on the spot.
TheologicalSignificance: Mist is a medical word for dimmed sight, and the verse does the preaching, not the noun — the sorcerer who blinded others was himself struck blind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achmetha (i.e. Ecbatana), the summer capital of Persia
BiblicalUsage: Achmetha — Ecbatana, the summer capital of Persia — is named once, where a roll was found in the palace: Cyrus's decree, whose finding restarted the building of the temple. As a place, Achmetha is covered in the Biblical Places collection rather than in a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: The place itself teaches nothing. But the finding does: a lost decree, found in an archive hundreds of miles away, was the hinge on which the temple was rebuilt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: backwards
BiblicalUsage: Backwards — achoranniyth describes walking with your face turned away. Shem and Japheth "went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father," refusing to look on Noah's shame; and Eli, when he heard the ark was taken, "fell from off the seat backward by the side of the gate, and his neck brake, and he died." One backward step covers shame; the other ends a life.
TheologicalSignificance: Walking backwards is a posture, not a doctrine, and the two scenes it describes — covering shame in honour, and falling in judgment — carry whatever lesson there is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achoach, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahoah is named once, as a son of Bela in the genealogy of Benjamin, listed with his brothers Abishua and Naaman.
TheologicalSignificance: His name sits in a list and nowhere else. The Chronicler kept the brothers together, and the tribe kept its families.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Achochite or descendant of Achoach
BiblicalUsage: The Ahohite was the family of Eleazar son of Dodo, one of the three mighty men who stood with David against the Philistines, and of Dodai, who commanded the second month's course. The clan is traced through Ahoah, whose name stands at the head of the family.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on a family name. But the honour roll it sits in says something plain: God remembers the men who stood their ground when the army fled.
RelatedPeople: King David; Eleazar, Son of Dodo
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the hinder part; hence (adverb) behind, backward; also (as facing north) the West
BiblicalUsage: Achowr means behind, the backside, the hinder part. Abraham looked up and saw "behind him a ram caught in a thicket"; Moses "led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God"; and David sang, "Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me." The word covers what is at our back — the provision we did not see, the place we did not expect, the God who surrounds us.
TheologicalSignificance: The word for 'behind' is a direction, not a teaching, and the comfort sits in the psalm it appears in, where God besets His people behind and before.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Burning Bush
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sister (used very widely (like brother), literally and figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: A sister — achowth is used very widely, literally and figuratively, from blood kin to fellow countrywomen. Abraham says of Sarah, "she is my sister"; Miriam "the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand"; and the law guards the sister's honour in Leviticus 18. The word runs through family, worship, and law alike.
TheologicalSignificance: Sisterhood in Scripture is never a small thing: it is the bond that holds families, and the bond the law protects. I hold that the word's breadth is the point — in God's people, sister means more than blood.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achrach, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aharah — Achrach in the Hebrew — was the third son of Benjamin, after Bela the firstborn and Ashbel the second.
TheologicalSignificance: The record gives me his name and nothing more, and I will not pretend otherwise. The tribe kept its sons' names, and the Chronicler kept the tribe's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G888; to render useless, i.e. spoil:--become unprofitable.
BiblicalUsage: To become unprofitable, to be spoiled, made useless — achreioo appears once, in Paul's verdict on all humanity: "They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one." The word is the hinge of Romans 3: every mouth stopped, the whole world guilty before God.
TheologicalSignificance: One verb for becoming useless is a small word, and the thunder in the verse comes from Paul's verdict on all humanity, not from the verb itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G5534 (compare G5532); useless, i.e. (euphemistically) unmeritorious:--unprofitable.
BiblicalUsage: Unprofitable, useless — achreios is the word for a servant who produces nothing. In the parable, the master commands, "cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness"; and Jesus tells His disciples, "when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do."
TheologicalSignificance: An unprofitable servant is a picture, not a system, and the two parables it serves — the buried talent and the servant who did only his duty — do the teaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5543; inefficient, i.e. (by implication) detrimental:--unprofitable.
BiblicalUsage: Unprofitable — achrestos appears once, in Paul's letter about Onesimus: "Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me." A runaway slave, useless to his master, has become useful — to Philemon, and to Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: A single verse about a runaway slave carries no doctrine in the adjective, and the gospel in the verse is that grace made the useless man useful.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἄχρις; akin to G206 (through the idea of a terminus); (of time) until or (of place) up to:--as far as, for, in(-to), till, (even, un-)to, until, while. Compare G3360.
BiblicalUsage: Until, as far as — achri marks the boundary. The days before the flood, when men ate and drank "until the day that Noe entered into the ark"; and the years in Egypt, "till another king arose, which knew not Joseph." The word draws a line and says: this far, and no further.
TheologicalSignificance: A boundary word like 'until' teaches nothing on its own, and the weight lies in what stands on either side of each line it draws.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bulrush or any marshy grass (particularly that along the Nile)
BiblicalUsage: Achu is marsh grass, the reeds along the Nile — the meadow where Pharaoh's fat kine fed in his dream, and the flag Bildad asks about: "Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?" The word appears only three times, always in a picture of life that needs its source.
TheologicalSignificance: Marsh grass is a detail of the Nile bank, and Bildad's question about the rush is what gives the word its meaning — nothing grows without its source.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achumai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahumai is named once, as a son of Jahath in the genealogy of Judah, among the families of the Zorathites.
TheologicalSignificance: The Bible leaves this name bare, and I refuse to dress it up into a lesson. The family is remembered because the tribe kept its records.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something seized, i.e. a possession (especially of land)
BiblicalUsage: A possession — achuzzah is what is seized and held, especially land. God promised Abraham the land of Canaan "for an everlasting possession"; Abraham bought a burial plot, saying, "give me a possession of a buryingplace"; and at the jubilee "ye shall return every man unto his possession." The word holds both gift and purchase, promise and homecoming.
TheologicalSignificance: The land was God's gift held in trust, and I hold that as a picture of everything we truly own: it is given, not taken, and it returns to its rightful owner in the end. Our true possession is the Lord Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achuzzam, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahuzam is named once, as a son of Naarah in the genealogy of Judah, one of four brothers in a single verse with no story following any of them.
TheologicalSignificance: Beyond his name the Bible says nothing, and I will leave it there. The Chronicler kept the brothers together, and the tribe kept its families.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achuzzath, a Philistine
BiblicalUsage: Ahuzzath is named once: he came with Abimelech and Phichol to Isaac at Beersheba to make a covenant, because they could see the Lord was with him.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on this friend. But the scene he walked into is worth keeping: enemies came to make a covenant because they could see God was with Isaac — and I hold that as a picture of what a godly life does to its neighbours.
RelatedPeople: Ahuzzath; Isaac; Abimelech, King of Gerar
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an utterance
BiblicalUsage: An utterance, a declaration — achvah appears once, when Job demands a hearing: "Hear diligently my speech, and my declaration with your ears." He is not whispering; he is insisting that his friends, and God Himself, listen to what he has to say.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an utterance is too small to preach from, and the honesty in the verse is Job's, demanding to be heard, not the noun's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achjan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahian is named once, as a son of Shemida in the genealogy of Manasseh, one of four brothers in a single verse with no story attached.
TheologicalSignificance: There is nothing more to say about him, and I will not pretend otherwise. The tribe kept its sons' names, and the Chronicler kept the tribe's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achio, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ahio drove the new cart carrying the ark of God from the house of Abinadab, walking before it with Uzzah his brother, on the day David learned that good intentions do not make an unholy way holy.
TheologicalSignificance: Ahio himself is not judged in the text, and I will not judge him either. But the scene is a sober one: the ark was to be carried on priests' shoulders, not hauled on a cart, and the cost of forgetting that fell on the man beside him.
RelatedPeople: Ahio, Son of Abinadab; King David; Uzzah, Son of Abinadab
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps remotely from χέω (to shed forth); chaff (as diffusive):--chaff.
BiblicalUsage: Chaff — achyron is the husk the wind carries away. John the Baptist preached it twice over: the Christ "will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire." The picture is the threshing floor: wheat kept, chaff burned.
TheologicalSignificance: Chaff is farm imagery, and the judgment it pictures is the point — the wind keeps the wheat and carries the husk away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Achzai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ahazai — Ahasai in the King James text — is named once, as an ancestor in a priestly family list running from Amashai back through Azareel and Ahasai to Meshillemoth and Immer.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching in this name. The list keeps it because the priests kept their lines, and the lines proved who could serve at the altar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: must or fresh grape-juice (as just trodden out)
BiblicalUsage: Sweet wine, new wine, juice fresh from the press — asiyc is the drink of joy and the drink of judgment both. The bride offers "spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate"; the oppressors are made "drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine"; and in the restored age "the mountains shall drop down new wine." The same cup, opposite ends.
TheologicalSignificance: Sweet wine is a drink, not a doctrine, and the verses hold both its faces — joy in the bride's offer and judgment in the oppressor's cup.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: gathered, i.e. (abstractly) a gathering in of crops
BiblicalUsage: The Feast of Ingathering — asiyph is the gathering in of the harvest at the end of the year, when the labour of the fields was done and Israel kept the feast. It is named twice, both times in the giving of the feasts: firstfruits, harvest, and ingathering, the three great feasts of the year.
TheologicalSignificance: A harvest feast's name is a calendar fact, and the teaching is the feast itself, closing the year with thanks to the Lord who gave the crop.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bound, i.e. a captive
BiblicalUsage: A prisoner, one who is bound — asiyr appears in Joseph's prison, where the keeper committed all the prisoners into his hand, and in the Psalm, where God bringeth out those which are bound with chains. Zechariah turns the word into a promise: 'Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope.'
TheologicalSignificance: God hears the groaning of the prisoner and sets him free — I hold that as a picture of the gospel itself. And Zechariah's phrase is one I love: prisoners, yes, but prisoners of hope.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; King David; Zechariah the Prophet
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asnah, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Asnah is named once, among the families of the Nethinim who returned from exile — the temple servants, given to the Levites for the work of the house of God, counted by name on the way home.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on this family. But the list that holds it shows something I will not miss: even the servants were counted, and even the servants came home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hurt
BiblicalUsage: Hurt, mischief — acown is the harm a father fears and a law measures. Jacob would not send Benjamin down to Egypt, "lest peradventure mischief befall him"; years later he repeats the fear, word for word; and the law of Moses fixes the price when hurt follows a fight. The word is a father's dread and a judge's standard in one.
TheologicalSignificance: Hurt is a plain word for harm, and the lesson sits in Jacob's fear and the law's fairness, not in the noun.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aspatha, a son of Haman
BiblicalUsage: Aspatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, named once in the list of the men the Jews slew in Shushan, whose bodies were hanged on the gallows their father had built for Mordecai.
TheologicalSignificance: The verse records judgment on a house that plotted murder, and I will not soften it. The gallows Haman raised for another became the end of his own sons — the Bible's own warning that the pit a man digs is the pit he falls into.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: gathered up together, i.e. a promiscuous assemblage (of people)
BiblicalUsage: The mixed multitude — acpecuph appears once, for the rabble that travelled with Israel out of Egypt: "the mixt multitude that was among them fell a lusting: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat?" Their craving set the whole camp complaining.
TheologicalSignificance: A rabble's name is a label, not a doctrine, and the verse does the work — a craving crowd set the whole camp complaining.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: collected (only in the plural), i.e. a collection of offerings)
BiblicalUsage: Asuppim — the storehouses. The word appears three times, always at the temple gates: the house of Asuppim fell to Obed-edom's lot among the porters, two Levites a day kept the storehouse, and the gatekeepers kept the ward "at the thresholds of the gates." The storehouse held the supplies of the house of God, guarded by men whose names were kept with the rest.
TheologicalSignificance: Storehouses are temple furniture, and the picture worth keeping is a house of God supplied, guarded, and counted by named men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a collection of (learned) men (only in the plural)
BiblicalUsage: A collection, an assembly — acuppah appears once, in the Preacher's closing: "The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd." The wise men's words are collected, fastened down, and traced to a single source.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about a collection of wise words is a small peg, and the claim in the verse is the Preacher's — all of it comes from one Shepherd.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: anointed, i.e. an oil-flask
BiblicalUsage: A pot of oil — acuwk appears once, in the widow's answer to Elisha: "Thine handmaid hath not any thing in the house, save a pot of oil." It was all she had, and it was the seed of her deliverance: Elisha told her to borrow vessels, pour, and sell, and the oil did not stop until the vessels ran out.
TheologicalSignificance: A pot of oil is a household object, and the miracle it belongs to is Elisha's story, not the flask's name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adadah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adadah was a town in the south of Judah, named once in the list of the tribe's cities, a border town counted among the twenty-nine cities of the southern district. As a place, Adadah is covered in the Biblical Places collection rather than in a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching in a town's name. The list keeps it because the land was divided by lot, town by town, and every town was counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: as far (or long, or much) as, whether of space (even unto) or time (during, while, until) or degree (equally with)
BiblicalUsage: Ad is the word for "until," "as far as" — of space, of time, of degree. "Till thou return unto the ground"; the raven that "went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up"; the Passover lamb, of which "ye shall let nothing of it remain until the morning." It is one of the commonest small words in the Bible, framing curse, deliverance, and command alike.
TheologicalSignificance: The word for 'until' is one of the commonest small words in the Bible, and it teaches nothing by itself — the curse, the flood, and the Passover do the teaching.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; Noah and the Flood; The Passover
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

BiblicalUsage: Ad is the word for "until," "as far as" — of space, of time, of degree. Definition: {to advance, i.e. pass on or continue; causatively, to remove; specifically, to bedeck (i.e. bring an ornament upon)}
BiblicalUsage: Ada is the Aramaic verb for passing on, being removed, taken away. "He removeth kings, and setteth up kings"; to Nebuchadnezzar the voice said, "The kingdom is departed from thee"; and of the Son of Man, "his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away." The same verb takes kingdoms away and promises one that will never be taken.
TheologicalSignificance: An Aramaic verb for passing away is a small word, and the contrast in Daniel does the preaching — kingdoms pass, and His dominion does not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to languish
BiblicalUsage: To languish, to grieve — adab appears once, in the sentence on Eli's house: those left alive "shall be to consume thine eyes, and to grieve thine heart." The man of God spoke it to a priest who had honoured his sons above the Lord, and the grief was the sentence.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for grieving is a small thing, and the sentence it sits in — the judgment on Eli's house — carries the whole weight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adad (or Hadad), an Edomite
BiblicalUsage: Hadad is the name of a king of Edom who smote Midian, and of Hadad the Edomite whom God raised up as an adversary to Solomon, who had fled to Egypt as a boy and returned when David and Joab were dead.
TheologicalSignificance: God raises up adversaries against unfaithful kings — that is what I hold this name to show. Solomon's heart had turned, and the Lord did not leave him comfortable in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adah, the name of two women
BiblicalUsage: The name Adah belongs to two women: Adah, wife of Lamech and mother of Jabal and Jubal, and Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite, one of Esau's wives.
TheologicalSignificance: The first Adah's family invented music and the wandering life; the second Adah's marriage grieved Isaac and Rebekah. I hold both as a sober picture: the line of Cain grew clever and godless at once, and Esau's choices cost his parents dear.
RelatedPeople: Adah, Wife of Lamech; Adah, Wife of Esau; Lamech, Father of Noah; Esau
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to advance, i.e. pass on or continue; causatively, to remove; specifically, to bedeck (i.e. bring an ornament upon)
BiblicalUsage: To adorn, to deck oneself with ornaments — adah is the verb of dressing up. The bride "adorneth herself with her jewels" in Isaiah's song of salvation; Jerusalem "deckest thee with ornaments of gold" to seduce her lovers in Jeremiah; and God says to Jerusalem, "I decked thee also with ornaments." The same verb dresses the bride, the harlot, and the beloved city.
TheologicalSignificance: Adorning is a picture with two faces in these verses, and the word itself is neutral — God dresses His people in salvation, and sin dresses itself for seduction.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adalja, a son of Haman
BiblicalUsage: Adalia was one of the ten sons of Haman, named once in the list of the men the Jews slew in Shushan, whose bodies were hanged on the gallows their father had built for Mordecai.
TheologicalSignificance: The verse hands down judgment on a house that plotted murder, and I will not soften it. The gallows Haman raised for another became the end of his own sons.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H121); Adam, the first man; typically (of Jesus) man (as his representative):--Adam.
BiblicalUsage: Adam the man — the first man, who named every living creature, whose generations are written in 'the book of the generations of Adam,' and who lived nine hundred and thirty years and died; Paul calls him 'the figure of him that was to come,' setting the first man against Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: The first man is the head of a fallen race, and the pattern of the One to come. I hold that as the Bible holds it: Adam's story is our story, and Christ's story is the answer to it.
RelatedTopics: Adam and Eve; The Fall; Creation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ruddy i.e. a human being (an individual or the species, mankind, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: Man, mankind — adam is the word for the human creature. "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness"; "the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life"; and David asks, "What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" The word holds both the dust and the image in one breath.
TheologicalSignificance: We are dust, and we are image-bearers — I hold both together, because the Bible does. The dust keeps us humble; the image keeps us from despair. Man is small, and yet God is mindful of him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adam the name of the first man, also of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adam the man — the first man, who named every living creature, whose generations are written in 'the book of the generations of Adam,' and who lived nine hundred and thirty years and died; Paul calls him 'the figure of him that was to come,' setting the first man against Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: The first man is the head of a fallen race, and the pattern of the One to come. I hold that as the Bible holds it: Adam's story is our story, and Christ's story is the answer to it.
RelatedTopics: Adam and Eve; The Fall; Creation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flush or turn rosy
BiblicalUsage: To be red, to flush rosy — adam is the verb of redness. Rams' skins "dyed red" covered the tabernacle; the Lord promises, "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool"; and the princes of Jerusalem "were more ruddy in body than rubies" before the siege broke them.
TheologicalSignificance: Redness is a colour, not a creed, and the thread it runs through the Bible — from tabernacle skins to scarlet sins washed white — is what gives it meaning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adamah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adamah was a town in Naphtali, named once in the list of the tribe's fenced cities, alongside Ramah and Hazor. As a place, Adamah is covered in the Biblical Places collection rather than in a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: A town's name teaches nothing by itself. The list keeps it because the land was divided town by town, and every town was counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: soil (from its general redness)
BiblicalUsage: Ground, soil, earth — adamah is the red earth man was made from and the ground that bears the curse. God "formed man of the dust of the ground"; then He said, "cursed is the ground for thy sake"; and to Cain, "the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood." The word holds creation, curse, and blood in one.
TheologicalSignificance: We are dust, and the ground itself bears the curse — I hold that as the plain reading. But the same ground that drank Abel's blood is the ground God promises to renew, and the whole creation waits for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: reddish
BiblicalUsage: Reddish — adamdam is the priest's word for a sore that is "somewhat reddish" on the skin, a white reddish sore on a bald head, or reddish hollows in the walls of a house. The priest looked, and looked again, and pronounced clean or unclean. The word is a diagnosis, repeated across the laws of leprosy.
TheologicalSignificance: A reddish sore is a priest's diagnosis, and the care behind the law is the point — the priest looked, and looked again, before declaring a man unclean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adami, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adami was a town on the border of Naphtali, named once, marking where one tribe's land met another's. As a place, Adami is covered in the Biblical Places collection rather than in a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching in a border town's name. The list keeps it because the borders were drawn line by line, and every line was counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be soft or pleasant; figuratively and reflexively, to live voluptuously
BiblicalUsage: To live softly, to delight oneself — adan appears once, in the Levites' great prayer: Israel took the fat land, "and became fat, and delighted themselves in thy great goodness." One word for the joy of the gift — and the prayer goes on to tell how they repaid it with rebellion.
TheologicalSignificance: One rare word for delighting in God's goodness is a small peg, and the prayer it sits in remembers both the delight and the ingratitude that followed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as negative particle); and G1160; costless, i.e. gratuitous:--without expense.
BiblicalUsage: Without expense, free of charge — adapanos appears once, in Paul's boast: he preached the gospel "without charge," refusing payment "that I abuse not my power in the gospel." He had the right to be paid; he gave the right up, so no one could say he sold the message.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for 'without charge' is a small thing, and Paul's boast is the sermon — he would rather work with his own hands than let the gospel look bought.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively, have) redundant
BiblicalUsage: To be over, left over, in excess — adaph is the word for what remains. He that gathered much manna "had nothing over"; the manna that "remaineth over" was kept for the Sabbath; and the remnant of the tabernacle curtains hung over the back of the tent. The word moves from the wilderness table to the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: Leftovers are a plain fact of the manna story, and the provision is the teaching — he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adar, the 12th Hebrew month
BiblicalUsage: Adar is the twelfth month of the Hebrew year: Haman cast the lot and it fell on Adar, in Adar the Jews instead destroyed their enemies, and in Adar the temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius. As a month, Adar has no People profile — its story is told in Esther and Ezra.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold the turn of Adar as one of the clearest pictures of providence in the Bible: the month chosen by lot for murder became the month of rescue, and the same month saw the house of God finished. The lot is cast, but the disposing is of the Lord.
RelatedEvents: Esther Saves Her People; Rebuilding of the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adar, the 12th Hebrew month
BiblicalUsage: Adar is the twelfth month of the Hebrew year: Haman cast the lot and it fell on Adar, in Adar the Jews instead destroyed their enemies, and in Adar the temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius. As a month, Adar has no People profile — its story is told in Esther and Ezra.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold the turn of Adar as one of the clearest pictures of providence in the Bible: the month chosen by lot for murder became the month of rescue, and the same month saw the house of God finished. The lot is cast, but the disposing is of the Lord.
RelatedEvents: Esther Saves Her People; Rebuilding of the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to arrange as a battle, a vineyard (to hoe); hence, to muster and so to miss (or find wanting)
BiblicalUsage: To be lacking, to fail, to miss — adar is the verb of the muster that comes up short. After the Amalekite raid, "there was nothing lacking to them, neither small nor great"; at the Jordan crossing, "there lacked not one of them"; and of the stars God calls by name, "not one faileth." The word counts what is missing — and finds nothing missing.
TheologicalSignificance: A verb for coming up short is a counter's word, and the promise in these verses is God's — nothing of His is lost, and not one is missing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to expand, i.e. be great or (figuratively) magnificent
BiblicalUsage: To be great, glorious, majestic — adar appears three times, all of them praise. "Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power"; "who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders"; and "he will magnify the law, and make it honourable." The word is a song, not a definition.
TheologicalSignificance: God's glory is not decoration; it is His power and His holiness on display. I hold those three verses together as the whole of it: glorious in power, glorious in holiness, and glorifying His own law.
RelatedTopics: Majesty of God; God's Holiness; God's Power
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a chief diviner, or astrologer
BiblicalUsage: The adargazer were the counsellors, the judges — Nebuchadnezzar's officials summoned to the dedication of the golden image: "the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces." They gathered to bow, and three men among them would not.
TheologicalSignificance: A counsellor's title is only a job in Nebuchadnezzar's court, and the scene it sits in — a whole court bowing, and three men standing — does the preaching.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a daric or Persian coin
BiblicalUsage: A daric, a dram of gold — adarkon is the Persian coin of the return. David's people gave "ten thousand drams" of gold for the temple, and Ezra weighed out twenty basins of gold "of a thousand drams" for the journey to Jerusalem. The word is money counted for God's house.
TheologicalSignificance: A Persian coin is money, not theology, and the generosity in the verses is the point — gold given freely, weighed and counted, for God's house.
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple; Ezra's Journey to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lentil
BiblicalUsage: Lentils — adash is the humble food that shows up at the hinges of great stories. Jacob gave Esau "bread and pottage of lentiles" for his birthright; lentils were brought to feed David's fugitives; Shammah stood his ground in "a piece of ground full of lentiles" while the army fled; and Ezekiel was told to take lentils for his bread in the siege.
