BiblicalUsage: Agnosia is ignorance — not knowing God — and it appears twice, both times as a rebuke. Paul tells the Corinthians to awake to righteousness and sin not, 'for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame'; and Peter says it is the will of God that by well-doing you put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.
TheologicalSignificance: Some have not the knowledge of God, Paul says, and this word names their ignorance — the shame is theirs, and the verse speaks it plainly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as negative particle) and G1110; unknown:--unknown.
BiblicalUsage: Agnostos is 'unknown' — and it appears once, on an altar in Athens: 'TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.' Paul found the altar as he walked through the city, and he took it as his text: the God they worshipped without knowing, he declared to them.
TheologicalSignificance: An altar to an unknown god is Athens confessing it does not know, and this word only reads the inscription — Paul supplies the God they missed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; properly, to lead; by implication, to bring, drive, (reflexively) go, (specially) pass (time), or (figuratively) induce:--be, bring (forth), carry, (let) go, keep, lead away, be open.
BiblicalUsage: Ago is to lead — to bring, to carry, to go. Jesus sends the disciples, 'Go into the village over against you'; He says, 'Let us go into Judaea again'; Paul says the goodness of God leadeth to repentance; and he tells the Galatians that if they are led by the Spirit they are not under the law. The word covers a journey, a command, and a life led by God — and the difference is always who is doing the leading.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word asks me a simple question: who is leading me? The goodness of God leads to repentance, the Spirit leads out from under the law, and the voice that says 'go' is the same voice that went to the cross — and I want to be led by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: reduplicated from G71; a bringing up, i.e. mode of living:--manner of life.
BiblicalUsage: Agoge is a manner of life — a bringing up, the way a person lives day by day — and it appears once, in Paul's charge to Timothy: 'But thou hast fully known my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, charity, patience.' Paul is not pointing to a single act but to a whole life Timothy had watched: the teaching and the living, side by side, for years.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul tells Timothy, you have followed my manner of life — and this word is just the life lived, not a doctrine about living.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: circular
BiblicalUsage: Agol means circular or round — and it appears only in the description of the temple's great bronze sea: 'a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about.' The word belongs to the craftsmen's measurements, to a basin so wide a man could not reach across it, standing on twelve oxen in the temple court. A round thing, named once, in the middle of the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: A round sea of bronze, ten cubits across — this word only says it was circular, and the measurement is the whole of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G71; properly, a place of assembly (as if led), i.e. (by implication) a contest (held there); figuratively, an effort or anxiety:--conflict, contention, fight, race.
BiblicalUsage: Agon is a contest — a fight, a race, a struggle. Paul says the Philippians share the same conflict he has; he tells the Colossians of the great conflict he has for them; he charges Timothy to fight the good fight of faith; and Hebrews pictures the Christian life as a race, run with patience, with a cloud of witnesses watching. The word holds the whole Christian life in one picture: a contest worth entering, and worth finishing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word will not let the Christian life go soft. Faith is a fight and a race, not a stroll — and the same Paul who fought it tells me to lay hold on eternal life, to run with patience, and to look to Jesus, who ran it first and finished it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G73; a struggle (properly, the state), i.e. (figuratively) anguish:--agony.
BiblicalUsage: Agonia is agony — a struggle, anguish — and it appears once, in Gethsemane: 'And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.' The word holds the whole weight of that night: the Saviour wrestling in prayer, alone, with the cup before Him, and praying harder as the anguish grew.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse holds the agony of Gethsemane, and the word is too small for what happened there — the sweat like blood does the preaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G73; to struggle, literally (to compete for a prize), figuratively (to contend with an adversary), or genitive case (to endeavor to accomplish something):--fight, labor fervently, strive.
BiblicalUsage: Agonizomai is to struggle — to compete for a prize, to contend with an adversary, to labour fervently. Jesus says to strive to enter the narrow gate; He says His servants would fight if His kingdom were of this world; Paul says every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things; and he commends Epaphras, who laboured fervently in prayer. The word covers the race, the fight, and the prayer closet — all of them a struggle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the call to take the Christian life seriously. The gate is narrow, the prize is real, and the striving is not anxiety but devotion — a life that fights, runs, and prays like it means it, because it does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀγείρω (to gather; probably akin to G1453); properly, the town-square (as a place of public resort); by implication, a market or thoroughfare:--market(-place), street.
BiblicalUsage: Agora is the marketplace — the town square, the public place where life happened. Jesus compares His generation to children sitting in the markets; the householder finds labourers standing idle in the marketplace; the sick are laid in the marketplaces hoping to touch Jesus' garment; and Paul disputed daily in the market at Athens with those who met him.
TheologicalSignificance: Children calling in the marketplace is the Lord's picture of a generation that would not dance — the place is the stage, not the lesson.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G58; relating to the market-place, i.e. forensic (times); by implication, vulgar:--baser sort, low.
BiblicalUsage: Agoraios means 'of the marketplace' — and in Acts it takes two very different shapes. In Thessalonica the Jews took 'certain lewd fellows of the baser sort,' marketplace loafers, and set the city in an uproar against Paul; in Ephesus the townclerk says 'the law is open' — literally, the court days are kept — and there are deputies, so let them accuse one another there.
TheologicalSignificance: Lewd fellows of the baser sort stirred the city against Paul, and this word only says where they lounged — the riot is the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G58; properly, to go to market, i.e. (by implication) to purchase; specially, to redeem:--buy, redeem.
BiblicalUsage: Agorazo is to buy — to go to market and purchase — and in the New Testament it becomes the great word for redemption. A man sells all to buy the field with the treasure; Paul says we were bought with a price and must glorify God in our bodies, and again, bought with a price, be not the servants of men; and heaven sings that the Lamb redeemed us to God by His blood. The word starts in the market and ends at the cross, where the price was paid in full.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one verb holds the whole gospel. I was bought — not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ — and being bought means I belong to the One who paid. That is why my body and my life are not my own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something gathered, i.e. perhaps a grain or berry; used only of a small (silver) coin
BiblicalUsage: Agowrah is a small silver coin — a piece of silver, the price of a loaf — and it appears only once, in the prophecy against the house of Eli: 'every one that is left in thine house shall come and crouch to him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread, and shall say, Put me, I pray thee, into one of the priests' offices, that I may eat a piece of bread.' The word holds the whole humiliation: the high priest's house, begging for a coin and a crust.
TheologicalSignificance: A piece of silver and a morsel of bread is all the humbled priest asks for, and this word names the scrap — the fall of Eli's house is the sermon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G71; (abstractly) a catching (of fish); also (concretely) a haul (of fish):--draught.
BiblicalUsage: Agra is a catch — a draught of fishes — and it appears only in the story of the miraculous catch. Jesus tells Simon to launch out and let down the nets, and they enclose a great multitude of fishes, so many the net breaks and the boats begin to sink; and Simon is astonished at the draught.
TheologicalSignificance: A great catch breaking the nets is the sign, and this word only names the haul — Peter's boats sinking is the wonder.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as negative particle) and G1121; unlettered, i.e. illiterate:--unlearned.
BiblicalUsage: Agrammatos means unlettered — illiterate, without formal schooling — and it appears once, in the council's reaction to Peter and John: 'they perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.' The word is the council's insult and the story's proof: men without letters, speaking with a boldness no school could teach.
TheologicalSignificance: Unlearned men stood bold before the council, and this word only says they had no schooling — their boldness said the rest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G68 and G832 (in the sense of G833); to camp out:--abide in the field.
BiblicalUsage: Agrauleo means to camp out — to abide in the field — and it appears once, in the Christmas story: 'there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night.' The word holds the whole scene: men sleeping rough under the sky, on duty in the dark, when the angel came. The first to hear of the Saviour's birth were men camping out with sheep.
TheologicalSignificance: Shepherds abiding in the field heard the good news first, and this word only says they were out there — the angels did the preaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G61; to hunt, i.e. (figuratively) to entrap:--catch.
BiblicalUsage: Agreuo means to hunt — to catch or entrap — and it appears once, in the trap set for Jesus: 'they send unto him certain of the Pharisees and of the Herodians, to catch him in his words.' The word is a hunter's word: they were not asking a question, they were laying a snare, hoping His own answer would be the rope. The tribute question was the bait.
TheologicalSignificance: They came to catch Him in His words, and this word names the trap — the Lord's answer is the teaching, not the verb.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G66 and G1636; an oleaster:--olive tree (which is) wild.
BiblicalUsage: Agrielaios is the wild olive tree — the uncultivated olive, growing where it was not planted — and it appears twice, both in Paul's picture of Israel and the Gentiles. The Gentiles were a wild olive branch, grafted in among the natural branches, partaking of the root and fatness of the olive tree; and Paul says if God could graft the wild branch in against nature, He can graft the natural branches back in again.
TheologicalSignificance: A wild branch grafted in among the natural ones is Paul's picture of us, and this word only says the tree was wild — the grafting is the gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G68; wild (as pertaining to the country), literally (natural) or figuratively (fierce):--wild, raging.
BiblicalUsage: Agrios is wild — of the country, untamed. John the Baptist ate locusts and wild honey in the wilderness — Matthew and Mark both tell it; and Jude calls false teachers raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame. The word covers the wildness of the desert and the wildness of men who will not be tamed — and the story always shows which wildness God uses and which He judges.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word draws a line I need to see. The wild honey fed the prophet — but the raging waves are reserved for judgment, and the difference is whether the wildness submits to God or rages against Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently from G66 and G2462; wild-horse tamer; Agrippas, one of the Herods:--Agrippa.
BiblicalUsage: Agrippa — Herod Agrippa II, the last of the Herods — came to Caesarea with Bernice to greet Festus, and stayed to hear Paul. Paul told him the whole gospel, from the light on the Damascus road to the resurrection, and Agrippa answered, 'Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.'.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Agrippa's 'almost' is the saddest word in Acts. He heard the gospel from Paul himself, he knew it was true, and he walked away a king who was almost persuaded — and almost is not enough, because the gospel demands a yes, not an almost.
RelatedPeople: Herod Agrippa II; Paul; Bernice; Festus
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G71; a field (as a drive for cattle); genitive case, the country; specially, a farm, i.e. hamlet:--country, farm, piece of ground, land.
BiblicalUsage: Agros is a field — the country, a farm, a piece of ground. The kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field, worth selling everything to buy; the invited guests went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise; the elder brother was in the field when the prodigal came home; and Jesus told His disciples to lift up their eyes, for the fields are white already to harvest.
TheologicalSignificance: Treasure hidden in a field is the kingdom's picture, and this word only names the ground — the man selling all he has is the point.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ultimately from G1 (as negative particle) and G5258; to be sleepless, i.e. keep awake:--watch.
BiblicalUsage: Agrypneo is to watch — to be sleepless, to keep awake. Jesus says, 'Take ye heed, watch and pray'; He tells His disciples to watch and pray always, that they may escape what is coming; Paul says to watch with all perseverance and prayer for all saints; and Hebrews says the leaders watch for your souls, as they that must give account. The word is the night watchman's word: eyes open, lamps lit, no one asleep on duty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word wakes me up in a sleepy world. The Lord is coming, the enemy is prowling, and the saints need prayer — and the watchman who sleeps on duty is no watchman at all. I want to be the one still awake when He comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G69; sleeplessness, i.e. a keeping awake:--watch.
BiblicalUsage: Agrypnia is sleeplessness — watchings — and it appears twice, both in Paul's list of his sufferings as a minister of God: 'in watchings, in fastings,' and again, 'in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness.' The word is not about insomnia but about nights spent awake for the gospel — travelling, praying, working, and watching over the churches.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul lists his watchings among his sufferings, and this word only names the sleepless nights — the apostle's endurance is the sermon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a band, bundle, knot, or arch
BiblicalUsage: Aguddah is a band or bundle — a bunch of hyssop dipped in blood and struck on the lintel at the first Passover, a troop of Benjamites gathered on a hill behind Abner, the bands of wickedness that true fasting looses, and the troop God has founded in the earth. The word ties things together: hyssop in a bunch, men in a troop, and the knots of oppression that God unties.
TheologicalSignificance: A bunch of hyssop to strike the blood on the doorposts — this word only names the bundle, and the blood is the whole meaning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably the swallow
BiblicalUsage: Aguwr is the swallow — the small bird that finds a nest even in God's house. The psalmist says the swallow has found a nest where she may lay her young, even at the altars of the Lord; Hezekiah chatters like a crane or a swallow in his sickness; and Jeremiah says the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming, while God's people do not know His judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: Even the swallow finds a nest by God's altars, and this word only names the bird — the longing for His courts is the psalm's heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Agur, a fanciful name for Solomon
BiblicalUsage: Agur is the name attached to the sayings of Proverbs 30: 'The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, even the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal.' Tradition has sometimes taken Agur as a fanciful name for Solomon, but the text gives us only the name, his father's name, and the words that follow — thirty-three verses of hard, humble wisdom, ending with the leech's daughters and the four things that are little on the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Agur's words are worth hearing whoever he was, because they begin where wisdom begins: 'I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man.' A man who knows he does not know is the man God can teach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: affection (in a good or a bad sense)
BiblicalUsage: Ahab is love as a noun — affection, in the plural, as a quality a person carries. Its one place in this study is Proverbs 5:19: "Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe." The wife is the loving hind — the word is her lovings, the delight she gives. It is love as delight, not duty: the kind that satisfies a husband at all times.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is honest about love in a way I need. Here love is not a hunger that takes but a delight that satisfies — a wife's lovings, the kind a husband is told to enjoy at all times. The test of love is what it does, not what it feels.
RelatedTopics: Love; Love for God; Love of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to have affection f or (sexually or otherwise)
BiblicalUsage: Ahab is the great verb 'to love' in the Old Testament, used hundreds of times. God tells Abraham to take Isaac, 'whom thou lovest'; Moses commands Israel, 'thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart'; Jonathan's soul was knit to David's and he loved him as his own soul; and God says to Israel, 'I have loved thee with an everlasting love.' The word covers love for God, love for a son, love for a friend, and God's love for His people — and it always means love that acts.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word is the whole Old Testament in a single verb. Love the Lord with all your heart — that is the command — and I have loved thee with an everlasting love — that is the promise. The command rests on the promise, and the promise is why the command can be obeyed.
RelatedTopics: Love; Love of God; Love for God; Covenant love
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Call of Abraham
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Oh!
BiblicalUsage: Ahahh is the cry 'Ah!' or 'Alas!' — the sound of a prophet overwhelmed. Jeremiah cries it when God calls him, because he cannot speak and he is a child; he cries it again when he prays over the siege of Jerusalem, 'Ah Lord GOD! thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power'; Ezekiel cries it when God tells him to cook over dung; and Joel cries it over the day of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: Jeremiah's cry — Ah, Lord God, I cannot speak, for I am a child — is the whole of it, and the word is only the gasp before the excuse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tent
BiblicalUsage: Only three times in the whole Bible, and all three are about moving a tent. Lot pitches his toward Sodom, Abram moves his to Mamre and builds an altar there, and Isaiah says no Arab will ever pitch a tent in ruined Babylon again.
TheologicalSignificance: The word itself is only a tent verb, and its weight lies in the scenes — Abram's tent beside his altar, Lot's pitched toward Sodom — not in the word alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tent
BiblicalUsage: Only three times in the whole Bible, and all three are about moving a tent. Lot pitches his toward Sodom, Abram moves his to Mamre and builds an altar there, and Isaiah says no Arab will ever pitch a tent in ruined Babylon again.
TheologicalSignificance: The word itself is only a tent verb, and its weight lies in the scenes — Abram's tent beside his altar, Lot's pitched toward Sodom — not in the word alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: aloe wood (i.e. sticks)
BiblicalUsage: Aloes are a fragrant wood, named four times and always as perfume. Balaam compares Israel's tents to aloes planted by the Lord, the king's robes smell of myrrh and aloes, a foolish woman perfumes her bed with them, and the Song names them among the garden's spices.
TheologicalSignificance: A fragrant wood carries no doctrine of its own; the same scent graces a king's robe and perfumes a seducer's bed, and the difference is in the hands, not the wood.
RelatedBooks: Numbers; Psalms; Proverbs; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aharon, the brother of Moses
BiblicalUsage: Aaron's name reaches the New Testament through the priesthood he began. Luke places John the Baptist's mother among Aaron's daughters, and Hebrews measures every priest against Aaron — called by God, never self-appointed — before showing Christ as the better priest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Aaron matters because God chose the priest; the priest never chose himself. That is the pattern Hebrews holds up, and the reason Christ's priesthood is better: He was called by God too, but He lives forever to intercede for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ahava, a river of Babylonia
BiblicalUsage: Ahava is a river in Babylonia where Ezra gathers the returning exiles before the long journey home. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: A place name carries little theology on its own, and I will not pretend otherwise. What matters is what happened there: God's people stopped, fasted, and asked Him for safe passage instead of asking the king for soldiers.
RelatedTopics: Exile and Return; Prayer; God's Protection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G164; captivity:--captivity.
BiblicalUsage: Paul quotes Psalm 68 when he says Christ led captivity captive — the ascended Lord takes His defeated enemies as His train of captives and gives gifts to men. Revelation uses the same word the other way round: he that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity, a warning that persecutors will share the fate they inflict.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word turns captivity inside out. Christ does not merely free prisoners; He parades the powers that held us, and the church's gifts — apostles, prophets, teachers — are the spoils of His victory.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G164; to capture (like G163):--lead captive.
BiblicalUsage: This verb occurs once, in Ephesians 4:8, where Paul says Christ led captivity captive when He ascended. The picture is a victorious king marching home with his prisoners behind him — except here the prisoners are the powers that once held humanity captive, and the triumph ends in gifts, not chains, for His people.
TheologicalSignificance: One verb in one verse carries no theology of its own; the weight is in the scene, Christ the ascended King leading captives and handing out gifts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G164; to make captive:--lead away captive, bring into captivity.
BiblicalUsage: Luke uses it of Jerusalem's people led away captive into all nations, and Paul uses it of the war inside himself — sin's law bringing him into captivity to the law of sin. Twice it turns hopeful: believers take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ, and Paul warns of teachers who lead captive silly women. Same verb, four very different captivities.
TheologicalSignificance: The word asks whose prisoner I am, and I believe the answer is the whole point. Sin takes captives, false teachers take captives, and Christ takes captives too — the difference is that His captivity is freedom, because every thought brought under His rule is a thought finally set right.
RelatedTopics: Sin; Spiritual Warfare; Freedom; False Teaching
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from αἰχμή (a spear) and a derivative of the same as G259; properly, a prisoner of war, i.e. (genitive case) a captive:--captive.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, on Jesus' own lips in the Nazareth synagogue, reading Isaiah: He has come to preach deliverance to the captives. The captives are not only prisoners in cells; in Isaiah's world they are exiles and the oppressed, and Jesus claims the whole promise as His mission.
TheologicalSignificance: The word itself is only a captive's label, and its weight lies in the lips that speak it — Jesus in Nazareth, claiming Isaiah's promise as His own mission.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G104; everduring (forward and backward, or forward only):--eternal, everlasting.
BiblicalUsage: Only twice in the New Testament, and both times of something that never began and never ends. Paul says God's eternal power and Godhead are clearly seen in creation, and Jude says the angels who left their first estate are kept in everlasting chains under darkness. One verse speaks of God's endless nature, the other of an endless judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is too big for anything but God and what God fixes forever. I hold that its force is the contrast: God's eternity is life and glory, while the eternity of judgment is the terrible mirror — what lasts forever depends entirely on whose side of it you stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to sing:--sing.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells believers to sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to one another, and John hears heaven doing the same — a new song to the Lamb who was slain, and the song of Moses and the Lamb beside the sea of glass. The word covers both the church's singing here and heaven's singing there.
TheologicalSignificance: Singing is how truth gets into the heart and stays there. I believe Paul puts it beside being filled with the Spirit for a reason: a singing church is a taught church, and heaven's song is the same one we are learning now.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1492 (through the idea of downcast eyes); bashfulness, i.e. (towards men), modesty or (towards God) awe:--reverence, shamefacedness.
BiblicalUsage: Once only. Paul says women should adorn themselves with shamefacedness and sobriety — modest dress, with a downcast, reverent spirit, not broided hair or gold or pearls or costly array.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for downcast modesty carries little weight on its own; its force lives in the one verse, where reverence before God shapes how His people dress.
RelatedTopics: Humility; Worship; Fear of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from αἴξ (a goat); belonging to a goat:--goat.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Hebrews 11:37, where the faithful wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented. The goatskin is the uniform of the persecuted — rough clothing for people the world drove out, who would rather wear an animal's hide than deny the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: A goatskin word carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the company it keeps, the faithful who wore it rather than deny the faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀΐσσω (to rush) and G251 (in the sense of the sea); a beach (on which the waves dash):--shore.
BiblicalUsage: The shore is where Jesus teaches the crowds from a boat, where the fishermen sort the catch in the parable of the net, where the risen Lord stands at dawn while the disciples fish, and where Paul's ship runs aground off Malta. It is the edge between the deep and dry land — a place of teaching, sorting, meeting, and shipwreck.
TheologicalSignificance: A beach is only a place, and the word carries no theology; the weight lies in the scenes on that shore, where Jesus taught, sorted, met His friends, and a ship went down.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Appears to Seven Disciples by the Sea of Galilee; Paul Shipwrecked on Malta
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G125; an Ægyptian or inhabitant of Ægyptus:--Egyptian.
BiblicalUsage: Stephen says Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, then tells how Moses killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew — the act that drove him into exile. This study covers only how the word is used; Egypt itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is a label, not a lesson, and I won't force one out of it. What it shows is how Israel's story keeps colliding with Egypt — first as a place of learning, then of oppression, then as a byword for rebellion.
RelatedEvents: Moses and Aaron Confront Pharaoh; Martyrdom of Stephen
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Ægyptus, the land of the Nile:--Egypt.
BiblicalUsage: Egypt is the land of refuge and the land of bondage, both at once. Egypt is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Egypt matters because God keeps using the same place both ways — a shelter for His Son and a prison for His people. The pattern is deliverance: what once enslaved becomes the road home, and the child who fled to Egypt grows up to lead a greater exodus.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Ænĕas, an Israelite:--Æneas.
BiblicalUsage: Aeneas is a paralyzed man at Lydda who has kept his bed eight years.
TheologicalSignificance: Aeneas carries no teaching of his own; he is a witness, not a theologian. What I take from him is simple: Christ's healing was immediate, public, and complete, and a whole town turned to the Lord because one bedridden man stood up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G136; to praise (God):--praise.
BiblicalUsage: The angels praise God over Bethlehem's fields, the shepherds go back glorifying and praising God, the crowds praise Him as Jesus rides into Jerusalem, and the lame man who has just been healed walks into the temple leaping, and praising God. Every use is praise that bursts out — angels, shepherds, crowds, and one healed man.
TheologicalSignificance: Praise here is never polite applause; it is the sound of people who have just seen God act. I believe that is the pattern for us too: praise is the right answer to a God who shows up, whether in a manger, on a road, or in a healed pair of legs.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Triumphal Entry; Peter Heals the Lame Man
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G134; a praising (the act), i.e. (specially) a thank(-offering):--praise.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Hebrews 13:15: let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. The word names the act itself — praise as an offering, laid on the altar like a sacrifice, and offered continually, not only when we feel like it.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse names praise as a sacrifice, and the word itself carries little beyond that picture; the weight is in Hebrews' command to keep offering it, with our lips, without stopping.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G136 (in its primary sense); an obscure saying ("enigma"), i.e. (abstractly) obscureness:--X darkly.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the most quoted verse about love's limits: For now we see through a glass, darkly. The word is enigma — a riddle, an obscure saying.
TheologicalSignificance: One riddle-word in one verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Paul's promise that the dim glass gives way to seeing face to face.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (a derivative of H5869, place of springs); Ænon, a place in Palestine:--Ænon.
BiblicalUsage: Aenon is the place near Salim where John was baptizing, because there was much water there. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: A place name with no sermon attached, and I will not invent one. What it marks is a moment: the last days of John's work, done faithfully in a small place with much water, while the greater ministry rose beside him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a prime word; properly, a story, but used in the sense of G1868; praise (of God):--praise.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times praise comes from the lips of the lowly. Jesus quotes Psalm 8 to the chief priests — Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise — while the children cry Hosanna in the temple; and the blind man of Jericho, his sight restored, follows Jesus glorifying God while all the people give praise.
TheologicalSignificance: I love that the word belongs to children and a blind beggar, not to the educated. God perfects praise from mouths the world would ignore, and the chief priests' anger only proves the point: true praise always threatens those who want worship on their own terms.
RelatedEvents: The Cleansing of the Temple; The Healing of Bartimaeus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G104; properly, an age; by extension, perpetuity (also past); by implication, the world; specially (Jewish) a Messianic period (present or future):--age, course, eternal, (for) ever(-more), (n-)ever, (beginning of the, while the) world (began, without end). Compare G5550.
BiblicalUsage: The word means an age — a stretch of time with a character of its own — and by extension the world shaped by that age. Jesus speaks of sins not forgiven neither in this world, neither in the world to come, of the harvest as the end of the world, and Paul says Christ is exalted above every name not only in this world, but also in that which is to come. Hebrews adds that God made the worlds by His Son.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that aion is the Bible's way of saying history has a shape and an end. This age is passing, the age to come is Christ's, and the line between them runs through the cross — which is why the same word can mean both the times we live in and the world itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G165; perpetual (also used of past time, or past and future as well):--eternal, for ever, everlasting, world (began).
BiblicalUsage: The young ruler asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life; Jesus tells Nicodemus God so loved the world that whoever believes should not perish, but have everlasting life; Paul sets the wages of sin is death against the gift of God is eternal life; and Timothy hears that God's purpose and grace were given before the world began. The word always points past time, in both directions.
TheologicalSignificance: Eternal life is not life that goes on and on — it is life of a different kind, God's own life, given as a gift and not earned. I believe that is the whole gospel in one adjective: what sin pays is death, and what God gives is forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G5316 (compare G1810) (meaning non-apparent); unexpected, i.e. (adverbially) suddenly:--sudden, unawares.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times it is a warning. Jesus says that day will come unawares on the careless, like a snare; Paul says that when people are saying Peace and safety, then sudden destruction comes upon them, like labour pains on a woman with child.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for suddenness carries little theology on its own; its weight is the warning in both verses, that the day finds the careless asleep.
RelatedTopics: Second Coming; Day of the Lord; Urgency
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary root; to lift up; by implication, to take up or away; figuratively, to raise (the voice), keep in suspense (the mind), specially, to sail away (i.e. weigh anchor); by Hebraism (compare H5375) to expiate sin:--away with, bear (up), carry, lift up, loose, make to doubt, put away, remove, take (away, up).
BiblicalUsage: The word does heavy work all through the Gospels. The devil quotes Psalm 91 to Jesus — the angels will bear thee up in their hands; John the Baptist points at Jesus and says, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world; the crowd takes up stones to kill Him; and Jesus tells anyone who will follow Him to take up his cross. Lift, bear, carry away, remove — one verb, and the cross gathers all its meanings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heart of this word is John 1:29: He takes away sin the way a servant carries a burden off someone else's back. And the call is the same shape in reverse — we take up our cross and follow the One who took up ours.
RelatedEvents: The Temptation in the Wilderness; The Baptism of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G150 and κέρδος (gain); sordid:--given to (greedy of) filthy lucre.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both times as a qualification for church leadership: a deacon must not be greedy of filthy lucre, and a bishop must not be given to filthy lucre. The word joins shame to gain — money got or wanted in a way that disgraces the man who takes it. Paul sets it beside a quick temper, wine, and striking, and holds up blamelessness and a steady life against it.
TheologicalSignificance: A leader who loves money will eventually sell the flock to feed himself. I hold that Paul puts this in the list for a reason: greed is the quiet rot that turns shepherds into hirelings, and the church must watch for it before the damage shows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G146; sordidly:--for filthy lucre's sake.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Peter's charge to the elders: Feed the flock of God which is among you, not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind. The word is the adverb — how the work is done.
TheologicalSignificance: One adverb in one verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Peter's test of the shepherd's motive, whether the work would go on if the pay stopped.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G150 and G3056; vile conversation:--filthy communication.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's list of what believers must put off: anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth. The word is foul talk — speech that is shameful to hear and shameful to say.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for foul talk carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Paul's list, where dirty speech sits beside anger and malice as a garment to be put off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G150; a shameful thing, i.e. indecorum:--shame.
BiblicalUsage: Three times, always in the phrase it is a shame. Paul says it is a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, a shame for a woman to speak in the church, and a shame even to speak of the things the disobedient do in secret.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for what is shameful carries little weight on its own; its weight is in Paul's line, that some deeds of darkness are not even fit for conversation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G153; shameful, i.e. base (specially, venal):--filthy.
BiblicalUsage: Four times, and three of them say it is a shame — for a woman to be shorn, for a woman to speak in the church, and even to speak of what the disobedient do in secret. The fourth is different: false teachers who subvert whole houses teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake. The adjective marks what is base and dishonourable, whether it is conduct, speech, or gain.
TheologicalSignificance: Shame here is a moral sense, not a feeling to be therapied away. I believe the word still convicts: gain that comes from corrupting households is filthy gain, and speech that drags darkness into the light for entertainment is shameful speech.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G150; shamefulness, i.e. obscenity:--filthiness.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Ephesians 5:4: Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks. Paul is listing the speech that does not belong in the saints' mouths, and filthiness heads the list — talk that is obscene, coarse, and unclean.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse sets filthiness against thanksgiving, and the word itself carries little beyond that contrast; the weight is Paul's cure, a mouth full of thanks instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G153; shame or disgrace (abstractly or concretely):--dishonesty, shame.
BiblicalUsage: The word runs both ways. Jesus warns the guest who takes the highest seat will be put down with shame; Paul says of enemies of the cross that their glory is in their shame; Hebrews says Jesus despised the shame of the cross; Jude calls false teachers wandering stars with shame like foam; and Laodicea is told to buy white raiment so the shame of thy nakedness do not appear. Shame is sometimes the punishment, sometimes the thing Christ bore for us.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gospel turns shame inside out. The world glories in what should shame it, and Christ took the shame that was ours so that we could be clothed instead of exposed. The cross is where shame ends — despised by Him, removed from us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from αἶσχος (disfigurement, i.e. disgrace); to feel shame (for oneself):--be ashamed.
BiblicalUsage: John says abide in Him, that when He appears we may have confidence, and not be ashamed before Him at His coming; Peter says a Christian who suffers, let him not be ashamed; and Paul says twice over that in nothing shall he be ashamed — neither of his authority, which the Lord gave for building up, nor of Christ being magnified in his body, whether by life, or by death. The verb always faces the same choice: hide Christ, or own Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the daily test of the Christian life. Shame is the pressure to keep quiet, and the answer is not boldness for its own sake but a clear sight of who Christ is — a Saviour no one need be ashamed of, and a coming no one who abides in Him need fear.
RelatedBooks: Mark; Luke; Romans; 2 Timothy; Hebrews; 1 Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; to apprehend (properly, by the senses):--perceive.
BiblicalUsage: Once, at a telling moment: after Jesus speaks of His coming betrayal, the disciples understood not this saying, and they perceived it not. The word is to take something in by the senses — to grasp it, to feel its weight.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about not perceiving carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the scene, disciples who heard Jesus plainly and were afraid to ask what He meant.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G143; perception, i.e. (figuratively) discernment:--judgment.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's prayer for the Philippians: that their love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment. The word is discernment — the trained sense that tells right from wrong, good from better.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, one prayer for discernment, and the word itself carries little weight; its weight is Paul's pairing of love with the judgment that tells good from better.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G143; properly, an organ of perception, i.e. (figuratively) judgment:--senses.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Hebrews 5:14: strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil. The word is the organ of perception — the senses themselves — and the writer says they are trained the way an athlete trains a muscle: by use.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse calls the senses a muscle trained by use, and the word itself carries little beyond that picture; its weight is Hebrews' training plan for maturity.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G154; a thing asked or (abstractly) an asking:--petition, request, required.
BiblicalUsage: Three times, and each one is a request laid before someone with power to grant it. Pilate grants the crowd's demand for Jesus' death; Paul tells believers to make their requests known to God by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving; and John says that if we know God hears our petitions, we know we have what we asked. One granted to a mob, one offered to God — the word itself does not judge the asking.
TheologicalSignificance: The contrast is the lesson. A request can be wicked or right, and the same word covers both — what matters is who we ask and what we ask for. I believe John's promise is the anchor: prayers laid before God in His will are already answered in His hearing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; to ask (in genitive case):--ask, beg, call for, crave, desire, require. Compare G4441.
BiblicalUsage: The great asking word of the New Testament. Ask, and it shall be given you — Jesus repeats it in the Sermon on the Mount, ties it to believing prayer, promises to do whatever is asked in His name, and James says the one who lacks wisdom should ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally. It is the simplest word in the Bible's vocabulary of prayer, and the most used.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God meant asking to be simple. He is not a miser who must be coaxed; He gives liberally, and the only condition James names is faith that does not waver. The door is open because the Father likes to be asked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from αἴθω (to scorch) and ὤψ (the face, from G3700); an Æthiopian (as a blackamoor):--Ethiopian.
BiblicalUsage: Once, for the Ethiopian eunuch — a man of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who had come to Jerusalem to worship and was reading Isaiah on the road home. This study covers only how the name is used in Acts 8 — the man's story is told there, in the one passage that names him.
TheologicalSignificance: One man, one word, and a whole door opens. I believe the Ethiopian's baptism is the proof that Isaiah's promise was for the nations — a foreigner, a eunuch, an outsider by every law of the old covenant, goes home rejoicing as a baptized believer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G154; a cause (as if asked for), i.e. (logical) reason (motive, matter), (legal) crime (alleged or proved):--accusation, case, cause, crime, fault, (wh-)ere(-fore).
BiblicalUsage: The word is a cause, a reason, or a formal charge. Over Jesus' head the soldiers nail His accusation — THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS — and Pilate keeps saying he finds no fault in him, no cause for death. Paul, years later, tells the Roman Jews he was delivered prisoner though I have committed nothing against the people. The word keeps appearing wherever men must say why someone stands accused.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the irony is the sermon. The only charge Rome could pin on Jesus was His kingship, and Pilate's no fault is the verdict of history: the innocent Man died under a true accusation — He is the King — and a false crime.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G156; a thing charged:--complaint.
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Paul stands before Festus and the Jews from Jerusalem laid many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove. The word is a formal charge, a complaint brought before a judge — and Luke's point is that the charges were many, heavy, and empty.
TheologicalSignificance: One complaint in one verse carries no doctrine; its weight is the scene, Paul's accusers bringing many grievous charges they could not prove.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G159; a reason or crime (like G156):--cause, fault.
BiblicalUsage: Luke uses it three times in the trial of Jesus — Pilate's repeated verdict, I find no fault in this man, and I have found no cause of death in him. The fourth use is the town clerk at Ephesus warning the riotous crowd that we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account. In every case the word is a reason that will stand up in court — and in Jesus' trial there was none.
TheologicalSignificance: Pilate said it three times, and the crowd shouted it down three times. I believe Luke records the repetition on purpose: the faultless Man was condemned by men who knew He was faultless, which is exactly why His death can count for the faulty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G154; causative, i.e. (concretely) a causer:--author.
BiblicalUsage: Once, and it is one of the weightiest verses in Hebrews: Christ, being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him. The word is causer — the one who brings something about.
TheologicalSignificance: One word, one verse, and the word itself is only a label — causer; its weight is the verse, Christ made the author of eternal salvation, and that weight belongs to the verse, not the word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a particle of affirmation, surely; hence (by limitation) only
BiblicalUsage: A small word that does big work — only, surely, truly. Noah only remained alive after the flood; David says Truly my soul waiteth upon God; Moses says Only ye shall not eat the blood.
TheologicalSignificance: A particle of only and surely carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is in the mouths that say it, Noah's only, David's truly, and the certainty of a soul that has settled.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to put on anklets
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Isaiah's judgment on the daughters of Zion, who walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet. The word is the tinkling — anklets worn to draw the eye and the ear.
TheologicalSignificance: One tinkling anklet in one verse carries no theology; its weight is Isaiah's judgment, that God sees the show and will strip it away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G2540 (meaning unseasonable); to be inopportune (for oneself), i.e. to fail of a proper occasion:--lack opportunity.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in a sentence full of grace: Paul tells the Philippians he rejoiced that their care for him hath flourished again; wherein ye were also careful, but ye lacked opportunity. The word is to have no season, no opening.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about a missed season carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Paul's grace toward the Philippians, whose love had not cooled but only lacked a door.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from the same as G170; inopportunely:--out of season.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's last charge to Timothy: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season. The word is unseasonable — the wrong time, the inconvenient moment.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for out of season carries little weight on its own; its weight is Paul's charge to Timothy, preach when the room is warm and when it is cold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2556; not bad, i.e. (objectively) innocent or (subjectively) unsuspecting:--harmless, simple.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, in opposite directions. Paul warns that smooth talkers deceive the hearts of the simple — the innocent, the unsuspecting; and Hebrews says our High Priest is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for harmless carries little weight on its own; its weight is the contrast between the simple sheep and the harmless Shepherd, one innocent by ignorance and one by holiness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {to eat (literally or figuratively)}
BiblicalUsage: One of the commonest verbs in the Bible — hundreds of times, from the first command in the garden (Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat) to the Passover lamb eaten in haste and the manna in the wilderness, where Israel learns man does not live by bread alone. The Aramaic form does the same work in Daniel and Ezra: Nebuchadnezzar, driven from men, did eat grass as oxen, and the king's officials tell Artaxerxes they eat the king's salt — literally, they have maintenance from the palace. Eating is where obedience and rebellion both begin, and in the Aramaic chapters it is humiliation, appetite, and loyalty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that eating is the Bible's first theology lesson. God gives food freely, forbids one tree, and the whole Fall turns on a bite — and the whole redemption turns on another meal, the Lamb eaten in haste on the night of deliverance.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; The Passover; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to eat (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: One of the commonest verbs in the Bible — hundreds of times, from the first command in the garden (Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat) to the Passover lamb eaten in haste and the manna in the wilderness, where Israel learns man does not live by bread alone. The Aramaic form does the same work in Daniel and Ezra: Nebuchadnezzar, driven from men, did eat grass as oxen, and the king's officials tell Artaxerxes they eat the king's salt — literally, they have maintenance from the palace. Eating is where obedience and rebellion both begin, and in the Aramaic chapters it is humiliation, appetite, and loyalty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that eating is the Bible's first theology lesson. God gives food freely, forbids one tree, and the whole Fall turns on a bite — and the whole redemption turns on another meal, the Lamb eaten in haste on the night of deliverance.
