Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Achan is the man whose sin cost Israel a battle. Joshua 7:1 names him — Achan, the son of Carmi, of the tribe of Judah — and says he took of the accursed thing, and the anger of the LORD was kindled against the children of Israel. The chapter tells the rest: Israel's defeat at Ai, the lots falling on Achan, his confession that he had taken a Babylonish garment and silver and gold from Jericho and hidden them in his tent, and the judgment in the valley of Achor. One man's hidden sin, and the whole camp paid for it.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that carries a warning, not a teaching to invent. Achan shows what one hidden sin does: it does not stay hidden, and it does not stay private. I hold that his story is in the Bible so I remember — the devoted thing in my tent is never only my business.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same as G188; a thorn:--thorn.
BiblicalUsage: Thorns are the Bible's picture of the curse and of the world's opposition. You do not gather grapes from thorns, Jesus says; thorns choke the seed in the parable of the sower; and the soldiers plait a crown of thorns and press it on His head.
TheologicalSignificance: A thorn is a picture, not a doctrine, and the word carries little weight on its own; its weight is the crown, where the curse of Eden is gathered onto the head of the King.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Parable of the Sower
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G173; thorny:--of thorns.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, always of the crown. Mark says the soldiers platted a crown of thorns and put it about His head; and John shows Jesus coming out wearing it, with Pilate's words, Behold the man!
TheologicalSignificance: An adjective that exists only for one crown carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is John's behold the man, the King wearing the curse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to urge
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Proverbs 16:26: He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him. The word is the press of hunger — the appetite that drives a man to his work.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about hunger's press carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Proverbs' plain honesty, that need is the foreman that never lets a man rest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once, in 1 Chronicles 2:7: And the sons of Carmi; Achar, the troubler of Israel, who transgressed in the thing accursed. The Chronicler spells him Achar where Joshua calls him Achan.
TheologicalSignificance: The Chronicler does not retell the story; he only names the man and his deed. I believe that is the Bible's own warning about hidden sin: one man's secret taking troubled a whole nation, and the record remembers the sinner by what he did, not by what he took.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to roil water; figuratively, to disturb or affict
BiblicalUsage: The verb means to stir up, to trouble, to roil the water. Jacob tells his sons they have troubled me to make me to stink among the inhabitants of the land; Joshua asks Achan, Why hast thou troubled us?; Jonathan says his father hath troubled the land; and Ahab greets Elijah with, Art thou he that troubleth Israel? In every case the trouble is real — and in every case the accuser has the wrong man, or the wrong reason.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word's sting is in who says it. Ahab calls the prophet the troubler when Ahab himself is the trouble; Jacob blames his sons for a trouble he helped make. The Bible keeps turning the charge around: the real troubler is the sin, not the one who names it.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin; Dinah and Shechem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2590; barren (literally or figuratively):--without fruit, unfruitful.
BiblicalUsage: The word is barren, without fruit. The seed among thorns is choked and becometh unfruitful; Paul says to have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness; and Peter says that if grace's virtues abound in us, they will keep us from being barren nor unfruitful. The picture is a tree that takes up ground and gives nothing back.
TheologicalSignificance: Fruit is the test Jesus Himself set. I believe this word is a warning to every comfortable Christian: a life with leaves and no fruit is not a growing life, and the cure Peter names is not trying harder but abounding in the graces God gives.
RelatedTopics: Fruit of the Spirit; Growth; Discipleship
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2607; unblamable:--that cannot be condemned.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's instruction to Titus about sound speech: Sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you. The word is unblamable — speech so sound that no accuser can find a fault in it.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about unblamable speech carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Paul's standard, that the gospel's best defence is a tongue its enemies cannot fault.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of a compound of G2596 and G2572; unveiled:--uncovered.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both in Paul's teaching on head coverings in worship: every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head, and then the question, Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered? The word is unveiled — the head without its covering — and the whole passage turns on what that sign means in the gathered church.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for uncovered carries little weight on its own; its weight is the passage, where worship is ordered and the church's gatherings show God's design rather than hiding it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2632; without (legal) trial:--uncondemned.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both times Paul's Roman citizenship saves him. At Philippi he refuses a quiet release: They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison — and the magistrates come trembling to apologize.
TheologicalSignificance: A legal word for uncondemned carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two scenes, where Paul's citizenship stops the scourge and shames the magistrates.
RelatedEvents: Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison; Paul Claims Roman Citizenship
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2647; indissoluble, i.e. (figuratively) permanent:--endless.
BiblicalUsage: Once, of the priesthood of Christ: He is made a priest not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life. The word is indissoluble — a life that cannot be broken apart, a priesthood that cannot end because the Priest cannot die.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an endless life carries little weight on its own; its weight is the verse, a Priest who cannot die and therefore saves to the uttermost.
RelatedTopics: Priesthood; Eternal Life; Superiority of Christ
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2664; unrefraining:--that cannot cease.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Peter's fierce portrait of false teachers: they have eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin. The word is unrefraining — an appetite that never rests.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about eyes that cannot cease carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Peter's warning, that unrepentant sin is not a stumble but a slavery.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2722; unrestrainable:--unruly.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in James's chapter on the tongue: the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. The word is unrestrainable — no bridle holds it, no cage contains it.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about an unruly tongue carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is James's bluntness, that no man can tame it and it needs a Master no man can supply.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G182; instability, i.e. disorder:--commotion, confusion, tumult.
BiblicalUsage: The word is instability, disorder, tumult. Jesus warns of commotions before the end; Paul says God is not the author of confusion, but of peace; he fears finding strifes, envyings, wraths, tumults in Corinth; and James says where envying and strife are, there is confusion and every evil work. In every case the word marks what God is not the author of.
TheologicalSignificance: Confusion is the fingerprint of the wrong spirit. I believe the test is simple and Paul gives it: God is the author of peace, so where there is settled disorder and strife, look for envy and selfish ambition behind it — and deal with those first.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2525; inconstant:--unstable.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both in James, both of what cannot settle. The double-minded man is unstable in all his ways; and the tongue can no man tame — an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for unstable carries little weight on its own; its weight is James's cure, ask in faith, and the anchor that holds is God's grip on us, not ours on Him.
RelatedPeople: James, Brother of Jesus; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G169; impurity (the quality), physically or morally:--uncleanness.
BiblicalUsage: The word is impurity in every sense — physical, moral, and spiritual. Jesus calls the Pharisees whitewashed tombs full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness; Paul says God gave men up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts; it heads the works of the flesh in Galatians; and Ephesians says it should not even be named among the saints. The same word covers a dirty tomb and a dirty heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word's force is in the contrast: uncleanness is what God gives people up to when they refuse Him, and it is the very thing the saints are told to leave unnamed. The gospel does not manage impurity; it washes it away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G169; impurity (the state), morally:--filthiness.
BiblicalUsage: This noun never occurs in the New Testament. Strong's lists it, but no verse uses it. The word readers actually meet is the adjective, akathartos — unclean — as in Revelation 17:4, where the woman holds a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornication. That word has its own study; this entry stands only to point you to it.
TheologicalSignificance: A word with no verse of its own carries no doctrine; its weight is the picture it points to — a golden cup full of filth, Babylon's glamour outside and corruption inside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G2508 (meaning cleansed); impure (ceremonially, morally (lewd) or specially, (demonic)):--foul, unclean.
BiblicalUsage: The great unclean word of the New Testament. Jesus gives His disciples power over unclean spirits; a man with an unclean spirit cries out in the synagogue; Peter refuses the sheet from heaven — I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean; and Paul quotes Isaiah, touch not the unclean thing. The word covers demons, forbidden foods, and a world the saints must come out of.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the arc of this word is the arc of the gospel: what was unclean — spirits, foods, Gentiles — is cleansed by Christ, and the church is told to stay clean not by ritual but by separation from what defiles. The sheet from heaven changed everything Peter thought he knew.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mouse (as nibbling)
BiblicalUsage: The mouse is named as an unclean creeping thing in Leviticus, then again when the Philistines send golden mice back with the ark as a guilt offering — five golden mice for five lords, a plague turned into tribute. Isaiah ends the story grimly: those who eat swine's flesh and the mouse shall be consumed together.
TheologicalSignificance: A mouse carries no theology, and the word itself has none to give; its weight is the law's thoroughness, that even the smallest creeping thing is named, and the plague turned into a golden idol.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akbor, the name of an Idumaean and of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Three men share the name: the father of Baal-hanan, a king of Edom, in Genesis 36; Josiah's courtier, the son of Michaiah, sent to inquire of Huldah the prophetess; and the father of Elnathan, whom Jehoiakim sent to fetch the prophet Uriah from Egypt to kill him. The three men are told apart by their errands — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: A shared name carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the Bible's honesty with ordinary people: one Akbor serves a reforming king, another's son serves a murdering one, and the name is remembered in both stories because God records the servants as well as the kings.
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aksah, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Achsah is Caleb's daughter, promised by her father to the man who takes Kirjath-sepher, and won by Othniel, her cousin.
TheologicalSignificance: I love Achsah's boldness. She does not apologize for asking, and Caleb does not scold her for it — he gives her the springs.
RelatedPeople: Caleb; Achsah, Daughter of Caleb; Othniel, Son of Kenaz
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (meaning field of blood; corresponding to H2506 and H1818); Akeldama, a place near Jerusalem:--Aceldama.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Acts 1:19: the field bought with Judas's blood money was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: A field with a terrible name, and Luke does not soften it. I believe the name matters because God lets consequences stand: the money for an innocent life bought a field no one would forget, and its name preaches the price of betrayal to every generation that passes it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: firmly; figuratively, surely; also (advers.) but
BiblicalUsage: A particle of certainty — surely, truly, but. Jacob wakes from his dream and says, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not; Agag says, Surely the bitterness of death is past; Asaph begins, Truly God is good to Israel; and Elihu says, But there is a spirit in man.
TheologicalSignificance: A particle of surely carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Jacob's surely, a man who went to sleep an exile and woke knowing God had been there all along.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G2767; unmixed, i.e. (figuratively) innocent:--harmless, simple.
BiblicalUsage: Three times, always of the believer's character. Jesus sends His disciples out as sheep among wolves and tells them to be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves; Paul wants the Romans to be wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil; and the Philippians are to be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke in a crooked generation. The word is unmixed — pure, without guile, with nothing harmful in it.
TheologicalSignificance: Harmless is not helpless. I hold that Jesus pairs it with serpent-wisdom on purpose: the dove without the serpent is a fool, and the serpent without the dove is a danger — and the Christian is called to be both, wise and harmless at once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something eatable, i.e. food
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the story of Elijah under the juniper tree: he rises, eats and drinks, and went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God. The word is the meal itself — the food the angel brought — and it carries a worn-out prophet forty days to the mountain where God will speak.
TheologicalSignificance: One meal in one verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the God who feeds His servant before He speaks to him, and the forty days of strength that followed.
RelatedEvents: Elijah at Horeb: The Still Small Voice
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akish, a Philistine king
BiblicalUsage: Achish is the Philistine king of Gath who shelters David twice.
TheologicalSignificance: Achish is a reminder that God's people sometimes find shelter in strange places. David's madness act is not his finest hour, but God used even a Philistine king's court to keep him alive — and I hold that the same God keeps His people in places they would never have chosen.
RelatedPeople: King David; Achish, Son of Maoch
RelatedEvents: David Among the Philistines; David Recovers Ziklag
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spider (as weaving a network)
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both times of something that looks strong and is not. Bildad says the hypocrite's hope shall be cut off and whose trust shall be a spider's web; Isaiah says the wicked weave the spider's web and hatch cockatrice eggs — works that cannot cover them and cannot save them.
TheologicalSignificance: A spider's web is a picture, not a doctrine, and the word carries little weight on its own; its weight is the warning, that a hope built on our own works tears when trouble leans on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Accad, a place in Babylon
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the table of nations: And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: A city name carries no sermon, and I will not invent one. What it marks is the start of something: the first kingdom after the flood, built by a mighty hunter, in the land where rebellion would take its tallest form.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akko (from its situation on a bay)
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the list of the conquest's failures: Neither did Asher drive out the inhabitants of Accho. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is a place name, and its lesson is the failure attached to it. I believe Judges keeps this list for a reason: the cities Israel did not take became the snares Israel could not escape, and a half-finished obedience is the seed of the whole book's trouble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2827; not leaning, i.e. (figuratively) firm:--without wavering.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in one of the great exhortations of Hebrews: Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; for he is faithful that promised. The word is firm, not leaning, not bending — a confession held straight and steady.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about holding fast without wavering carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the reason given, not our grip but His faithfulness, because He promised.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G188; to make a point, i.e. (figuratively) mature:--be fully ripe.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the vision of the harvest: an angel cries to the one with the sharp sickle, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe. The word is ripeness at its peak — the moment when the fruit can wait no longer, and the harvest must come.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for fully ripe carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the harvest vision, where evil ripens like grapes and judgment comes at exactly the right time.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; Day of the Lord; End Times
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: accusative case of a noun ("acme") akin to ἀκή (a point) and meaning the same; adverbially, just now, i.e. still:--yet.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in a question full of surprise: And Jesus said, Are ye also yet without understanding? The word is even now, still — the disciples have walked with Him, seen the miracles, heard the teaching, and still they do not understand.
TheologicalSignificance: One small word for still carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Jesus' question, Are ye also yet without understanding, and the patience that explains again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G191; hearing (the act, the sense or the thing heard):--audience, ear, fame, which ye heard, hearing, preached, report, rumor.
BiblicalUsage: The word is hearing itself — the act, the sense, and the report. His fame went out through all Syria; Isaiah's prophecy is fulfilled in those who hear and never understand; Paul says faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God; and Hebrews says the readers have become dull of hearing. The same word covers the fame of Jesus, the deafness of Israel, and the birth of faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Romans 10:17 is the hinge of the whole word: faith comes by hearing. The gospel is a message before it is anything else, and it enters through the ear — which is why dull hearing is so dangerous, and why preaching matters so much.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a particle of union) and κέλευθος (a road); properly, to be in the same way with, i.e. to accompany (specially, as a disciple):--follow, reach.
BiblicalUsage: The great discipleship word. The fishermen leave their nets and follow Him; Jesus says, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me; He promises, He that followeth me shall not walk in darkness; and the sheep follow because they know his voice. Following is the whole of the Christian life in one verb: leave, deny, take up, walk.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that following is not agreeing with Jesus — it is going where He goes. The fishermen left their nets in the middle of the workday, and the cross Jesus names is carried daily, not once. That is the cost, and it is also the promise: the sheep who follow never walk in darkness.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples; The Sermon on the Mount
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2967; in an unhindered manner, i.e. freely:--no man forbidding him.
BiblicalUsage: Once, and it is the last word of Acts: Paul preaches the kingdom of God and teaches about the Lord Jesus Christ with all confidence, no man forbidding him. The word is unhindered — no one stopping him, no one in the way.
TheologicalSignificance: One word, the last word of Acts, carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Luke's ending, a prisoner under arrest preaching freely, because the Word cannot be bound.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1635; unwilling:--against the will.
BiblicalUsage: Once only. Paul says if he preaches against his will, a dispensation of the gospel is committed unto him — the work is his whether he likes it or not.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for unwilling carries little weight on its own; its weight is Paul's point, that the gospel was committed to him whether he felt like it or not — the calling stands whether the willingness does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to hear (in various senses):--give (in the) audience (of), come (to the ears), (shall) hear(-er, -ken), be noised, be reported, understand.
BiblicalUsage: The commonest hearing word in the New Testament — hundreds of times. Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time; He that hath ears to hear, let him hear; The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. Hearing is the doorway of the whole gospel: the dead hear His voice and live.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hearing is the Bible's first act of faith. The deaf hear, the dead hear, and the living are told to hear — and the promise is that the voice of the Son of God does not merely inform, it raises. That is why Jesus keeps saying, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
RelatedTopics: Faith; Listening Well; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akor, the name of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Achor is the valley where Achan is stoned for taking the devoted spoil — the valley of trouble, named for what happened there. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Hosea's promise is the gospel in a place name. The valley where sin was judged becomes the valley where hope opens — and the God who named the trouble is the same God who turns it into a doorway.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G193; want of self-restraint:--excess, incontinency.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times of a lack of self-control. Jesus tells the Pharisees their cups are clean outside but within they are full of extortion and excess; and Paul tells married couples not to deprive one another except it be with consent for a time, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency. The word is the absence of restraint — appetite with no master.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is a warning about what happens when nothing says no. I believe both uses point the same way: excess is not freedom, it is slavery to appetite, and the cure is the self-control the Spirit gives, not the willpower we wish we had.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2904; powerless, i.e. without self-control:--incontinent.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's portrait of the last days: men will be without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good. The word is powerless over oneself — without self-control.
TheologicalSignificance: One word in a dark list carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the company it keeps, affection gone, promises broken, restraint gone, in a world that calls appetite freedom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G2767; undiluted:--without mixture.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the most terrible verse in Revelation: whoever worships the beast shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation. The word is undiluted — wine with no water in it, wrath with nothing to soften it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for undiluted carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the cup in Revelation, wrath with nothing to soften it, and the urgency of the One who drank it for us.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; God's wrath and refuge; Second Coming
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G196; exactness:--perfect manner.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's defence before the Jerusalem crowd: I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers. The word is exactness — the strict, precise, careful way he was taught the law.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for exactness is a credential, not a doctrine, and it carries little weight on its own; its weight is the man, Paul trained in precision and turned to grace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: superlative of ἀκρίβης (a derivative of the same as G206); most exact:--most straitest.
BiblicalUsage: Once, before Agrippa: Paul says the Jews knew him from the beginning, that after the most straitest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee. The word is the superlative — the strictest, the most exact.
TheologicalSignificance: One superlative in one verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Paul's point, that the strictest sect produced the greatest apostle of grace.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of the comparative of the same as G196; (adverbially) more exactly:--more perfect(-ly).
BiblicalUsage: Three times, always of knowing or explaining more exactly. Priscilla and Aquila take Apollos aside and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly; the Jews ask the chief captain to bring Paul down as though ye would enquire something more perfectly concerning him; and Felix, having more perfect knowledge of that way, defers Paul's case.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for more exactly carries little weight on its own; its weight is the scene, two friends taking a gifted preacher aside to teach him more perfectly, and his gladness to learn.
RelatedEvents: Apollos Taught at Ephesus; Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G196; to be exact, i.e. ascertain:--enquire diligently.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both in the Christmas story's dark side. Herod enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared, and then, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, he kills the children of Bethlehem according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for diligent enquiry carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast, Herod inquiring exactly to plan a murder and the wise men inquiring to worship.
RelatedEvents: The Magi Visit Jesus; The Massacre of the Innocents
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from the same as G196; exactly:--circumspectly, diligently, perfect(-ly).
BiblicalUsage: The adverb of exactness. Herod tells the wise men to search diligently for the young child; Luke writes to Theophilus that he has had perfect understanding of all things from the very first; Paul tells believers to walk circumspectly, exactly, carefully; and the Thessalonians know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night.
TheologicalSignificance: An adverb of exactness carries little weight on its own; its weight is the lives it describes, Luke investigating carefully, Paul commanding careful walking, and the diligence that serves the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently from the same as G206; a locust (as pointed, or as lighting on the top of vegetation):--locust.
BiblicalUsage: The locust is John the Baptist's food — his meat was locusts and wild honey — and the plague of Revelation, where locusts come out of the smoke of the bottomless pit with power to torment men for five months. Same creature, two pictures: the prophet's plain diet in the wilderness, and the judgment that falls like a swarm.
TheologicalSignificance: A locust is an insect, not a doctrine, and the word carries no weight of its own; its weight is the two pictures, the prophet's plain diet and the judgment that falls like a swarm.
RelatedPeople: John the Baptist; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G202; an audience-room:--place of hearing.
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Festus brings Paul before Agrippa: on the morrow, when Agrippa was come, and Bernice, with great pomp, and was entered into the place of hearing, with the chief captains, and principal men of the city. The word is the audience room — the hall where the hearing happens.
TheologicalSignificance: A room name carries no teaching, and the word itself has none; its weight is the scene it frames, earthly pomp on one side and a chained apostle speaking the Word on the other.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀκροάομαι (to listen; apparently an intensive of G191); a hearer (merely):--hearer.
BiblicalUsage: The hearer who only hears. Paul says not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified; James says be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves, and compares the hearer who forgets to a man who looks in a mirror and walks away. The word always carries the warning: hearing without doing is self-deception.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the most practical word in the New Testament. The mirror does not lie — the man who hears and forgets has deceived himself — and the blessed man is the one James names last: the doer, who looks into the perfect law of liberty and continues in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G206 and probably a modified form of πόσθη (the penis or male sexual organ); the prepuce; by implication, an uncircumcised (i.e. gentile, figuratively, unregenerate) state or person:--not circumcised, uncircumcised (with G2192), uncircumcision.
BiblicalUsage: The word for the uncircumcised state — and, by extension, the Gentiles themselves. Paul argues that circumcision profits only if you keep the law, that Abraham was counted righteous while still in uncircumcision, that the called man should stay as he is, and that in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but faith which worketh by love. The word is the old dividing line, and Paul erases it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word is where Paul's gospel to the nations turns. The mark in the flesh never saved anyone — Abraham believed before he was circumcised — and what counts now is faith working through love. The wall is down, and the Gentiles are in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G206 and G1137; belonging to the extreme corner:--chief corner.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both of Christ as the cornerstone. Paul says the church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; Peter quotes Isaiah, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious. The word is the extreme corner — the stone that sets the angle for the whole building and holds it square.
TheologicalSignificance: Every stone in the building is measured from the corner stone. I believe that is why Paul and Peter both reach for it: Christ is not one stone among many, He is the stone that decides whether the whole house stands straight — and the house is us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of an adjective probably akin to the base of G188; the extremity:--one end… other, tip, top, uttermost part.
BiblicalUsage: The extremity — the tip, the top, the uttermost part. The angels gather the elect from the uttermost part of heaven; the rich man begs for Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water; and Jacob, dying, worships leaning upon the top of his staff.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the tip or the uttermost part carries little weight on its own; its weight is Jacob's use, a dying man worshipping on the top of his staff.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G206 and θίς (a heap); properly (in the plural) the top of the heap, i.e. (by implication) best of the booty:--spoils.
BiblicalUsage: Once, of Abraham's gift to Melchizedek: Now consider how great this man was, unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils. The word is the top of the heap — the best of the booty, the choicest part of what was taken in battle.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the best of the spoils carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Hebrews' argument, that the patriarch gave his best tenth to a greater priest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Acshaph, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Acshaph is a Canaanite city whose king joins Jabin's alliance against Joshua, is defeated at the waters of Merom, and is listed among the thirty-one kings Joshua struck. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: A place name carries no doctrine, and I will not invent one. What it records is the conquest's completeness: the kings who gathered against Israel fell one by one, and the land they lost became the inheritance of God's people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an asp (from lurking coiled up)
BiblicalUsage: Once, in David's prayer against violent men: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips. The word is the asp — the coiled, lurking snake — and David uses it for the poison hidden under a smooth tongue.
TheologicalSignificance: One asp in one verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is David's prayer, that God sees the poison under smooth lips and is the refuge from it.
RelatedTopics: Speech; God's Protection; Evil and Suffering
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably for Latin aquila (an eagle); Akulas, an Israelite:--Aquila.
BiblicalUsage: Aquila is a Jewish tentmaker from Pontus, driven from Rome by Claudius, who meets Paul in Corinth and becomes his fellow worker.
TheologicalSignificance: I love that Aquila is remembered with his wife, in every mention. The two of them taught a great preacher, hosted a church, and risked their lives for Paul — and the work of the gospel has always run on people like them, whose names history nearly forgets.
RelatedEvents: Apollos Taught at Ephesus; Paul at Corinth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2964; to invalidate:--disannul, make of none effect.
BiblicalUsage: The word is to invalidate, to make void. Jesus charges the Pharisees with making God's word of none effect by your tradition; Mark repeats it; and Paul says the law, which came four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul the covenant God made with Abraham. In every case something human tries to cancel something divine — and fails.
TheologicalSignificance: Tradition cannot void the Word, and the law cannot void the promise. I hold that this word is the Bible's own guarantee: what God has spoken stands, and no human addition or later rule can annul it.
RelatedTopics: Covenant; Promises of God; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: falsehood; by implication treachery
BiblicalUsage: Twice, both of something that fails when you lean on it. Jeremiah, in his pain, asks God, wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail? — a stream that runs dry when you need it most. Micah says the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel — a wordplay on the town's own name, which sounds like deception.
TheologicalSignificance: The word stings because the picture is so plain: a stream that fails in the dry season, a town whose name means lie. I believe the two verses belong together — one is a prophet's honest question, the other is God's answer to a nation that trusted in failing things.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: violent; by implication deadly; also (in a good sense) brave
BiblicalUsage: Four times, and the word never softens. The wine of false gods is the cruel venom of asps; Job says God has become cruel to me; of Leviathan, none is so fierce that dare stir him up; and Lamentations says the daughter of God's people is become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. Cruelty is laid at the door of idols, of Leviathan, of a ruined city — and once, in his agony, at the door of God.
TheologicalSignificance: Job's charge is the one that stops me. He says it to God's face, in his suffering, and God does not strike him for it — He answers him. I hold that this is the Bible's honesty about pain: the sufferer may say the hard thing, and God is big enough to hear it and answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: terrible
BiblicalUsage: Eight times, always of cruelty in human hands. The adulterer's years go to the cruel one; the wicked man's tender mercies are cruel; a cruel messenger is sent against the rebel; and the invaders from the north are cruel, and have no mercy. The word moves from the bedroom to the battlefield, and in every place it names the same thing: power without pity.
TheologicalSignificance: Proverbs keeps putting mercy and cruelty side by side, and the contrast is the lesson. The merciful man does good to his own soul; the cruel man troubles his own flesh — I believe that is the Bible's own verdict: cruelty is not strength, it is a wound the cruel inflict on themselves.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fierceness
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Proverbs 27:4: Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? The word is cruelty itself — the abstract noun, fierceness as a quality.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, one proverb, and the word itself carries little weight; its weight is the ranking, that envy outlasts wrath and anger and stands when the loud sins have spent themselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akzib, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Achzib is a town named three times: once in Judah's inheritance, once in Asher's, and once in Micah's prophecy, where its houses shall be a lie to the kings of Israel — a pun, since the town's name sounds like the word for deception. The place is covered in the Biblical Places collection — this study covers only how the name is used.
TheologicalSignificance: A town whose name means deception, and the prophet makes the name come true. I will not force a moral out of a boundary list; the point is Micah's, and it is plain: a place you trust can fail you, and the kings who trusted Achzib found a lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {not (the qualified negation, used as a deprecative); once (Job 24:25) as a noun, nothing}
BiblicalUsage: The Aramaic word for not — the small word that turns a sentence around. Daniel tells the guard, Destroy not the wise men of Babylon; Nebuchadnezzar tells Daniel, no secret troubleth thee; and Job, in his last defence, says if his words are not true, who will make me a liar, and make my speech nothing worth?
TheologicalSignificance: A negative carries no doctrine, and the word itself has none to give; its weight is how much of faith hangs on a not — destroy not the wise men, no secret troubles the dreamer.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, the top; specifically, the highest (i.e. God); also (adverb) aloft, to Jehovah
BiblicalUsage: The word means the height — the top, the highest place. Isaac blesses Esau with the dew of heaven from above; Jacob's blessing speaks of blessings above; David is called the man raised up on high; and twice Hosea names God Himself the most High — the One Israel will not return to, though the prophets call them upward.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the height carries little weight on its own; its weight is Hosea's accusation, that Israel calls God the Most High with its lips and walks away with its feet.
RelatedTopics: God; God's Sovereignty; Majesty of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: 'Thou must not destroy'; probably the opening words to a popular song
BiblicalUsage: The words stand at the head of four psalms — To the chief Musician, Altaschith — meaning Destroy thou not. It is probably the opening line of a well-known song, and David's psalms borrow its tune: one written in the cave fleeing Saul, one against unjust judges, one against Saul's watchmen, and one of thanksgiving for God's judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: A tune title carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the plea inside it, do not destroy, and the four psalms underneath it that show God hearing, judging, and saving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rib
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Daniel's vision of the bear: it raised up itself on one side, and it had three ribs in the mouth of it between the teeth of it. The word is a rib — the bones of prey still in the beast's teeth.
TheologicalSignificance: One rib in one verse carries no teaching of its own; its weight is Daniel's vision, a beast with the bones of devoured kingdoms still in its teeth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to sip up
BiblicalUsage: Twice, in the same proverb repeated word for word: The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly. The word is to sip up, to swallow down — gossip goes down like a dainty morsel, swallowed whole, and settles in the deepest place.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for sipping up carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the proverb, repeated twice because the warning needs repeating, that gossip is swallowed and settles deep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of ἀλάβαστρος (of uncertain derivation), the name of a stone; properly, an "alabaster" box, i.e. (by extension) a perfume vase (of any material):--(alabaster) box.
BiblicalUsage: The alabaster box holds the ointment poured on Jesus — in Matthew and Mark by a woman at Bethany, anointing His head before His burial, and in Luke by the sinful woman who weeps at His feet, kisses them, and anoints them. The box is broken to pour it out, and the perfume fills the house.
TheologicalSignificance: An alabaster box is a vessel, not a doctrine, and the word carries little weight on its own; its weight is the broken box, the costliest thing poured out without keeping any back.
RelatedEvents: The Anointing at Bethany; The Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to leap for joy, i.e. exult, wave joyously
BiblicalUsage: Three times, and the word never means the same thing twice. The wicked man shall not rejoice in his ill-gotten gain; the ostrich's wing flaps joyously in the wilderness; and the adulteress says, let us solace ourselves with loves. The same root covers a joy denied, a bird's exulting wing, and a sin invited — delight itself is neutral, and the heart decides what it serves.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is delight, and delight is a test. I believe the three uses belong together on purpose: joy in gain that must be given back, joy in a creature doing what it was made to do, and joy offered as a snare. The question is never whether we rejoice, but in what.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to muddle, i.e. (figuratively and intransitive) to turn (morally) corrupt
BiblicalUsage: Three times, always of a corruption that spreads. David says twice, in two psalms, They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one; and Eliphaz asks, How much more abominable and filthy is man, which drinketh iniquity like water?
TheologicalSignificance: A word for turning foul carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the verse Paul quotes in Romans, that there is none that does good, no, not one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to adjure, i.e. (usually in a bad sense) imprecate
BiblicalUsage: The word is to adjure — to bind someone by an oath, or to lay a curse. Leviticus makes the man who hears a curse and hides it guilty; Numbers puts the suspected wife under oath; Deuteronomy warns the man who hears the curse of the covenant and blesses himself anyway; and Joshua lays a curse on whoever rebuilds Jericho. Oaths and curses both run on the same word, because both call God to witness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word warns me about the weight of words. An oath calls God as witness, a curse calls Him as judge — and the Bible treats both as real, binding, and dangerous. That is why Jesus says to let our yes be yes: a people who speak plainly have no need to swear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to ascend, in transitively (be high) or actively (mount); used in a great variety of senses, primary and secondary, literal and figurative
BiblicalUsage: This is the ordinary Hebrew word for going up, and it carries everything from climbing a hill to Elijah's whirlwind ride into heaven. Jacob watches angels ascending and descending on the ladder at Bethel; Moses goes up the mountain to meet God; Elijah is taken up and Elisha is left staring after him. The word does not change its meaning — what changes is who is going up, and where.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the going up matters because God is the one who calls us upward. He comes down to us first, in the ladder, in the burning bush, in Christ, and then He lifts us up with Him. Isaiah's promise still stands: those who wait on the LORD mount up with wings as eagles, and I hold that this is not poetry about escape but about strength — God gives tired people the lift they cannot give themselves.
RelatedEvents: Jacob's Dream at Bethel; Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a holocaust
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the Aramaic of Ezra, where Darius orders supplies for the rebuilt temple: young bullocks, rams, lambs, and the burnt offering, with wheat, salt, wine and oil, day by day without fail. The word is the whole burnt offering, given over entirely to God on the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: One Aramaic word in one verse carries no theology of its own; its weight is the temple worship it supplied, the daily offering that kept going once the exiles came home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to enter; causatively, to introduce
BiblicalUsage: In Daniel's Aramaic this is the word for going in, and Daniel does it twice in ways that matter: he goes in to the king to ask for time before the dream is interpreted, and the magicians come in before Nebuchadnezzar and fail where Daniel will succeed. Entering the king's presence is the doorway of the whole book.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for walking through a door carries no deep theology; what it shows is Daniel's nerve, that he went in and asked while the wise men of Babylon could only come in and confess they could not.
RelatedEvents: Daniel's Resolve in Babylon; Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to effect thoroughly; specifically, to glean (also figuratively); by implication (in a bad sense) to overdo, i.e. maltreat, be saucy to, pain, impose (also literal)
BiblicalUsage: This word gathers two opposite pictures under one root. In the law it is gleaning, going back over the olive tree and the vineyard so the stranger, the fatherless and the widow can gather what is left. In Exodus it is God dealing with Egypt, showing Pharaoh what He can do to a proud king; the same word covers the harvest left behind and the judgment that strips a nation bare.
TheologicalSignificance: One word doing two jobs carries no single doctrine; its weight is the two pictures side by side, that God leaves enough for the poor and yet deals thoroughly with the proud.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀλαλή (a shout, "halloo"); to vociferate, i.e. (by implication) to wail; figuratively, to clang:--tinkle, wail.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and the two uses could hardly be further apart. In Corinth it is the clanging cymbal, a loud noise with no love behind it, which is what a gifted tongue becomes without love. In Capernaum it is the wailing at Jairus's house, the hired mourners making a tumult around a dead girl before Jesus takes her by the hand.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for making a loud noise carries no theology of its own; its weight is the contrast, that noise without love is nothing and grief without hope is answered by a word from Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2980; unspeakable:--unutterable, which cannot be uttered.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the one place the Bible needs it. The Spirit helps our weaknesses, Paul says, and makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. The word is for the prayers that have no words in them, the groaning too deep for speech.
TheologicalSignificance: One word in one verse carries no system of doctrine; its weight is the comfort in it, that when I cannot find the words, the Spirit is already praying them for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2980; mute:--dumb.
BiblicalUsage: Three times in Mark, and always about a mouth that will not open. A father brings a boy with a dumb spirit that tears him and throws him down; Jesus rebukes it, and the boy speaks. And the crowd marvels at a different healing, that He makes the deaf to hear and the dumb to speak.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a sealed mouth carries no theology of its own; its weight is the two healings, that the same Christ who casts out the spirit also opens the ears and the tongue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to veil from sight, i.e. conceal (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: To hide, to veil from sight, and the Bible uses it both ways. The law forbids hiding yourself from your brother's lost ox, and commands you not to look away. Isaiah turns it on God: when your hands are full of blood, He hides His eyes and will not hear. And the psalm knows the other side, that our secret sins stand in the light of His countenance, hidden from everyone but Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hiding is the oldest human instinct after the fall, and God answers it both ways: He will not be hidden from, and He will not hide from the one who comes honestly. The same God who hides His face from bloodied hands is the one who sees the secret sin and still makes a way back, and I hold that is why confession works — nothing I hide is hidden from Him, and nothing I bring Him is turned away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tie fast; hence (of the mouth) to be tongue-tied
BiblicalUsage: The word binds a mouth shut. Joseph's sheaf stands upright while his brothers' sheaves bow, and the binding is in the dream, sheaves tied fast together. Isaiah uses the same root for the Suffering Servant, who is brought as a lamb to the slaughter and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so He openeth not His mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a tied tongue carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the Servant's silence, that the one who could have spoken chose not to, and His silence was part of the offering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, girls, i.e. the soprano or female voice, perhaps falsetto
BiblicalUsage: Once in the body of the text, when David brings the ark to Jerusalem and the Levites play psalteries on Alamoth, the high soprano voice, above the harps. The word also heads Psalm 46, where the sons of Korah sing a song upon Alamoth over the psalm that begins, God is our refuge and strength.
TheologicalSignificance: One musical direction in one verse carries no theology of its own; its weight is the scene, that the ark came home to singing, and the highest voices led it.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: causative, to make a thousandfold
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the psalm of David's blessing on the land: that our sheep may bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our streets. The word is the thousandfold, the flock multiplying beyond counting, and it sits in a prayer for a people at peace, sons like plants, daughters like corner stones, garners full.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a thousandfold flock carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture of blessing, that God's provision multiplies past what anyone could number.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {hence (the ox's head being the first letter of the alphabet, and this eventually used as a numeral) a thousand}
BiblicalUsage: Twice in Daniel, and both times the thousand is a crowd. Belshazzar makes a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and the wine flows while the fingers write on the wall. And the Ancient of Days sits down, and thousand thousands minister unto Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stand before Him.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a thousand carries no theology of its own; its weight is the contrast, that Belshazzar's thousand drink themselves into judgment while heaven's thousand thousands stand ready to serve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to veil or cover; figuratively, to be languid
BiblicalUsage: The word covers and it faints. Tamar veils herself and sits by the wayside, covered so Judah will not know her. And Jonah sits east of the city under his gourd, the sun beats on his head, and he faints and wishes himself dead; the same root covers a face and drains the strength from a body.
TheologicalSignificance: A word that means both to cover and to faint carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two scenes, a woman hiding her face to get justice and a prophet wilting in the sun because God would not do what he wanted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

BiblicalUsage: Once, in the psalm of David's blessing on the land: that our sheep may bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our streets. Definition: dusk
BiblicalUsage: Four times, and always at the edge of the day. When the sun went down and it was dark, the smoking furnace and burning lamp passed between the pieces of Abraham's covenant. And Ezekiel is told to dig through the wall and carry his stuff out in the twilight, a sign of an exile leaving under cover of dark.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for dusk carries no theology of its own; its weight is the hour it marks, that God's covenant was cut after dark and His prophet acted out an exile's flight at twilight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to jump for joy, i.e. exult
BiblicalUsage: To jump for joy, to exult — and the Bible saves it for the joy that has a reason. Hannah sings it when the barren woman bears seven and the bows of the mighty are broken. The psalms sing it when God is trusted, when enemies fall back, when the righteous are glad before Him. This is not a vague happiness; it is joy with its feet off the ground because God has acted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe joy like this is the right answer to what God does, not an extra. Hannah's song and the psalms agree: when God lifts the poor and breaks the bow of the mighty, the heart does not sit still. I hold that exulting is worship with the body in it, and a church that never jumps for joy has not yet heard what Hannah heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to press
BiblicalUsage: Once, and it is Delilah wearing Samson down: she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death. The word is pressure applied day after day until the strongest man alive gives up the secret of his strength.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for pressing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning in it, that a will can be worn down a little at a time until it breaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
