Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle (compare G427)) and G127; impudence, i.e. (by implication) importunity:--importunity.
BiblicalUsage: The word is used once only, in the parable of the friend at midnight: though the man will not rise and give him bread because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth. Importunity is shameless persistence — knocking until the door opens, not because the friendship demands it but because the asking will not stop.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for shameless asking carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the parable — the friend who keeps knocking until he is heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and (the active of) G138; to take up, i.e. adopt; by implication, to take away (violently), i.e. abolish, murder:--put to death, kill, slay, take away, take up.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to take up — and to take away. Pharaoh's daughter took Moses up when he was cast out and nourished him for her own son, and Hebrews says Christ takes away the first covenant that He may establish the second. In Acts the word is mostly used for killing — Herod slew the children, the Jews sought to kill Paul — but the taking up and the taking away are the same motion.
TheologicalSignificance: A word that means both taking up and taking away carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two takings — a baby lifted from the river, and an old covenant lifted away so the new one can stand.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G337; (the act of) killing:--death.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, and it is death: Saul was consenting unto the death of Stephen, and at that time there was a great persecution against the church at Jerusalem. It is the noun for the killing itself — the act Stephen's death is named by, in the verse where the scattering of the church begins.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a killing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the verse — Stephen's death, Saul consenting, and the church scattered abroad by the persecution that followed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G159 (in the sense of G156); innocent:--blameless, guiltless.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears twice, both times on Jesus' lips in the same argument: He reminds them that the priests in the temple profane the sabbath and are blameless, and that if they had known what 'I will have mercy, and not sacrifice' means, they would not have condemned the guiltless. It is the word for someone with no guilt on them — the priests doing their work, the disciples picking grain — and the Pharisees condemning them anyway.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about the guiltless carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is Jesus' charge — mercy over sacrifice, and no condemnation for the innocent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: according to most a plumb-line, and to others a hook
BiblicalUsage: The word appears twice, both times in Amos's vision: the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in His hand, and said, 'Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more.' A plumbline is a builder's line with a weight on it, held against a wall to see whether it stands straight — and God holds it against Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about a plumbline carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the measuring — God holding His line against His people and finding the wall crooked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and a derivative of G2537; to restore:--renew.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the warning of Hebrews 6: if they shall fall away, it is impossible to renew them again unto repentance, seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh. It is the renewing that cannot happen twice — the one who has tasted the heavenly gift and turned away cannot be made new again by the same repentance.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for renewing again carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning — a renewal that, once thrown away, cannot simply be repeated.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and a derivative of G2537; to renovate:--renew.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says our outward man perishes, but the inward man is renewed day by day — and the new man we have put on is renewed in knowledge after the image of Him that created him. It is not a single event but a daily work: the body wears down while the inner life is made new again every morning, growing back toward the likeness of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe renewal is daily, not once: the outward man perishes a little every day, and the inward man is renewed a little every day, and the two run side by side until the end. The new man is renewed in knowledge — knowing God better is what makes us more like Him — and that is the work I can ask for every morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G341; renovation:--renewing.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the Romans not to be conformed to this world but to be transformed by the renewing of their minds, so they can prove what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God — and he tells Titus that God saved us not by works of righteousness we have done, but by the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost. The renewing is both a mind made new and a life washed new, and in both places God is the one who does it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that renewal starts in the mind and shows in the life: a mind renewed by God's word stops being shaped by the world, and a life washed by the Spirit stops trusting its own works. It is not my effort that renews me — it is the Holy Ghost — but the renewed mind is mine to use, proving God's will day by day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 (in the sense of reversal) and G2572; to unveil:--open, (un-)taken away.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the minds of Israel were blinded, for until this day the same veil remains untaken away in the reading of the old testament, a veil done away in Christ — and then, 'we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.' The veil is taken away in Christ, and the face is uncovered, and the looking itself changes the looker.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the veil is the heart of the gospel: what Moses covered, Christ uncovers, and I do not read the old Scriptures through a veil anymore. The open face beholds the glory of the Lord, and the beholding changes me into the same image — glory to glory, by the Spirit, not by my effort.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2578; to turn back:--(re-)turn.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to turn back, to return: the wise men, warned of God in a dream not to return to Herod, departed into their own country another way, and Hebrews says the patriarchs, if they had been mindful of the country they came out of, might have had opportunity to have returned. It is the turning back that obedience refuses and homesickness invites.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for turning back carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two turnings — the wise men who would not go back to Herod, and the fathers who would not go back to the country they had left.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2523; properly, to set up, i.e. (reflexively) to sit up:--sit up.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears twice, and both times a dead person sits up: the widow of Nain's son sat up and began to speak, and Jesus delivered him to his mother — and Tabitha opened her eyes when she saw Peter, and sat up. It is the sitting up of someone who was lying dead, the first movement of a life given back.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about sitting up carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the moment — the dead sitting up and speaking, and a mother getting her son back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2749; to recline (as a corpse or at a meal):--guest, lean, lie, sit (down, at meat), at the table.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to recline at table, the way people ate in the ancient world: when evening came, Jesus sat down with the twelve at the last supper, and at that table one of His disciples was leaning on Jesus' bosom, the one Jesus loved. It appears fourteen times, almost always at a meal — guests reclining, the sick lying down, and once a corpse laid out.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for reclining carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the table — Jesus eating with His twelve, and the beloved disciple leaning on His breast.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2775 (in its original sense); to sum up:--briefly comprehend, gather together in one.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to sum up, to gather together under one head: every commandment — thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not covet — is briefly comprehended in this saying, 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself'; and in the fullness of times God will gather together in one all things in Christ, both in heaven and on earth. One verse sums up the law in love, and the other sums up the whole creation in Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for summing up carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two gatherings — the whole law gathered into loving your neighbour, and all things gathered into Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2827; to lean back:--lay, (make) sit down.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to lay down, or to make to sit down: Mary brought forth her firstborn son and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn, and Jesus commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass before He broke the bread. It is used for a mother laying a baby down and for a host seating a crowd of five thousand.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for laying down carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two layings — a baby in a manger, and five thousand seated on the grass to be fed.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2875; to beat back, i.e. check:--hinder.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: 'Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?' Paul asks the Galatians who cut in on them and broke their stride — they were running the race well, and someone stepped across their path and stopped them. It is the word for a runner tripped up mid-course.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for hindering carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the race — the Galatians were running well, and someone cut in and broke their stride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2896; to scream up (aloud):--cry out.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to cry out, to scream aloud: a man with an unclean spirit in the synagogue cried out when Jesus came near, and the crowd before Pilate cried out all at once, 'Away with this man, and release unto us Barabbas.' It is a shout, not a conversation — the cry of a spirit being driven out, and the cry of a crowd demanding a death.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for crying out carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two shouts — a demon crying out before Jesus, and a crowd crying out for Barabbas.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2919; properly, to scrutinize, i.e. (by implication) investigate, interrogate, determine:--ask, question, discern, examine, judge, search.
BiblicalUsage: The Bereans were more noble than those in Thessalonica, Luke says, because they received the word with all readiness of mind and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. Paul says the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged of no man, and that an unbeliever who comes into the assembly is convinced of all and judged of all. Pilate uses the same word when he tells the chief priests he has examined Jesus before them and found no fault in Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the heart of how Christians are meant to think: examine everything, including the preaching you hear on a Sunday. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily, and that is still the test — not whether a teacher sounds convincing, but whether what he says is so. And I hold that the same examination falls on me: the spiritual man judges all things, and I should expect my own life to stand up to the same searching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G350; a (judicial) investigation:--examination.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Festus tells Agrippa he has brought Paul before them, 'that, after examination had, I might have somewhat to write.' It is a judicial investigation — the formal hearing where the charges are sifted so the governor can write an honest report to Caesar.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an examination carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the hearing — Festus needing something certain to write to his master about Paul.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 (in the sense of reversal) and G2955; to unbend, i.e. rise; figuratively, be elated:--lift up, look up.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to unbend, to lift yourself up: a woman bound together for eighteen years could in no wise lift up herself, until Jesus laid His hands on her — and Jesus tells His disciples that when these things begin to come to pass, they should look up and lift up their heads, for their redemption draws near. It is the straightening of a bent back, and the lifting of a bowed head.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for lifting up carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the straightening — a woman bent double for eighteen years, and a people told to lift their heads because redemption is near.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Woman Bent Double
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2983; to take up:--receive up, take (in, unto, up).
BiblicalUsage: The word means to take up, and it holds both the taking up of Jesus and the taking up of His people: the angels tell the men of Galilee that this same Jesus, taken up from them into heaven, shall so come in like manner; Mark says He was received up into heaven and sat on the right hand of God; Paul says to take unto you the whole armour of God, that you may withstand in the evil day; and the hymn of 1 Timothy says He was received up into glory. The taking up is both His ascension and our equipment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the taking up of Christ is the pattern of the Christian life: He was received up into glory, and I am told to take up the armour He left for me. He went up so that I could stand, and the same word that describes His ascension describes my daily taking up of the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G353; ascension:--taking up.
BiblicalUsage: The word is used once, and it is the ascension: when the time was come that He should be received up, Jesus steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem. It is the noun for the taking up itself — the moment the road turns toward Jerusalem and the cross, because the time of His receiving up has come.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the taking up carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the set face — Jesus turning toward Jerusalem because His ascension was coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and a form of the alternate of G138; properly, to use up, i.e. destroy:--consume.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to use up, to consume: James and John ask whether they should command fire to come down from heaven and consume the Samaritans, even as Elijah did, and Paul warns the Galatians that if they bite and devour one another, they should take heed that they are not consumed one of another. Fire from heaven in the one verse, and a church eating itself alive in the other.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for consuming carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning — the disciples wanted fire on Samaria, and Paul warns that a biting church will be consumed by its own teeth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G303 and G3056; proportion:--proportion.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: having gifts differing according to the grace given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith. It is the measure — the proportion — and Paul ties the exercise of prophecy to the measure of faith God has given.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for proportion carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the measure — prophesy according to the faith you have been given, no more and no less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G356; to estimate, i.e. (figuratively) contemplate:--consider.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: 'For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds.' It is the act of weighing something up, turning it over in the mind — and the thing to consider is Christ, enduring the contradiction of sinners so that we do not grow weary.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for considering carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the looking — consider Him, and you will not faint.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G251; saltless, i.e. insipid:--X lose saltness.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Jesus' saying about salt: salt is good, but if it has lost its saltness, nothing can season it again — so have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another. It is salt without saltiness — the thing that has lost the very quality that made it useful, and cannot get it back.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for saltless carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the question — salt that has lost its saltness, and what it is good for then.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3089; to break up, i.e. depart (literally or figuratively):--depart, return.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to break up, to depart — and to return: be like men that wait for their lord when he will return from the wedding, that when he comes and knocks they may open to him immediately, and Paul says he is in a strait between two, having a desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better. The same word is the lord returning and the apostle departing, and both are a breaking up of camp.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for departing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two directions — the lord returning to his servants, and Paul longing to depart and be with Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G360; departure:--departure.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Paul's last letter: 'For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.' It is the noun for the departing itself — the breaking up of camp, the loosening of the ropes — and Paul uses it for his own death, already in sight.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for departure carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Paul's calm — the time of his departure at hand, and he is ready to be offered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G264; sinless:--that is without sin.
BiblicalUsage: The word is used once, and the whole argument is in that one word: when the scribes and Pharisees kept asking Jesus about the woman taken in adultery, He lifted Himself up and said, 'He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.' Sinless — the one qualification for throwing the first stone, and no one there had it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for sinless carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the silence that followed — no one without sin stepped forward, and the stones stayed on the ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3306; to await:--wait for.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: the Thessalonians turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead, even Jesus, which delivered us from the wrath to come. It is waiting with the eyes up — not idle waiting, but the waiting of people who have turned from idols and are looking for the Son.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for waiting carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the posture — turned from idols, serving the living God, and waiting for His Son from heaven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3403; to remind; (reflexively) to recollect:--call to mind, (bring to, call to, put in), remember(-brance).
BiblicalUsage: The word means to call to mind, to remind: the second time the cock crew, Peter called to mind the word Jesus had said to him — before the cock crow twice, you will deny me three times — and he wept; and Paul tells Timothy to stir up the gift of God in him, putting him in remembrance of the laying on of hands. One remembering brings tears, and the other brings courage, and both are the same word.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for remembering carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two rememberings — Peter weeping when he called the word to mind, and Timothy stirred up by being put in remembrance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anamim, a son of Mizraim and his descendants, with their country
BiblicalUsage: Anamim is named twice, in the same list both times: Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim. He was a son of Mizraim — Egypt — and the name stands for both the man and his descendants, a people of Egypt whose land and story the Bible never tells beyond the list.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a list is all we have of Anamim, and I believe the list is enough: the sons of Mizraim are counted, and Egypt's peoples are named, because the table of nations is God's record of the whole earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anammelek, an Assyrian deity
BiblicalUsage: Anammelech is named once, as one of the gods of Sepharvaim: the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim. He was an Assyrian god, brought into the land of Israel by the people settled there after Samaria fell, and his worship cost children their lives.
TheologicalSignificance: A false god named once still shows the truth about idolatry: the Sepharvites burnt their own children to Anammelech, and I believe that is what false gods always demand in the end — the most precious thing you have.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G363; recollection:--remembrance (again).
BiblicalUsage: Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, 'This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me' — and Paul repeats the words to Corinth, adding that the cup is the same. But Hebrews turns the word the other way: in the old sacrifices there is a remembrance again made of sins every year. The same word is the remembering that saves and the remembering that accuses — the supper that remembers Christ, and the sacrifices that only remembered sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the difference between the two remembrances is the whole difference between the covenants: the old sacrifices remembered sins every year and never took them away, but the bread and the cup remember Christ, who took them away once for all. That is why I come to the table — not to remember my sins, but to remember the One who bore them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: figuratively, to act covertly, i.e. practise magic
BiblicalUsage: The word means to practise hidden arts — to observe times, to read the clouds for omens, to deal in what God has forbidden. The law says there shall not be found among you an observer of times, and Leviticus says neither shall you use enchantment nor observe times; Manasseh did exactly what the law forbade, observing times and using enchantments and dealing with familiar spirits; and Micah promises a day when God will cut off witchcrafts and there will be no more soothsayers. The root is the same as the word for cloud — the arts of reading the sky for what only God knows.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the ban on these arts is a mercy, not a restriction: God forbids them because they are a shortcut around trusting Him, and a shortcut that ends in serving what is not God. Manasseh's reign shows where the shortcut leads, and Micah's promise shows where it ends — a day when no one needs a soothsayer, because God Himself speaks plainly to His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a cloud (as covering the sky), i.e. the nimbus or thunder-cloud}
BiblicalUsage: The Aramaic word for cloud appears once, in Daniel's night vision: 'I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.' It is the cloud of heaven itself, carrying the Son of man to the throne — the same cloud the Hebrew word carries through the whole Old Testament, here in Aramaic for the one verse.
TheologicalSignificance: One cloud in one verse carries the weight of the whole vision: the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive His kingdom, and I believe that is the day every other cloud in Scripture was pointing toward.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cloud (as covering the sky), i.e. the nimbus or thunder-cloud
BiblicalUsage: The cloud is God's covering through the whole Old Testament: the LORD went before Israel by day in a pillar of a cloud to lead them the way; the cloud covered the tent of the congregation and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle; the LORD came down in the pillar of the cloud and stood in the door of the tabernacle and called Aaron and Miriam; and when the priests came out of the holy place, the cloud filled the house of the LORD. The cloud leads, the cloud covers, and the cloud is where God speaks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cloud tells the truth about God: He is near enough to lead us and hidden enough that we cannot manage Him. He goes before His people in the cloud and He fills the house in the cloud, and I hold that is still how He works — present and guiding, and still beyond my full sight, which is why I trust what He has said rather than what I can see.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Building of Solomon's Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Anan is named once, in the list of those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day: 'And Ahijah, Hanan, Anan.' He was one of the men who put his name to the sealed promise that the returned exiles would keep God's law, and the Bible tells us nothing more about him.
TheologicalSignificance: A name on a sealed covenant is all we have of Anan, and I believe it is enough: he put his name to God's law with the rest of the returned people, and the list remembers him for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to mourn, i.e. complain
BiblicalUsage: The word means to complain, to murmur against what God has done: when the people complained, it displeased the LORD, and the fire of the LORD burnt among them. Jeremiah asks why a living man should complain at all, a man punished for his sins. The same word is the crowd grumbling in the wilderness and the prophet's question.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for complaining carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Jeremiah's question — a living man, punished for his sins, has nothing to complain about.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: cloudiness
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Job's curse on the day of his birth: 'Let darkness and the shadow of death stain it; let a cloud dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.' It is cloudiness — not a cloud that leads or covers, but a gloom that settles on a day Job wishes had never been.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for cloudiness carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Job's grief — a day he wishes darkness would swallow whole.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and a derivative of G3501; to renovate, i.e. reform:--renew.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: 'And be renewed in the spirit of your mind.' It is the renewing of the mind itself — not new information, but a mind made new in its spirit, the way of thinking itself changed, so that the new man can be put on.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for being renewed in the mind carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the command — be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and the new man follows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3525; to become sober again, i.e. (figuratively) regain (one's) senses:--recover self.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Paul prays that those who oppose themselves may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will. It is waking up sober — coming back to your senses after being caught in a trap you did not see, and finding the way out.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for coming back to your senses carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the escape — the snare of the devil, and the recovery God gives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and the base of G32; to announce (in detail):--declare, rehearse, report, show, speak, tell.
BiblicalUsage: John says, 'This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all' — and Jesus promises the Spirit of truth will show His people things to come. Paul tells the Ephesian elders he has not shunned to declare all the counsel of God, and he tells Rome that those to whom Christ was not spoken of shall see. The word is declaring in full: the message heard, the counsel told, the future shown, and the name carried to those who never heard it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe declaring is the duty that follows hearing: John heard the message and declared it, Paul knew the counsel and would not shun it, and the Spirit shows things to come so that we can tell them. The gospel was never meant to stop with the hearer — it was heard so it could be declared, and I hold that is still the chain: hear it, then tell it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2608); Ananias, the name of three Israelites:--Ananias.
BiblicalUsage: Three men share the name Ananias, and their stories could not be more different: the first sold a possession with his wife Sapphira, kept back part of the price, and fell dead when Peter exposed the lie, while the second was a disciple at Damascus whom the Lord sent in a vision to lay hands on Saul, so that the persecutor could see again. The third was the high priest who commanded that Paul be struck on the mouth, and whom Paul called a whited wall.
TheologicalSignificance: One name, three men: a liar struck dead, a faithful disciple who baptised the apostle to the Gentiles, and a high priest who struck Paul. I believe the name carries no lesson of its own — what it shows is that God judges the heart, not the name, and the same name can belong to a warning and to a faithful servant.
RelatedPeople: Ananias, Husband of Sapphira; Ananias of Damascus; Ananias, the High Priest; Sapphira; Paul
RelatedEvents: Ananias and Sapphira; The Conversion of Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anani, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Anani is named once, at the end of the genealogy of David's line: the sons of Elioenai were Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah, and Anani, seven. He is the last name in a long line of David's descendants, counted among the sons of the kingdom after the exile.
TheologicalSignificance: A name at the end of a genealogy still counts: Anani is one of the seven sons who carried David's line forward after the exile, and the list remembers him for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G318; necessary; by implication, close (of kin):--near, necessary, necessity, needful.
BiblicalUsage: The word means necessary, needful — and it is used for both duty and love: Paul and Barnabas tell the Jews it was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to them, and Paul tells the Philippians that to abide in the flesh is more needful for them, though his desire is to depart and be with Christ. It appears eight times, always for what cannot be left undone.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for necessary carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the necessity — the word that had to be spoken first, and the apostle who stayed because his people needed him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of G315; compulsorily:--by constraint.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind. It is the adverb for doing something because you are forced to — and Peter forbids it in shepherds. The flock is not to be fed under compulsion.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for by constraint carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the willing shepherd — feed the flock willingly, not because you must.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G318; to necessitate:--compel, constrain.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to compel, to constrain: the lord tells his servant to go out into the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, that his house may be filled — and Paul asks Peter, before them all, why he compels the Gentiles to live as the Jews. The same word is the urgency of the invitation and the pressure of a false demand, and the difference is everything.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for compelling carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the difference — compel them to come in to the feast, but do not compel Gentiles to live as Jews.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and the base of G43; constraint (literally or figuratively); by implication, distress:--distress, must needs, (of) necessity(-sary), needeth, needful.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says necessity is laid upon him — woe unto me if I preach not the gospel — and he takes pleasure in necessities, in distresses for Christ's sake, for when he is weak then he is strong. Jesus warns of great distress in the land in the days to come, and Hebrews says that when the priesthood is changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law. The word is constraint, distress, the thing that must be: the pressure that drives the preacher, the trouble that proves the apostle, and the necessity that changes the priesthood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe necessity is the pressure that shows what a man is made of: Paul preached because he must, and he took pleasure in the necessities because they proved Christ's strength in his weakness. And I hold that the greatest necessity in the Bible is the one in Hebrews — the priesthood had to change, because the old one could not finish the work, and the new Priest could.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G368; promptly:--without gainsaying.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Peter tells Cornelius, 'Therefore came I unto you without gainsaying, as soon as I was sent for.' It is the adverb for coming at once, without arguing or objecting — Peter did not dispute the vision, did not argue with the messengers, but came as soon as he was sent for.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for without gainsaying carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Peter's obedience — he came as soon as he was sent for, without arguing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of a compound of G473 and G4483; indisputable:--cannot be spoken against.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: the town clerk of Ephesus tells the crowd, 'Seeing then that these things cannot be spoken against, ye ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly.' It is the word for what cannot be denied — the facts about Artemis and her temple are beyond dispute, and the crowd should go home.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for cannot be spoken against carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the clerk's calm — the facts are beyond dispute, so be quiet and do nothing rash.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ananjah, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ananiah is named twice, once as a man and once as a place: Azariah the son of Maaseiah the son of Ananiah repaired the wall by his house, and Ananiah is listed among the towns where the children of Benjamin settled after the exile. The man and the town share the name, and the lists keep them apart by the context.
TheologicalSignificance: A man and a town with one name still tell the same story: the wall was rebuilt house by house, and the people settled town by town, and Ananiah's name is on both lists.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3973; (reflexively) to repose (literally or figuratively (be exempt), remain); by implication, to refresh:--take ease, refresh, (give, take) rest.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says, 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' — and He tells His disciples to come apart into a desert place and rest a while, for there were many coming and going. Paul tells Philemon the bowels of the saints are refreshed by his love, and the voice from heaven says blessed are the dead which die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labours. The word is rest, refreshment, and the laying down of a burden — given by Christ, shared among the saints, and finished in death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rest is a gift before it is a duty: Jesus gives it to the heavy laden, the disciples take it apart from the crowds, the saints refresh one another with love, and the dead rest from their labours. I hold that the rest He gives now is the same rest the voice promises at the end — not an escape from work, but the end of labouring without Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G373; intermission; by implication, recreation:--rest.
BiblicalUsage: The word means rest, and it appears five times — twice as a promise and twice as its opposite. Jesus says take His yoke and learn of Him, and you shall find rest unto your souls; and Revelation says those who worship the beast have no rest day nor night. The same word is the rest the soul finds in Christ and the rest the lost never find.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for rest carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast — rest for the soul in Christ, and no rest day nor night for those who refuse Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3982; to incite:--persuade.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the charge against Paul at Corinth: 'This fellow persuadeth men to worship God contrary to the law.' It is inciting, stirring up — the accusers say Paul is talking people into a worship the law forbids, and Gallio throws the case out.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for persuading carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the charge — Paul persuading men to worship God, and the charge itself proving the gospel was spreading.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3992; to send up or back:--send (again).
BiblicalUsage: The word means to send up, or to send back: Pilate, learning that Jesus belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, sent Him to Herod — and Paul tells Philemon, 'Whom I have sent again: thou therefore receive him, that is, mine own bowels,' sending Onesimus back to his master. The same word sends a prisoner up to a higher court and sends a runaway slave back home with a letter.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for sending back carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two sendings — Jesus sent to Herod, and Onesimus sent back to Philemon as Paul's own heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 (in the sense of intensity) and πῆρος (maimed); crippled:--maimed.
BiblicalUsage: The word means maimed, crippled: when you make a feast, Jesus says, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind — and the servant reports that the master has ordered him to bring in the poor and the maimed and the halt and the blind. It appears only twice, both times in the same parable, and both times the maimed are the ones invited in off the streets.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for maimed carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the guest list — the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind, brought in from the streets and lanes to fill the house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the face
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic the word means the face: Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel, and later the form of his visage — his face — was changed against Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and he ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter. The same word is the king's face bowed to the ground in worship and the king's face twisted with fury.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the face carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two faces — Nebuchadnezzar bowed down before Daniel, and Nebuchadnezzar raging against the three friends.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a twig (as covering the limbs)}
BiblicalUsage: The word means a twig, a branch — the limbs of a tree. In Aramaic it describes the great tree of Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the leaves were fair, the fruit was much, the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof; and in the interpretation Daniel repeats it, the branches where the birds had their habitation. In Hebrew the same word is the twig of Ezekiel's cedar and the boughs of the feast of tabernacles.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a twig carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the tree — the great tree of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, whose branches sheltered the beasts and the birds until it was cut down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a twig (as covering the limbs)
BiblicalUsage: The word means a twig, a branch — the limbs of a tree. In Aramaic it describes the great tree of Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the leaves were fair, the fruit was much, the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof; and in the interpretation Daniel repeats it, the branches where the birds had their habitation. In Hebrew the same word is the twig of Ezekiel's cedar and the boughs of the feast of tabernacles.

Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to breathe hard, i.e. be enraged
BiblicalUsage: The word means to breathe hard, to be enraged: in Horeb Israel provoked the LORD to wrath, so that the LORD was angry with them to have destroyed them — and the psalm asks how long He will be angry, and whether He will draw out His anger to all generations. It is the anger that snorts, the breath that comes hard, and it is used of God's anger against Israel and of Israel asking how long it will last.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for being enraged carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the question — how long will God be angry, and the answer the psalm trusts, that His anger does not last for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an unclean bird, perhaps the parrot (from its irascibility)
BiblicalUsage: The word appears twice, in the same list both times: among the unclean birds, after the stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat. It is the heron — a wading bird, named from its irascibility, the anger in its cry — and the law counts it unclean, not to be eaten.
TheologicalSignificance: One bird in two lists carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the list — the clean and the unclean set apart, and the heron on the unclean side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G5316; to show, i.e. (reflexively) appear, or (passively) to have pointed out:--(should) appear, discover.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to show, to appear: Jesus added a parable because He was near Jerusalem and they thought the kingdom of God should immediately appear — and on the voyage to Jerusalem, when the ship had discovered Cyprus, they left it on the left hand and sailed on. It is the appearing of a kingdom the crowds expected at once, and the appearing of an island on the horizon.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for appearing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the expectation — the kingdom the crowds thought should appear at once, and the parable Jesus told to correct them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G5342; to take up (literally or figuratively):--bear, bring (carry, lead) up, offer (up).
BiblicalUsage: The word means to take up, to carry up, to offer up — and it holds the whole ladder of sacrifice. Abraham offered Isaac his son upon the altar, and James says he was justified by works when he did it; the high priest offers up sacrifice daily, but Christ offered up Himself once; Peter says He bore our sins in His own body on the tree; and Jesus takes Peter, James and John up into a high mountain apart, and is transfigured before them. The offering goes up, and the Lord goes up, and both are the same word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds the gospel in both directions: Abraham carried his son up the mountain to offer him, and God carried His Son up the mountain to offer Him — and the difference is everything. Isaac came down alive, and Christ bore our sins in His own body on the tree so that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness. The offering that Abraham could not finish, God finished Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G5455; to exclaim:--speak out.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, spake out with a loud voice and said, 'Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.' It is the speaking out — the cry of recognition when Mary comes through the door, and Elizabeth knows who the child is before Mary says a word.
TheologicalSignificance: One loud voice carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the greeting — Elizabeth speaking out what the Spirit showed her, that the mother of her Lord had come to her.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G4098; to fall back, i.e. lie down, lean back:--lean, sit down (to meat).
BiblicalUsage: The word means to fall back, to lean back, to sit down at table: the disciple lying on Jesus' breast asks Him who it is — and when the hour was come, Jesus sat down, and the twelve apostles with Him. It appears eleven times, always at a meal or a leaning — the posture of those who eat together, and of the disciple who leans on Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for leaning back carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the table — the disciple on Jesus' breast, and the twelve sitting down with Him at the hour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G4137; to complete; by implication, to occupy, supply; figuratively, to accomplish (by coincidence ot obedience):--fill up, fulfill, occupy, supply.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to fill up, to complete: in the hearers of the parables the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, hearing and not understanding; Paul says bear one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ; the unlearned man cannot say Amen because he does not understand, though he occupies the room; and Epaphroditus risked his life to supply the Philippians' lack of service toward Paul. The filling up is a prophecy completed, a law fulfilled, a place occupied, and a lack supplied.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is about completion: the prophecy is fulfilled in the very people who refuse to hear it, and the law of Christ is fulfilled when I carry a burden that is not mine. The filling up is never about adding to what God said — it is about His word coming true, and His people supplying what is lacking in one another's service.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G626; indefensible:--without an excuse, inexcusable.
BiblicalUsage: The word means without excuse, without defence: the invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation of the world, so that men are without excuse — and therefore, Paul says, you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are that judges, for in judging another you condemn yourself, because you do the same things. It appears only twice, and the second verse turns the first one on the reader.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for without excuse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the turn — the creation leaves no one an excuse, and the judge finds he has none either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G5594; properly, to cool off, i.e. (figuratively) relieve:--refresh.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: 'The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain.' It is cooling off, catching your breath — the refreshment of a friend who keeps coming to a prisoner in chains, when others have walked away.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for refreshing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Onesiphorus — the friend who kept coming, and was not ashamed of the chain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G404; properly, a recovery of breath, i.e. (figuratively) revival:--revival.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: 'Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord.' It is a recovery of breath, a revival — the cool air after the heat, and Peter ties it to repentance: sins blotted out, and then the refreshing comes.
TheologicalSignificance: The times of refreshing carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the order — repent, be converted, sins blotted out, and then the refreshing comes from the presence of the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G681; to enkindle:--kindle, light.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to kindle, to light: Jesus says He has come to send fire on the earth, and wishes it were already kindled — and James says the tongue is a little member that boasts great things, and behold how great a matter a little fire kindleth. The same word is the fire Jesus came to send and the fire a tongue can start.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for kindling carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two fires — the fire Christ came to send on the earth, and the little fire of the tongue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 (in the sense of reversal) and G4428; to unroll (a scroll or volume):--open.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: in the synagogue at Nazareth, there was delivered unto Jesus the book of the prophet Isaiah, and when He had opened the book, He found the place where it was written, 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.' It is the unrolling of a scroll — the book opened to the exact place, and the reading that followed.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unrolling carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the opening — the scroll unrolled to Isaiah, and Jesus finding the place where it was written.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to collar, i.e. adorn with a necklace; figuratively, to fit out with supplies
BiblicalUsage: The word means to collar, to adorn with a necklace — and by extension, to fit out with supplies: the psalm says pride compasses the wicked about as a chain, and Moses commands that a freed servant shall be furnished liberally out of the flock, the floor, and the winepress. The same word is a chain of pride around a neck and a generous provision for a man going free.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for putting a collar on carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast — pride worn like a chain, and a freed servant sent out laden with gifts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a necklace (as if strangling)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a necklace, a chain about the neck: Proverbs says a father's instruction and a mother's law shall be an ornament of grace unto your head and chains about your neck — and the spoil of Midian included collars and purple raiment that were on the kings, and chains about their camels' necks. The same word is wisdom worn as an ornament and gold stripped from a defeated king.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a necklace carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the wearing — wisdom as chains about the neck, and a king's collars carried off as spoil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anak, a Canaanite
BiblicalUsage: Anak was a Canaanite, the father of the Anakim — the giants the spies saw in the land, strong people in walled cities, and the name stands for the giants themselves and for the fear they put in Israel. A generation later Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the children of Anak.
TheologicalSignificance: A name for a giant carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the fear — the spies saw the children of Anak and said the land could not be taken, and Caleb drove them out anyway.
RelatedPeople: Anak; Sheshai, Son of Anak; Ahiman, Son of Anak; Talmai, Son of Anak
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shriek
BiblicalUsage: The word means to shriek, to groan aloud: the LORD tells the man with the inkhorn to set a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and cry for the abominations done in Jerusalem — and Jeremiah says that in the day of Babylon's judgment, through all her land the wounded shall groan. It is the cry of the wounded and the sigh of the faithful, and God hears both.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for shrieking carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the cry — the men who sigh over Jerusalem's sins marked for life, and the wounded of Babylon groaning under judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: some kind of lizard, probably the gecko (from its wail)
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the list of unclean creeping things: 'the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.' It is one of the small creatures of the ground — probably the gecko, named from its wail — and the law counts it unclean, not to be touched or eaten.
TheologicalSignificance: One small creature in one list carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the list — the clean and the unclean set apart down to the smallest creeping thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: some kind of lizard, probably the gecko (from its wail)
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the list of unclean creeping things: 'the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.' It is one of the small creatures of the ground — probably the gecko, named from its wail — and the law counts it unclean, not to be touched or eaten.
TheologicalSignificance: One small creature in one list carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the list — the clean and the unclean set apart down to the smallest creeping thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Anakite or descendant of Anak
BiblicalUsage: The Anakim were the descendants of Anak — the giants of the land. Moses tells Israel the Emim who lived in Moab were a people great and many and tall, as the Anakim; and Caleb, at eighty-five, asks for the mountain where the Anakim were and the cities were great and fenced, trusting the LORD would be with him to drive them out. The word is always the giants, and always the question of whether Israel will face them.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for giants carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the asking — Caleb at eighty-five asking for the mountain where the Anakim were, because the LORD was with him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G705; unnumbered, i.e. without number:--innumerable.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: 'Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable.' It is the number that cannot be numbered — Abraham's descendants, from one man as good as dead, as many as the stars and the sand.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for innumerable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the promise — from one man as good as dead, a people like the stars and the sand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G4579; figuratively, to excite:--move, stir up.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to stir up, to excite: the chief priests moved the people to ask for Barabbas instead of Jesus, and the accusers said Jesus stirreth up the people, teaching throughout all Jewry, beginning from Galilee to this place. It is the stirring of a crowd — the priests moving the people one way, and the charge that Jesus moved them the other.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for stirring up carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the crowd — moved by the chief priests to choose Barabbas, and charged with being stirred up by Jesus.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to urge; by implication, to inflict a penalty, specifically, to fine
BiblicalUsage: The word means to fine, to lay a penalty on someone: if men strive and hurt a woman with child, the offender shall be surely punished as the husband lays upon him and the judges determine; and a man who falsely accuses his bride shall be amerced a hundred shekels of silver and give them to her father. In Hebrew the word is the fine itself, and in Aramaic it is the same penalty in Ezra's decree — death, banishment, confiscation, or imprisonment for whoever will not keep the law.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a fine carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the penalty — the law setting a price on the wrong, and the judges determining what is owed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mulct
BiblicalUsage: The word means to fine, to lay a penalty on someone: if men strive and hurt a woman with child, the offender shall be surely punished as the husband lays upon him and the judges determine; and a man who falsely accuses his bride shall be amerced a hundred shekels of silver and give them to her father. In Hebrew the word is the fine itself, and in Aramaic it is the same penalty in Ezra's decree — death, banishment, confiscation, or imprisonment for whoever will not keep the law.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a fine carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the penalty — the law setting a price on the wrong, and the judges determining what is owed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be frail, feeble, or (figuratively) melancholy
BiblicalUsage: The word means frail, feeble, sick past healing: the child of David and Bathsheba was struck and was very sick; Jeremiah says the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked, past knowing; and twice the wound is called incurable — thy bruise is incurable, thy wound is grievous, and her wound is incurable, for it has come unto Judah. The word is used for a dying child, a deceitful heart, and a wound no physician can heal.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the Bible's honest diagnosis: the heart is desperately wicked, and the wound is incurable — no man can heal it and no effort can fix it. That is why the gospel has to be a new heart and not a repaired one, and why I hold that only God can do what Jeremiah says no one can: know the heart, and heal the wound that is past healing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 (in the sense of reversal) and a derivative of G4632; properly, to pack up (baggage), i.e. (by implication, and figuratively) to upset:--subvert.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the letter from the Jerusalem council: 'Forasmuch as we have heard, that certain which went out from us have troubled you with words, subverting your souls, saying, Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law: to whom we gave no such commandment.' It means to pack up and upset — to turn a soul upside down — and the council says plainly that the men who did it had no authority from them.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for subverting carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the letter — the council disowning the men who troubled the Gentiles with a law they never gave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G4685; to take up or extricate:--draw up, pull out.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to draw up, to pull out: which of you, Jesus asks, shall have an ass or an ox fallen into a pit and will not straightway pull him out on the sabbath day? And Peter's vision of the sheet was drawn up again into heaven, all three times. It is the pulling out of a pit and the drawing up of a vision — the same motion, up out of where it was.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for pulling out carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two drawings — the ox pulled from the pit on the sabbath, and the sheet drawn up into heaven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G450; a standing up again, i.e. (literally) a resurrection from death (individual, genitive case or by implication, (its author)), or (figuratively) a (moral) recovery (of spiritual truth):--raised to life again, resurrection, rise from the dead, that should rise, rising again.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus told Martha, 'I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.' Paul says that as by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead, and the apostles gave witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus with great power. He adds that if we have been planted together in the likeness of His death, we shall be also in the likeness of His resurrection. The resurrection is not only something that happened to Jesus — it is something that will happen to us, in His likeness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the resurrection is the whole Christian hope in one word: Christ rose, so death is not the end, and I will rise in His likeness because I have been planted together with Him. It is not a doctrine I hold at arm's length — it is the reason I can face death without fear, and the reason the apostles preached with great power when everything was against them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G450 (in the sense of removal); properly, to drive out of home, i.e. (by implication) to disturb (literally or figuratively):--trouble, turn upside down, make an uproar.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to turn upside down, to drive out of house and home: the rulers of Thessalonica cried, 'These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also' — and Paul wishes those who trouble the Galatians were even cut off. It is the uproar the gospel causes: the world turned upside down, and the troublers who ought to be cut off.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for turning upside down carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the charge — the world turned upside down, and the accusers meant it as a complaint when it was really a compliment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G4717; to recrucify (figuratively):--crucify afresh.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: if they shall fall away, it is impossible to renew them again unto repentance, seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put Him to an open shame. It is crucifying again — not a second cross on Calvary, but the apostate's fresh rejection, treating the Son of God as though His crucifixion were not finished.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for crucifying afresh carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning — to fall away after tasting the heavenly gift is to crucify the Son of God again, and put Him to open shame.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G4727; to sigh deeply:--sigh deeply.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit over a generation seeking a sign, and said there would be no sign given to it. It is a deep sigh, from the spirit, not the lungs — the sigh of a man who sees the demand for proof and knows it will not believe anyway.
TheologicalSignificance: One deep sigh carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the sigh itself — Jesus sighing in His spirit at a generation that asks for a sign and will not believe one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G4762; to overturn; also to return; by implication, to busy oneself, i.e. remain, live:--abide, behave self, have conversation, live, overthrow, pass, return, be used.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says his rejoicing is the testimony of his conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity he has had his conversation — his whole way of life — in the world, and more abundantly toward Corinth; and he reminds the Ephesians that they all once had their conversation in the lusts of the flesh. Peter tells the scattered believers to pass the time of their sojourning in fear, and Hebrews says the writers trust they have a good conscience, in all things willing to live honestly. The word is a life lived, day after day, in the world and before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the test of everything else I claim: my conversation — the way I actually live — is the evidence, and the conscience knows whether it is simplicity and godly sincerity or not. I once lived in the lusts of the flesh like everyone else, and now I am to pass my sojourning in fear, living honestly in all things. That is the life I want my own to be, and I hold that God judges the walk, not just the words.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G390; behavior:--conversation.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says they have heard of his conversation in time past in the Jews' religion, how beyond measure he persecuted the church of God and wasted it — and he tells the Ephesians to put off, concerning the former conversation, the old man, corrupt according to the deceitful lusts. Timothy is told to be an example of the believers in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity; and Peter says, as He who called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation. The word is the whole conduct of a life: the old one put off, the new one an example, and holiness in all of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that conduct is the sermon people actually hear: Paul's old conversation persecuted the church, and his new one built it, and the difference was Christ. Timothy is told to be an example in conversation before anything else, and Peter says holiness belongs in all manner of it — not just on Sundays, but in the whole manner of living. I believe God cares about the way I live on a Tuesday as much as what I say on a Sunday.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and the middle voice of G5021; to arrange:--set in order.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the first verse of Luke's gospel: 'Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us.' It is the arranging, the setting in order — Luke taking the accounts others had written and putting them in order, so Theophilus could know the certainty of what he had been taught.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for setting in order carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the gospel itself — Luke arranging the story so that certainty could follow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and the base of G5056; to (cause to) arise:--(a-, make to) rise, at the rising of, spring (up), be up.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to rise, to spring up: God makes His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust — and James says the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat than it withers the grass, and the flower thereof falls. It is used for the sun rising, for a plant springing up, and for the day dawning, and it appears nine times.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for rising carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the sun — rising on the evil and the good alike, and withering the grass by noon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anath, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Anath is known only as the father of Shamgar, the judge who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. Judges names him twice, both times to place Shamgar, and says nothing more about the man himself.
TheologicalSignificance: A name with no story of its own still matters, because God remembers the father behind the deliverer, and Shamgar's victory is tied to a real family, not a legend.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and θάλλω (to flourish); to revive:--flourish again.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this one word once, telling the Philippians that their care for him has flourished again, like a plant putting out fresh growth after winter. The picture is of something coming back to life, not starting from nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: One picture of care blooming again carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Paul's joy that the Philippians' love for him had found fresh expression.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G394 (like G331, but in a good sense); a votive offering:--gift.
BiblicalUsage: Luke records this word once, where some speak of the temple adorned with goodly stones and gifts. Here it means a votive offering, something dedicated and set out in honour of God, the opposite sense of the curse-word that shares its spelling.
TheologicalSignificance: A single mention of temple gifts holds no teaching of its own; what matters is the contrast, that the same root can name a gift given to God or a person cut off from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G394; a (religious) ban or (concretely) excommunicated (thing or person):--accused, anathema, curse, X great.
BiblicalUsage: Anathema is a ban, a person or thing handed over to destruction, cut off from God and His people. Paul says he could wish himself accursed for his brethren's sake, warns that no one speaking by the Spirit calls Jesus accursed, and pronounces the curse on anyone who preaches another gospel or does not love the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line that love cannot blur: there is a real curse for rejecting Christ and for twisting His gospel. Paul's willingness to be accursed himself shows how seriously he took it, and I hold that the gospel is worth defending with that same gravity.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G331; to declare or vow under penalty of execration:--(bind under a) curse, bind with an oath.
BiblicalUsage: This is the verb of binding oneself under a curse. In Acts the Jews bind themselves with an oath to kill Paul before they eat, and in Mark Peter begins to curse and to swear that he does not know Jesus. Both times the curse is a man's own doing, laid on himself to make his words stick.
TheologicalSignificance: A verb for swearing a curse on oneself carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that men will call down God's judgment on themselves rather than tell the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2334; to look again (i.e. attentively) at (literally or figuratively):--behold, consider.
BiblicalUsage: Twice the New Testament tells us to look carefully at something. Paul in Athens says he beheld the Athenians' devotions as he passed by, and Hebrews tells its readers to consider the end of their leaders' conversation. In both cases the word means a slow, attentive look, not a glance.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for looking closely holds no theology by itself; what it asks is simple, that we pay attention to what people worship and to how faithful lives end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anathoth, the name of two Israelites, also of a place in Pal
BiblicalUsage: Anathoth is a town of Benjamin, a city of the priests, and the home of Jeremiah the prophet. Solomon sends the priest Abiathar there in disgrace, Isaiah names it among the towns trembling before the Assyrian advance, and Jeremiah's whole ministry begins as the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth.
