TheologicalSignificance: A priestly town that produced both a disgraced priest and a faithful prophet shows me that God does not choose by address; He calls whom He will, even from a place men had written off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and the middle voice of G5087; to set forth (for oneself), i.e propound:--communicate, declare.
BiblicalUsage: Festus lays Paul's case before King Agrippa, setting it forth for counsel, and Paul goes up to Jerusalem to lay the gospel he preaches before the leaders there. The word means to lay something out plainly before others so they can weigh it.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for laying a matter before others carries no doctrine of its own; its value is the example, that even Paul put his gospel before the church to be examined.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G393; a rising of light, i.e. dawn (figuratively); by implication, the east (also in plural):--dayspring, east, rising.
BiblicalUsage: Anatole is the rising, the dawn and the east where the sun comes up. The wise men come from the east following His star, Zechariah sings that the dayspring from on high has visited us, and Jesus says His coming will be like lightning shining from the east to the west. The word joins the direction of sunrise to the hope of a new day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God tied His promises to the sunrise on purpose: every morning rehearses the coming of the Light. The dayspring has already visited us in Christ, and I hold that His return will be just as unmistakable as the dawn.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Magi Visit Jesus; The Annunciation to Mary
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G5142; to rear (physically or mentally):--bring up, nourish (up).
BiblicalUsage: Stephen says Moses was nourished up in his father's house for three months, and Paul says he was brought up in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel. The word covers both kinds of raising, fed as a child and taught as a young man.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for being brought up carries no doctrine of its own; its interest is biographical, that both Moses and Paul were shaped by the homes and teachers God gave them.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and the base of G5157; to overturn (figuratively):--overthrow, subvert.
BiblicalUsage: False teachers overthrow the faith of some, Paul warns, and in Crete they subvert whole houses, teaching things they ought not for money's sake. The word pictures a table overturned: what stood firm is thrown down.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for overturning faith carries no teaching of its own; its warning is plain, that wrong doctrine does real damage to real households.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: depressed (figuratively), in mind (gentle) or circumstances (needy, especially saintly)
BiblicalUsage: The meek and the afflicted poor are one people in this word's family: the lowly whom God defends and lifts up. Moses is called the meekest man on earth, the good tidings are preached to the meek, and the humble boast in the Lord who hears them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe meekness is not weakness but strength held low before God, and the afflicted poor are not forgotten by Him but chosen as His special care. I hold that God still lifts the lowly and brings down the proud, and that is where my hope sits.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: condescension, human and subjective (modesty), or divine and objective (clemency)
BiblicalUsage: The meek and the afflicted poor are one people in this word's family: the lowly whom God defends and lifts up. Moses is called the meekest man on earth, the good tidings are preached to the meek, and the humble boast in the Lord who hears them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe meekness is not weakness but strength held low before God, and the afflicted poor are not forgotten by Him but chosen as His special care. I hold that God still lifts the lowly and brings down the proud, and that is where my hope sits.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G370; irreverently:--unworthily.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns that whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. The adverb names the manner, not the man: taking the Supper lightly, without discerning what it is.
TheologicalSignificance: One adverb in one warning carries no system of its own; its weight is Paul's, that the Lord's Supper is not a common meal to be taken carelessly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G514; unfit:--unworthy.
BiblicalUsage: Paul asks the Corinthians if they are unworthy to judge the smallest matters, when the saints will judge the world. The word is a rebuke: men fit for the greatest judgment were acting as if they could not settle a small dispute.
TheologicalSignificance: A single rebuke about fitness to judge holds no doctrine of its own; its point is Paul's, that Christians who will judge the world should be able to settle their own quarrels.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anajah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Two men share this name in Nehemiah's day: one stands beside Ezra on the pulpit of wood as the law is read to the returned exiles, and the other sets his seal to the covenant the people make afterward. The name appears only in the work of rebuilding.
TheologicalSignificance: Two men with one name, both standing where the law was read and the covenant sealed, remind me that God's work is carried by ordinary men who simply show up and stand in their place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2198; to recover life (literally or figuratively):--(be a-)live again, revive.
BiblicalUsage: To live again. The father cries that his son was dead and is alive again, and Paul says that when the commandment came, sin revived and he died. The word carries both pictures: a dead son coming home alive, and a dead sin waking up at the sound of God's law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds the whole gospel in miniature: what was dead can live again, and what was dormant can wake. The prodigal's return is my own story, and I hold that God's life is stronger than any death I have known.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2212; to search out:--seek.
BiblicalUsage: Mary and Joseph search for the boy Jesus among their company on the road home from Jerusalem, and Barnabas goes to Tarsus to seek out Saul and bring him to Antioch. The word is a thorough searching, looking until the one sought is found.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for searching out holds no doctrine of its own; its charm is the picture, of parents hunting for their child and a friend hunting for a man the church needed.
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Barnabas; Paul
RelatedEvents: The Boy Jesus in the Temple; The Church at Antioch
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2224; to gird afresh:--gird up.
BiblicalUsage: Peter tells his readers to gird up the loins of their mind, be sober, and hope to the end. The picture comes from a man tucking up his long robe so he can run or work without tripping, applied to the mind getting ready for what is coming.
TheologicalSignificance: One call to gird up the mind carries no system of its own; its force is Peter's, that hope is not daydreaming but a mind made ready to run.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and a compound of the base of G2226 and G4442; to re-enkindle:--stir up.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells Timothy to stir up the gift of God that is in him by the laying on of his hands. The picture is a fire banked low and blown back into flame, a gift that needs tending rather than a new gift altogether.
TheologicalSignificance: A single picture of a fire rekindled holds no doctrine of its own; its encouragement is Paul's, that Timothy's gift was still there, waiting to be stirred.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of a compound of G435 and G4228; an enslaver (as bringing men to his feet):--menstealer.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists menstealers among the lawless and disobedient for whom the law is made, alongside murderers, liars, and perjurers. The word names the slave trader, the man who steals people to sell them.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a slave trader carries no teaching of its own; its weight is Paul's list, that stealing a person to sell him stands among the plain sins the law condemns.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G435; manly; Andreas, an Israelite:--Andrew.
BiblicalUsage: Andrew is Simon Peter's brother, a fisherman of Bethsaida, and the first of the apostles to follow Jesus. He brings his brother to Christ, and later he brings the boy with the five loaves and two fishes, always quietly bringing someone to Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: Andrew never takes the centre of the story, and I love him for it: his work is bringing people to Jesus and then stepping back. I believe the kingdom runs on men like him, faithful in the introductions no one remembers.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples; The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G435; to act manly:--quit like men.
BiblicalUsage: Paul closes his first letter to Corinth with a soldier's call: watch, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. The word means to act like a man in the old sense, to show courage and hold your ground.
TheologicalSignificance: A single soldier's call holds no doctrine of its own; its force is Paul's, that faith is not passive but a stand to be held.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G435 and G3534; man of victory; Andronicos, an Israelite:--Adronicus.
BiblicalUsage: Andronicus appears once, in Paul's greetings, as his kinsman and fellow prisoner, of note among the apostles, and in Christ before Paul was. One verse gives him a whole history: kin, prison, honour, and an earlier faith than Paul's own.
TheologicalSignificance: A man known from a single greeting still shows me something real: faithfulness before fame, prison shared with an apostle, and a name Paul thought worth remembering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G435 and G5408; a murderer:--manslayer.
BiblicalUsage: Paul names manslayers among those for whom the law is made, beside murderers of fathers and mothers. The word is the plain name for a man who kills another man.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a manslayer carries no teaching of its own; its place in Paul's list says enough, that taking a life stands among the sins the law was written to restrain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G303 and G2192; to hold oneself up against, i.e. (figuratively) put up with:--bear with, endure, forbear, suffer.
BiblicalUsage: To bear with, to put up with, to hold oneself up against the weight of another person's faults. Paul tells the churches to forbear one another in love and to forgive as Christ forgave, Jesus asks how long He shall suffer a faithless generation, and Hebrews asks its readers to suffer the word of exhortation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bearing with one another is the daily proof of love, harder than any single act of forgiveness and longer than any single argument. Christ bore with me first, and I hold that His patience with me is the measure of the patience I owe His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G1555; not expounded in full, i.e. indescribable:--unspeakable.
BiblicalUsage: Paul ends his appeal for generous giving with thanks for God's unspeakable gift, a gift too great to be told out in full. The word means what cannot be fully narrated, a gift beyond the reach of words.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a gift beyond telling carries no system of its own; its wonder is Paul's, that God's gift outruns every attempt to describe it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G1583; not spoken out, i.e. (by implication) unutterable:--unspeakable.
BiblicalUsage: Peter writes of joy unspeakable and full of glory for believers who have not seen Christ yet love Him. The word names a joy that cannot be spoken out, too deep for the tongue to carry.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for unspeakable joy holds no doctrine of its own; its beauty is Peter's, that love for an unseen Christ gives a joy words cannot hold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G1587; not left out, i.e. (by implication) inexhaustible:--that faileth not.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus tells His disciples to provide bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not. The word describes a treasure that never runs out, that no thief approaches and no moth corrupts.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a treasure that never fails carries no teaching of its own; its comfort is Jesus', that what we lay up in heaven is the only wealth that cannot be lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2240; to attain to, i.e. (figuratively) be proper:--convenient, be fit.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this word for what is fitting: filthiness and foolish talking are not convenient, and wives are to submit to their husbands as it is fit in the Lord. The word draws the line between what suits a Christian and what does not.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for what is fitting carries no doctrine of its own; its use is practical, that some speech and some behaviour simply do not suit people who belong to Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: comparative of a derivative of G430; more endurable:--more tolerable.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says it shall be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for the city that rejects His disciples. The word is a comparison of judgment: some refusals are worse than others, and the judgment fits the light that was refused.
TheologicalSignificance: One comparison about tolerable judgment carries no system of its own; its warning is Jesus', that rejecting the gospel after hearing it is worse than never having heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1655; merciless:--unmerciful.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists the unmerciful among the marks of a mind given over to itself: without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful. The word names the heart that refuses pity to anyone.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for mercilessness holds no doctrine of its own; its darkness is Paul's, that a heart without mercy is one of the signs of a heart God has left to itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anem, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Anem is a town of Issachar, given to the Levites of the family of Gershom, and it appears only once in the whole Bible. The chronicler lists it among the towns where the Levites lived, and says nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once and never again still has its place in the record, and I take comfort in that: God keeps the small places too, and no corner of His people's story is forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and ἥμερος (lame); savage:--fierce.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns that in the last days men will be fierce, despisers of those that are good, traitors, heady, highminded. The word means savage, untamed, like a wild animal that cannot be gentled.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for savagery carries no teaching of its own; its warning is Paul's, that the last days will be marked by men who cannot be reasoned with or softened.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G417; to toss with the wind:--drive with the wind.
BiblicalUsage: James says the doubter is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed. The word is the wind's work on the water, and James uses it for a mind that cannot settle, blown one way and then the other.
TheologicalSignificance: A single picture of wind-tossed water holds no doctrine of its own; its lesson is James's, that a doubting heart is at the mercy of every wind that blows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G109; wind; (plural) by implication, (the four) quarters (of the earth):--wind.
BiblicalUsage: The wind is the Bible's picture of power no man controls and of teaching that blows men about. Jesus rebukes the winds on the sea and they obey Him, the sea rises with a great wind against the disciples, and Paul warns against being tossed to and fro by every wind of doctrine. The same wind that frightens the disciples is the one Christ commands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wind teaches me two things at once: my helplessness, because I cannot steer it, and Christ's authority, because He can. I hold that the winds of doctrine will keep blowing, and the only safety is staying anchored to the word He has spoken.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Calms the Storm; Jesus Walks on Water
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of the same as G1735; unadmitted, i.e. (by implication) not supposable:--impossible.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says it is impossible but that offences will come, and then warns of the woe on the one through whom they come. The word means what cannot be admitted or allowed in, here the plain fact that stumbling blocks are unavoidable in this world.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for what cannot be kept out carries no doctrine of its own; its sobriety is Jesus', that offences will come, and the woe falls on the one who causes them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G1458; unaccused, i.e. (by implication) irreproachable:--blameless.
BiblicalUsage: Deacons must first be proved and then found blameless, and an elder must be blameless, the husband of one wife, with faithful children. The word names the man against whom no charge can be laid, not a perfect man but one no one can fairly accuse.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for blamelessness in church office carries no system of its own; its standard is Paul's, that leaders must be men no honest charge can stick to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of a compound of G1909 and G153; not ashamed, i.e. irreprehensible: --that needeth not to be ashamed.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells Timothy to study to show himself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. The word describes the workman who has nothing to be ashamed of, because his work stands inspection.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for an unashamed workman holds no doctrine of its own; its charge is Paul's, that handling God's word rightly is the work that leaves a man with nothing to hide.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: branching
BiblicalUsage: Ezekiel pictures Israel's mother as a vine planted by the waters, fruitful and full of branches. The word is the branching itself, the spreading limbs of the vine in the prophet's lament for the princes of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a vine's branches carries no theology of its own; its sorrow is Ezekiel's, that a vine planted by good waters was cut down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G1949; not arrested, i.e. (by implication) inculpable:--blameless, unrebukeable.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells Timothy a bishop must be blameless, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach. The word names the man who cannot be seized upon, no handle for an accuser to grab.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a leader no one can lay hold of carries no system of its own; its standard is Paul's, that a bishop's life must give his accusers nothing to grip.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a particle of union) and an obsolete νέπος (a brood); properly, akin, i.e. (specially) a cousin:--sister's son.
BiblicalUsage: Paul calls Mark his sister's son, his fellow worker, and tells the Colossians to receive him if he comes to them. The word is simply cousin, the nearest kin after brother and sister.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for cousin carries no doctrine of its own; its interest is the family tie, that Mark was Barnabas's cousin and Paul's fellow worker.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word (compare G444); a man (properly as an individual male):--fellow, husband, man, sir.
BiblicalUsage: Man, husband, fellow, sir: the word covers the individual male in every relation. Joseph is called the husband of Mary, a man is to love his wife as Christ loved the church, and Peter stands up to say, ye men of Israel, hear these words.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this plain word carries the whole weight of manhood as Scripture sees it: a man is known by what he does with those given to him. Joseph's quiet righteousness, the husband's love like Christ's, the men of Israel called to listen, all of it says the same thing, that being a man means answering for others. I hold that standard, and I know it is higher than any man can meet alone.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Husband of Mary; Simon Peter; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aner, a Amorite, also a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Aner is one of the Amorite chiefs who joined Abram in the rescue of Lot, and the name also belongs to a town of Manasseh given to the Levites. Genesis remembers him as Abram's ally, and the chronicler remembers the town that bore his name.
TheologicalSignificance: A minor ally in Abram's war still earns a place in the record, and I take that as God's way: the men who stand beside His people in a hard hour are not forgotten, even if their own story is only a line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2064; to ascend:--go up.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this word for going up to Jerusalem, three years after his conversion, and Jesus goes up into a mountain to teach. The word is the plain act of ascending.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for going up carries no theology of its own; its use is geographical, that Jerusalem and the mountains of Galilee were reached by climbing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G447; relaxation or (figuratively) relief:--eased, liberty, rest.
BiblicalUsage: Relief, rest, ease after pressure. Paul finds no rest for his spirit in Troas, the churches are promised rest with us when the Lord Jesus is revealed, and Felix keeps Paul in liberty, giving him leave to receive his friends. The word is the loosening of a grip.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rest is one of God's promises, not a luxury: the rest He gives now to troubled spirits and the rest He will give when Christ is revealed. Paul's restless spirit in Troas is honest about the waiting, and I hold that the waiting itself ends in rest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and ἐτάζω (to test); to investigate (judicially):--(should have) examined(-d).
BiblicalUsage: Paul is examined by the chief captain, who commands him to be examined by scourging, and the next day the examination is dropped when they learn Paul is a Roman. The word is a judicial investigation, questioning under authority.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a Roman examination carries no doctrine of its own; its interest is the scene, that Paul's citizenship stopped the scourge before it began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; dill:--anise.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for tithing mint and anise and cummin while omitting the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith. The word is dill, a garden herb measured out to the tenth part.
TheologicalSignificance: One herb in one rebuke holds no theology of its own; its point is Jesus', that men will measure dill to the tenth part and skip justice altogether.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle; without:--without. Compare G1.
BiblicalUsage: Without. Two sparrows fall not without the Father, and wives may be won without a word by the conversation of their husbands. The word marks the absence of something, a thing done apart from another.
TheologicalSignificance: A small particle for without carries no doctrine of its own; its comfort is Jesus', that not even a sparrow falls apart from the Father.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2147; to find out:--find.
BiblicalUsage: The disciples find the child Jesus sitting in the temple, and in Troas the brethren find Paul and urge him to stay seven days. The word means to find out after looking, to come upon what was sought.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for finding after seeking holds no doctrine of its own; its pleasure is the scene, of shepherds finding the child and friends finding Paul.
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Paul
RelatedEvents: The Boy Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2111; not well set, i.e. inconvenient:--not commodious.
BiblicalUsage: Paul's ship is caught in a storm and the sailors fear the place is not commodious to winter in, so they sail on toward Crete. The word means an inconvenient harbour, a place not fit to wait out the winter.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an unfit harbour carries no teaching of its own; its interest is the voyage, that a bad wintering place pushed Paul's ship on toward the storm.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G1830; not searched out, i.e. (by implication) inscrutable:--unsearchable.
BiblicalUsage: Paul writes of judgments and ways past finding out, and then cries out at the depth of the riches of God's wisdom. The word names what cannot be searched out, the bottom that no sounding line reaches.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for what cannot be searched out carries no system of its own; its wonder is Paul's, that God's judgments have a depth no mind can sound.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of a compound of G1537 and a derivative of G2487; not tracked out, i.e. (by implication) untraceable:--past finding out; unsearchable.
BiblicalUsage: Paul reaches for the word for untraceable when he speaks of the unsearchable riches of Christ, and for the past tracing out of God's judgments. The word names a path no foot has left a print on, a way that cannot be followed back.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a trackless path holds no doctrine of its own; its wonder is Paul's, that Christ's riches cannot be traced to their end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G430 and G2556; enduring of ill, i.e. forbearing:--patient.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells Timothy the servant of the Lord must be patient, enduring evil without striking back, apt to teach and gentle to all. The word is the patience that absorbs a wrong and does not return it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for patient endurance carries no system of its own; its standard is Paul's, that the Lord's servant answers evil with teaching, not with temper.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (compare H104); properly, to be a courier, i.e. (by implication) to press into public service:--compel (to go).
BiblicalUsage: To press into service. A Roman soldier compels Simon of Cyrene to bear the cross, and Jesus says whoever compels you to go a mile, go with him two. The word is the power of a stronger man laying a burden on a weaker one, and Jesus turns it into a command to give more than is demanded.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus took the ugliest picture of power, a soldier pressing a man into carrying a cross, and made it the picture of His people: go further than you were forced to go. Simon carried the cross once, and I hold that every act of going the second mile still follows His steps.
RelatedEvents: Simon of Cyrene Carries Jesus' Cross
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄγγος (a pail, perhaps as bent; compare the base of G43); a receptacle:--vessel.
BiblicalUsage: The wise virgins take oil in their vessels with their lamps, while the foolish take none. The word is the plain jar that holds the oil, the container that makes the difference between readiness and ruin.
TheologicalSignificance: One jar in one parable carries no doctrine of its own; its lesson is the parable's, that readiness is oil in the vessel before the bridegroom comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G32; an announcement, i.e. (by implication) precept:--message.
BiblicalUsage: John writes that the message we have heard from the beginning is that God is light and in Him is no darkness at all. The word is the announcement itself, the thing declared and handed on.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the message itself carries no teaching of its own; its weight is John's, that the message is simple, God is light, and we are to love one another.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀγγέλλω (probably derived from G71; compare G34) (to bring tidings); a messenger; especially an "angel"; by implication, a pastor:--angel, messenger.
BiblicalUsage: An angel is a messenger, and Scripture gives the word its widest work: the angel who announces Jesus' birth to Mary, the angels who minister to Him after the temptation, the angel who rolls the stone from the tomb, the angels who will gather the elect, and the fallen angels kept in chains. The same word names the herald of good news and the warrior of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe angels are real and busy, and the Bible never lets me treat them as decoration: they announce, they guard, they fight, and they will gather. I hold that God sends His messengers to His people still, and that the angels who stood at the empty tomb are the same kind of servants who watch over us now.
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Jesus; Gabriel
RelatedEvents: The Annunciation to Mary; The Temptation in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and ἵημι (to send); to let up, i.e. (literally) slacken or (figuratively) desert, desist from:--forbear, leave, loose.
BiblicalUsage: The prison doors are opened and the bands loosed at Philippi, and the writer of Hebrews promises God will never leave us nor forsake us. The word means to slacken, to let go, to leave off.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for letting go carries no doctrine of its own; its comfort is Hebrews', that the God who never leaves us is the reason we can loosen our grip on fear.
RelatedEvents: Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2436; inexorable:--without mercy.
BiblicalUsage: James warns that judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has shown no mercy. The word names the pitiless verdict, mercy refused to the merciless.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for judgment without mercy carries no system of its own; its warning is James's, that the mercy we refuse is the mercy we will not receive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G3538; without ablution:--unwashen.
BiblicalUsage: The Pharisees eat with unwashen hands, and Jesus says it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man. The word means unwashed in the ceremonial sense, hands not cleansed by the ritual washing.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for unwashed hands carries no doctrine of its own; its point is Jesus', that defilement comes from the heart, not from the hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G2476; to stand up (literal or figurative, transitive or intransitive):--arise, lift up, raise up (again), rise (again), stand up(-right).
BiblicalUsage: To rise, to stand up, and by extension to be raised from the dead. Peter stands up with the eleven on the day of Pentecost, God raised up Jesus from the dead, the prodigal rises and goes to his father, and the dead in Christ shall rise first. The word joins the simplest act of standing to the greatest hope of the gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe standing up is the gospel in a single motion: the dead Christ stood up, the prodigal stood up, and the dead in Christ will stand up. I hold that resurrection is not an idea but a rising, and my own rising is already promised in His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aniam, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aniam is named once, as a son of Shemida in the genealogy of Manasseh. The chronicler gives him a place in the family list and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A name with a single mention still sits in the record, and I take comfort in that: God counts the men whose stories are only a line in a genealogy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: depressed, in mind or circumstances
BiblicalUsage: The meek and the afflicted poor are one people in this word's family: the lowly whom God defends and lifts up. Moses is called the meekest man on earth, the good tidings are preached to the meek, and the humble boast in the Lord who hears them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe meekness is not weakness but strength held low before God, and the afflicted poor are not forgotten by Him but chosen as His special care. I hold that God still lifts the lowly and brings down the proud, and that is where my hope sits.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: I
BiblicalUsage: I is the first word of a speaker about himself, and the Bible is full of it: God's I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur, His I am the LORD to Moses, David's I have sinned, Paul's I am chief of sinners. The word itself is only a pronoun, but the sentences built on it carry the whole of confession and covenant.
TheologicalSignificance: A pronoun carries no weight of its own; its power is in the mouths that use it, from God's I am the LORD to the sinner's I have sinned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: groaning
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah says the Lord will make Jerusalem's Ariel, her groaning, heavy with sorrow, and Lamentations takes up the groaning of a city in mourning. The word is the sound of a people in distress, a groan that has no words left.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for groaning holds no doctrine of its own; its sorrow is the prophets', that a city can be brought so low its only speech is a groan.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Anim is a town in the hill country of Judah, listed once among the cities of Judah's inheritance. Joshua's account gives it a place on the map and says nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once still has its place on the map of Judah, and I take comfort in that: God records the small towns as carefully as the great cities.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄγκος (a bend, "ache"); an arm (as curved):--arm.
BiblicalUsage: Simeon takes the child Jesus up in his arms and blesses God, saying his eyes have seen salvation. The word is the bent arm that cradles, the crook of the elbow where a child is held.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a cradling arm carries no doctrine of its own; its tenderness is Simeon's, that salvation could be held in a man's arms.
RelatedPeople: Simeon; Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus
RelatedEvents: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G43; a hook (as bent):--hook.
BiblicalUsage: Peter finds a coin in the mouth of the first fish he catches, enough to pay the temple tax for Jesus and himself. The word is the hook that caught the fish, a bent piece of metal with a job to do.
TheologicalSignificance: A single hook in a single miracle carries no teaching of its own; its wonder is the coin, that Jesus provided the tax from the sea.
RelatedEvents: The Coin in the Fish's Mouth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2584); Anna, an Israelitess:--Anna.
BiblicalUsage: Anna is the prophetess of the tribe of Asher, eighty-four years old, who lived in the temple with fastings and prayers and spoke of the child Jesus to all who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. Luke gives her a husband, seven years of marriage, a long widowhood, and a life spent waiting in the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: Anna waited in the temple for decades, and I believe her waiting is the pattern for mine: prayer and fasting in the dark, and then the child in her sight at last. I hold that no long waiting is wasted when it ends in seeing Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: oh now!
BiblicalUsage: Anna is the Hebrew word for O now, I pray, the cry of a man pleading with God. Hezekiah prays it on his sickbed, and the psalmist sings it at the feast, Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: A cry like this one teaches me that prayer needs no fine words, only an honest O now before God, and He hears the shortest prayers as well as the longest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2608); Annas (i.e. G367), an Israelite:--Annas.
BiblicalUsage: Annas is the high priest who had Jesus brought before him first, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, and the power behind the priesthood for years. John names him in the trial, Luke names him at the start of John the Baptist's ministry, and Acts names him among the rulers who threatened Peter and John.
TheologicalSignificance: Annas shows me how power can outlive office: he was no longer high priest, yet Jesus was brought to him first. I believe the trial of Jesus exposes every kind of corruption, and I hold that no council of men can condemn what God has appointed.
RelatedPeople: Annas; Caiaphas; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: Jesus Before the Sanhedrin; Peter and John Before the Sanhedrin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G473; upward or on the top:--above, brim, high, up.
BiblicalUsage: Above, on high, upward. The Jerusalem above is free and the mother of us all, and Paul presses toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. The word lifts the eyes from earth to heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for above carries no doctrine of its own; its direction is the point, that the Christian life is lived looking up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G430; self-restraint, i.e. tolerance:--forbearance.
BiblicalUsage: Forbearance, the patience that holds back judgment. Paul asks if we despise the riches of God's goodness and forbearance and longsuffering, which leads us to repentance, and says God set forth Christ to declare His righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God. The word is God waiting before He judges.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forbearance is the space God gives me to repent, the judgment He holds back so that I can turn. His goodness is not His blindness, and I hold that every day of His patience is a day meant for turning back to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3539; unintelligent; by implication, sensual:--fool(-ish), unwise.
BiblicalUsage: Paul calls the Galatians foolish for turning back to the law after beginning in the Spirit, and Jesus calls the two on the road fools and slow of heart to believe. The word names a mind that will not understand, not because it cannot but because it will not.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for foolishness carries no doctrine of its own; its sting is Paul's and Jesus', that the failure to understand is often a refusal, not an inability.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: luxurious
BiblicalUsage: The word describes delicate luxury, the tender and delicate woman of Deuteronomy who would not set the sole of her foot on the ground for delicateness, and the tender, delicate daughter of Babylon whom Isaiah mocks. It is soft living carried to excess.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for soft luxury carries no theology of its own; its warning is the prophets', that a people grown tender with ease will not endure the day of trouble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G507 and G1093; above the ground, i.e. (properly) the second floor of a building; used for a dome or a balcony on the upper story:--upper room.
BiblicalUsage: The upper room is where Jesus eats the Passover with His disciples, and where the disciples wait after His ascension. Mark and Luke both call it the large upper room, furnished and prepared, the room above the ground floor where the last supper was kept.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for an upper room carries no doctrine of its own; its memory is the supper, that the Lord chose an upstairs room for His last meal with His friends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G3563; stupidity; by implication, rage:--folly, madness.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the folly of Jannes and Jambres shall be manifest to all, and Luke says the Pharisees were filled with madness when Jesus healed on the Sabbath. The word is senselessness turned to rage, a mind that has lost its way and lashes out.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for senseless rage holds no doctrine of its own; its picture is the Pharisees', that opposition to Jesus ends in fury without reason.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and οἴγω (to open); to open up (literally or figuratively, in various applications):--open.
BiblicalUsage: To open: eyes, doors, mouths, heavens, and the book of life. Jesus says ask and it shall be opened unto you, the blind man's eyes are opened, the angel opens the prison doors, and the Lord opens a door in heaven before John. The word runs from the smallest opening to the greatest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe opening is God's work from first to last: He opens eyes that cannot see, doors that cannot be forced, and a heart that cannot open itself. I knock because He promised the door would open, and I hold that the open door in Revelation is the same promise, that no man can shut what Christ opens.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Man Born Blind; The Apostles Before the Council
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G3618; to rebuild:--build again.
BiblicalUsage: Amos quotes the promise to rebuild the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and James takes up the same words at the council in Jerusalem. The word is the rebuilding of what has fallen down, stone set back on stone.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for rebuilding carries no doctrine of its own; its promise is Amos's, that God will raise up again what has fallen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G455; opening (throat):--X open.
BiblicalUsage: Paul asks for the opening of his mouth, that utterance may be given him to make known the mystery of the gospel. The word is the opening itself, here the opening of the lips to speak boldly.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an opening mouth carries no doctrine of its own; its plea is Paul's, that he might speak the gospel boldly as he ought.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: I
BiblicalUsage: I is the longer form of the Hebrew pronoun, the word Moses, David, and the prophets use when they speak of themselves before God. I am the LORD thy God, I am a worm and no man, I will sing unto the LORD: the word is only a pronoun, but the sentences built on it hold the whole of prayer and promise.
TheologicalSignificance: The longer I carries no doctrine by itself; its weight is in the mouths that use it, from God's I am the LORD to the psalmist's I am a worm.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G459; illegality, i.e. violation of law or (genitive case) wickedness:--iniquity, X transgress(-ion of) the law, unrighteousness.
BiblicalUsage: Lawlessness is sin's own name: John says sin is the transgression of the law, Jesus will tell the workers of iniquity to depart from Him, and Paul says the mystery of iniquity already works in the world. The word names life lived as if God's law did not exist.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lawlessness is not freedom but rebellion with the label torn off: a life that answers to no law but its own. John names it plainly, sin is the transgression of the law, and I hold that the cure is not a lighter law but a new heart that loves the law it once broke.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G459; lawlessly, i.e. (specially) not amenable to (the Jewish) law:--without law.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says those who have sinned without law shall perish without law, while those under the law shall be judged by the law. The adverb names the state of being outside the law, Gentiles judged apart from Moses' law.
TheologicalSignificance: One adverb about sinning without law carries no system of its own; its point is Paul's, that no one escapes judgment by never having heard the law.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3551; lawless, i.e. (negatively) not subject to (the Jewish) law; (by implication, a Gentile), or (positively) wicked:--without law, lawless, transgressor, unlawful, wicked.
BiblicalUsage: The lawless are those who live outside God's law, whether men who never had it or the man of sin who defies it. Paul lists the lawless among those the law was made for, and the man of sin is revealed as the lawless one.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the lawless carries no doctrine of its own; its warning is the apostles', that the law was written for those who live as if it did not exist.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and the base of G5624; useless or (neuter) inutility:--unprofitable(-ness).
BiblicalUsage: The law is set aside for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof, Hebrews says, and Paul calls Jewish fables and endless genealogies unprofitable and vain. The word names what serves no purpose, a thing that cannot do the job it was made for.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for what is useless carries no teaching of its own; its point is Hebrews', that the old law could not perfect, and endless arguments about it profit no one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and a derivative of the base of G3717; to straighten up:--lift (set) up, make straight.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus lifts up the woman bowed together for eighteen years, and the writer of Hebrews tells his readers to lift up the hands which hang down. The word is the straightening of what was bent.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for straightening what was bent carries no doctrine of its own; its beauty is the bent woman's, that Jesus sets straight what eighteen years had bowed.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Woman Bent Double
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3741; wicked:--unholy.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists the unholy among those for whom the law is made, and warns that in the last days men will be unholy, without natural affection, trucebreakers. The word names the man with no reverence left in him.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the unholy carries no teaching of its own; its darkness is Paul's, that a heart without reverence ends among the marks of the last days.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G511; superior, i.e. (locally) more remote:--upper.
BiblicalUsage: Paul comes into the upper coasts on his way to Ephesus, travelling the inland road rather than the coast. The word means the higher, more remote country, the uplands away from the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the upper country carries no doctrine of its own; its interest is the journey, that Paul reached Ephesus by the inland road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: comparative degree of G507; upper, i.e. (neuter as adverb) to a more conspicuous place, in a former part of the book:--above, higher.
BiblicalUsage: Hebrews quotes the psalm, sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, and the writer says God speaks of a higher place, a more conspicuous one. The word means upper, set above, given the better seat.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for the upper place carries no teaching of its own; its use is Hebrews', that the old sacrifices were set aside for something higher.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G507; from above; by analogy, from the first; by implication, anew:--from above, again, from the beginning (very first), the top.
BiblicalUsage: From above, from the first, anew. Jesus tells Nicodemus a man must be born from above, James says every good gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights, and John says Jesus was born from above and speaks of heavenly things. The word joins the new birth to heaven itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being born from above is the only beginning that counts: no man climbs into God's kingdom, he is born into it from above. James says the good gifts come down from the same place, and I hold that my life, my birth, and my hope all come from above, not from below.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Nicodemus; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G75; to struggle against (figuratively) ("antagonize"):--strive against.
BiblicalUsage: Hebrews says believers have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin. The word is the struggle itself, a fight carried on against an enemy that will not yield.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for striving against sin carries no doctrine of its own; its challenge is Hebrews', that the fight against sin is a real struggle, not a shrug.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: thou
BiblicalUsage: Thou is the Aramaic word for you, the address Daniel uses to the king: thou, O king, sawest a great image, and thou art the head of gold. It is the plain second person, the word a prophet uses to a king.
TheologicalSignificance: A pronoun in Aramaic holds no doctrine; its interest is the scene, a captive prophet telling a king what he dreamed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G473 and G236; an equivalent or ransom:--in exchange.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus asks what a man shall give in exchange for his soul, and what shall be given for the world if a man gains it and loses himself. The word is the price paid in return, the thing offered to buy back what was lost.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for an exchange price carries no doctrine of its own; its question is Jesus', that no price can buy back a lost soul.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G378; to supplement:--fill up.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he fills up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in his flesh for the church's sake. The word means to fill up what is lacking, to complete the measure.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for filling up what remains carries no system of its own; its mystery is Paul's, that his sufferings somehow complete what is lacking for the church.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G591; to requite (good or evil):--recompense, render, repay.
BiblicalUsage: To repay, to recompense, to give back what is owed, good or evil. God will repay tribulation to those who trouble His people, no man can first give to God and be repaid, vengeance belongs to the Lord, and the good who cannot repay you now will be repaid at the resurrection of the just. The word covers both sides of the same coin: God's repayment to the wicked and His reward to the faithful.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the accounts, and that is both my warning and my comfort: vengeance is His, not mine, and the kindness no one repaid will be repaid at the resurrection. I hold that no good deed is ever lost and no wrong ever forgotten, because the Lord repays, in His time and in His way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G467; a requital (properly, the thing):--recompense.
BiblicalUsage: To repay, to recompense, to give back what is owed, good or evil. God will repay tribulation to those who trouble His people, no man can first give to God and be repaid, vengeance belongs to the Lord, and the good who cannot repay you now will be repaid at the resurrection of the just. The word covers both sides of the same coin: God's repayment to the wicked and His reward to the faithful.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the accounts, and that is both my warning and my comfort: vengeance is His, not mine, and the kindness no one repaid will be repaid at the resurrection. I hold that no good deed is ever lost and no wrong ever forgotten, because the Lord repays, in His time and in His way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G467; requital (properly, the act):--reward.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the reward of the inheritance is what believers receive from the Lord, the recompense for serving Christ. The word names the repayment itself, the act of giving back.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a reward holds no doctrine of its own; its comfort is Paul's, that serving Christ carries an inheritance as its recompense.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G611; to contradict or dispute:--answer again, reply against.
BiblicalUsage: The Pharisees cannot answer Jesus again, and Paul asks who has replied against God, as the clay against the potter. The word is an answer back, a contradiction offered in return.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for answering back carries no doctrine of its own; its rebuke is Paul's, that the clay has no standing to argue with the potter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and the middle voice of G2192; to hold oneself opposite to, i.e. (by implication) adhere to; by extension to care for:--hold fast, hold to, support.
BiblicalUsage: To hold fast to the faithful word, to cleave to a master and despise the other. Jesus says no man can serve two masters, for he will hold to the one and despise the other, and Paul tells Titus to hold fast the faithful word so he can exhort and convince the gainsayers. The word is a grip that will not let go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe holding fast is the whole of faithfulness in one grip: you cannot serve two masters, so you hold to one and let the other go. Paul's charge to Titus is my charge too, to hold the faithful word tight enough to teach it and defend it. I hold that the hand that grips Christ will not be shaken loose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G2036; to refute or deny:--gainsay, say against.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus promises His disciples a mouth and wisdom which all their adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist. The word means to speak against, to deny or refute, and here the promise is that no adversary will be able to do it.
TheologicalSignificance: One promise about gainsaying carries no doctrine of its own; its comfort is Jesus', that the wisdom He gives cannot be answered by its enemies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G2476; to stand against, i.e. oppose:--resist, withstand.
BiblicalUsage: To stand against, to resist, to withstand. Jesus says resist not evil but turn the other cheek, James says resist the devil and he will flee, and Paul says to put on the armour of God so you may withstand in the evil day. The same word names the refusal to fight back and the refusal to give ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe standing against the devil and refusing to strike back at a man are the same courage worn two ways. James promises the devil will flee from the one who resists, and I hold that promise when I stand my ground: the enemy runs from a heart that will not yield, and the cheek turned is not defeat but victory.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; James, Brother of Jesus; Paul; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and the middle voice of G3670; to confess in turn, i.e. respond in praise:--give thanks.
BiblicalUsage: Anna the prophetess gives thanks to the Lord over the child Jesus, answering the praise of Simeon with her own. The word means to answer in praise, to confess in turn, as one voice answers another.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for answering praise carries no doctrine of its own; its beauty is Anna's, that an old woman's thanks answered Simeon's song over the child.
RelatedEvents: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word; a blossom:--flower.
BiblicalUsage: Peter and James both say the flower of the grass falls and withers, and the glory of man is as the flower of the field. The word is the blossom itself, brief and bright and gone.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a flower holds no doctrine of its own; its lesson is the apostles', that the glory of man fades like grass, and only the word of the Lord endures.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Antothite or inhabitant of Anathoth
BiblicalUsage: The Antothite is a man of Anathoth, and the name belongs chiefly to Abiezer, one of David's thirty mighty men, who led the ninth monthly course of the army. The chronicler names him among the Benjamites who came to David, and the army lists keep his name across the books.
TheologicalSignificance: A man known by his town, Anathoth, stands among David's mighty men, and I take that as God's way: He raises warriors from small towns and remembers them by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anthothijah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Anthothijah is named once, as a son of Jeroham in the genealogy of Benjamin. The chronicler gives him a place in the family list and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: One mention in a genealogy is still a place in the record, and I take comfort in that: God counts the men whose stories are only a line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G440; a bed of burning coals:--fire of coals.
BiblicalUsage: A fire of coals is where the disciples warm themselves on the night of Jesus' arrest, and where the risen Jesus cooks fish for them on the shore. The word is the bed of burning coals itself, the small fire that gives warmth and cooks a meal.
TheologicalSignificance: A coal fire carries no doctrine of its own; its poignancy is the contrast, that Peter warms himself at one fire while denying Jesus, and is fed beside another after the resurrection.
RelatedEvents: The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane; Jesus Appears to Seven Disciples by the Sea of Galilee
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a live coal:--coal of fire.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the Romans to heap coals of fire on the head of an enemy by feeding him when he is hungry. The word is the live coal itself, the burning ember that the proverb turns into a picture of kindness.
TheologicalSignificance: One live coal in one proverb holds no doctrine of its own; its picture is Paul's, that kindness to an enemy burns hotter than revenge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G444 and G700; man-courting, i.e. fawning:--men-pleaser.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns servants to serve with singleness of heart, not with eyeservice as menpleasers, but as the servants of Christ. The word names the man who works only to be seen, courting the favour of men rather than God.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for menpleasers carries no teaching of its own; its warning is Paul's, that work done only for watching eyes is not service to Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G444; human:--human, common to man, man(-kind), (man-)kind, men's, after the manner of men.
BiblicalUsage: Paul speaks of human wisdom, the common lot of mankind, and the human way of speaking about spiritual things. The word marks what belongs to men as men: ordinary, shared, after the manner of men.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for what is merely human carries no doctrine of its own; its use is Paul's, that the gospel is not spoken in man's wisdom but in the Spirit's power.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G444 and κτείνω (to kill); a manslayer:--murderer. Compare G5406.
BiblicalUsage: John says no murderer has eternal life abiding in him, and that the devil was a murderer from the beginning. The word is the plain name for a man-killer, and John ties it to hatred: whoever hates his brother is a murderer.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a murderer holds no doctrine of its own; its terror is John's, that hatred is murder in the heart before it is murder with the hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G435 and ὤψ (the countenance; from G3700); man-faced, i.e. a human being:--certain, man.
BiblicalUsage: Man, the human being, man-faced, made in God's image and fallen from it. The first man Adam brought sin into the world, the second man Christ brings life, and every man will give account for the deeds done in the body. The word runs the whole length of the Bible, from the man formed of the dust to the man who will judge the world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe man is the Bible's great subject because God made him for Himself: dust that God breathed into, a sinner Christ died for, and a creature who will stand before his Maker. Adam's fall and Christ's life are both told in this one word, and I hold that no man is beyond the reach of the second Adam.
RelatedEvents: The Temptation in the Wilderness; The Fall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G446; to act as proconsul:--be the deputy.
BiblicalUsage: Gallio is called the deputy of Achaia when the Jews bring Paul before his judgment seat, and he refuses to judge a matter of words and names. The word is the office itself, to act as proconsul, the Roman governor's seat in Corinth.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a deputy carries no doctrine of its own; its interest is the scene, that Gallio's refusal to judge Paul left the gospel free in Corinth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and a superlative of G5228; instead of the highest officer, i.e. (specially) a Roman proconsul:--deputy.
BiblicalUsage: The proconsul is the Roman governor of a province, and Luke names two: Sergius Paulus in Cyprus, who believes, and Gallio in Corinth, who refuses to judge Paul. The word is the office of the highest Roman authority in the province.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a Roman governor carries no teaching of its own; its interest is the story, that the gospel reached the highest seats of Rome and found both belief and indifference there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle; opposite, i.e. instead or because of (rarely in addition to):--for, in the room of. Often used in composition to denote contrast, requital, substitution, correspondence, etc.
BiblicalUsage: Anti is the small word that does heavy work: instead of, because of, in place of, as when Christ gave Himself a ransom for many and a man is told to render evil for evil to no man. The word marks exchange, one thing standing in the room of another.
TheologicalSignificance: A particle carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is in the exchange it names, that Christ stood in our place and gave His life a ransom for many.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G906; to bandy:--have.
BiblicalUsage: Luke says the two on the road to Emmaus talked together of all these things which had happened, communing as they walked. The word means to bandy words back and forth, to talk a matter over between friends.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for talking over carries no doctrine of its own; its tenderness is the road to Emmaus, that two sad friends talked their grief out until Jesus joined them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G5547; an opponent of the Messiah:--antichrist.
BiblicalUsage: Antichrist is the opponent of the Messiah, and John is the only writer who names him. He writes that many antichrists have already come, that the spirit of antichrist denies that Jesus is the Christ, and that the one who denies the Father and the Son is the antichrist.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe John wrote about antichrist so that we would not be fooled: the test is not signs or wonders but the confession of Jesus Christ come in the flesh. Many antichrists have already come, and I hold that the spirit that denies the Son is the same spirit in every age, and it is to be resisted, not debated.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G1303; to set oneself opposite, i.e. be disputatious:--that oppose themselves.
BiblicalUsage: In his charge to Timothy, Paul says the servant of the Lord must be gentle, able to teach those who oppose themselves, if God will give them repentance. The word names the disputatious, the ones set against the truth.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for the disputatious carries no doctrine of its own; its hope is Paul's, that even those who oppose themselves may yet be given repentance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G1349; an opponent (in a lawsuit); specially, Satan (as the arch-enemy):--adversary.
BiblicalUsage: The adversary is the opponent in a lawsuit, and Peter says the devil walks about as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour. Jesus tells His people to agree with their adversary quickly while on the way, and the widow cries to the judge to avenge her of her adversary.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the adversary is real, and Peter's picture of him as a lion is the one I keep: he walks about, he seeks, and he devours the unwary. Jesus' counsel is practical, settle quickly, and I hold that the only safe answer to the adversary is a sober mind and a steadfast faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G2564; to invite in return:--bid again.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus tells His disciples to invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind to their feasts, for they cannot bid you again, and you shall be recompensed at the resurrection of the just. The word is the return invitation, the favour paid back in kind.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a return invitation carries no teaching of its own; its lesson is Jesus', that the feast that cannot be repaid is the one God repays.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G2525; to set down (troops) against, i.e. withstand:--resist.
BiblicalUsage: The writer of Hebrews tells his readers they have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin. The word is the resistance that holds its ground, setting oneself down against an enemy and not moving.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for withstanding carries no doctrine of its own; its challenge is Hebrews', that the fight against sin has not yet cost us blood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G2749; to lie opposite, i.e. be adverse (figuratively, repugnant) to:--adversary, be contrary, oppose.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says there is a great door opened to him and many adversaries, and the Thessalonians hear of the man of sin who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God. The word names the one who lies across the path, set against the work.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for adversaries carries no teaching of its own; its realism is Paul's, that an open door and many adversaries come together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prolonged from G473; opposite:--over against.
BiblicalUsage: Paul sails past Chios and comes the next day over against Samos, the ship holding its course on the far side. The word means directly opposite, facing across the water.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for over against carries no doctrine of its own; its interest is the voyage, that Paul's ship passed Samos on the far side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and the middle voice of G2983; to take hold of in turn, i.e. succor; also to participate:--help, partaker, support.
BiblicalUsage: To take hold of in turn, to succour, to help. Paul tells the strong to support the weak, remembering the Lord's words that it is more blessed to give than to receive, and the Lord takes hold of Israel His servant in remembrance of His mercy. The word is a hand laid on the shoulder of the weak.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for taking hold to help carries no teaching of its own; its beauty is the Lord's, that He took hold of Israel His servant and remembered His mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G3004; to dispute, refuse:--answer again, contradict, deny, gainsay(-er), speak against.
BiblicalUsage: To dispute, to speak against, to deny. The Jews contradict Paul's preaching at Antioch, and Simeon tells Mary the child is set for the fall and rising again of many and for a sign which shall be spoken against. The word is opposition spoken aloud.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for speaking against carries no doctrine of its own; its pattern is the gospel's, that the sign of Christ is spoken against wherever He is preached.
RelatedEvents: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G482; relief:--help.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists helps among the gifts God has set in the church, alongside apostles, prophets, teachers, and miracles. The word is the gift of relief, the helping hand that carries what others cannot.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for helps carries no doctrine of its own; its honour is Paul's, that the gift of helping stands in the church beside apostles and prophets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G483; dispute, disobedience:--contradiction, gainsaying, strife.
BiblicalUsage: Contradiction, gainsaying, dispute: Hebrews says no contradiction is greater than the contradiction of sinners against Christ, and the men of Jude's day perished in the gainsaying of Core. The word names the argument that will not yield.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for contradiction holds no doctrine of its own; its warning is Hebrews', that Christ endured the contradiction of sinners, and we are not to grow weary.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G3058; to rail in reply:--revile again.
BiblicalUsage: Peter says Christ, when He was reviled, reviled not again, and when He suffered, He threatened not, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously. The word is the answering rail, the insult thrown back, and Christ refused it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for reviling again carries no teaching of its own; its power is Christ's, that when He was reviled He reviled not again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G3083; a redemption-price:--ransom.
