BiblicalUsage: Paul calls Christ Jesus the one mediator who gave Himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time. The word is the redemption price itself, the payment made in place of the captive.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for a ransom price carries no system of its own; its weight is Paul's, that Christ gave Himself as the price for all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G3354; to mete in return:--measure again.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says with what measure you mete it shall be measured to you again, and the same measure you give will be given back to you. The word is the measuring returned in kind, the measure meted back.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for measuring again carries no teaching of its own; its warning is Jesus', that the measure we give is the measure we will receive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G473 and G3408; requital, correspondence:--recompense.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the men who left the natural use of the woman received in themselves the recompense of their error which was meet, and the Corinthians are asked to give him the same requital, to be enlarged in return for his open heart. The word is the return made in kind, the fitting answer to what was done.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a fitting return carries no doctrine of its own; its gravity is Paul's, that error is repaid in the error itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Ἀντίοχυς (a Syrian king); Antiochia, a place in Syria:--Antioch.
BiblicalUsage: Antioch is the great city of Syria where the disciples were first called Christians, where Barnabas brought Saul, and where Paul and Barnabas were sent out by the church. The same name belongs to the city in Pisidia where Paul preached on his first journey, and Antioch is where the gospel first became a church that sent missionaries.
TheologicalSignificance: Antioch shows me what a church is for: it is not only a place to be fed but a place that sends. The disciples were first called Christians there, and I believe that name is still earned the same way, by a people so joined to Christ that the city has to call them something new.
RelatedEvents: The Church at Antioch; Barnabas and Saul Sent Out from Antioch
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G490; an Antiochian or inhabitant of Antiochia:--of Antioch.
BiblicalUsage: Antioch is the great city of Syria where the disciples were first called Christians, where Barnabas brought Saul, and where Paul and Barnabas were sent out by the church. The same name belongs to the city in Pisidia where Paul preached on his first journey, and Antioch is where the gospel first became a church that sent missionaries.
TheologicalSignificance: Antioch shows me what a church is for: it is not only a place to be fed but a place that sends. The disciples were first called Christians there, and I believe that name is still earned the same way, by a people so joined to Christ that the city has to call them something new.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G3928; to go along opposite:--pass by on the other side.
BiblicalUsage: The priest and the Levite pass by on the other side of the wounded man on the road to Jericho, and the Samaritan stops. The word is the walk that keeps its distance, going along the far side of the road.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for passing by on the other side carries no doctrine of its own; its shame is the parable's, that the priest and the Levite saw the wounded man and kept to the far side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contracted for a compound of G473 and a derivative of G3962; Antipas, a Christian:--Antipas.
BiblicalUsage: Antipas is named once, in the letter to Pergamos, as the Lord's faithful martyr who was slain among them where Satan dwells. The risen Christ remembers him by name, and that is all the Bible tells of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A martyr known from a single verse still shows me the whole of faithfulness: he held the Lord's name where Satan dwelt, and he died for it. I believe Christ remembers His faithful by name, and Antipas is proof of it.
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Pergamum
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G493; Antipatris, a place in Palestine:--Antipatris.
BiblicalUsage: Antipatris is the town to which the soldiers bring Paul by night on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea, the halfway point of his escape from the plot against his life. Luke names it once, as the place where the escort stops and the horsemen carry Paul on alone.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once, on a night march to save Paul's life, reminds me that God guards His servants by ordinary roads and ordinary towns, and no step of the journey is wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G4008; on the opposite side:--over against.
BiblicalUsage: Paul's ship sails over against Chios on its way to Jerusalem, holding its course on the far side of the island. The word means on the opposite side, across the water from where you stand.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the opposite shore carries no doctrine of its own; its interest is the voyage, that the ship made for the country on the far side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G4098 (including its alternate); to oppose:--resist.
BiblicalUsage: Stephen charges the council that they always resist the Holy Ghost, as their fathers did. The word is the plain act of opposing, setting oneself against what God is doing.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for resisting the Spirit carries no teaching of its own; its charge is Stephen's, that a people can resist God as their fathers did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and G4754; (figuratively) to attack, i.e. (by implication) destroy:--war against.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he sees another law in his members, warring against the law of his mind and bringing him into captivity to the law of sin. The word is the war itself, the inner battle between the two laws.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an inner war carries no doctrine of its own; its honesty is Paul's, that the law of sin still fights the law of the mind in every believer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G473 and the middle voice of G5021; to range oneself against, i.e. oppose:--oppose themselves, resist.
BiblicalUsage: To range oneself against, to oppose, to resist. Peter says God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble, and James says the same. The word is the stance of opposition, and Scripture turns it both ways: God resists the proud, and the proud resist God.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for opposing carries no doctrine of its own; its warning is the apostles', that God Himself resists the proud, and the humble are the ones He lifts.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; James, Brother of Jesus; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G473 and G5087; opposition, i.e. a conflict (of theories):--opposition.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns Timothy to avoid profane and vain babblings and oppositions of science falsely so called, the arguments that set themselves against the faith. The word names the conflict of theories, the rival teaching that claims to know better.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for oppositions carries no teaching of its own; its warning is Paul's, that clever arguments dressed as knowledge can shipwreck the faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a compound of G473 and G5179; corresponding ("antitype"), i.e. a representative, counterpart:--(like) figure (whereunto).
BiblicalUsage: The antitype is the figure that answers to the type, the reality that matches the shadow. Peter says baptism is the antitype of Noah's ark, the water that saved eight souls, and Hebrews says the earthly tabernacle is the figure of the true, into which Christ entered. The word joins the shadow to the substance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the types were never meant to stand alone: the ark pointed to baptism, and the tabernacle pointed to heaven itself. The shadow is real because the substance is real, and I hold that every figure in the old covenant finds its answer in Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G501; a baling-vessel:--thing to draw with.
BiblicalUsage: The Samaritan woman leaves her waterpot and asks for the living water, that she may not have to come and draw. The word is the vessel for drawing, the bucket let down into the well.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a drawing vessel carries no doctrine of its own; its thirst is the woman's, that she might never have to draw again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄντλος (the hold of a ship); to bale up (properly, bilge water), i.e. dip water (with a bucket, pitcher, etc.):--draw (out).
BiblicalUsage: To draw water from a well. The servants draw the water made wine at Cana, and Jesus asks the Samaritan woman to give Him to drink from Jacob's well. The word is the plain work of lifting water from a well.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for drawing water holds no doctrine of its own; its wonder is the well, that the water Jesus gives becomes a well springing up to everlasting life.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana; Jesus and the Samaritan Woman
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G473 and G3788; to face:--bear up into.
BiblicalUsage: Paul's ship is caught in the storm and cannot bear up into the wind, so the sailors give way and let her drive. The word means to face into the wind, to hold the ship's head against the gale, and here the wind is too strong for it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for facing into the wind carries no doctrine of its own; its drama is the storm, that the ship could not bear up and had to let herself drive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ye
BiblicalUsage: Ye is the Aramaic word for you, the address of the Chaldeans to the king: ye have said the thing is gone from me, and Daniel answers that the king's word is sure. It is the plain plural you, the word of men speaking to a king.
TheologicalSignificance: A pronoun in Daniel's Aramaic carries no teaching; its weight is the scene, the Chaldeans answering the king who demands his dream.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: we
BiblicalUsage: We is the Hebrew word for us, the voice of the remnant answering Jeremiah: we will obey the voice of the LORD our God, whether it be good or whether it be evil. The word is the people's own answer, spoken together.
TheologicalSignificance: A pronoun carries no doctrine of its own; its poignancy is the remnant's, that they promised to obey and then did the opposite.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anub, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Anub is named once, as a son of Coz in the genealogy of Judah. The chronicler gives him a place in the family list and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A single line in Judah's genealogy is still a place in God's book, and that comforts me: no name is too small for Him to keep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mildness (royal); also (concretely) oppressed
BiblicalUsage: The word is the gentleness of the king's majesty, the mildness that belongs to a royal bow: the psalmist says God's gentleness has made him great, and the king's majesty rides prosperously in meekness and truth. It is strength worn gently, the king's hand made soft toward his people.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for royal gentleness holds little theology of its own, but it shows me the kind of king God is: His gentleness is what makes His people great, and I would rather be ruled by a gentle king than a hard one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5204; waterless, i.e. dry:--dry, without water.
BiblicalUsage: Peter calls false teachers wells without water and clouds carried by a tempest, and Jude calls them clouds without water, carried about of winds. The word is the dry place, the well with no water in it and the land with no rain.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for waterless places carries no doctrine of its own; its picture is the apostles', that false teachers promise water and have none to give.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G5271; undissembled, i.e. sincere:--without dissimulation (hypocrisy), unfeigned.
BiblicalUsage: Unfeigned, without hypocrisy, sincere and undisguised. Paul speaks of unfeigned love and unfeigned faith, Peter of unfeigned love of the brethren, and James of the wisdom from above that is without partiality and without hypocrisy. The word names the love and faith that are what they seem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe unfeigned love is the mark of real faith: love without hypocrisy, faith without acting, wisdom without partiality. Paul puts it at the head of his list of the marks of the ministry, and I hold that sincerity is not a nicety but the test of whether the faith is real.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; Timothy; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G5293; unsubdued, i.e. insubordinate (in fact or temper):--disobedient, that is not put under, unruly.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists the unruly among those for whom the law is made, and warns that elders' children must not be accused of riot or unruly. The word names the man who will not be ruled, the one who refuses every yoke.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the unruly carries no doctrine of its own; its place in Paul's lists says enough, that refusing to be ruled is one of the plain marks of a lawless heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3707; invisible:--invisible (thing).
BiblicalUsage: The invisible things of God, the unseen God, the King eternal, immortal, invisible. Paul says the invisible things of God are clearly seen by the things that are made, the Son is the image of the invisible God, and Moses endured as seeing Him who is invisible. The word names what the eye cannot see and faith must take hold of.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the invisible is more real than the visible: the God no eye has seen made the world every eye sees, and Moses endured by seeing Him who is invisible. I hold that faith is not believing in nothing but seeing what is truly there, and the invisible God is the most solid thing I know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G71; to take off (in various senses):--bring, carry away, lead (away), put to death, take away.
BiblicalUsage: To lead away, to carry off, to bring before a judge. The soldiers lead Jesus away to the high priest, and the mob leads Him to Pilate. The word is the taking of a man where he does not choose to go.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for leading away carries no doctrine of its own; its sorrow is the passion's, that Jesus was led from one judgment seat to another for us.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Before the Sanhedrin; Jesus Before Pilate
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3811; uninstructed, i.e. (figuratively) stupid:--unlearned.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns Timothy to avoid foolish and unlearned questions, knowing they do gender strifes. The word names the question no one has taught the asker to ask, the argument that has nothing to teach.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unlearned questions carries no teaching of its own; its wisdom is Paul's, that some arguments are only good for breeding strife.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G142; to lift off, i.e. remove:--take (away).
BiblicalUsage: When the bridegroom is taken away, then shall the disciples fast, Jesus says, and the bridegroom's friends cannot mourn while He is with them. The word is the lifting off, the taking away of the one whose presence made the feast.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for taking away carries no doctrine of its own; its sorrow is the disciples', that the Bridegroom would one day be taken from them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G154; to demand back:--ask again, require.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus tells His disciples to give to every man that asks, and says the rich man's soul shall be required of him that night. The word is the demanding back, the claim laid on what was given.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for demanding back carries no teaching of its own; its warning is the rich fool's, that the soul lent to us will one day be required.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and ἀλγέω (to smart); to grieve out, i.e. become apathetic:--be past feeling.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the Gentiles, being past feeling, have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness. The word names the heart that has grieved itself out, grown numb to what once stung.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for being past feeling carries no doctrine of its own; its terror is Paul's, that a heart can grow so used to sin it no longer feels it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G236; to change away, i.e. release, (reflexively) remove:--deliver, depart.
BiblicalUsage: To deliver, to depart, to be released. The evil spirits depart from those touched by Paul's handkerchiefs, and Christ came to deliver those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. The word is the release itself, the going free.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for deliverance carries no teaching of its own; its hope is Hebrews', that Christ came to free those who lived their whole lives in fear of death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and a derivative of G245; to estrange away, i.e. (passively and figuratively) to be non-participant:-- alienate, be alien.
BiblicalUsage: To estrange, to alienate, to make a stranger of. Paul says the Gentiles were aliens from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God, and that the understanding is darkened and men are alienated from the life of God through ignorance. The word names the distance sin puts between man and God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe alienation is the truest name for what sin did: it made strangers of us, far from the covenants and without hope in the world. Paul says we were alienated from the life of God, and I hold that the gospel is the end of that estrangement, Christ bringing near those who were far off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; soft:--tender.
BiblicalUsage: The fig tree puts forth tender leaves, and then you know summer is near. The word is the soft, tender leaf of spring, the sign that the season has turned.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a tender leaf carries no doctrine of its own; its sign is Jesus', that when the branch is tender you know summer is nigh.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and ἄγχω (to choke; akin to the base of G43); to strangle oneself off (i.e. to death):--hang himself.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for Judas hanging himself after he betrayed Jesus. It appears only once, and the Bible does not soften what it describes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this single, terrible verse shows where guilt without repentance ends, and why turning back to God matters more than anything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G32; to announce:--bring word (again), declare, report, shew (again), tell.
BiblicalUsage: This is the ordinary word for bringing news back to someone — the apostles reporting to their own people after their release, Peter telling the household what the angel had done, the women returning from the empty tomb to tell the eleven, and John passing on what he had seen and heard. The word covers good news and hard news alike, and it always carries a report from someone who was there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel travels the same way it always has: one person telling another what they saw and heard. John says he writes so that others may share the fellowship he found, and I hold that no report in Scripture matters more than the one that says Christ is risen and seen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and a derivative of G473; to meet away, i.e. encounter:--meet.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to meet someone coming the other way — the ten lepers meeting Jesus as he entered the village, and the man carrying water meeting the two disciples in the city. It is an encounter, not an accident.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe these meetings remind me that Jesus is found on the road, in the middle of ordinary errands and desperate cries alike.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G528; a (friendly) encounter:--meet.
BiblicalUsage: A meeting, and a joyful one — the cry at midnight that sends the virgins out to meet the bridegroom, the believers from Rome coming as far as Appii Forum to meet Paul, and the promise that we will meet the Lord in the air. In each case someone goes out to welcome the one who is coming.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word turns waiting into welcome. We are not bracing for a stranger; we are going out to meet the Lord we already know, and I believe that meeting is the hope that steadies every hard day now.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3845; not passing away, i.e. untransferable (perpetual):-- unchangeable.
BiblicalUsage: This word describes a priesthood that cannot be passed on to anyone else, because Jesus lives forever. No successor is needed, and none will ever take his place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is why my hope is safe: the priest who stands for me never dies and never retires.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3903; unready:--unprepared.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this word for being caught unprepared — the embarrassment of boasting about the Corinthians' readiness and then finding the gift not ready when the brothers from Macedonia arrive. It is the one place the word appears, and it is all about readiness.
TheologicalSignificance: I take this as a plain warning: promises about giving should be ready before they are made.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and G756; a beginning of sacrifice, i.e. the (Jewish) first-fruit (figuratively):--first-fruits.
BiblicalUsage: The firstfruits are the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a promise of the rest to come. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, and calls believers the firstfruits of God's creatures; Romans speaks of the firstfruits of the Spirit in us now, and Revelation sees the redeemed as firstfruits to God and the Lamb.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the firstfruits tell me the harvest is certain. Christ rose first, so those who belong to him will follow, and the Spirit already living in us is God's down payment on the day the whole harvest comes in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G720; to deny utterly, i.e. disown, abstain:--deny.
BiblicalUsage: To deny utterly — Peter swearing he never knew Jesus, and the Lord turning to look at him while the cock crowed a second time. The same word is the one Jesus uses for the disciple's daily calling: deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow me.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Peter's failure and Jesus' command belong together. Denying myself is the way I stop denying him, and the look Jesus gave Peter tells me that even after the worst denial, his face is still turned toward me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G737; from now, i.e. henceforth (already):--from henceforth.
BiblicalUsage: From now on — Jesus telling the council that from this moment they will see the Son of man seated at God's right hand, and the voice from heaven calling the dead who die in the Lord blessed from henceforth. The phrase marks a turning point, and what follows is different from what came before.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this little phrase carries real weight: once Christ has spoken, the future is already decided.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G534; completion:--finishing.
BiblicalUsage: The finishing of a tower — Jesus' picture of the man who sits down first and counts the cost, so he does not lay the foundation and then run out of money before the tower is done. The word is about completing what was begun.
TheologicalSignificance: I take this as Jesus' plain demand: following him is a whole-life decision, and it should be counted before it is started.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; to cheat, i.e. delude:--deceive.
BiblicalUsage: To cheat or delude — Eve was deceived, Paul says, and Adam was not; empty words deceive the sons of disobedience; and a man who thinks himself religious while his tongue runs loose deceives his own heart. Deception always works the same way: it promises something and delivers nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe deception is the oldest trick in the book, and it still starts with a lie about God's word. The guard against it is simple and hard: listen to what God actually said, and let it judge my heart before my heart judges it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G538; delusion:--deceit(-ful, -fulness), deceivableness(-ving).
BiblicalUsage: Deceit — the thorns in the parable of the sower, choking the word with the deceitfulness of riches; the old man corrupted by deceitful lusts; and sin itself, which hardens hearts by deceiving them day after day. The word never describes an honest mistake; it describes a lure.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that deceit is dangerous precisely because it feels good while it works. Riches promise security, lust promises life, and sin promises freedom, and I believe only the daily honesty of God's word keeps me from believing any of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3962; fatherless, i.e. of unrecorded paternity:--without father.
BiblicalUsage: Without father — Melchizedek appears in the record with no father or mother named, no genealogy, no beginning or end of days given. The silence is the point: he stands as a picture of a priesthood that does not depend on descent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this deliberate silence points straight to Christ, whose priesthood rests on his own endless life rather than on any family line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and G826; an off-flash, i.e. effulgence:--brightness.
BiblicalUsage: The brightness of God's glory — Christ is the radiance shining out from the Father, the exact imprint of his nature, upholding all things by his word of power. The word is a flash of light thrown off from its source, and it never leaves the source behind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one picture settles who Jesus is: not a reflection at second hand, but God's own glory shining out in a person I can know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: third person singular present indicative active of G568 used impersonally; it is sufficient:--it is enough.
BiblicalUsage: It is enough — Jesus' words to the sleeping disciples in Gethsemane: sleep on now, take your rest, it is enough, the hour is come. The word is a single, tired full stop, and it appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even in Gethsemane, Jesus sets the limit: the hour has come, the waiting is over, and what must be faced will be faced.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2192; (actively) to have out, i.e. receive in full; (intransitively) to keep (oneself) away, i.e. be distant (literally or figuratively):--be, have, receive.
BiblicalUsage: The word runs in two directions. On one side it means to have received in full — the hypocrites have their reward already, and Paul says he has received everything the Philippians sent. On the other side it means to be far off, like the prodigal still a great way from home when his father saw him. Full payment and far distance share one word, and both turn on whether something is already in hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the warning and the comfort sit side by side here. A reward taken now is a reward already spent, while a father who sees his son a long way off is already running to meet him, and I hold that God's kind of fullness is the second one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice (reflexively) of G568; to hold oneself off, i.e. refrain:--abstain.
BiblicalUsage: Hold yourself off — abstain from fornication, Paul tells the Thessalonians, and abstain from fleshly lusts, Peter tells the scattered believers. The middle voice makes it personal: nobody abstains for you; you hold yourself back.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe abstaining is not about missing out but about staying free for the life God has for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the same as G1492; to see fully:--see.
BiblicalUsage: To see how things will turn out — Paul, in prison, telling the Philippians he hopes to send Timothy as soon as he sees how it will go with him. The word stands in the received text here, where other manuscripts read a form of the word for looking toward something, and the sense is the same either way: Paul is waiting to see what God does next.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this single verse shows me how to wait: hope in prison still plans, and still trusts God with the outcome it cannot see yet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G546; a menace:--X straitly, threatening.
BiblicalUsage: A threat — the rulers threatening Peter and John, Saul breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples, and Paul warning masters to forbear threatening, because their Master is in heaven. Threats are the language of people who want obedience without love.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that threats belong to the old way of ruling, not to Christ's. The church's answer to threatening was prayer for boldness, and I believe that is still the answer: speak the word freely, and leave the consequences to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; to menace; by implication, to forbid:--threaten.
BiblicalUsage: To threaten — the council threatening the apostles not to speak in Jesus' name, and Christ himself, when reviled, threatening not, but committing himself to the one who judges righteously. The same verb, two opposite uses.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ's silence under threat is the pattern for mine: I do not have to win the argument to be safe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and εἶμι (to go); to go away:--go. Compare G548.
BiblicalUsage: To be away, or to go away — the brethren sending Paul and Silas away by night from Berea, Paul writing that whether present or absent he is the same man, and his joy that even though absent in body he is present in spirit with the Colossians. Distance changes the body, not the bond.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word comforts every separated church: Paul's absence did not break his care. Distance never broke the bond the gospel made, and I hold that the same gospel binds believers across any distance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and εἶμι (to go); to go away:--go. Compare G548.
BiblicalUsage: To be away, or to go away — the brethren sending Paul and Silas away by night from Berea, Paul writing that whether present or absent he is the same man, and his joy that even though absent in body he is present in spirit with the Colossians. Distance changes the body, not the bond.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word comforts every separated church: Paul's absence did not break his care. Distance never broke the bond the gospel made, and I hold that the same gospel binds believers across any distance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: reflexive past of a compound of G575 and G2036; to say off for oneself, i.e. disown:--renounce.
BiblicalUsage: To renounce — Paul says we have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, refusing to walk in craftiness or handle God's word deceitfully. The word is a public disowning: those things are not mine any more.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that honesty in ministry starts here, with renouncing every shortcut that hides the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G3987; untried, i.e. not temptable:--not to be tempted.
BiblicalUsage: Not to be tempted — God cannot be tempted with evil, James says, and he tempts no one. The word appears only here, guarding God's character at the exact point where suffering people are most tempted to blame him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this guards my view of God when life hurts: my trials never come from a God who is himself drawn toward evil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3984; inexperienced, i.e. ignorant:--unskilful.
BiblicalUsage: Unskilful — the one who still lives on milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness, a babe rather than a grown man. The word is about inexperience, not stupidity: the skill comes with use.
TheologicalSignificance: I take this as a push toward maturity: the word is meant to be practised, not just heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G545; disbelief (obstinate and rebellious):--disobedience, unbelief.
BiblicalUsage: Disobedience — the wrath of God coming on the children of disobedience, the spirit working in them now, and the mercy shown to us who once were disobedient too. Paul will not let me forget I was one of them before mercy found me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe disobedience is never just breaking rules; it is refusing the God who made me. And I hold that the mercy I received is the only reason I can now obey with joy instead of fear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G545; to disbelieve (wilfully and perversely):--not believe, disobedient, obey not, unbelieving.
BiblicalUsage: To disbelieve, to refuse to be persuaded — the one who believes not the Son shall not see life, the disobedient people God stretched out his hands to all day long, the generation that could not enter his rest because of unbelief, and the stone the builders rejected. Refusal, not ignorance, is the heart of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that unbelief is a decision, not a fog, and that makes the gospel's offer all the more urgent. God holds his hands out all day long, and I believe the only right answer is to take them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3982; unpersuadable, i.e. contumacious:--disobedient.
BiblicalUsage: Disobedient — the angel's promise that John would turn the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, Paul's claim that he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, and the blunt lists that name disobedience to parents among the marks of a godless age. The word covers children who will not listen and adults who will not obey heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe obedience is the shape love takes when God speaks. John prepared the way by turning disobedient hearts, and I hold that the same turning is what repentance still does in me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1551; to expect fully:--look (wait) for.
BiblicalUsage: To wait eagerly, looking for what is coming — creation waiting for the revealing of the sons of God, believers waiting with patience for what they hope for, our citizenship in heaven from which we look for the Saviour, and Christ appearing a second time to those who look for him. This is not idle waiting; it leans forward.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe waiting like this changes how I live today. If creation itself is on tiptoe for the revealing of God's children, then I hold that my hope is not an escape from the world but the world's own future arriving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G575 and G1562; to divest wholly oneself, or (for oneself) despoil:--put off, spoil.
BiblicalUsage: To strip off — Christ stripping the rulers and authorities bare and triumphing over them, and believers stripping off the old man with his deeds. The word is a soldier's word: take the armour off the defeated enemy, and take the old life off yourself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cross stripped my enemies before it stripped me, and that is why I can lay the old life down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G554; divestment:--putting off.
BiblicalUsage: The putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh — Paul calls circumcision made without hands the putting off of the old nature, done by Christ himself. It happens once, and it is God's work, not mine.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that my old life was not improved but put off, and Christ did the putting off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1643; to dismiss:--drive.
BiblicalUsage: To drive away — Gallio driving the accusers from the judgment seat, refusing to judge a dispute about words and names. The word appears only here, and it is a judge washing his hands of a case.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Gallio's dismissal as a small mercy: the gospel was left alone to spread while its enemies were shown the door.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and G1651; refutation, i.e. (by implication) contempt:--nought.
BiblicalUsage: Contempt, or coming to nothing — Demetrius warning that Paul's preaching would bring the temple of Artemis into disrepute, and his whole craft into contempt. The word measures what people fear losing when the gospel arrives.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel still threatens every idol's reputation, and that is a sign it is working.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1658; one freed away, i.e. a freedman:--freeman.
BiblicalUsage: A freedman — the one called in the Lord while a slave is the Lord's freeman, just as the one called while free is Christ's servant. The word turns the world's ranks upside down in a single sentence.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Christ's freedom does not depend on my circumstances: called by him, I am free wherever I stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Apelles, a Christian:--Apelles.
BiblicalUsage: Apelles is greeted by name in Paul's letter to Rome, among the believers Paul calls approved in Christ. One verse is all we have, and it is enough to know he stood the test and Paul wanted Rome to know it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Apelles matters because faithfulness does not need a long story to be real. Approved in Christ is the whole verdict, and I hold that it is the verdict I want for myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1679; to hope out, i.e. fully expect:--hope for again.
BiblicalUsage: To hope for again, to expect back — Jesus telling his people to lend, hoping for nothing again, and love their enemies anyway. The word is about giving up the claim to be repaid.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the hardest kind of generosity: giving without keeping a ledger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1725; from in front, i.e. opposite, before or against:--before, contrary, over against, in the presence of.
BiblicalUsage: Over against, before — Mary Magdalene sitting over against the sepulchre, watching where they laid him, and the plain charge that there is no fear of God before the eyes of the godless. The word places things face to face.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what stands before my eyes shapes what I do next, and Mary watching the tomb is the right picture of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a secondary derivative of G4008; unfinished, i.e. (by implication) interminable:--endless.
BiblicalUsage: Endless — Paul warning against endless genealogies, which minister questions rather than godly edifying in faith. The word is not about long lists; it is about lists that never arrive anywhere.
TheologicalSignificance: I take this as a rule for my own study: if it produces arguments instead of faith, it is a distraction.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2064; to go off (i.e. depart), aside (i.e. apart) or behind (i.e. follow), literally or figuratively:--come, depart, go (aside, away, back, out, … ways), pass away, be past.
BiblicalUsage: To go away, to depart — the Samaritan woman leaving her waterpot and running to the city, Jesus rising early to go apart and pray, Peter running to the tomb and going away wondering, and the promise that one day tears and death and sorrow will depart for good. The word follows people leaving, and it follows sorrows leaving too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every departure in this word points to the last one: the day God himself wipes away tears, and nothing that hurts us now is left to come back. Until then, I hold that following Jesus means going where he goes, even when it means leaving the waterpot behind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G4049; undistractedly, i.e. free from (domestic) solicitude:--without distraction.
BiblicalUsage: Without distraction — Paul's reason for his counsel about marriage: that believers may attend upon the Lord without distraction. The word is about an undivided gaze, not a busy schedule.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the goal of every counsel about my life is the same: fewer distractions between me and the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G4059; uncircumcised (figuratively):--uncircumcised.
BiblicalUsage: Uncircumcised — Stephen's charge to the council: stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, always resisting the Holy Ghost. The word is not about the body; it is about a heart that will not listen.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Stephen's rebuke personally: a heart that will not hear is uncircumcised whatever its outward marks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an eyelash (as fluttering); figuratively, morning ray
BiblicalUsage: The eyelids — Job cursing the day of his birth and longing for the eyelids of the morning never to open on it, the psalmist's eyes watching the sons of men, and the wise man's call to let your eyelids look straight before you. The same word names the first light of dawn, the eyelids of the morning breaking over Leviathan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this small word shows how closely God watches and how plainly I am told to watch too. His eyes are on the sons of men, and my eyes are meant to look straight ahead, not wander after trouble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {meaning accession (used as an adverb or conjunction); also or yea; adversatively though}
BiblicalUsage: Also, yea, even — Daniel telling the king that he has done no hurt before God, and also none before the king, and the elders of Judah asking the names of the men building the temple. The word adds one more thing to the list, and in Daniel's mouth it is the whole defence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's little word carries his whole case: innocent before God, and innocent before the king too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {meaning accession (used as an adverb or conjunction); also or yea; adversatively though}
BiblicalUsage: Also, yea, even — Daniel telling the king that he has done no hurt before God, and also none before the king, and the elders of Judah asking the names of the men building the temple. The word adds one more thing to the list, and in Daniel's mouth it is the whole defence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's little word carries his whole case: innocent before God, and innocent before the king too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {meaning accession (used as an adverb or conjunction); also or yea; adversatively though}
BiblicalUsage: Also, yea, even — Daniel telling the king that he has done no hurt before God, and also none before the king, and the elders of Judah asking the names of the men building the temple. The word adds one more thing to the list, and in Daniel's mouth it is the whole defence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's little word carries his whole case: innocent before God, and innocent before the king too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gird on (the ephod)
BiblicalUsage: To gird on — Moses girding Aaron with the ephod when he dressed him for the priesthood, and the same dressing repeated at the consecration. The word is the fastening of the garment that marks the priest for service.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the girding matters because God dresses his priests himself: the service starts with what he puts on, not with what we bring.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cook, especially to bake
BiblicalUsage: To bake — Lot baking unleavened bread for his guests in Sodom, Israel baking unleavened cakes in the rush out of Egypt, the woman of Endor baking unleavened bread for Saul, and the two wave loaves baked with leaven for the feast. Bread baked in a hurry and bread baked for a feast share the one word.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that bread in the Bible is never just food: it is hospitality in Sodom, deliverance in Egypt, and worship at the feast. I believe the God who provides the bread is the one the bread always points to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G138; to remove (literally or figuratively):--cut (smite) off, take away.
BiblicalUsage: To take away, to cut off — the Lord taking away Elizabeth's reproach, the servant's ear cut off in the garden, and the promise that God will take away sins. The word removes things: shame, an ear, and sin itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the best taking away in this word is the last one: God taking away sins is the promise the whole covenant stands on. Shame lifted, and sin removed: that is the taking away I live on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to swell; figuratively, be elated
BiblicalUsage: To swell, to be puffed up — the proud soul that is not upright, set against the just who shall live by faith, and the people presuming to go up the hill after God had told them not to. Swelling is the picture of pride that will not stay in its place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pride is a swelling that always bursts: the just live by faith, not by being lifted up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5316; non-apparent:--that is not manifest.
BiblicalUsage: Not manifest, hidden from sight — nothing is hidden from God, the writer says; all things are naked and opened before him. The word appears only here, at the exact point where the word of God is described as a discerner of thoughts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is both comfort and warning: nothing about me is hidden from the God who loves me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G853; disappearance, i.e. (figuratively) abrogation:--vanish away.
BiblicalUsage: Vanishing away — the old covenant is ready to vanish away, made old by the new one. The word is about something fading out because its time is done.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the old covenant vanished because the new one arrived, and Christ is the reason it could go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G852; to render unapparent, i.e. (actively) consume (becloud), or (passively) disappear (be destroyed):-- corrupt, disfigure, perish, vanish away.
BiblicalUsage: To make disappear, to consume — the fading of earthly treasure before moth and rust, the rich man's life vanishing like a vapour, and the scoffers in the synagogue told to behold and perish. The word destroys what it touches, whether treasure, life, or the proud.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word preaches the sermon itself: what I store on earth will vanish, and what I store in heaven will not. James calls my life a vapour, and I believe him — which is why I want it spent on what lasts.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G5316; non-manifested, i.e. invisible:--vanished out of sight.
BiblicalUsage: Vanished out of their sight — Jesus, known in the breaking of bread at Emmaus, vanishing from the two disciples' eyes. One verse, and the whole resurrection morning in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe he vanished so they would carry the news rather than keep the sight, and that is still how it works.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to surround
BiblicalUsage: To surround, to wrap around — the waves of death compassing David, the weeds wrapped about Jonah's head in the deep, and evils compassing the psalmist on every side. The word is a closing circle, and it is always trouble closing in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is honest about trouble: it does surround us, like water closing over a drowning man. But I hold that the same psalms that name the surrounding end with deliverance, and Jonah's weeds gave way to dry land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to contain, i.e. (reflex.) abstain
BiblicalUsage: To hold back, to restrain oneself — Joseph refraining himself before his brothers, and then unable to refrain himself any longer when he made himself known; Saul forcing himself to offer the sacrifice while he waited for Samuel; and Haman refraining himself, holding his fury until he got home. The word is self-control under pressure, for good and for ill.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe restraint is a power, not a weakness, and Joseph shows both sides of it: he held himself back until the right moment, and then he let love out. Haman shows the other side: restraint that only stores up hate. I hold that what I restrain myself for is what my restraint is worth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dust (as powdered or gray); hence, clay, earth, mud
BiblicalUsage: Dust — God forming man from the dust of the ground, the sentence that dust we are and to dust we shall return, Abraham calling himself dust and ashes before the Lord, and Job repenting in dust and ashes. The word is our beginning, our end, and our confession.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dust keeps me honest: I am made from it, I return to it, and the God who breathed life into it is the only reason dust can speak at all. Job's repentance in dust is where my pride ends and my hope begins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be dust
BiblicalUsage: To be dust — Shimei going along the hill throwing dust as David passed, cursing him as he went. The word appears once, in a handful of dust thrown at a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Shimei's dust shows how low a king can be brought, and David's refusal to answer it shows how a king ought to bear it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Apharsekite or Apharsathkite, an unknown Assyrian tribe
BiblicalUsage: The Apharsathkites are named among the peoples who wrote to the king against the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and again among the officials beyond the river who were told to leave the work of God alone. Three verses, one role: they stand on the other side of the wall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe their name is a small warning: opposition to God's work often comes dressed as official business. The wall went up anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Apherasite or inhabitant of an unknown region of Assyria
BiblicalUsage: The Apharsites appear once, named among the peoples settled in Samaria who wrote to Artaxerxes against the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem. A single mention, and it is a letter of complaint.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one verse is enough to place them: they are remembered for standing against the work, and the work went on without them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to disappear, i.e. cease
BiblicalUsage: To cease, to disappear — money failing in Egypt in the famine, and Joseph answering that the cattle would do; the extortioner coming to an end in Isaiah's vision; and the psalmist asking whether God's mercy is clean gone for ever. The word asks what happens when the supply runs out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the psalmist's question is mine too, in the lean years: is his mercy clean gone for ever? And I hold that the answer of the whole psalm is no — the God who remembered Joseph in the famine remembers his mercy too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and the base of G1476; a place of sitting apart, i.e. a privy:--draught.
BiblicalUsage: A privy, a draught — Jesus' plain teaching that what goes into the mouth passes into the draught and is cast out, so it cannot defile a man. The word appears only in this teaching, and it is deliberately earthy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus chose the plainest picture on purpose: defilement comes from the heart, not from the stomach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G5339; unsparingness, i.e. austerity (asceticism):--neglecting.
BiblicalUsage: Unsparingness — Paul naming the show of wisdom in self-made religion: will-worship, humility, and neglecting of the body, all with no honour in them. The word is severity without value, harshness that God never asked for.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe harshness toward the body is not holiness; Christ's yoke is easy, and severity I invent for myself is not devotion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dusky
BiblicalUsage: Dusky — the day of the Lord described as darkness and not light, darkness with no brightness in it. One verse, and the whole warning in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day of the Lord is darkness for those who trusted in their own religion, and that is why Amos still frightens me in a good way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: duskiness, figuratively, misfortune; concrete, concealment
BiblicalUsage: Darkness — the thick darkness over Egypt that could be felt, the blind groping of a disobedient people at noonday, and the promise that light will rise in obscurity for the one who feeds the hungry. The word names both judgment and the place where light is promised.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that darkness in Scripture is never just the absence of light; it is the judgment of God and the cry of his people at once. And I believe the promise stands with it: those who spend themselves for the hungry will see their darkness become noonday.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and φέλλος (in the sense of a stone as stubbing the foot); smoothness, i.e. (figuratively) simplicity:--singleness.
BiblicalUsage: Smoothness, simplicity — the believers breaking bread with gladness and singleness of heart, day by day in the temple and from house to house. The word is about a heart without folds in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe singleness of heart is the mark of the early church I most want back: glad, simple, and together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aphek (or Aphik), the name of three places in Palestine
KeyPassages: 1 Samuel 4:1; 1 Samuel 29:1; 1 Kings 20:26; 2 Kings 13:17; Joshua 12:18; Judges 1:31
BiblicalUsage: Aphek is the name of three places, and the Bible keeps returning to it: Israel camped at Aphek before the ark was taken, the Philistines gathered there before Gilboa, Ben-Hadad's army was routed there, and the arrow Elisha told Joash to shoot was aimed toward it. One name, three towns, and a long history of battles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Aphek matters because battles were fought there again and again: the ground where God's people lost the ark is also the ground where God gave them victory, and I hold that no place is lost to him for good.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aphekah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Aphekah is named once, among the towns of Judah in the hill country, listed between the valleys and the wilderness. A single mention on a map of the inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a town named once belongs to the story: the inheritance was counted town by town, and none of it was forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a turban
BiblicalUsage: A turban — the prophet disguising himself with a headband over his eyes to wait for Ahab on the road, and then removing it so the king would know him. Two verses, one disguise, and the message it carried.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the turban shows how God's word comes to kings: not in splendour, but in a disguise on the road, plain and impossible to ignore.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G863; freedom; (figuratively) pardon:--deliverance, forgiveness, liberty, remission.
BiblicalUsage: Forgiveness, release — the blood of the covenant shed for the remission of sins, Peter's call to repent and be baptized for the remission of sins, the redemption we have through Christ's blood, and the plain rule that without shedding of blood there is no remission. The word is a release from a debt and a letting go from prison at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forgiveness is the centre of the whole gospel, because it is the one thing I could never do for myself. Christ's blood paid the debt and opened the cell, and I hold that every other blessing in the Christian life flows out of that release.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and ἵημι (to send; an intensive form of εἶμι, to go); to send forth, in various applications (as follow):--cry, forgive, forsake, lay aside, leave, let (alone, be, go, have), omit, put (send) away, remit, suffer, yield up.
BiblicalUsage: To send away, to let go — forgive us our debts, the master forgiving his servant's whole debt out of pity, the woman whose many sins are forgiven because she loved much, and the church given the charge to remit sins or retain them. The word covers letting go of a debt, leaving a boat, and leaving a place, because all of them are a sending away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forgiveness is the clearest picture of what God did for me: he sent my sins away, as far as the east is from the west, and he did it because of Christ. And I hold that the same sending away is now my own calling toward everyone who owes me anything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G2425; to go (i.e. spread) forth (by rumor):--come abroad.
BiblicalUsage: To come abroad, to spread by report — Paul's joy that the Romans' obedience has come abroad unto all men, and his wish that they be wise unto good and simple concerning evil. One verse, and a whole church's reputation in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a church's obedience speaks further than its preaching, and Rome's had travelled everywhere.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5358; hostile to virtue:--despiser of those that are good.
BiblicalUsage: Despisers of those that are good — one mark of the perilous last days, named beside the loveless and the unthankful. The word is hatred aimed at goodness itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the ugliest mark on Paul's list: hating what is good is the last step away from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5366; unavaricious:--without covetousness, not greedy of filthy lucre.
BiblicalUsage: Without covetousness — a bishop must not be greedy of filthy lucre, and every believer's manner of life is to be without covetousness, content with such things as we have. The word is freedom from the love of money.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe contentment is the other side of this word: God has said he will never leave me, and that is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2476; to remove, i.e. (actively) instigate to revolt; usually (reflexively) to desist, desert, etc.:--depart, draw (fall) away, refrain, withdraw self.
BiblicalUsage: To depart, to fall away — the devil departing from Jesus until a more convenient season, Gamaliel's counsel to refrain from these men and let them alone, the warning that some shall depart from the faith, and the call to take heed lest there be an evil heart of unbelief in departing from the living God. The word can describe a devil leaving, a council standing back, or a soul walking out on God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that departing from the living God is the one departure this word warns me about above all others. The devil left Jesus and came back; those who leave the faith in the last days may not. I believe the guard is the one Hebrews names: take heed, and hold fast.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G864; properly, arrival, i.e. (by implication) departure:--departing.
BiblicalUsage: A departing — Paul warning the Ephesian elders that after his departing, grievous wolves will enter in among them, not sparing the flock. The word is his leaving, and the danger that follows it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's farewell is a shepherd's last duty: warn the flock plainly, then leave them to the God who keeps them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aphiach, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aphiah is named once, in the genealogy of Saul: the son of Becorath, of the tribe of Benjamin, standing four generations above the first king of Israel. His name is the root of a royal line.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept in a genealogy is never wasted: Aphiah's line led to a king, and the king's story led to David, and David's line led to Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: unripe
BiblicalUsage: Unripe — the wheat and the rye not smitten by the hail, because they were not grown up. One verse, in the middle of the plagues, and the detail is God's mercy in the middle of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the unripe wheat is a small sign of God's restraint: even in the plague, he left something standing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, containing, i.e. a tube; also a bed or valley of a stream; also a strong thing or a hero
KeyPassages: Ezekiel 6:3; Joel 1:20; Song of Solomon 5:12; 2 Samuel 22:16
BiblicalUsage: Channels, valleys, beds of streams — the rivers of water running in the valleys, the beasts crying for the water brooks, the eyes of the beloved like doves by the rivers of waters, and the channels of the sea laid bare at the rebuke of the Lord. The word is the hollow the water runs in, and it can be full or dry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the channels show me how God's blessing flows: it runs in low places, like water in a valley, and the beasts of the field know to cry for it when it is dry. I hold that my own dry places are where his water is meant to run.
RelatedBooks: 2 Samuel; Ezekiel; Joel; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G852 (contraction); unawares, i.e. unexpectedly:--suddenly.
BiblicalUsage: Suddenly — the sound from heaven filling the house at Pentecost, the great earthquake shaking the prison at Philippi so the doors stood open, and the islanders watching Paul for the swelling that never came. The word marks the moment God breaks in without warning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still comes suddenly, as he did at Pentecost and in the prison: no announcement, no slow build, just the sound and the shaking and the doors standing open. I hold that suddenness is not God's absence from my plans but his freedom from them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G5401; fearlessly:--without fear.
BiblicalUsage: Without fear — serving God in holiness and righteousness without fear, Timothy working without fear among the Corinthians, the brethren waxing confident to speak the word without fear, and the false shepherds feeding themselves without fear. The same word praises the fearless and exposes them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fearlessness is good only when it serves God: Timothy's quiet courage and the false teachers' bold self-feeding wear the same word, and the difference is whom they serve. I hold that my own fearlessness is worth having only if it is spent on speaking his word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G3666; to assimilate closely:--make like.
BiblicalUsage: Made like — Melchizedek made like unto the Son of God, abiding a priest continually. The word is a likeness, not an identity: the priest of Salem pictures the Son, and the picture holds because the Son is the reality.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Melchizedek is a shadow drawn to show me the substance, and the substance is Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5456; voiceless, i.e. mute (by nature or choice); figuratively, unmeaning:--dumb, without signification.
BiblicalUsage: Voiceless, mute — the dumb idols the Corinthians once followed, the voices in the world that all have their meaning, the dumb ass speaking with man's voice to rebuke the prophet, and the Lamb led as a sheep to the slaughter, silent before his shearers. The word is silence, whether of an idol that cannot speak or a Saviour who will not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the whole sermon: idols are dumb because they have nothing to say, and Christ was silent because he had everything to bear. I hold that his silence before his shearers is the loudest thing in the Bible.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G3708; to consider attentively:--look.
BiblicalUsage: To look toward, to consider — looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, and Paul waiting to see how it will go with him in prison. The word is a fixed gaze, whether on the Saviour or on the outcome God will give.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe looking unto Jesus is the whole of the Christian life in one verb: I look away from everything else, and I keep looking at him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G3724; to set off by boundary, i.e. (figuratively) limit, exclude, appoint, etc.:--divide, separate, sever.
BiblicalUsage: To set apart, to separate — Paul separated unto the gospel of God, the Spirit saying separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work, God separating Paul from his mother's womb, and the call to come out from among them and be separate. The word draws a boundary, and the boundary is for a purpose.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe separation is not rejection but appointment: God sets his people apart so he can send them. And I hold that being set apart for the gospel is the highest calling there is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and G3729; a starting-point, i.e. (figuratively) an opportunity:--occasion.
BiblicalUsage: An aphormē is a starting-point, a base of operations — the place an army launches from, or the excuse a person launches an argument from. Paul says sin took occasion by the commandment in Romans 7:8, and again in Romans 7:11 that sin deceived him by it and slew him; the law itself was good, but sin used it as its launching ground. The word cuts both ways: in 2 Corinthians 5:12 Paul gives the Corinthians an occasion to glory on his behalf, and in Galatians 5:13 he warns them not to use their liberty for an occasion to the flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word exposes how sin works: it never attacks head-on if it can find a foothold instead. A good law, a real liberty, even a fair boast — any of them can become sin's starting-point once I hand it over. That is why Paul's answer is not to abandon the law or liberty, but to watch what I am launching from them — love serving one another, not the flesh serving itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G876; to froth at the mouth (in epilepsy):--foam.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times about the same boy. His father tells Jesus the spirit tears him and he foams at the mouth in Mark 9:18, and when the boy is brought to Jesus in Mark 9:20 the spirit throws him down and he wallows foaming on the ground.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is only a symptom in the story; the point is the boy's torment and the disciples' failure, and then Jesus casting the spirit out.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5424; properly, mindless, i.e. stupid, (by implication) ignorant, (specially) egotistic, (practically) rash, or (morally) unbelieving:--fool(-ish), unwise.
BiblicalUsage: Paul calls the man who doubts the resurrection a fool in 1 Corinthians 15:36 — ‘thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die’ — because the seed in the ground already teaches what he denies. Jesus uses the same word for the rich man in Luke 12:20, whose soul is required of him the very night his barns are full, and Paul turns it into a command in Ephesians 5:17: be not unwise, but understand what the will of the Lord is. Romans 2:20 shows the other side, the Jew who claims to be an instructor of the foolish while holding only the form of knowledge.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that foolishness in Scripture is never about being slow; it is about living as though God will not call the account. The fool sows nothing, plans for decades he does not have, and teaches others from a form of truth he never obeyed. Wisdom, by contrast, is simply understanding what the Lord wills — and doing it while there is still time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; froth, i.e. slaver:--foaming.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Luke's account of the boy with the spirit. The spirit takes him, he cries out, it tears him until he foams again, and bruising him, it hardly leaves him — the froth at the mouth is the visible mark of the torment.
TheologicalSignificance: A single ugly detail, and it does its work: the boy's suffering is real and bodily, not a figure of speech.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G878; senselessness, i.e. (euphemistically) egotism; (morally) recklessness:--folly, foolishly(-ness).
BiblicalUsage: Paul borrows the word to defend himself in 2 Corinthians 11:1, asking the church to bear with him a little in his folly, and in 2 Corinthians 11:17 he speaks as it were foolishly, boasting only because the false apostles have forced his hand. But Jesus puts the word in its proper place in Mark 7:22, listing foolishness among the evils that come out of the heart — thefts, deceit, pride, blasphemy — not a manner of speaking but a moral condition.
