Paul says put off the old man with its deceitful lusts, put off anger and malice and filthy language, lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and lay apart all filthiness and receive the word with meekness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that putting off is not a one-time act, it is the daily work of a Christian. The old clothes come off so the new man can be seen, and the race is run lighter without the weights we chose to carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5111; to venture plainly:--be very bold.
BiblicalUsage: Paul quotes Isaiah being very bold, saying God was found by those who did not seek Him and made known to those who did not ask for Him. The word is boldness that speaks plainly, without hedging.
TheologicalSignificance: God's grace is bold enough to find people who were not even looking.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G664; (figuratively) decisiveness, i.e. rigor:--severity.
BiblicalUsage: Paul sets God's goodness and His severity side by side: severity toward those who fell, goodness toward those who continue in His goodness. The word is decisiveness, the sharp edge of a God who means what He says.
TheologicalSignificance: A God with no severity would have no goodness worth trusting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of a comparative of G575 and τέμνω (to cut); abruptly, i.e. peremptorily:--sharply(-ness).
BiblicalUsage: The adverb means sharply, abruptly, without softening. Paul tells Titus to rebuke the false teachers sharply so they may be sound in the faith, and he writes sharply from a distance so he will not have to use sharpness when he arrives.
TheologicalSignificance: Sharp words, spoken in love, can be the kindest thing a church hears.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G5157; to deflect, i.e. (reflexively) avoid:--turn away.
BiblicalUsage: Paul describes people with a form of godliness but denying its power, and his instruction is short: from such turn away. The word is a deliberate turning aside, refusing to walk with them.
TheologicalSignificance: A form of godliness with no power in it is not harmless, and the wise move is to walk away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the participle of G548; a being away:--absence.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the Philippians to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, not only in his presence but much more in his absence. The word is simply being away, and Paul counts on their obedience holding when no one is watching.
TheologicalSignificance: Faithfulness that only works under watch is not faithfulness at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Appajim, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Appaim is named in the genealogy of Judah as a son of Nadab, and then as the father of Ishi. He appears only in the family record, one link in the line that runs from Judah toward David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the names of people the world forgets, and a single line in a genealogy is still a life He counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pavilion or palace-tent
BiblicalUsage: Daniel's vision ends with the king planting the tents of his palace between the seas and the glorious holy mountain, and coming to his end with no one to help him. The word is a royal pavilion, a palace-tent pitched as a claim of power.
TheologicalSignificance: A king can pitch his tent against God's mountain, but the tent does not last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: revenue; others at the last
BiblicalUsage: The enemies of the returning exiles warn the king that if Jerusalem is rebuilt, the Jews will pay no more tribute, custom, or toll, and the revenue of the kings will be hurt. The word is that revenue, the money a king counts on.
TheologicalSignificance: Opposition to God's work often wears the clothes of money.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; Apphia, a woman of Collosæ:--Apphia.
BiblicalUsage: Apphia is greeted in Paul's letter to Philemon as beloved, named beside Philemon and Archippus, and the letter is addressed to the church in their house. She is one of the few women named in the New Testament letters, and her name sits at the head of a letter about forgiveness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a woman named once in a letter about a runaway slave still matters, because the church that met in her house was the place where forgiveness had to be lived out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; (in the genitive, i.e. possessive case) of Appius, the name of a Roman:--Appii.
BiblicalUsage: Appii Forum was a market town on the road to Rome, and the brothers came out from Rome to meet Paul there, as far as Appii Forum and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them he thanked God and took courage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sends encouragement on the road, and sometimes it looks like friends walking out to meet you a long way from home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a palanquin
BiblicalUsage: King Solomon made himself a palanquin of the wood of Lebanon, a covered litter carried in procession. The word is that royal carriage, built for a king's coming.
TheologicalSignificance: Even a king's finest carriage is only the frame; the glory is the one who rides in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of a compound of G4314 and εἶμι (to go); inaccessible:--which no man can approach.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says God alone has immortality and dwells in light which no man can approach unto, whom no man has seen or can see. The word is inaccessible, light too bright to enter.
TheologicalSignificance: God's light is not dim, it is too bright, and that is why we come to Him through Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G4350; actively, inoffensive, i.e. not leading into sin; passively, faultless, i.e. not led into sin:--none (void of, without) offence.
BiblicalUsage: The word means giving no offence, not causing anyone to stumble. Paul says give no offence to Jews, Greeks, or the church of God; he exercises himself to have a conscience void of offence toward God and men; and he prays the Philippians will be sincere and without offence until the day of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a blameless life is not about never offending anyone, it is about never putting a stumbling block where Christ should be. Conscience kept clear before God and men is the quiet work of a lifetime.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of a presumed compound of G4383 and G2983 (compare G4381); in a way not accepting the person, i.e. impartially:--without respect of persons.
BiblicalUsage: Peter says to call on the Father who without respect of persons judges according to every man's work, and to pass the time of your sojourning in fear. God weighs the work, not the face, the standing, or the name.
TheologicalSignificance: God does not play favourites, and that is both our comfort and our warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5579; veracious:--that cannot lie.
BiblicalUsage: Paul opens his letter to Titus with the hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began. The word is simply that God cannot lie, and the promise rests on it.
TheologicalSignificance: A promise is only as good as the one who makes it, and God cannot lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; wormwood (as a type of bitterness, i.e. (figuratively) calamity):--wormwood.
BiblicalUsage: When the third angel sounds, a star falls and its name is Wormwood, and a third of the waters become wormwood, bitter and deadly, so that many men die. The word is a bitter herb, and John makes it the name of a judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: Bitterness that falls from heaven is not an accident, it is a judgment, and it turns sweet water deadly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5590; lifeless, i.e. inanimate (mechanical):--without life.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says even lifeless things that give sound, whether pipe or harp, must give a distinction in the sounds, or no one will know what is being played. The word is without life, an instrument with no breath of its own.
TheologicalSignificance: Sound without sense is noise, and worship without sense is no better.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G4417; not stumbling, i.e. (figuratively) without sin:--from falling.
BiblicalUsage: Jude closes by praising Him who is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before His glory with exceeding joy. The word is not stumbling, kept steady on feet that would fall on their own.
TheologicalSignificance: We do not keep ourselves from falling; He keeps us, and that is the whole hope of the verse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to seize by the heel; figuratively, to circumvent (as if tripping up the heels); also to restrain (as if holding by the heel)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to take by the heel, and it is Jacob's story in a single verb. Esau says his brother is rightly named Jacob, for he has supplanted him twice; Jeremiah warns that every brother will utterly supplant his neighbour; and Hosea looks back to the womb, where Jacob took his brother by the heel before he had done anything at all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jacob's name tells the truth about all of us: we grab for the blessing with our own hands before we learn to receive it. God did not change Jacob by renaming him first; He wrestled with him until the supplanter became Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tie with thongs
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, when Abraham built the altar, laid the wood in order, and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar upon the wood. It is the binding itself, the tying that makes the offering complete.
TheologicalSignificance: Isaac let himself be bound, and the ram took his place, and that is the whole gospel in one picture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: constraint
BiblicalUsage: David says the wicked press him because of the voice of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked, for they cast iniquity on him and hate him in anger. The word is constraint, the weight of being hemmed in by people who mean harm.
TheologicalSignificance: Oppression is real, and David's answer is to cry out to God rather than to carry it alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wrest
BiblicalUsage: Habakkuk complains that the law is slacked and judgment never goes forth, because the wicked compass about the righteous and wrong judgment proceeds. The word is to wrest, to twist justice until it comes out crooked.
TheologicalSignificance: When the law is twisted to serve the wicked, the prophet's complaint is itself an act of faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: tortuous
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah says the Lord will punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent, with His sore and great and strong sword. The word is tortuous, winding and twisted, and it names the enemy's shape.
TheologicalSignificance: The crooked serpent is not too twisted for God's sword.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: winding
BiblicalUsage: In Deborah's song the highways stood empty and travellers walked through crooked byways, and the psalm warns that those who turn aside to their crooked ways will be led away with the workers of iniquity. The word is winding, a path that will not run straight.
TheologicalSignificance: Crooked roads feel safer when the highways are dangerous, but the psalm says they end with the workers of iniquity.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akan, an Idummaean
BiblicalUsage: Akan is named in the genealogy of Esau as a son of Ezer, among the Horite chiefs of Seir. He is the Horite Akan, not Achan of Jericho, and his name survives only in the family record of Edom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Bible keeps Edom's lines as carefully as Israel's, because God is the God of all nations, not only of one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {to pluck up (especially by the roots); specifically, to hamstring; figuratively, to exterminate}
BiblicalUsage: In Daniel's vision of the four beasts, a little horn comes up among ten horns, and three of the first horns are plucked up by the roots before it. The word is that uprooting, power torn out to make room for a smaller, louder power.
TheologicalSignificance: Horns that look immovable can be plucked up overnight, and the vision says to watch what grows in their place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sterile (as if extirpated in the generative organs)
BiblicalUsage: Barren is the word for a womb that has not borne, and it follows the mothers of the promise. Sarai was barren, Rebekah was barren until Isaac prayed for her, Hannah sings that the barren has borne seven, and Isaiah tells the barren woman to sing because her children will outnumber the married wife's.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that barrenness in Scripture is never the end of the story. God opens closed wombs, and He turns the song of the barren into the song of the church, which bears children it never carried.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pluck up (especially by the roots); specifically, to hamstring; figuratively, to exterminate
BiblicalUsage: To pluck up by the roots is the word for uprooting, and for hamstringing a horse so it can never run again. There is a time to plant and a time to pluck up what is planted, Jacob's sons houghed oxen in their anger, God tells Joshua to hough the Canaanites' horses, and David does the same to the chariot horses he captures.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe uprooting is God's way of making sure a power stays down. He does not only defeat the enemy's army, He takes away the horses it would ride back on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to knot or distort; figuratively, to pervert (act or declare perverse)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to knot or distort, to make crooked what should run straight. The upright walk surely, but the one who perverts his ways will be found out; Israel has made crooked paths for itself; Micah accuses the rulers of perverting all equity; and the perverse in his ways will fall at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that perversity is not a mistake, it is a choice to knot the straight path. God sees the knot, and He promises that the one who walks uprightly is safe while the twisted way collapses.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lier in wait
BiblicalUsage: The psalmist asks why he should fear in days of evil, when the iniquity of his heels compasses him about. The word is a heel, and by extension a lying in wait, the sins that dog a man's steps and wait for him at the heel.
TheologicalSignificance: The sins at our heels are not a reason to fear, when God is the one who keeps our steps.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lier in wait
BiblicalUsage: The psalmist asks why he should fear in days of evil, when the iniquity of his heels compasses him about. The word is a heel, and by extension a lying in wait, the sins that dog a man's steps and wait for him at the heel.
TheologicalSignificance: The sins at our heels are not a reason to fear, when God is the one who keeps our steps.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (transitive) fraudulent or (intransitive) tracked
BiblicalUsage: The word means fraudulent or tracked, crooked or followed by footprints. Jeremiah says the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked; Isaiah promises the crooked shall be made straight; and Hosea calls Gilead a city tracked with blood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heart's deceit is the deepest problem in the Bible, deeper than any enemy outside us. The promise is that God Himself makes the crooked straight, and no one can do that work for himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: striped (with bands)
BiblicalUsage: The word is striped with bands, ringstraked, and it belongs to Jacob's flocks. The flocks conceived before the rods and brought forth ringstraked cattle, Jacob dreamed that the rams leaping on the cattle were ringstraked, and Laban removed all the ringstraked and spotted from the flock the day Jacob named them as his wages.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the striped sheep are a quiet sign of God's hand in an unfair bargain. Laban kept changing the wages, and God kept marking the flock Jacob's way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: slender, i.e. the ibex
BiblicalUsage: The ibex, the wild goat of the hills, is listed among the clean animals Israel may eat. It is a shy mountain animal, named once in the law's list of food that is permitted.
TheologicalSignificance: Even the wild goat of the hills has a place in God's law, and nothing clean is beneath His notice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Akkub, the name of five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Akkub is the name of several Israelites. One is a gatekeeper of the temple in the days of the return, one is listed among the Nethinim who came back with Zerubbabel, one is a Levite who helps the people understand the law when Ezra reads it, and one is a descendant of David in the royal line.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gatekeepers and the Levites who explain the law are as much a part of the story as the kings, because the temple only stands when ordinary faithful people hold its doors.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a scorpion; figuratively, a scourge or knotted whip
BiblicalUsage: A scorpion is the desert's sting, and it becomes the picture of a scourge. Moses reminds Israel that God led them through a wilderness of fiery serpents and scorpions; Ezekiel is told not to fear, though he dwells among scorpions; and Rehoboam threatens that his father chastised with whips, but he will chastise with scorpions.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God lets His people walk among scorpions and still keeps them. A king who reaches for the scorpion instead of the staff has already lost his kingdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: naked, i.e. (figuratively) poor
BiblicalUsage: The word means naked, or in the psalm's use, poor and destitute. The Lord will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer.
TheologicalSignificance: The prayer of the destitute is not despised, and that is the whole hope of the poor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Areli (or an Arelite, collectively), an Israelite and his descendants
BiblicalUsage: Areli is named as a son of Gad who went down into Egypt with Jacob's household, and his descendants are counted in the wilderness as the family of the Arelites. His name carries the line from Egypt to the plains of Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a family counted in the wilderness is a family God has not forgotten, even when all we have of them is a name in a list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a foe (as watchful for mischief)
BiblicalUsage: This word means a foe, one who watches for a chance to do harm. Samuel's spirit tells Saul the Lord has become his enemy, and the psalm says God's enemies take His name in vain. The word is not a stranger, it is an enemy made by turning away.
TheologicalSignificance: Becoming God's enemy is not something that happens to us, it is something we choose, and Saul's story shows where the choice ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a foe (as watchful for mischief)
BiblicalUsage: This word means a foe, one who watches for a chance to do harm. Samuel's spirit tells Saul the Lord has become his enemy, and the psalm says God's enemies take His name in vain. The word is not a stranger, it is an enemy made by turning away.
TheologicalSignificance: Becoming God's enemy is not something that happens to us, it is something we choose, and Saul's story shows where the choice ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the bottom
BiblicalUsage: The word is the bottom, and it appears once, when the men who accused Daniel are cast into the lions' den with their families, and the lions break their bones before they ever reach the bottom of the den.
TheologicalSignificance: The accusers fell to the very bottom they had dug for Daniel, and the den did the work they meant for him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ar, a place in Moab
BiblicalUsage: Ar is a city of Moab, given to the children of Lot for a possession, and Israel is told not to distress the Moabites for its sake. The brook runs down to the dwelling of Ar, and Isaiah's burden on Moab says Ar is laid waste in a night.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ar shows that God gives land even to nations outside the promise, and that a city can be given by God and still be laid waste when its day comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G142; properly, prayer (as lifted to Heaven), i.e. (by implication) imprecation:--curse.
BiblicalUsage: Paul's catalogue of human sin says their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. The word is a curse, a prayer lifted up that calls down harm instead of blessing.
TheologicalSignificance: A mouth full of cursing shows a heart full of bitterness, and both need the same cure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G142 (through the idea of drawing a conclusion); a particle denoting an inference more or less decisive (as follows):--haply, (what) manner (of man), no doubt, perhaps, so be, then, therefore, truly, wherefore. Often used in connection with other particles, especially G1065 or G3767 (after) or G1487 (before). Compare also G687.
BiblicalUsage: This little particle draws a conclusion: then, so, therefore. Paul argues that if Christ is not risen, then our preaching is vain, and he concludes that faith comes by hearing. The word does the quiet work of logic in Paul's letters.
TheologicalSignificance: Small words carry big arguments, and Paul's therefore is where doctrine turns into consequence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a form of G686, denoting an interrogation to which a negative answer is presumed:--therefore.
BiblicalUsage: This particle asks a question that expects no for an answer. Jesus asks whether the Son of man will find faith on the earth when He comes, and Philip asks the Ethiopian whether he understands what he is reading. Both questions hang in the air, waiting for the hearer to answer.
TheologicalSignificance: A question that expects no answer can still change a life, if the hearer refuses to give it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the earth; by implication (figuratively) low
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this is the word for earth, the ground beneath every kingdom. The stone cut without hands becomes a mountain and fills the whole earth, a second kingdom will bear rule over all the earth, Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a tree in the midst of the earth, and the four beasts are four kings who rise out of the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that earth is the stage where kingdoms rise and fall. Daniel's message is that every one of them is measured against the kingdom that will fill the whole earth and never be destroyed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ara, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ara is named once, as a son of Jether among the sons of Asher. His name sits in the genealogy of the tribe, one of the sons of Jether beside Jephunneh and Pispah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept in the record of Asher is a person God counted, even when the story gives us nothing more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to braid, i.e. intermix; technically, to traffic (as if by barter); also or give to be security (as a kind of exchange)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to give a pledge, to stand surety for another, and it runs through the whole Bible. Judah becomes surety for Benjamin, the Proverbs warn against becoming surety for a friend or striking hands for a stranger, and Job asks God to put him in surety with Himself, since no one else will strike hands for him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe surety is the shape of love that puts its own name on the line. Judah did it for Benjamin, and Christ did it for us, standing surety where no one else could.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to braid, i.e. intermix; technically, to traffic (as if by barter); also or give to be security (as a kind of exchange)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to give a pledge, to stand surety for another, and it runs through the whole Bible. Judah becomes surety for Benjamin, the Proverbs warn against becoming surety for a friend or striking hands for a stranger, and Job asks God to put him in surety with Himself, since no one else will strike hands for him.

Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to commingle
BiblicalUsage: In Nebuchadnezzar's dream the iron is mixed with miry clay, and the peoples shall mingle themselves with the seed of men, but they shall not cleave one to another. The Aramaic word is to commingle, to mix what does not truly join.
TheologicalSignificance: Mixtures that look strong can be the weakest kingdoms of all, because iron and clay never truly hold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arab (i.e. Arabia), a country East of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Arabia is the land east of Palestine, the country of the spice merchants and the kings who brought tribute to Solomon. Isaiah lays a burden upon Arabia, and Jeremiah makes all the kings of Arabia drink the cup of God's wrath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Arabia's place in Scripture is a reminder that the nations around Israel were never outside God's reach, neither in trade nor in judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a willow (from the use of osiers as wattles)
BiblicalUsage: The willow grows by the water, and it carries two feelings at once. The redeemed spring up as willows by the water courses, the feast of tabernacles takes willows of the brook in joy, the exiles hang their harps on the willows of Babylon, and the willows shade the great beast in Job.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the willow is the tree of both joy and sorrow, because the same branches that shade the feast can hold the harps of the exiles. God meets His people by the water in both places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arab, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Arab is named once, as a town in the hill country of Judah, listed beside Dumah and Eshean in the inheritance of the tribe. It is a place on the map of Judah's allotment, nothing more and nothing less.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every town in Judah's inheritance matters, because the promise was measured out town by town, and God keeps the whole map.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lurk
BiblicalUsage: To lurk, to lie in ambush, is the word for waiting in secret to strike. God tells Joshua to lay an ambush behind Ai, the men of Shechem set liers in wait on the mountains, the gang in Proverbs invites the young man to lie in wait for blood, and Jeremiah says God was to him as a bear lying in wait.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ambush is the devil's favourite posture, hidden and patient, and the only defence is to walk openly with God. But when God Himself is the one lying in wait, it is because judgment has been earned, not because He is cruel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a desert; especially (with the article prefix) the (generally) sterile valley of the Jordan and its continuation to the Red Sea
BiblicalUsage: The Arabah is the desert valley of the Jordan, the long sterile plain that runs from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. Moses speaks to Israel in the Arabah, the waters of the Jordan stand up as Israel crosses, and Isaiah promises the wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad, with a highway for God prepared in the desert.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Arabah is where God does His best work, because a desert has nothing to offer but room for Him. The highway in the wilderness is the promise that He comes to dry places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H6152); Arabia, a region of Asia:--Arabia.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says that after his conversion he went into Arabia before returning to Damascus, and he says Mount Sinai is in Arabia, answering to the Jerusalem that is in bondage with her children. Arabia is where Paul went to be alone with the gospel he had received.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's years in Arabia matter because the gospel he preached came by revelation, not by committee, and the desert was his classroom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arabian or inhabitant of Arab (i.e. Arabia)
BiblicalUsage: The Arabians appear as neighbours of Israel, sometimes bringing flocks as tribute to Jehoshaphat, sometimes standing with Sanballat and Tobiah to mock Nehemiah's wall. The word is simply an Arabian, a man of Arabia.
TheologicalSignificance: Neighbours can bring tribute one generation and mockery the next, and the wall gets built either way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pawn (given as security)
BiblicalUsage: A pledge or pawn is something given as security until a promise is kept. Judah promises Tamar a kid from the flock and gives her his signet, his bracelets, and his staff as a pledge, and when he sends the kid to redeem the pledge, she cannot be found.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a pledge is only as good as the man who gives it. Judah gave what identified him, his signet and staff, and the story will not let him forget it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arach, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Arach is the name of several Israelites. One is a son of Ulla among the sons of Asher, one is the father of a family of 775 who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, one is the father of Shechaniah, whose son married Tobiah's daughter, and the family of Arah is counted again in Nehemiah's census.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the returning families are the quiet proof that exile did not end Israel, because God kept the names and brought the people home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to travel
BiblicalUsage: To travel, to go on the road, is the word for a wayfaring man. An old man in Gibeah sees a traveller in the street and takes him in, Jeremiah asks why God is like a wayfaring man who turns aside to tarry for a night, Elihu accuses Job of walking in company with the workers of iniquity, and Nathan tells of a traveller who came to the rich man.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the road is where character shows, because a traveller has no home to hide in. The question is always whose company we keep on the way, and where we turn aside to spend the night.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an onager
BiblicalUsage: The word is the onager, the wild ass of the desert, and it appears once, when Nebuchadnezzar is driven from men and dwells with the wild asses, eating grass like oxen until he learns that the Most High rules.
TheologicalSignificance: A king who forgets God ends up living with the wild asses, and the desert is a hard school.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arad, the name of a place near Palestine, also of a Canaanite and an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Arad is the name of a Canaanite king and his city in the south, a Benjamite, and a place. King Arad fought Israel and took some prisoners, Joshua lists the king of Arad among the thirty-one kings he struck down, the Kenites settled in the wilderness south of Arad, and a son of Beriah in Benjamin is also named Arad.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Arad shows that a city can fight Israel, fall to Israel, and still give its name to the land, because God writes the whole map, not only the victories.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to long for
BiblicalUsage: The word means to long for, to pant after, and the psalm gives it its famous shape: as the hart pants after the water brooks, so pants my soul after God. Joel says the beasts of the field cry out to God in the drought, longing the same way.
TheologicalSignificance: Longing for God is as natural as thirst, and the hart by the brook is the picture of a soul that knows what it needs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to plait or weave
BiblicalUsage: To weave is the work of the loom, and it runs from the holy to the terrible. The robe of the ephod is woven work, the craftsmen of the tabernacle work in weaving, Goliath's spear staff is like a weaver's beam, and the wicked weave the spider's web.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that weaving is a picture of how a life is made, thread by thread. The same craft that clothes the priest can arm a giant or spin a spider's web, and the difference is whose hands are on the loom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively, make) bare; hence, to empty, pour out, demolish
BiblicalUsage: The word means to make bare, to empty out or pour out. The Servant pours out His soul unto death, Rebekah hastens and empties her pitcher into the trough for the camels, God lays bare the foundation of the wicked house, and the law speaks of uncovering what should stay covered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pouring out is the shape of the Servant's life. He emptied Himself completely, and the emptying is what makes Him able to divide the spoil with the strong.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively, make) bare; hence, to empty, pour out, demolish
BiblicalUsage: The word means to make bare, to empty out or pour out. The Servant pours out His soul unto death, Rebekah hastens and empties her pitcher into the trough for the camels, God lays bare the foundation of the wicked house, and the law speaks of uncovering what should stay covered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pouring out is the shape of the Servant's life. He emptied Himself completely, and the emptying is what makes Him able to divide the spoil with the strong.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pluck
BiblicalUsage: The word means to pluck or gather. The psalm asks why God has broken down the vine's hedges, so that all who pass by pluck her fruit, and the beloved in the Song says he has gathered his myrrh with his spice.
TheologicalSignificance: A vine with no hedge is plucked by every passer-by, and the psalm's complaint is really a prayer for the hedge to be rebuilt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to set in a row, i.e. arrange, put in order (in a very wide variety of applications)
BiblicalUsage: To set in order, to arrange in a row, is the word for laying the wood on the altar, laying the pieces of the offering on the fire, setting the battle in array in the valley of Elah, and ordering a cause before God. It is the same careful arranging, whether the thing set in order is wood, an offering, an army, or an argument.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God is a God of order, and setting things in order before Him is itself an act of worship. Abraham laid the wood, the priests laid the offering, and Job laid out his case, each trusting that what is set in order before God is heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to suit
BiblicalUsage: The word is Aramaic for suiting or being fitting, and it appears once, when the adversaries of Judah write to the king that they have maintenance from the king's palace, and it is not fitting for them to see the king dishonoured.
TheologicalSignificance: Even enemies of God's work can sound reasonable when they talk about what is fitting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causative, make) long (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to be long, and it carries the promise of long days. Honour your father and mother, that your days may be long on the land; a man's discretion makes him slow to anger; and the Servant, having made His soul an offering for sin, shall prolong His days and see His seed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe long life is not a reward for being lucky, it is the fruit of honour and patience. The longest life of all belongs to the Servant who died and yet prolongs His days forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H7410); Aram (i.e. Ram), an Israelite:--Aram.
BiblicalUsage: Aram, also called Ram, is named in the genealogy of Jesus as the son of Hezron and the father of Aminadab, one link in the line from Judah through Perez to David. He appears only in the genealogy, carrying the promise forward one generation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in the genealogy of Jesus is never filler, because the promise travelled through ordinary men who did nothing else worth recording.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be (or make) bare; but used only in the derivative sense (through the idea perhaps of smoothness) to be cunning (usually in a bad sense)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to be crafty or subtle, to deal slyly. Smite a scorner and the simple will beware, the enemies take crafty counsel against God's people, and Saul is told that David deals very subtly in hiding. Craftiness can be a warning, a threat, or a fugitive's survival.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that craftiness is a tool, and the hand that holds it decides what it is. God's enemies use it to plot, David uses it to survive, and the Proverbs use it to teach the simple to watch and learn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be (or make) bare; but used only in the derivative sense (through the idea perhaps of smoothness) to be cunning (usually in a bad sense)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to be crafty or subtle, to deal slyly. Smite a scorner and the simple will beware, the enemies take crafty counsel against God's people, and Saul is told that David deals very subtly in hiding. Craftiness can be a warning, a threat, or a fugitive's survival.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that craftiness is a tool, and the hand that holds it decides what it is. God's enemies use it to plot, David uses it to survive, and the Proverbs use it to teach the simple to watch and learn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aram of (the) two rivers (Euphrates and Tigris) or Mesopotamia
BiblicalUsage: Aram-naharaim is Aram of the two rivers, Mesopotamia, the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris. Abraham's servant goes there to find a wife for Isaac, Balaam is called from Pethor in Mesopotamia to curse Israel, Cushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia oppresses Israel for eight years, and the Ammonites hire chariots from Mesopotamia to fight David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mesopotamia is the land Israel kept coming from and going back to, the old country that held both the promise and the enemy, and God ruled over both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aram of Tsoba (or Coele-Syria)
BiblicalUsage: Aram-zobah is named only in the title of Psalm 60, which says the psalm was written when David strove with Aram-naharaim and with Aram-zobah, and Joab returned and smote twelve thousand Edomites in the valley of salt. The name itself never appears in a numbered verse.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept only in a psalm's title is still part of the story, because the title tells us what David was fighting when he wrote the song.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aram or Syria, and its inhabitants; also the name of the son of Shem, a grandson of Nahor, and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aram is both a man and a nation. Aram the son of Shem stands in the table of nations, the Syrians of Damascus come to help Hadadezer and fall before David, Naaman captains the host of the king of Syria, and Rezin of Syria marches on Jerusalem in the days of Ahaz.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Aram is the neighbour Israel could never ignore, sometimes the enemy at the gate and sometimes the servant who carries God's healing home, and God used them both ways.
RelatedPeople: Aram, Son of Shem; Naaman; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only adverbial) in Aramean
BiblicalUsage: The word means in Aramaic, the language of Syria. Hezekiah's officers ask the Rabshakeh to speak to them in the Syrian language so the people on the wall will not understand, and the Chaldeans answer Nebuchadnezzar in Syriac.
TheologicalSignificance: The language of the enemy's court and the language of the common people are not the same, and the officers knew which one to ask for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Aramite or Aramaean
BiblicalUsage: The word means a Syrian or Aramean. Israel confesses that a Syrian ready to perish was their father, and Isaac marries Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Padan-aram.
TheologicalSignificance: Israel's own confession begins with a Syrian ready to perish, and the promise runs through a Syrian bride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aran, an Edomite
BiblicalUsage: Aran is named as a son of Dishan among the Horite chiefs of Seir, in the genealogy of Esau and again in the chronicle of Adam's line. His name survives only in the two lists.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Horite lists are kept because Esau's house, like Jacob's, was counted by God, even when the story moves on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to break the neck; hence (figuratively) to destroy
BiblicalUsage: The word means to break the neck, and by extension to destroy. The firstling of an ass is redeemed or its neck is broken, the heifer's neck is struck off in the valley for an unsolved murder, the man who kills an ox in rebellion is as one who cuts off a dog's neck, and God says He will break down the altars and spoil the images.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that breaking the neck is the law's way of saying some things cannot be left half alive. What is devoted to God is redeemed, and what is devoted to idols is destroyed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to break the neck; hence (figuratively) to destroy
BiblicalUsage: The word means to break the neck, and by extension to destroy. The firstling of an ass is redeemed or its neck is broken, the heifer's neck is struck off in the valley for an unsolved murder, the man who kills an ox in rebellion is as one who cuts off a dog's neck, and God says He will break down the altars and spoil the images.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that breaking the neck is the law's way of saying some things cannot be left half alive. What is devoted to God is redeemed, and what is devoted to idols is destroyed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: gloom (as of a lowering sky)
BiblicalUsage: Thick darkness, gloom as of a lowering sky, is where God meets His people. Moses draws near to the thick darkness where God is, the mountain burns with darkness and cloud, Solomon says the Lord will dwell in the thick darkness, and Joel says the day of the Lord is a day of darkness and gloominess.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thick darkness is not God's absence, it is His nearness in a form we cannot bear to look at. Moses went in where the people stood afar off, and the darkness was where God was.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G688; an Arab or native of Arabia:--Arabian.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, on the day of Pentecost, when the crowd hears the disciples speak in their own tongues. The Arabians are named among them, hearing the wonderful works of God in their own language.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Arabians at Pentecost are the proof that no nation is left out of the gospel, because God speaks to each in the tongue they were born to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gnaw, i.e. (figuratively) eat (by hyberbole); also (participle) a pain
BiblicalUsage: The word means to gnaw, and Job uses it for the misery that eats at him. The outcasts gnaw in the wilderness for want and famine, and in the night his bones are pierced, gnawed, and his sinews take no rest.
TheologicalSignificance: Suffering gnaws like a wild thing in the dark, and Job names it plainly instead of pretending it is not there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the earth
BiblicalUsage: The word is Aramaic for the earth, and it appears once, in the one Aramaic verse in Jeremiah: the gods that have not made the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from under these heavens.
TheologicalSignificance: A single Aramaic sentence in the middle of Jeremiah is enough to doom every false god.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bare; figuratively, to demolish
BiblicalUsage: The word means to bare, to strip and demolish. The Chaldeans raise up Tyre's palaces and bring it to ruin, the careless women are told to strip and make themselves bare, and the broad walls of Babylon shall be utterly broken and her gates burned.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that stripping a city bare is God's judgment on pride that dressed itself in palaces. What is built to impress men is laid bare before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to execrate
BiblicalUsage: To curse, to execrate, is the word that falls on the serpent in Eden, that God promises to Abraham's enemies, that Moses pronounces on the maker of idols, and that Balaam is forbidden to speak against Israel. The curse is God's sentence, spoken by His mouth or by His prophets.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the curse is real and it is not ours to speak. God cursed the serpent, blessed Abraham, and told Balaam he could not curse a people God had blessed, and that is where our safety lies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ararat (or rather Armenia)
BiblicalUsage: Ararat is the mountain land where the ark rested when the waters went down, the land where Sennacherib's sons fled after murdering their father, and one of the kingdoms called to march against Babylon. The name runs from the flood to the fall of empires.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Ararat is where the old world ended and the new one began, because the ark came to rest there, and every story after it starts on dry ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to engage for matrimony
BiblicalUsage: To betroth, to engage for marriage, is a binding promise before the wedding itself. A man who has betrothed a wife and not taken her is sent home from battle, the law protects a betrothed virgin, a man who lies with an unbetrothed maid must endow her as his wife, and David demands Michal, whom he espoused, back from her second husband.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe betrothal in Scripture is not a casual promise, it is a covenant already binding. God treats a pledge of marriage as a marriage, and so should we.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to awe or (intransitive) to dread; hence, to harass
BiblicalUsage: The word means to be in awe, to dread, and by extension to be the thing that terrifies. Moses says fear not, for the Lord goes with you; Isaiah says let the Lord be your fear and your dread; Joshua is told to be strong and not afraid; and the spies' report had already taught Israel to dread the giants instead of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that dread has to go somewhere, and God means it to land on Him. Fear the Lord and you need not fear the enemy; fear the enemy and you will never enter the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aravnah (or Arnijah or Ornah), a Jebusite
BiblicalUsage: Araunah the Jebusite owned the threshingfloor on the hill where the angel stayed his hand from destroying Jerusalem. Gad told David to build an altar there, Araunah offered the floor and the oxen for nothing, and David refused the gift, saying he would not offer to the Lord what cost him nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Araunah's threshingfloor is where Jerusalem's temple would stand, and the whole story turns on David's refusal of a free offering. A sacrifice that costs nothing is not a sacrifice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of cedar
BiblicalUsage: The word means of cedar, and it appears once, among the merchants of Tyre, trading in chests of rich apparel bound with cords and made of cedar. It is a word for the finest wood, in the finest cargo, of the proudest city.
TheologicalSignificance: Tyre traded in cedar and fine cloth, and the cargo outlasted the city that carried it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {four}
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this is the number four. Four winds strive on the great sea, four great beasts come up from the sea, the four beasts are four kings who rise from the earth, and at the dedication of the house of God the people offer four hundred lambs.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that four in Daniel is the number of the kingdoms of the earth, complete in their pride. Every one of them is measured against the kingdom that has no number and no end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arba, one of the Anakim
BiblicalUsage: Arba is named as the greatest man among the Anakim, the father of Anak, whose name the city of Hebron bore before it was Hebron. Kirjath-arba, the city of Arba, is where Sarah died and where Caleb was given his inheritance among the children of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Arba matters because his name is still on the city when the promise is fulfilled, and the greatest of the giants gives way to the inheritance of Caleb.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: forty
BiblicalUsage: Forty is the number of testing and of a generation's wandering. It rained forty days on the earth, Israel ate manna forty years, God led them forty years in the wilderness to humble and prove them, and Elijah walked forty days and forty nights to the mount of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forty is God's number for a work that cannot be hurried. The rain, the manna, the wilderness, and the prophet's journey all teach the same thing: God finishes what He starts, and He takes the time it takes.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; Wilderness Wanderings
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fourfold
BiblicalUsage: The word means fourfold, and it appears once, when Nathan tells David the rich man must restore the poor man's lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and had no pity.
TheologicalSignificance: Fourfold is the law's arithmetic for a theft without pity, and David pronounces his own sentence before he knows it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {four}
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this is the number four. Four winds strive on the great sea, four great beasts come up from the sea, the four beasts are four kings who rise from the earth, and at the dedication of the house of God the people offer four hundred lambs.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that four in Daniel is the number of the kingdoms of the earth, complete in their pride. Every one of them is measured against the kingdom that has no number and no end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arbathite or inhabitant of (Beth-) Arabah
BiblicalUsage: The word means an Arbathite, a man of Beth-arabah, and it appears twice, naming Abi-albon the Arbathite among David's mighty men and Abiel the Arbathite in the chronicler's list of the same men.
TheologicalSignificance: A man from a little town in the Arabah can stand among David's mighty men, and the lists keep his name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a locust (from its rapid increase)
BiblicalUsage: The locust is the plague that eats a land bare, and it multiplies faster than any army. God sends the locusts over Egypt, Joel says what the palmerworm left the locust has eaten, the psalm remembers that God spoke and the locusts came, and the Proverbs note that locusts have no king yet go forth all of them by bands.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the locust is the smallest picture of the largest judgment. No king, no army, no plan, only a swarm that does what God says, and a land that cannot stop it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arbite or native of Arab
BiblicalUsage: The word means an Arbite, a man of Arab, and it appears once, naming Paarai the Arbite among David's mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: One line in the list of mighty men is enough to keep a man's name, and God counts the men from little towns too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746; original or primeval:--(them of) old (time).
BiblicalUsage: The word means of old time, ancient, from the beginning. Jesus says you have heard it said by them of old time, James says Moses of old time is preached in every city, Peter says God spared not the old world, and Paul says if any man is in Christ, old things are passed away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe old does not mean outdated, and it does not mean safe either. The old world was drowned, the old things pass away in Christ, and the old words of Moses are still preached, because what is ancient can be either judged or kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G757 and G32; a chief angel:--archangel.
BiblicalUsage: The word is archangel, a chief angel, and it appears twice. The Lord will descend with the voice of the archangel and the trump of God, and Michael the archangel contended with the devil over the body of Moses.
TheologicalSignificance: The archangel's voice is the sound of the Lord's return, and Michael's restraint with the devil is the model for how angels fight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G756; (properly abstract) a commencement, or (concretely) chief (in various applications of order, time, place, or rank):--beginning, corner, (at the, the) first (estate), magistrate, power, principality, principle, rule.
BiblicalUsage: The word means beginning, first in time or in rank, and it opens the Bible's biggest claims. In the beginning was the Word, that which was from the beginning we declare to you, Christ is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, and He calls Himself the beginning of the creation of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that every beginning in Scripture points back to one Beginning. Christ was there before anything began, and He is the first in rank over all that was made, so the beginning is not a moment, it is a Person.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and G71; a chief leader:--author, captain, prince.
BiblicalUsage: The word means a chief leader, the author or captain, the one who goes first. Peter says the Jews killed the Prince of life, God exalted Christ to be a Prince and a Saviour, He is the captain of our salvation made perfect through sufferings, and He is the author and finisher of our faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Captain does not send us where He has not gone first. He went through suffering to bring us to glory, and He authors the faith He also finishes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G757 and G2994; people-ruling; Archelaus, a Jewish king:--Archelaus.
BiblicalUsage: Archelaus is named once, when Joseph hears that Archelaus reigns in Judaea in the room of his father Herod. Being afraid to go there, Joseph turns aside to Galilee and settles in Nazareth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a tyrant's son can change the road a family takes, and God used Joseph's fear of Archelaus to bring Jesus to Nazareth.
RelatedPeople: Archelaus; Herod the Great; Joseph, Husband of Mary
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and a derivative of G2413; high-priestly:--of the high-priest.
BiblicalUsage: The word means of the high priest, of his kindred and household, and it appears once, when Peter and John stand before Annas the high priest and as many as were of the kindred of the high priest.
TheologicalSignificance: The high priest's whole household stood against the apostles, and the apostles stood anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and G2409; the high-priest (literally, of the Jews, typically, Christ); by extension a chief priest:--chief (high) priest, chief of the priests.
BiblicalUsage: The high priest is the chief priest, and the word carries both the office and its failure. Caiaphas, high priest that year, says it is expedient that one man die for the people, and Jesus is led to Caiaphas the high priest; but Hebrews says we have a great high priest passed into the heavens, holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the contrast is the whole point. Caiaphas used the office to kill, and Christ fills the office to save, and the better high priest is the one who lives forever to intercede for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and G4166; a head shepherd:--chief shepherd.
BiblicalUsage: The word is chief shepherd, and it appears once, when Peter promises the elders that when the chief Shepherd appears, they shall receive a crown of glory that does not fade away.
TheologicalSignificance: Every shepherd answers to the chief Shepherd, and His appearing is the payday for faithful ones.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and G2462; horse-ruler; Archippus, a Christian:--Archippus.
BiblicalUsage: Archippus is named twice, both times beside Philemon's household. Paul tells the church to say to Archippus, take heed to the ministry you have received in the Lord, that you fulfil it, and he greets Archippus as a fellow soldier in the letter to Philemon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a short word to Archippus is worth a long sermon, because a ministry received in the Lord is a ministry to be fulfilled, not started and dropped.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and G4864; director of the synagogue services:--(chief) ruler of the synagogue.
BiblicalUsage: The ruler of the synagogue directed its services, and the word follows the gospel's hardest moments. Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, falls at Jesus' feet for his dying daughter, a messenger comes from the ruler's house saying she is dead, Crispus the chief ruler believes with all his house, and the rulers of the synagogue invite Paul to speak a word of exhortation.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the rulers of the synagogue show both sides of the gospel's welcome. Some fall at Jesus' feet and some invite Paul to speak, and the synagogue that was meant to keep the law becomes the place where the gospel is first heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and G5045; a chief constructor, i.e. "architect":--masterbuilder.
BiblicalUsage: The word is masterbuilder, a chief constructor, and it appears once, when Paul says that by the grace of God he has laid the foundation as a wise masterbuilder, and another builds on it.
TheologicalSignificance: A wise masterbuilder lays a foundation no one else can move, and Paul laid Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and G5057; a principle tax-gatherer:--chief among the publicans.
BiblicalUsage: The word is chief among the publicans, a principal tax collector, and it appears once, naming Zacchaeus, who was rich, and who climbed a tree to see Jesus pass by.
TheologicalSignificance: The chief tax collector climbed a tree like a child, and Jesus stopped for him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G746 and a compound of G5140 and G2827 (a dinner-bed, because composed of three couches); director of the entertainment:--governor (ruler) of the feast.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the governor of the feast, the master of the banquet, and it appears at Cana, when Jesus tells the servants to draw out the water made wine and bear it to the governor, who tastes it and calls the bridegroom.
TheologicalSignificance: The governor of the feast did not know where the good wine came from, but the servants did, and that is often how a miracle works.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to be first (in political rank or power):--reign (rule) over.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to be first, in rank or in time, to rule or to begin. The rulers of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, the root of Jesse shall rise to reign over the Gentiles, Paul takes bread and begins to eat before the shipwreck, and Jesus begins to warn His disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being first cuts both ways in the Bible. The Gentiles' rulers use first place to lord it over others, but Christ rises to reign by serving, and the beginning of His teaching is a warning against the pride that loves first place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of G757 (through the implication, of precedence); to commence (in order of time):--(rehearse from the) begin(-ning).
BiblicalUsage: The word is the middle voice of to rule, used for beginning, and it marks the great beginnings. From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand, and Jesus Himself began to be about thirty years of age when He stepped into His ministry.
TheologicalSignificance: The beginning of Jesus' preaching is a call to repent, and the kingdom it announces is still the same call today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: present participle of G757; a first (in rank or power):--chief (ruler), magistrate, prince, ruler.
BiblicalUsage: A ruler, a first in rank or power, is the word for the men who run the world. The rulers gather against Peter and John, Moses is asked who made him a ruler and a judge, Nicodemus comes as a ruler of the Jews, and Jesus says now shall the prince of this world be cast out.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that rulers come in two kinds, and Jesus names them both. There are the rulers who gather against the gospel, and there is the prince of this world, who is cast out, and neither of them is the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ard, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ard is named among Benjamin's sons who went down into Egypt with Jacob, and in the wilderness his descendants are numbered as the Ardites. The name is all that survives of him, yet it still marks a family that crossed from Egypt to Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a name preserved through the wilderness count means God kept track of this family too, even when Scripture gives us nothing more than the name itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ardite (collectively) or descendant of Ard
BiblicalUsage: The word means an Ardite, a descendant of Ard, and it appears once, in the census of Benjamin in the plains of Moab, where the family of the Ardites is counted beside the family of Naaman.
TheologicalSignificance: A family named after one man can outlast the man by generations, and the census keeps the count.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ardon, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ardon is named once, as a son of Caleb by Azubah his wife, beside Jesher and Shobab in the genealogy of Judah. His name sits in the line that runs from Judah toward David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in the line of Judah is a name in the line of the promise, even when the story gives us nothing more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pleasant
BiblicalUsage: The word means pleasant or sweet. Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet for a moment, but the mouth ends up full of gravel, and the beloved in the Song says sweet is the voice of the one she loves.
TheologicalSignificance: Sweetness that comes by deceit turns to gravel, and sweetness that comes by love stays sweet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pleasant
BiblicalUsage: The word means pleasant or sweet. Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet for a moment, but the mouth ends up full of gravel, and the beloved in the Song says sweet is the voice of the one she loves.
TheologicalSignificance: Sweetness that comes by deceit turns to gravel, and sweetness that comes by love stays sweet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Ἄρης (the name of the Greek deity of war) and a derivative of G4078; rock of Ares, a place in Athens:--Areopagus, Mars' Hill.
BiblicalUsage: The Areopagus, Mars' Hill, is the rock in Athens where the council sat, and Paul is brought there to explain his new teaching. He stands in the midst of Mars' Hill and speaks to the men of Athens about the unknown God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Areopagus is where the gospel met philosophy on its own ground, and Paul did not flinch, because the unknown God was not unknown to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: long
BiblicalUsage: The word means long, and it is the Bible's picture of God's patience. The Lord proclaims Himself longsuffering, slow to anger, Moses pleads the same name when Israel rebels, Jonah complains that God is slow to anger and ready to relent, and Nehemiah remembers that God was gracious and merciful and slow to anger when His people refused to listen.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's longsuffering is the reason any of us are still here. He is slow to anger and ready to pardon, and Jonah's complaint about it is the best news in the Bible for sinners.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: uncircumcised (i.e. still having the prepuce uncurtailed)
BiblicalUsage: Uncircumcised is the word for one outside the covenant sign, and it becomes the Bible's insult and its warning. The uncircumcised child is cut off from his people, no uncircumcised person may eat the passover, David asks who this uncircumcised Philistine is to defy the armies of the living God, and Jeremiah says God will punish all who are circumcised with the uncircumcised.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the outward sign was never the point, and Jeremiah proves it. A circumcised heart is what God looks for, and an uncircumcised heart in a circumcised body is judged the same as a Philistine's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: uncircumcised (i.e. still having the prepuce uncurtailed)
BiblicalUsage: Uncircumcised is the word for one outside the covenant sign, and it becomes the Bible's insult and its warning. The uncircumcised child is cut off from his people, no uncircumcised person may eat the passover, David asks who this uncircumcised Philistine is to defy the armies of the living God, and Jeremiah says God will punish all who are circumcised with the uncircumcised.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the outward sign was never the point, and Jeremiah proves it. A circumcised heart is what God looks for, and an uncircumcised heart in a circumcised body is judged the same as a Philistine's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a heap; specifically, a sheaf
BiblicalUsage: The word is a heap, a pile of grain or spoil, and it marks both blessing and ruin. The people bring tithes and lay them by heaps in the temple, the sabbath-breakers carry sheaves into Jerusalem, Babylon is to be cast up as heaps, and a man who came to a heap of twenty measures found only ten.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that heaps tell the truth about a nation. Heaps of tithes mean a people giving freely, heaps of spoil mean a city judged, and a heap that shrinks when you measure it means God has withheld the blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps the same as G730; a lamb (as a male):--lamb.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a lamb, a young male sheep, and it appears once, when Jesus sends out the seventy and says, I send you forth as lambs among wolves.
TheologicalSignificance: Lambs among wolves is not a mistake in the plan, it is the plan.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G697; an Areopagite or member of the court held on Mars' Hill:--Areopagite.
BiblicalUsage: The word means an Areopagite, a member of the council that met on Mars' Hill. It appears once, naming Dionysius the Areopagite, who believed when Paul preached in Athens.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one man from the council believing is enough to show that the gospel can reach the highest seats in the city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a longing for
BiblicalUsage: The word is a longing, the request of the lips, and it appears once, when the psalm says God has given the king his heart's desire and has not withheld the request of his lips.
TheologicalSignificance: A longing laid before God is not withheld when the heart is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G700; complaisance:--pleasing.
BiblicalUsage: The word is pleasing, complaisance, and it appears once, when Paul prays that the Colossians will walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work.
TheologicalSignificance: A life that pleases the Lord is a life that bears fruit, and the two cannot be separated.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G142 (through the idea of exciting emotion); to be agreeable (or by implication, to seek to be so):--please.
BiblicalUsage: To please, to seek to be agreeable, is the word for the aim of a Christian's life, and Paul draws the line sharply. He pleases all men in all things, seeking not his own profit but the profit of many; yet if he still pleased men he would not be the servant of Christ; the strong ought to bear the weak and not please themselves; and the gospel is spoken not as pleasing men, but God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that pleasing people and pleasing God are not the same work, and they cannot both be the master. Paul pleased men only where it served their salvation, and the moment pleasing men would cost the truth, he stopped.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G700; agreeable; by implication, fit:--(things that) please(-ing), reason.
BiblicalUsage: The word means pleasing, agreeable, fit. Jesus says He always does the things that please the Father, the apostles say it is not fitting to leave the word of God and serve tables, Herod sees that killing James pleases the Jews, and John says we receive from God because we do the things that are pleasing in His sight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pleasing God is the only measure that matters, because men are pleased by the wrong things as often as the right ones. Jesus pleased the Father, and that is the pattern.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; John the Apostle; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin; Aretas, an Arabian:--Aretas.
