Definition: from G765; to be (by implied act) impious or wicked:--commit (live, that after should live) ungodly.
BiblicalUsage: To commit ungodly deeds is used once, in Enoch's prophecy quoted by Jude. The Lord cometh with ten thousands of His saints, to execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for ungodly deeds carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the courtroom in it, that the deeds will be named, and the ungodly convinced of them, when the Lord comes with His saints.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G4576; irreverent, i.e. (by extension) impious or wicked:-- ungodly (man).
BiblicalUsage: The ungodly are those without God, and the New Testament will not soften the word. God justifieth the ungodly, and faith is counted for righteousness; the law is made for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners; Peter asks where the ungodly and the sinner shall appear if the righteous scarcely be saved; and the heavens and earth are reserved unto fire against the day of judgment of ungodly men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'ungodly' is the word that makes the gospel good news: God justifies the ungodly, not the deserving. The same word names the men the fire is reserved for, and I hold that the difference between the two is faith, the ungodly who believe are counted righteous, and the ungodly who will not are left to the judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed σελγής (of uncertain derivation, but apparently meaning continent); licentiousness (sometimes including other vices):--filthy, lasciviousness, wantonness.
BiblicalUsage: Lasciviousness is wantonness without shame, the flesh let loose, and the apostles name it in their lists of sins. It is a work of the flesh in Galatians, the Gentiles give themselves over to it to work all uncleanness with greediness, Peter says the time past of our life may suffice to have wrought it, and Lot is delivered, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lasciviousness is the sin of a conscience gone numb: not a fall in a weak moment, but a life given over to uncleanness with greediness. Lot is the proof that a righteous soul can live in the middle of it and be vexed day by day, and I hold that the gospel's answer is not better management but a new heart that wants to be clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and the base of G4591; unmarked, i.e. (figuratively) ignoble:--mean.
BiblicalUsage: This word is used once, when Paul is seized in Jerusalem and asks to speak. He says, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city, and he asks leave to speak unto the people.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a city of no mean standing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the moment, that Paul claims his citizenship before he claims his gospel, and the captain lets him speak.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H836); Aser (i.e. Asher), an Israelite tribe:--Aser.
BiblicalUsage: Aser is Asher in the Greek spelling, and the name turns up twice in the New Testament. Anna the prophetess is of the tribe of Aser, an old widow who serves God with fastings and prayers night and day; and twelve thousand of the tribe of Aser are sealed among the servants of God.
TheologicalSignificance: A tribe named for a prophetess and for the sealed tells me that Asher's blessing has not run out: the tribe that was promised bread and royal dainties still has a widow praying in the temple, and a sealed remnant in the last days.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a moth
BiblicalUsage: The moth eats what men trust, and the prophets use it for the enemies of God and the pride of man. Isaiah says the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool; and Eliphaz asks how much less man, who dwells in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who is crushed before the moth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the moth is God's answer to everything that looks lasting: the garment is eaten, the house of clay is crushed, and only the righteousness that is for ever stands. And I hold that the man who knows he is dust before the moth is the man who is ready to hear that God's salvation is for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: guilt; by implication, a fault; also a sin-offering
BiblicalUsage: The guilt offering is the offering for the sin a man did not mean to do, and for the sin he did not know he did. If a soul commit a trespass through ignorance, he shall bring a ram for a trespass offering; Isaiah says thou shalt make His soul an offering for sin, and He shall see His seed; and the Philistines are told to return the ark with a trespass offering, lest His hand be not removed from them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the guilt offering is the most merciful part of the law, because it covers the sin you did not know you did: ignorance is no excuse, but it is not beyond atonement either. And Isaiah takes the offering and lays it on the Servant, whose soul is made the offering for sin, and I hold that there is the whole gospel, that Christ was made the guilt offering for the sins we never even knew we committed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be guilty; by implication to be punished or perish
BiblicalUsage: To be guilty is to owe God for a sin, whether you knew it or not, and the law will not let you plead ignorance. If the whole congregation sin through ignorance and the thing be hid, yet are they guilty; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty; Hosea says God will go and return to His place till they acknowledge their offence; and the law says when a man or woman shall commit any sin, and be guilty, they shall confess.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe guilt in the Bible is a debt, not a feeling: you can be guilty and not feel it, and you can feel guilty and not be. The debt is real either way, and the only way out of it is the confession the law commands and the offering the law provides, and I hold that Christ paid the debt the law could only point to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: smoke, literally or figuratively (vapor, dust, anger)
BiblicalUsage: Smoke is the sign of God's presence, and it fills the Bible from the covenant to the temple. A smoking furnace and a burning lamp pass between the pieces of Abram's sacrifice, Mount Sinai is altogether on a smoke because the LORD descends on it in fire, the house of the temple is filled with smoke when the seraphim cry Holy, and David says there went up a smoke out of His nostrils.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe smoke is the visible sign of a God who cannot be looked at: fire on the mountain, a furnace in the dark, a temple full of cloud. It hides Him and it shows Him at once, and I hold that the smoke over Sinai and the smoke in the temple are the same sign, that God has come down to meet His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ashan is a town in the low country of Judah, given to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's inheritance. Joshua lists it among the cities of Judah, and again among the cities of Simeon, and the chronicler names it among the villages where the Simeonites dwelt.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named three times in the lists of the inheritance tells me that the land was given out town by town, and that Simeon's share inside Judah was measured and written down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to smoke, whether literal or figurative
BiblicalUsage: To smoke is what God's anger and God's mountain do, and the Bible uses it for both. The whole mount quaked greatly and smoked as a furnace when the LORD descended, Moses warns that the anger of the LORD and His jealousy shall smoke against the man who blesses himself in his heart, and the psalm says He looketh on the earth, and it trembleth, He toucheth the hills, and they smoke.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smoking of the mountain and the smoking of anger are the same picture: God is a consuming fire, and what He touches trembles. The man who blesses himself while he walks in his own heart is warned plainly, and I hold that the warning is mercy, that he might turn before the fire falls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to press upon, i.e. oppress, defraud, violate, overflow
BiblicalUsage: To oppress is to press a man down and keep him down, and the prophets name it as plainly as the law forbids it. The law says thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy, Amos cries against the cows of Bashan who oppress the poor and crush the needy, the Preacher sees the tears of the oppressed with no comforter, and Samuel asks the people, whom have I defrauded, whom have I oppressed?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe oppression is the sin the prophets never let go of, because it is the sin of the strong against the weak, and God hears the tears of the oppressed even when no man comforts them. Samuel could ask the question and get silence for an answer, and I hold that the ruler who can ask it is the ruler God is pleased with.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to accumulate; chiefly (specifically) to grow (causatively, make) rich
BiblicalUsage: To grow rich is God's work and man's temptation, and the Bible holds both together. Hannah sings that the LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich, He bringeth low, and lifteth up; Abram refuses so much as a thread from the king of Sodom, lest he say I have made Abram rich; and the proverb says the blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and He addeth no sorrow with it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe riches are God's to give and God's to take, and the difference between Abram's riches and the rich fool's is who made him rich. The blessing of the LORD makes rich without sorrow, and I hold that the man who lets God make him rich is the only rich man who sleeps well.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be straight (used in the widest sense, especially to be level, right, happy); figuratively, to go forward, be honest, proper
BiblicalUsage: To be straight is to be right, level and happy, and the Bible uses the word for the way that leads to blessing. Leah says happy am I, for the daughters will call me blessed, and calls her son Asher; wisdom is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her, and happy is every one that retaineth her; Isaiah says learn to do well, seek judgment, relieve the oppressed; and Malachi says all nations shall call you blessed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe straight and happy are the same word for a reason: the life that walks straight is the life that ends blessed. Leah's happiness, wisdom's tree of life and the nations calling Israel blessed are all one promise, and I hold that the straight way is the happy way, because God made it so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably to be sleek, i.e. glossy; hence (through the idea of polishing) to excogitate (as if forming in the mind)
BiblicalUsage: This word is used twice, for growing sleek and for thinking upon. Jeremiah says the wicked are waxen fat, they shine, they overpass the deeds of the wicked; and the shipmaster comes to Jonah in the storm and says, arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for sleekness and for thought carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast, that the sleek rich shine while the poor go unjudged, and the heathen sailor begs God to think upon them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asbea, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ashbea is named once, as the head of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea, in the families of Shelah the son of Judah. The verse gives his house and his trade and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A linen worker named once in a list of Judah's families tells me that God counts the tradesmen as well as the kings, and that fine linen for the house of God was a family calling.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashbel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ashbel is a son of Benjamin, named three times, in the list of those who went down into Egypt with Jacob, in the census of the wilderness, and in the chronicler's genealogy of Benjamin. His sons are the Ashbelites, and the name is counted in every list.
TheologicalSignificance: A son of Benjamin counted going into Egypt, counted in the wilderness, and counted after the exile tells me that God keeps the tribes by name through every generation, and none is lost on the way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ashbelite (collectively) or descendant of Ashbel
BiblicalUsage: The Ashbelites are the family of Ashbel the son of Benjamin, named once, in the census in the plains of Moab. The sons of Benjamin after their families are counted, and of Ashbel comes the family of the Ashbelites.
TheologicalSignificance: The family of Ashbel counted in the wilderness carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the record, that Benjamin's sons were numbered family by family before they entered the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashchur, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ashchur is named twice, as the father of Tekoa, in the families of Judah. After Hezron died in Calebephratah, his wife Abiah bare him Ashur the father of Tekoa, and the chronicler names him again among the sons of Hezron.
TheologicalSignificance: A father of a town named twice in a genealogy tells me that Tekoa had a founder worth naming, and that the towns of Judah were built by men whose names the chronicler kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashdod, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ashdod is a city of the Philistines, and its story is the ark's story. The Philistines take the ark to Ashdod and set it by Dagon, and the hand of the LORD is heavy on them of Ashdod, smiting them with emerods; Amos says God will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod, and Uzziah breaks down the wall of Ashdod and builds cities among the Philistines.
TheologicalSignificance: A Philistine city that kept the ark for seven months and was smitten for it tells me that God's presence is no trophy: Dagon falls on his face, the people are smitten, and the city that took the ark is glad to send it away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ashdodite (often collectively) or inhabitant of Asdod
BiblicalUsage: The Ashdodites are the people of Ashdod, and they turn up where Israel meets the Philistines. The men of Ashdod rise early and find Dagon fallen on his face before the ark, Joshua names Ashdod among the land that remains to be taken, and Nehemiah finds Jews who have married wives of Ashdod, whose children speak half in the speech of Ashdod.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Ashdodites matter because they are the neighbours Israel could never quite conquer and never quite keep away from: their god falls before the ark, their land is left untaken, and their speech creeps into the children's mouths. And I hold that Nehemiah's anger is the right one, that a people who lose their language have lost more than words.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only adverb) in the language of Ashdod
BiblicalUsage: The speech of Ashdod is named once, in Nehemiah's grief over the marriages with foreign wives. Their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a foreign tongue carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the sorrow in it, that a generation of Judah's children could not speak the language of their fathers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashdoth-Pisgah, a place east of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Ashdothpisgah is the slopes of Pisgah, the place east of the Jordan where the land drops down to the salt sea. Moses names it as the border of the land Reuben and Gad inherit, and again as the far edge of the Arabah under Pisgah, and Joshua gives its slopes to Reuben.
TheologicalSignificance: A place named for the slopes under a mountain tells me how God measures out the land: mountain, slope and sea, each with its name, and the tribes take up their inheritance where the mountain runs down to the water.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ravine
BiblicalUsage: The slope is the hillside running down to the plain, and it is used for the borders of the land. Moses gives Reuben the plain under the springs of Pisgah, Joshua smites all the country of the hills and the south and the vale and the springs, and the kings he defeats are listed by the same country, hills and valleys and springs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the springs and slopes are named so often because the land is the promise made visible: every hillside and spring has its place in the gift, and the God who promised the land knows it hill by hill. And I hold that the God who counts the slopes is the God who keeps the promise, down to the last spring in the valley.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: guilty; hence, presenting a sin-offering
BiblicalUsage: Guilty is the word Joseph's brothers use when they remember the pit, and the word the wise woman of Tekoa turns back on David. They say we are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul; the woman says the king is as one which is faulty, in that he does not fetch home again his banished; and the men who married strange wives give their hands and offer a ram for their trespass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'guilty' is the word that opens the door to mercy: the brothers say it at last, the woman says it to the king, and the men who married foreign wives own it with a ram in their hands. Confession is the beginning of the way home, and I hold that God never turns away the man who says he is guilty and brings the offering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: smoky
BiblicalUsage: Smoky is used twice, for the mountain and for the firebrands. The people see the thunderings and the lightnings and the mountain smoking, and stand afar off; and Isaiah tells Ahaz not to fear the two tails of smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin and of the son of Remaliah.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for smoky carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the mountain smokes with God's presence, and the kings who threaten Judah are only smoking ends, already going out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: happy; Asher, a son of Jacob, and the tribe descended from him, with its territory; also a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Asher is the son of Jacob by Zilpah, and the tribe that comes from him, and his name means happy. Leah says happy am I and calls him Asher, Jacob blesses him that out of Asher his bread shall be fat and he shall yield royal dainties, Moses says let Asher be blessed with children and dip his foot in oil, and Joshua gives his tribe the coast from Helkath to the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: A son named Happy, blessed with fat bread and oil and a coast by the sea, tells me that God's blessing is not thin: Asher gets the best of the land, and the name his mother gave him in joy is the name his tribe carries into the inheritance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: who, which, what, that; also (as an adverb and a conjunction) when, where, how, because, in order that, etc.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for who, which, what and that, the little word that joins one clause to the next, and it is used thousands of times. God saw every thing that He had made, and behold, it was very good, and the LORD says, I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: One small joining word carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is that the whole Bible hangs on it, that God made all that He made, and that He brought His people out of Egypt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asherah (or Astarte) a Phoenician goddess; also an image of the same
BiblicalUsage: Asherah is the goddess of the Canaanites, and the grove that bears her name, and the Bible names her wherever Israel goes wrong. Judah builds high places and images and groves under every green tree, Asa removes his mother Maachah from being queen because she made an idol in a grove, and Gideon is told to throw down the altar of Baal and cut down the grove that is by it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Asherah is the proof that idolatry in Israel was not a foreign import but a home-grown sin: the groves stand under every green tree, a queen mother makes the idol, and it takes a king and a judge to cut them down. And I hold that the groves are still cut down the same way, by men who will obey God at night with ten men and a new altar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Asherite (collectively) or descendant of Asher
BiblicalUsage: The Asherites are the tribe of Asher, named once, in the conquest that was never finished. The Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a tribe that dwelt among the Canaanites carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the failure in it, that Asher kept the land but not the victory, and lived among the people God told them to drive out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably to shrink, i.e. fail
BiblicalUsage: To waste away is what grief does to the eyes and the strength, and David uses it three times in his sorrow. Mine eye is consumed because of grief, it waxeth old because of all mine enemies; mine eye is consumed with grief, yea, my soul and my belly; and my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wasting away is the honest language of a man who knows his sin has cost him his strength: the eye dims, the bones are consumed, and the grief is not only sorrow but iniquity. And I hold that David's answer is the same in both psalms, to cry for mercy, and the Lord who hears is the Lord who restores.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to purpose
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is used once, for the king's thought about Daniel. Daniel is preferred above the presidents and princes because an excellent spirit is in him, and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a king's purpose carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the moment, that a heathen king sees the Spirit in a captive and decides to set him over everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashima, a deity of Hamath
BiblicalUsage: Ashima is named once, as the god of Hamath, one of the peoples the king of Assyria settles in the cities of Samaria. Every nation makes gods of their own, the men of Hamath make Ashima, and they set them in the high places the Samaritans had made.
TheologicalSignificance: A god named once for a people moved into Samaria tells me how the land filled with idols: each nation brings its own, and the high places hold them all side by side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rich, whether literal or figurative (noble)
BiblicalUsage: Rich is used for the man with much and for the man with more than he needs, and the Bible watches him closely. Nathan tells David of a rich man with exceeding many flocks and herds, the rich shall not give more than half a shekel for the ransom of the soul, the Preacher says curse not the rich in thy bedchamber, for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and the Servant is appointed a grave with the wicked and with the rich in His death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rich is a dangerous word in the Bible, because the rich man in Nathan's story is the thief, the rich man's half shekel buys no more than the poor man's, and the rich man's grave is where they lay the Servant. And I hold that the only safe riches are the ones God gives, because the rich who trust in riches fall, and the rich who trust in God are rich indeed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (ruined) foundation
BiblicalUsage: The foundation is named once, for the ruined city of Moab. Moab shall howl for Moab, every one shall howl, for the foundations of Kirhareseth shall ye mourn, surely they are stricken, and the vineyards and the summer fruits are gone with them.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a city's foundations carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that when God judges Moab He takes the foundations too, and the mourning is for what held the city up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something closely pressed together, i.e. a cake of raisins or other comfits
BiblicalUsage: The cake of raisins is the festival food, pressed together and sweet, and it is used for feasting and for love. David deals to every one of Israel a cake of bread and a good piece of flesh and a flagon of wine when the ark comes home, the beloved asks to be stayed with flagons and comforted with apples, for she is sick of love, and Hosea is told to love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, as the children of Israel love flagons of wine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cake of raisins says that God gives His people sweet things for the feast, and that love asks for them plainly: stayed with flagons, comforted with apples, sick of love. And Hosea's flagons are the warning with it, that the same sweetness Israel loves becomes the love of an adulteress, and I hold that the heart must choose which love it will feed on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashkenaz, a Japhethite, also his descendants
BiblicalUsage: Ashkenaz is a son of Gomer, named three times, in the table of nations, in the chronicler's copy of it, and in Jeremiah's call to the nations against Babylon. The prophet says set ye up a standard in the land, blow the trumpet among the nations, prepare the nations against her, and call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni and Ashchenaz.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that runs from the table of nations to the fall of Babylon tells me that God calls the far nations by name, and that the same Ashkenaz who descends from Japheth is summoned to march against the greatest city on earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: guiltiness, a fault, the presentation of a sin-offering
BiblicalUsage: Guiltiness is the guilt that stays on a people, and the Bible uses it for Israel's sin after the return and for the sin that brings the sword. Ezra says our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens; the people leave the house of the LORD and serve groves and idols, and wrath comes upon Judah for this their trespass; and Amos says they that swear by the sin of Samaria shall fall, and never rise up again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe guiltiness is guilt that has grown up to heaven and will not be put down: Ezra is ashamed to lift his face, the chronicler says wrath came for it, and Amos says those who swear by it shall fall and never rise. And I hold that the only answer to guilt grown up to heaven is the confession Ezra makes, on his knees, with his face to the ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fat-field
BiblicalUsage: This word is used once, for the desolate places where the blind grope. Isaiah says we grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes, we stumble at noonday as in the night, we are in desolate places as dead men.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a desolate place carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that sin leaves a people groping in the dark at noon, as if they were dead men already.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a night watch
BiblicalUsage: The night watch is the division of the night when the guard changes, and God moves in it. In the morning watch the LORD looks through the pillar of fire and of the cloud and troubles the host of Egypt, Gideon comes to the camp in the beginning of the middle watch, and Saul smites the Ammonites in the morning watch.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the morning watch is God's hour: the Egyptians are troubled in it, Gideon strikes in it, and Saul wins in it. The night is divided into watches, and I hold that the God who keeps the last watch is the God who fights for His people while they sleep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashnah, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ashnah is the name of two towns in the low country of Judah, both listed in the inheritance. One stands in the valley with Eshtaol and Zoreah, and the other with Jiphtah and Nezib, and the verse gives the name and the neighbours and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: Two towns sharing one name in the same inheritance tell me that the land was given out village by village, and that even the doubled names were written down, so no town would be lost from the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: oppressive (as noun, a tyrant)
BiblicalUsage: This word is used once, for the oppression Jeremiah forbids the king of Judah. Execute ye judgment and righteousness, he says, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor, and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the oppressor carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the command, that the king's first duty is to deliver the spoiled from the hand of the man who presses them down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: shining, i.e. polished
BiblicalUsage: This word is used once, for the bright iron in the market of Tyre. Dan and Javan go to and fro in her fairs, and bright iron, cassia and calamus are in her market, among the goods the nations bring to the great city of the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for polished iron carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that Tyre's wealth is made of bright metal and sweet spice, and it will all sink with her.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a quiver or arrow-case
BiblicalUsage: The quiver is the case for arrows, and it is used for the Servant and for the enemy. The LORD has made my mouth like a sharp sword, and made me a polished shaft, and hid me in His quiver; and Jeremiah says the enemy's quiver is as an open sepulchre, they are all mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a quiver carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the Servant is kept hidden in God's quiver until He is drawn, and the enemy's quiver is an open grave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashpenaz, a Babylonian eunuch
BiblicalUsage: Ashpenaz is named once, as the prince of the eunuchs in Babylon, the master of the king's chamber. Nebuchadnezzar commands him to bring certain of the children of Israel, of the king's seed and of the princes, to be taught the learning of the Chaldeans, and Daniel is among them.
TheologicalSignificance: A Babylonian official named once because he chooses Daniel's food and his name tells me that the exile begins with small things, what a boy eats and what he is called, and that Daniel's stand starts there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a heap of rubbish or filth
BiblicalUsage: The dunghill is the heap of filth outside the city, and the Bible uses it for the lowest place a man can be, and the highest lift God gives. Hannah sings that He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes; Nehemiah rebuilds the dung gate and the wall by it; and the psalm sings the same song, that He lifteth the needy out of the dunghill.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dunghill is the gospel in one word: the poor are raised out of the dust, the beggar is lifted from the filth, and set among princes. God does not wait for men to climb out of the heap, He lifts them out of it Himself, and I hold that the dung gate Nehemiah builds is the gate we all come in by.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashkelon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ashkelon is a city of the Philistines on the coast, and it is named for Samson's vengeance, for David's lament and for the prophets' judgment. Samson goes down to Ashkelon and slays thirty men for their garments, David says tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon, Amos says God will cut off the inhabitant from Ashkelon, and Jeremiah says baldness is come upon Gaza, and Ashkelon is cut off.
TheologicalSignificance: A Philistine city named for a lament and for judgments tells me that Ashkelon is the place Israel's grief and God's judgment meet: David will not have Saul's death published in its streets, and the prophets say the city will be cut off all the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a conjurer}
BiblicalUsage: The enchanter is the wise man of Babylon, the one the king calls when no one else can answer. The Chaldeans say there is no man on earth who can shew the king's matter, for no king has asked such things of any magician or astrologer or Chaldean; Daniel says the secret the king demands cannot be shewed by the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians or the soothsayers; and the queen remembers that in Daniel's father there is the spirit of the holy gods, and the king made him master of the magicians and astrologers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the enchanters matter because they are the best Babylon has, and the best is not enough: no magician can tell the king his dream, and the man who can is the captive who prays. And I hold that the queen's memory is the verdict, that the Spirit of God in Daniel is greater than all the wisdom of Babylon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a conjurer}
BiblicalUsage: The enchanter is the wise man of Babylon, the one the king calls when no one else can answer. The Chaldeans say there is no man on earth who can shew the king's matter, for no king has asked such things of any magician or astrologer or Chaldean; Daniel says the secret the king demands cannot be shewed by the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians or the soothsayers; and the queen remembers that in Daniel's father there is the spirit of the holy gods, and the king made him master of the magicians and astrologers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the enchanters matter because they are the best Babylon has, and the best is not enough: no magician can tell the king his dream, and the man who can is the captive who prays. And I hold that the queen's memory is the verdict, that the Spirit of God in Daniel is greater than all the wisdom of Babylon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashshur, the second son of Shem; also his descendants and the country occupied by them (i.e. Assyria), its region and its empire
BiblicalUsage: Asshur is the son of Shem, and the nation and the land that bear his name, and it grows from a man into an empire. Out of the land of Shinar went forth Asshur and builded Nineveh, Isaiah calls Assyria the rod of God's anger and the staff of His indignation, and in the days of Hezekiah Sennacherib king of Assyria comes up against the fenced cities of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that grows from a son of Shem to the rod of God's anger tells me how God uses nations: Assyria is His staff to punish, and then His staff is broken for its pride. And I hold that the God who raised Assyria up is the God who shuts its king outside the walls of Jerusalem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashtaroth, the name of a Sidonian deity, and of a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Ashtaroth is the city of Og king of Bashan, and the name of the goddess whose house holds Saul's armour. Moses names Og, who dwelt at Astaroth, Samuel tells Israel to put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth and serve the LORD only, and the Philistines put Saul's armour in the house of Ashtaroth after they take his body.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that is both a city of giants and a house for a dead king's armour tells me that Ashtaroth stands for the old powers Israel had to leave behind: the gods of the Canaanites and the armour of a fallen king both end up in her house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: increase
BiblicalUsage: The increase is the young of the flock and the herd, and the blessing of the land, and Moses promises it to obedience and takes it away for disobedience. The LORD will love thee and bless thee, and bless the fruit of thy womb and the fruit of thy land, and the increase of thy kine and the flocks of thy sheep; blessed shall be the fruit of thy body and the fruit of thy ground and the fruit of thy cattle; and the enemy shall eat the increase of thy cattle and the fruit of thy land until thou be destroyed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the increase of the flock is the test of the covenant: obedience fills the folds, and disobedience empties them. The same flocks are the blessing and the loss, and I hold that God means it when He says the land's fruitfulness follows His people's faithfulness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ashterathite or inhabitant of Ashtaroth
BiblicalUsage: The Ashterathite is Uzzia, named once, in the list of David's mighty men. He stands among the thirty, a man of Ashtaroth east of Jordan, and the verse gives his name and his town and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: Uzzia's hometown is all we know of him, and that carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the reminder that David's mighty men came from both sides of the Jordan, and their towns were worth writing down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashteroth-Karnaim, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Ashteroth Karnaim is named once, as the place where Chedorlaomer and the kings with him smite the Rephaims. The kings come in the fourteenth year and smite the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim.
TheologicalSignificance: A place named once for a battle with giants tells me that the land east of Jordan was a land of Rephaim before it was a land of Israel, and that the kings who smote them were only the beginning of the wars for the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: eleven or (ordinal) eleventh
BiblicalUsage: Eleven is used for journeys and curtains and captains, and it is the number just short of twelve. In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, Moses speaks to Israel all the LORD commanded him; the tabernacle has eleven curtains of goats' hair for a covering; and Benaiah the Pirathonite is captain of the eleventh course, with twenty-four thousand in his course.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eleven is the number that says almost: eleven months into the fortieth year Moses speaks, eleven curtains cover the tabernacle, and the eleventh captain stands in a roster of twelve. It is the count that reminds me the promise is nearly kept, and the last month and the last captain are still to come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashtoreth, the Phoenician goddess of love (and increase)
BiblicalUsage: Ashtoreth is the goddess of the Zidonians, and Solomon's fall is told by her name. Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites; the LORD says they have forsaken Me and worshipped Ashtoreth; and Josiah defiles the high places Solomon built for Ashtoreth, the abomination of the Zidonians, on the right hand of the mount of corruption.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ashtoreth is the name that marks Solomon's fall: the wisest king in Israel builds high places for a goddess, and the kingdom breaks in his son's days. And I hold that Josiah's defiling of those high places is the answer, that what one king builds in folly another must tear down in faithfulness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: cogitation
BiblicalUsage: This word is used once, for the thought of a man at ease about a man who slips. Job says he that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease, and the friends who sit in comfort despise the lamp that is going out.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the thought of the comfortable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that the man at ease despises the lamp that is about to go out, and calls it wisdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the cedar tree or some other light elastic wood
BiblicalUsage: This word is used once, for the timber of Tyre's benches. Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars, and the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim, and the wood is the light, springy timber the shipwrights chose for the benches.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a shipwright's timber carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that Tyre's glory is built of oaks and ivory and fine wood, and it all goes down with the ship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a step
BiblicalUsage: The step is the going of a man's feet, and the Bible watches where they go. Job says my foot hath held His steps, His way have I kept, and not declined; again, if my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes; and the proverb says the simple believeth every word, but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the step is the smallest unit of the Christian life: Job held His steps and did not decline, and the prudent man looks well to his going. The way is walked one step at a time, and I hold that the man who watches his steps is the man who stays on the way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: used in plural masculine as abstractly, tyranny
BiblicalUsage: Oppression is the cry of the pressed-down, and the prophets and the Preacher hear it together. Amos is told to publish in the palaces of Ashdod that there are great tumults and oppressions within her; the Preacher returns and considers all the oppressions done under the sun, and beholds the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and Elihu says men cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe oppression is the sin God hears first, because the oppressed cry and the cry goes up to Him: the tumults in the palaces, the tears with no comforter, the arm of the mighty pressing down. And I hold that the God who hears the cry is the God who will answer it, and the oppressor's arm is not the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ashurite (collectively) or inhabitant of Ashur, a district in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: The Ashurites are named twice, once among the sons of Dedan, the grandsons of Abraham by Keturah, and once among the peoples over whom Abner makes Ishbosheth king. The name marks a people of the south, and the verse gives the family and the kingdom and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A people named twice, once in a genealogy and once in a kingdom, tells me that Abraham's house by Keturah spread wide, and that the Ashurites were counted among the tribes when Israel was divided.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: foundation
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for a foundation, and it shows up only once, in the judgment on Babylon. Her foundations are fallen, her walls thrown down, because the vengeance of the LORD has come on her.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that no foundation built against God stands, and Babylon's fall is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ashvath, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ashvath appears once, in the genealogy of Asher, listed among the sons of Japhlet. His name survives only in that family record, as one of the heads counted among Asher's descendants.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept in the record matters even when nothing else is told about the man, because God counts His people one by one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Asia, i.e. Asia Minor, or (usually) only its western shore:--Asia.
BiblicalUsage: Asia was the Roman province on the western edge of Asia Minor, and it shows up all through the New Testament. Men from Asia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost, Paul's teaching in Ephesus reached everyone living in Asia within two years, John wrote to the seven churches there, and Peter addressed his letter to believers scattered through Asia and the regions around it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Asia matters because it shows how fast the gospel moved beyond Jerusalem, into cities and provinces that had never heard it. The churches there were real congregations with real struggles, and the Lord's letters to them still speak to any church that has lost its first love or grown cold.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; John the Apostle; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G773; an Asian (i.e. Asiatic) or an inhabitant of Asia:--of Asia.
BiblicalUsage: Only one verse uses this word, naming Tychicus and Trophimus as Asians travelling with Paul toward Jerusalem. They were part of the company carrying the gift for the believers there.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gospel made travelling companions out of strangers, and Asia's sons walked beside Paul as brothers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G773 and G746; an Asiarch or president of the public festivities in a city of Asia Minor:--chief of Asia.
BiblicalUsage: The chiefs of Asia were the wealthy men who sponsored the games and festivals in the province, and some of them were Paul's friends. When the riot broke out in Ephesus they sent him a message, begging him not to go into the theatre.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can put friends in unexpected places, and these officials risked their standing to keep Paul safe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G777; fasting (the state):--abstinence.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for going without food, and it appears once, in the storm that carried Paul's ship toward Malta. After many days of abstinence the men were worn down, and Paul stood up among them to speak.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that fear and hunger had done their work on that ship, and Paul's calm in the middle of it pointed to a God who was still in charge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G4621; without (taking) food:--fasting.
BiblicalUsage: Paul told the men on the ship that this was the fourteenth day they had waited and gone without food, and he urged them to eat for their health. The word describes the empty stomachs of men who had been too afraid to eat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's care for their bodies showed the same gospel he preached, that God looks after the whole person.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asiel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Asiel is named once, among the princes of Simeon listed in the tribal record. He stands in the genealogy as one of the leaders of his father's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the chronicler kept these names because every family and every leader counted in Israel's story, even when their deeds are not told.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: tenth; by abbreviation, tenth month or (feminine) part
BiblicalUsage: This word counts tenths, and it turns up in three different corners of the law and the calendar. It marks the tenth generation barred from the congregation, the tenth part of an ephah offered by Aaron and his sons, the tenth month when the mountain tops were seen after the flood, and the fast of the tenth month that Zechariah says will become joy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tenth keeps showing up because God claims a portion of everything, time and grain and generations alike. The fasts that once marked judgment would turn to feasting, and I hold that the God who counts tenths is the same God who turns mourning into joy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same as G4632; to elaborate, i.e. (figuratively) train (by implication, strive):--exercise.
BiblicalUsage: Paul told Felix that he trained himself, like an athlete in the games, to keep a conscience clear before God and men. It is the only place this word appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a clear conscience is not an accident, it is the result of daily training, and Paul's example still sets the pattern.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G778; a leathern (or skin) bag used as a bottle:--bottle.
BiblicalUsage: A bottle in the ancient world was a skin bag, and Jesus used it for one of His plainest pictures. New wine bursts old skins, so it must go into new ones, and the point was that His teaching could not be poured into the old forms without breaking them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus was telling His hearers that the new covenant is not a patch on the old one, it is something fresh that needs room to grow. Trying to hold it in the old skins only spills the wine and ruins the skins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of the base of G2237; with pleasure:--gladly.
BiblicalUsage: When Paul reached Jerusalem the brothers received him gladly, and the word carries the warmth of that welcome. It is a small word for a large kindness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a glad welcome is itself a ministry, and the Jerusalem believers gave Paul one when he needed it most.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G4680; unwise:--fool.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells believers to walk carefully, not as fools but as wise, making the most of the time. The word is the opposite of wisdom, a life lived without seeing clearly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wisdom shows itself in how we walk day by day, not in what we claim to know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G4982; properly, unsavedness, i.e. (by implication) profligacy:--excess, riot.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for a life thrown away on excess, the riot that Paul sets against being filled with the Spirit. An elder's children must not be accused of it, and Peter says the world thinks it strange when believers refuse to run with them into the same flood of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the whole point: a life can be filled with wine or filled with the Spirit, but not both. The world's surprise at our refusal is itself a witness, and I hold that self-control is the quiet proof of a changed heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from the same as G810; dissolutely:--riotous.
BiblicalUsage: The younger son in Jesus' story took his share and wasted it in riotous living in a far country. The word sums up the whole prodigal slide in a single stroke.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the far country always looks like freedom until the money runs out, and the road home starts when a person comes to himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ten; by abbreviated form ten strings, and so a decachord
BiblicalUsage: This word means ten, and it shows up in two places that could not be more different. It fixes the tenth day of the seventh month as the Day of Atonement, and it names the instrument of ten strings on which the psalms were sung. The same number counts a holy day and strings a song.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gave His people both a calendar and a song, and the number ten ties them together. Atonement and praise belong in the same life, and I hold that the God who sets the day also tunes the instrument.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G782; a greeting (in person or by letter):--greeting, salutation.
BiblicalUsage: A greeting in the ancient world was more than politeness, and this word carries its weight in both directions. Mary was troubled at Gabriel's greeting, Elizabeth's child leaped when she heard Mary's, the Pharisees loved greetings in the marketplaces, and Paul signed his own greeting at the end of his letter to Corinth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a greeting shows what a person is reaching for, whether it is honour from men or grace from God. Mary's greeting carried the Saviour Himself into Elizabeth's house, and I hold that the simplest hello can carry Christ with it.
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Jesus; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a particle of union) and a presumed form of G4685; to enfold in the arms, i.e. (by implication) to salute, (figuratively) to welcome:--embrace, greet, salute, take leave.
BiblicalUsage: To greet, in the New Testament, is to embrace, to welcome, and to take leave, all in one word. Paul ends his letters with a long roll of greetings by name, the believers of old greeted the promises from afar and embraced them, and John closes his short letter hoping to greet his friends face to face.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the greetings at the ends of the letters are not filler, they are the church being the church, naming names and holding people close. Faith greets the promises before it ever holds them, and I hold that heaven will feel like that final greeting, face to face at last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G804; security (literally or figuratively):--certainty, safety.
BiblicalUsage: This word means safety and certainty, and Luke uses it for the very purpose of his Gospel, that Theophilus might know the certainty of the things he had been taught. The prison keepers claimed the apostles were shut up safely, and Paul warns that the world will cry peace and safety just before sudden destruction comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe real safety is not a locked door or a comforting slogan, it is knowing the truth for certain. The keepers' safety was an empty cell and the world's safety is a trap, but Luke's certainty still stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and σφάλλω (to "fail"); secure (literally or figuratively):--certain(-ty), safe, sure.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for what cannot slip or fail. The hope set before us is an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, Paul says writing the same things again is safe for his readers, and the chief captain wanted to know the certainty of the charges against Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the anchor holds because of where it is fastened, inside the veil where Christ has gone before us. That is the whole ground of our safety, and I hold it fast when everything else feels like it is giving way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G804; to render secure:--make fast (sure).
BiblicalUsage: To make fast is to lock down, and men used this word twice against Christ. The chief priests asked Pilate to make the tomb secure, the stone was sealed and the watch set, and the jailer at Philippi thrust Paul and Silas into the inner prison and made their feet fast in the stocks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every lock men set failed in the same way, because no seal can hold the One who is life itself. The tomb was made as sure as men could make it, and it stood empty by morning.
RelatedEvents: The Guards Report the Empty Tomb
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G804; securely (literally or figuratively):--assuredly, safely.
BiblicalUsage: Peter told the crowd at Pentecost to know assuredly that God had made Jesus both Lord and Christ, and Judas gave the soldiers a sign to take Jesus safely, without a stir. The same adverb covers certainty and caution.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Peter's assurance is the one that matters, because it rests on what God has done, not on what men can guard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G4695; unblemished (physically or morally):--without spot, unspotted.
BiblicalUsage: Without spot is how Peter describes the blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish, and how James describes pure religion, keeping oneself unspotted from the world. Peter tells believers to be diligent to be found of Him in peace, without spot, and Paul charges Timothy to keep the commandment without spot until Christ appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spotless Lamb is the reason spotless living is possible at all. We are not made clean by keeping ourselves apart, we are kept clean by the One who was never stained, and I hold that His purity is the pattern and the power for ours.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; James, Brother of the Lord; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a buckler (or round shield); used of a serpent (as coiling itself), probably the "asp":--asp.
BiblicalUsage: Paul quotes the psalm that says the poison of asps is under men's lips, and the asp is the serpent whose bite kills quietly. The word appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul chose the serpent on purpose, because deadly speech does its harm before anyone feels the bite.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G4689; literally, without libation (which usually accompanied a treaty), i.e. (by implication) truceless:--implacable, truce-breaker.
BiblicalUsage: In Paul's picture of the last days, men are without natural affection and trucebreakers, people who will not keep a treaty even when one is offered. The word is built from the libation poured out when a covenant was made, and these men refuse the cup.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a world that will not keep its word has lost the very thing that holds families and nations together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Asrielite (collectively) or descendant of Asriel
BiblicalUsage: The Asrielites were the family descended from Asriel, counted among the sons of Gilead in the wilderness census. The name marks a clan, not a single man.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counted the clans as carefully as the men, and no family was lost in the crowd.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asriel, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Two men carry this name in Scripture, and the record keeps them apart. One is Asriel the son of Manasseh, named in the genealogy of the tribe, and the other is Asriel the son of Gilead, whose family was counted in the wilderness and given a share in the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Asriels show how carefully the record is kept, because the same name can belong to an uncle and a great-grandson, and God knows which is which.
RelatedPeople: Asriel, Son of Gilead; Ashriel, Son of Manasseh
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; an assarius or as, a Roman coin:--farthing.
BiblicalUsage: A farthing was the smallest Roman copper coin, and Jesus used it to price the sparrows. Two sparrows sold for one, five for two, and not one of them falls without the Father.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the farthing is the whole point: if God watches the cheapest bird in the market, He is certainly watching me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter comparative of the base of G1451; more nearly, i.e. very near:--close.
BiblicalUsage: When the south wind blew softly, the sailors thought their plan had worked, and they sailed close by Crete. The word means near at hand, and it is the calm before the storm that wrecked them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a gentle wind can still carry a ship the wrong way, and closeness to shore is no safety when the storm comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; Assus, a city of Asia MInor:--Assos.
BiblicalUsage: Assos was the port where Paul's companions went ahead by ship while he walked the land road to meet them there. Luke names it twice in the same journey, once as the place they sailed to and once as the place where they took Paul aboard.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the detail matters because Luke was there, keeping the journey honest mile by mile, and a seaport most readers would never see still stands in the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G2476; to be non-stationary, i.e. (figuratively) homeless:--have no certain dwelling-place.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the apostles hunger and thirst and are buffeted and have no certain dwelling place, and this is the word for that homelessness. It means to have nowhere to settle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the apostles' wandering was not a failure of God's care, it was the shape of their calling, and Christ Himself had nowhere to lay His head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄστυ (a city); urbane, i.e. (by implication) handsome:--fair.
BiblicalUsage: Moses was fair to God as a child, and his parents hid him by faith because they saw he was a beautiful child. The word means handsome, but both places tie his beauty to God's purpose for him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can mark a child for His work before anyone knows what that work will be, and a mother's eyes saw it first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G4766; a star (as strown over the sky), literally or figuratively:--star.
BiblicalUsage: The star led the wise men from the east to Bethlehem, and when they saw it again they rejoiced with exceeding great joy. John sees Christ as the bright and morning star, and Paul says one star differs from another star in glory.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the star over Bethlehem and the star of the resurrection are the same light, Christ Himself guiding His people home. The stars differ in glory, and I hold that the glory of the risen body will outshine them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G4741; unfixed, i.e. (figuratively) vacillating:--unstable.
BiblicalUsage: Peter warns about unstable souls who are beguiled, and about untaught and unstable people who twist Paul's letters as they do the other Scriptures. The word means unfixed, like a tent peg that will not hold.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a faith with no anchor drifts into whatever error is nearest, and the cure is to be settled in the Scriptures.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G772; feebleness (of mind or body); by implication, malady; morally, frailty:--disease, infirmity, sickness, weakness.
BiblicalUsage: Weakness in the New Testament covers sickness of the body, frailty of the mind, and the limits of our praying. Lazarus's sickness was for the glory of God, Paul's thorn taught him that grace is enough, our High Priest is touched with the feeling of our infirmities, and the Spirit helps our weaknesses when we do not know what to pray.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe weakness is not the opposite of faith, it is the place where faith learns to lean. Christ was never weak toward us, and I hold that His strength shows itself most clearly in the people who know they have none of their own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G770; a scruple of conscience:--infirmity.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and the word means the scruples and tender consciences that make a brother hesitate. It is the only place it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that bearing with a weaker brother is not a burden to resent, it is the way Christ bore with us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G772; to be feeble (in any sense):--be diseased, impotent folk (man), (be) sick, (be, be made) weak.
BiblicalUsage: To be weak is to be sick in body or feeble in faith, and the word covers both. Lazarus was sick, James says the sick should call for the elders to pray over them, Paul tells the church to receive the weak in faith without doubtful disputations, and he takes pleasure in weaknesses because when he is weak, then he is strong.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God never treats weakness as a reason to set a person aside, He treats it as a reason to draw near. The church that prays for its sick and makes room for its weak is doing what Christ does, and I hold that His power rests on the people who admit they need it.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Lazarus; Paul; James, Brother of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and the base of G4599; strengthless (in various applications, literal, figurative and moral):--more feeble, impotent, sick, without strength, weak(-er, -ness, thing).
BiblicalUsage: The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, and Jesus said it to disciples who could not watch one hour with Him. God chose the weak things of the world to confound the mighty, the weaker members of the body are necessary, and Christ died for the ungodly when we were yet without strength.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God chooses weakness on purpose, because it leaves no doubt about whose power is at work. The flesh will always be weak, and I hold that the answer is not to pretend otherwise but to watch and pray.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and στοίχος (an aim); to miss the mark, i.e. (figuratively) deviate from truth:--err, swerve.
BiblicalUsage: To miss the mark is to swerve from the truth, and Paul uses it three times for the same danger. Some turned aside to vain jangling, some erred concerning the faith by chasing what is falsely called science, and Hymenaeus and Philetus erred by saying the resurrection is past already.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the target is small and the pull is constant, and a little swerve at the start becomes a wide miss by the end. Holding the pattern of sound words is how a person stays on the mark, and I hold that the faith once delivered is worth aiming at with everything I have.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of στέργω (to cherish affectionately); hard-hearted towards kindred:--without natural affection.
BiblicalUsage: Without natural affection is Paul's charge against a world that has traded God's truth for a lie, and he puts it in his list of the last days too. The word means a heart gone hard toward its own kindred.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that affection for one's own family is part of God's design, and a heart that cannot love its own has already wandered far from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G797; lightning; by analogy, glare:--lightning, bright shining.
BiblicalUsage: Lightning is how Jesus describes His coming, flashing from the east even to the west, and how He saw Satan fall from heaven. The angel at the tomb had a countenance like lightning, and lightnings come out of the throne in John's vision.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lightning tells the truth about power: it is sudden, it is seen by all, and no one can mistake it for anything else. Christ's return will be like that, and I hold that the safest place to be when it flashes is on His side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G792; to flash as lightning:--lighten, shine.
BiblicalUsage: The Son of man will lighten like the lightning that shines from one part of heaven to the other, and the two men at the empty tomb stood in shining garments. The word is the flash itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the brightness at the tomb was the first flash of the resurrection morning, and the world has never been dark since.
RelatedEvents: The Guards Report the Empty Tomb
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter from G792; properly, a constellation; put for a single star (natural or artificial):--star.
BiblicalUsage: Stephen charges Israel with carrying the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of their god Remphan, and the writer to the Hebrews says Abraham's descendants became as many as the stars of heaven. Jesus says there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on Paul's ship neither sun nor stars appeared for many days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stars keep two records at once: the idols men worshipped and the promises God kept. Abraham's seed outnumbered the stars, and I hold that the same God who counts them also counts His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G4859; inharmonious (figuratively):--agree not.
BiblicalUsage: After Paul quoted Isaiah to the Jews in Rome, they departed and disagreed among themselves, and the word means out of tune with one another. It is the only place it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word of God still divides hearers the same way, and the disagreement is not with Paul but with the message itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G4908; unintelligent; by implication, wicked:--foolish, without understanding.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus asked His disciples, are ye also yet without understanding, when they missed the point about what defiles a man. Paul says the hearts of men were darkened because they became vain in their imaginations, and he lists the foolish and the without understanding among the marks of a mind given over.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe understanding is not a matter of cleverness, it is a matter of a heart willing to hear. The disciples learned it slowly and so do I, and I hold that Christ is patient with slow learners who keep listening.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G4793; incomparable; Asyncritus, a Christian:--Asyncritos.
BiblicalUsage: Asyncritus is named once, in Paul's long list of greetings to the believers in Rome, alongside Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren with them. Nothing else is told about him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in Paul's greeting is no small thing, because it means a brother known and loved by the apostle, and known by God besides.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G4934; properly, not agreed, i.e. treacherous to compacts:-- covenant-breaker.
BiblicalUsage: Covenantbreakers stand in Paul's list of the sins of a mind that has refused God, people who make agreements and break them without a second thought. The word means not agreed, untrue to a compact.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a promise kept is a small picture of God's faithfulness, and a promise broken is a small picture of what sin does to the world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (as a noun) a necromancer (from their soft incantations), (as an adverb) gently
BiblicalUsage: This little word carries two meanings that seem far apart, and both turn on softness. Jacob promises to lead his flocks on softly, David begs his men to deal gently with Absalom, and Isaiah says the waters of Shiloah go softly. But the same root names the mutterers and charmers whose soft incantations Egypt would seek in the day of her judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word warns me that gentleness and sorcery can sound alike, and the difference is not the tone but the master. David's gentleness came from a father's heart, and Egypt's whispering came from idols, and I hold that God knows which soft voice I am listening to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a thorn-tree (especially the buckthorn)
BiblicalUsage: The thornbush gives its name to the threshing floor of Atad, where Joseph mourned his father for seven days, and it speaks in Jotham's parable, offering the trees its shade if they will make it king. The psalm says the wicked will be taken away before their pots can feel the thorns.
