TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thorn is the Bible's picture of a small thing with a sharp edge, a mourning place named for a bush and a king no one should choose. The trees were right to refuse it, and I hold that God still warns His people against crowning what can only wound them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wrap, i.e. cover, veil, cloth, or roll
BiblicalUsage: To wrap is to cover, and the word moves from clothing to judgment without changing its shape. God covers Himself with light as with a garment, the leper must cover his upper lip, Isaiah says the LORD put on righteousness as a breastplate, and the psalm prays that shame would cover the enemy like the garment he wears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe covering tells the story of who we are: God covers Himself in light, we cover ourselves in shame, and Christ covers us in righteousness. The garment a person wears shows where they stand, and I hold that His is the only covering that never wears thin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G813; to be (i.e. act) irregular:--behave self disorderly.
BiblicalUsage: Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he did not behave disorderly among them, working night and day so as not to be a burden. The word means to break ranks, like a soldier out of step.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that order in the church is not about rules for their own sake, it is about love that refuses to be a burden on others.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G813, irregularly (morally):--disorderly.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the church to withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly, and he had heard that some were walking disorderly, working not at all but acting as busybodies. The word is the adverb form, describing the walk itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a disordered walk harms the whole church, because idleness and meddling travel together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G5021; unarranged, i.e. (by implication) insubordinate (religiously):--unruly.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the church to warn the unruly, to comfort the feebleminded, to support the weak, and to be patient toward all. The unruly are the ones out of step, and the cure begins with a warning, not a punishment.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that patience is part of the command, because the unruly need a shepherd's voice before they need a judge's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bat
BiblicalUsage: The bat is named among the unclean birds in the law, and Isaiah says men will cast their idols to the bats in the day the LORD rises to shake the earth. It is a creature of the dark, and it ends up owning what men once worshipped.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bat's story is a warning about idols: what we bow to in the light we will throw to the dark when judgment comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to close (the lips or ears); by analology to contract (a window by bevelled jambs)
BiblicalUsage: To close is to shut the ear, the lips, or the window, and the word covers all three. The man who stops his ears at the cry of the poor will cry himself and not be heard, the righteous man stops his ears from hearing of blood, the wicked are like the deaf adder that stops her ear, and Solomon's temple had windows that were narrowed from within.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what a person shuts out decides what they will hear, and a closed ear to the poor is a closed door to God. The temple windows let in light while keeping out the weather, and I hold that wisdom is knowing which openings to guard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shroud, i.e. clothe (whether transitive or reflex.); hence (from the idea of darkness) to languish
BiblicalUsage: To be overwhelmed is to faint under a weight too heavy to carry, and the psalms use this word for the spirit at its lowest. David cries from the end of the earth when his heart is overwhelmed, Asaph says his spirit was overwhelmed when he remembered God, the hungry and thirsty fainted in the wilderness, and Jonah's soul fainted within him in the belly of the fish.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the overwhelmed heart is not the end of the story, it is the place where prayer begins. Jonah remembered the LORD when his soul fainted, and I hold that God hears the cry that comes from the very bottom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to encircle (for attack or protection); especially to crown (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: To crown is to encircle, and the psalms use this word for God's favour, man's glory, the year's goodness, and a life redeemed. The LORD crowns the righteous with favour as with a shield, He crowned man with glory and honour, He crowns the year with His goodness, and He crowns our lives with lovingkindness and tender mercies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every crown in these psalms comes down from God's hand, not up from our effort. The year, the life, and the man are all crowned by Him, and I hold that the favour that surrounds us is the reason we stand at all.
RelatedTopics: Blessing; Love of God; God's mercy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to close up
BiblicalUsage: David prays that the pit would not shut her mouth upon him, and this is the word for that closing. It appears only here, in a psalm of drowning and distress.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the pit's mouth is the picture of despair itself, and David's prayer is the cry of a man who still believes God can keep it open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atarah, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Atarah was the second wife of Jerahmeel, and the record names her as the mother of Onam. She appears once, in the genealogy of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept in the family record is no small thing, because it means a mother remembered by name among the sons of Judah.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a crown
BiblicalUsage: A crown is the mark of honour, and this word follows it through the whole Bible. David took the crown of the Ammonite king, wisdom gives a crown of glory to the one who holds her, Isaiah says Zion will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and the king in the psalm received a crown of pure gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crown that matters is the one God sets on, not the one men take off. David could lift a crown from a conquered king, but only the LORD can make His people a crown of glory, and I hold that the honour He gives is the only one that lasts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ataroth, the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ataroth was a town claimed by the children of Gad when they asked for land east of the Jordan, and they built it up again as their own. The name also marks a boundary town in Ephraim's allotment, on the border running down toward the Jordan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Ataroths show how the land was divided and settled by real families, and a town's name in the record is a deed as much as a place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5043; childless:--childless, without children.
BiblicalUsage: The Sadducees posed their riddle about the childless man who dies leaving his wife to his brother, and the word means without children. Jesus answered that the question itself misunderstands the resurrection.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Sadducees' trap failed because they could not imagine a life beyond this one, and the childless are not forgotten in the life to come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a particle of union) and τείνω (to stretch); to gaze intently:--behold earnestly (stedfastly), fasten (eyes), look (earnestly, stedfastly, up stedfastly), set eyes.
BiblicalUsage: To look intently is to fasten the eyes, and this word marks the moments when looking matters. Peter fastened his eyes on the lame man at the temple gate, the eyes of the synagogue were fastened on Jesus as He read Isaiah, Stephen looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and the Israelites could not look steadfastly at Moses' face for its glory.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the eyes go where the heart already is, and every one of these gazes landed on something worth seeing. Stephen's last sight was the glory of God, and I hold that a life spent looking at Christ will end the same way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a particle probably akin to G427; aloof, i.e. apart from (literally or figuratively):--in the absence of, without.
BiblicalUsage: Judas sought a chance to betray Jesus in the absence of the multitude, and Jesus asked His disciples whether they had lacked anything when He sent them out without purse or scrip. The word means apart from, or in the absence of.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two uses stand against each other: Judas wanted Jesus without the crowd, and the disciples found they lacked nothing without their supplies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ater, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Three men carry the name Ater in the records of the return, and the lists keep their families apart. One is the head of a family that came back with Zerubbabel, one is the father of the porters, and one sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three Aters show how the returned exiles rebuilt by family, and each household had its part in the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a portent
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means a sign or a wonder, and Nebuchadnezzar uses it twice when he tells what the high God has done for him. He thought it good to show the signs and wonders wrought toward him, and he says how great are His signs and how mighty His wonders. Darius uses it the same way after Daniel came out of the lions' den, saying God works signs and wonders in heaven and in earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the signs did their work on the very kings who ordered them, because the men who built the furnaces and dug the dens ended up praising the God they had defied. A sign that turns a king's heart is no small thing, and I hold that God's wonders still speak to the proud.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to prepare
BiblicalUsage: To prepare is to make ready beforehand, and the word appears twice. Eliphaz says the wicked dwell in desolate cities ready to become heaps, and the proverb tells a man to prepare his work outside and make his field ready before he builds his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that preparation shows the heart: one man prepares for ruin and another prepares for a home, and wisdom is knowing which work comes first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {to arrive}
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means to come or to arrive, and it carries the turning points of Daniel. Nebuchadnezzar came near the furnace and called the three men out, the vessels of God's house were brought into Belshazzar's feast, and Daniel saw one like the Son of man come with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word keeps pointing forward, because the coming that matters most is the Son of man coming to receive His kingdom. The furnace and the feast both ended in judgment, and I hold that His coming will end in a kingdom that never passes away.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; King Nebuchadnezzar; Belshazzar; Shadrach; Meshach; Abednego
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {to arrive}
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means to come or to arrive, and it carries the turning points of Daniel. Nebuchadnezzar came near the furnace and called the three men out, the vessels of God's house were brought into Belshazzar's feast, and Daniel saw one like the Son of man come with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word keeps pointing forward, because the coming that matters most is the Son of man coming to receive His kingdom. The furnace and the feast both ended in judgment, and I hold that His coming will end in a kingdom that never passes away.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; King Nebuchadnezzar; Belshazzar; Shadrach; Meshach; Abednego
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Athak, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Athak was one of the places David sent a share of the spoil to, after he recovered everything the Amalekites had taken. It appears only here, in the list of towns that had sheltered him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe David's gift remembered the friends who had stood by him when he had nothing, and a town's name in that list is a mark of honour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Athaljah, the name of an Israelitess and two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Two very different people share this name, and the record keeps them apart. One is Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, who seized the throne of Judah and ruled six years after killing her own grandchildren, until Jehoiada crowned the boy Joash and she was put to death, and the other is a man of the house of Elam whose son Jeshaiah came back with Ezra.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the queen's story is the Bible's plainest warning that a throne taken by murder cannot stand, because God had already hidden the true king in His house. The other Athaliah's son simply came home, and I hold that the contrast is the point: one name, two roads, and only one of them ends in life.
RelatedPeople: Athaliah; Joash, King of Judah; Jehoiada, High Priest; Ahaziah, King of Judah; Ezra; Jeshaiah, Son of Athaliah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably to glow, i.e. (figuratively) be desolated
BiblicalUsage: The word means to burn or glow, and Isaiah uses it for wickedness that burns like a fire and for a people burned up by the anger of the LORD. It appears once in this form, in the judgment on a nation that would not turn.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that wickedness is its own fire, and it burns the very people who feed it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G2288; deathlessness:--immortality.
BiblicalUsage: Immortality is the word for deathlessness, and Paul uses it for the change that is coming and for God Himself. This corruptible must put on incorruption and this mortal must put on immortality, and when it does, death is swallowed up in victory. God alone has immortality, dwelling in light no man can approach.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promise is as plain as it is wonderful: what God has in Himself He will give to His people, and death will not get the last word. Mortality puts on immortality the way a garment is put on, and I hold that the resurrection morning will show what that looks like.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: impudent
BiblicalUsage: This word means impudent or arrogant, and it describes hard speech against God and His people. Hannah warns against proud and arrogant talk, and the lying lips that speak grievous things against the righteous will be silenced.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that arrogant speech is not a small sin, because it lifts the neck against the very God who hears it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to remove (intransitive or transitive) figuratively, to grow old; specifically, to transcribe
BiblicalUsage: To move away or grow old is the sense here, and the word covers a journey, a well, and a weary eye. Abram moved on from Bethel toward the south, Isaac moved away from the strife over the wells and found room at Rehoboth, the proverbs of Solomon were copied out by Hezekiah's men, and David says his eye grows old because of all his enemies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds two kinds of moving: the moving on of faith and the wearing down of sorrow. Abram and Isaac moved toward the promise, and I hold that God makes room for the ones who keep moving in trust.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; King David; King Hezekiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to burn incense in worship, i.e. intercede (reciprocally, listen to prayer)
BiblicalUsage: To entreat is to pray for another, and this word is the hinge of the plague story. Pharaoh begged Moses to entreat the LORD for him when the frogs covered Egypt, and Moses agreed and set the time, and Pharaoh promised to let the people go. Isaac entreated the LORD for Rebekah because she was barren, and the LORD was entreated of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe intercession is one of the highest works a person can do, because it stands between a need and the God who can meet it. Pharaoh asked for it and then broke his word, Isaac asked for it and received a son, and I hold that God still listens when His people pray for others.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to burn incense in worship, i.e. intercede (reciprocally, listen to prayer)
BiblicalUsage: To entreat is to pray for another, and this word is the hinge of the plague story. Pharaoh begged Moses to entreat the LORD for him when the frogs covered Egypt, and Moses agreed and set the time, and Pharaoh promised to let the people go. Isaac entreated the LORD for Rebekah because she was barren, and the LORD was entreated of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe intercession is one of the highest works a person can do, because it stands between a need and the God who can meet it. Pharaoh asked for it and then broke his word, Isaac asked for it and received a son, and I hold that God still listens when His people pray for others.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: incense (as increasing to a volume of smoke); hence a worshipper
BiblicalUsage: This word means incense rising in a cloud, and the suppliant who offers it. Ezekiel saw seventy elders burning incense to idols in the dark, and Zephaniah says God's dispersed people will bring Him an offering from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that incense shows what worship really is: something rising to God, and the question is always whether it rises to Him or to an idol.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a place; (adverb) after
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means a place, and then, by a small step, what comes after. The stone cut out without hands became a mountain and filled the whole earth, a kingdom would arise after Nebuchadnezzar's, Daniel saw a beast like a leopard, and after it another, and Cyrus ordered the house of God rebuilt in its place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word fits Daniel's whole message, because kingdoms rise in their place and fall to make room for the next, until the stone fills the earth. What comes after is God's doing, and I hold that His kingdom is the one that has no after.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; King Nebuchadnezzar; Cyrus the Great
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atharim, a place near Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Atharim was the place near which the Canaanite king of Arad heard that Israel was coming, and he fought against them and took some of them prisoner. It appears only here, at the edge of the wilderness road.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a place named once still matters, because Israel's road to the land ran past it, and God was with them on every mile.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Athajah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Athaiah the son of Uzziah was one of the children of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the return, listed among the heads of families who lived in the holy city. He appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the men who moved into Jerusalem after the exile were rebuilding more than houses, they were rebuilding a people, and Athaiah's name stands among them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of θέμις (statute; from the base of G5087); illegal; by implication, flagitious:--abominable, unlawful thing.
BiblicalUsage: Peter told Cornelius it was unlawful for a Jew to keep company with a man of another nation, and he wrote that believers had already spent enough time in the abominable idolatries of their past life. The word means what the law forbids.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the wall Peter thought the law built was the very wall God was pulling down, because Christ had made the two one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plural of Ἀθήνη (the goddess of wisdom, who was reputed to have founded the city); Athenæ, the capitol of Greece:-- Athens.
BiblicalUsage: Athens was the city of philosophers where Paul waited for Silas and Timothy, and his spirit was stirred when he saw it wholly given to idolatry. He reasoned in the synagogue and in the marketplace and spoke on the Areopagus, then went on to Corinth, and later wrote that he had been left at Athens alone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Athens shows the gospel meeting the world's wisdom on its own ground, and Paul did not flinch. The city that had an altar to the unknown god heard the name of the God it did not know, and I hold that no city is too clever for the cross.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G116; an Athenæan or inhabitant of Athenæ:--Athenian.
BiblicalUsage: Luke says the Athenians and the strangers there spent their time in nothing else but telling or hearing some new thing, and Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill and addressed them as men of Athens. The word names the citizens of the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a city hungry for the newest thing is a city ready for the oldest news of all, that Christ is risen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2316; godless:--without God.
BiblicalUsage: Paul reminds the Gentile believers that they were once without Christ, aliens from Israel, strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. The word is godless, and it describes a life with no share in Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that without God is the bleakest phrase in the Bible, and the wonder of the verse is the word that follows it in the next breath: but now in Christ Jesus.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: antique, i.e. valued
BiblicalUsage: Wisdom says riches and honour are with her, yea, durable riches and righteousness, and the word means antique or valued, like a treasure kept for years. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wisdom's riches are the kind that do not wear out, because they were valuable before we were born and will be after we are gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: copiousness
BiblicalUsage: God promises to bring health and cure to His people and to reveal to them the abundance of peace and truth, and the word means copiousness, a full measure poured out. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's healing never comes in a small measure, because abundance is His way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G5087 (in the sense of enacting); lawless, i.e. (by implication) criminal:--wicked.
BiblicalUsage: Peter says God delivered righteous Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked, and he warns believers to beware lest they be led away with the error of the wicked. The word means lawless, living as though no law binds.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Lot's vexation is the mark of a righteous soul in a lawless place, and the warning still stands for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G5087; to set aside, i.e. (by implication) to disesteem, neutralize or violate:--cast off, despise, disannul, frustrate, bring to nought, reject.
BiblicalUsage: To set aside is to reject what God has given, and the word carries that weight in every place it falls. Paul says he does not frustrate the grace of God, the writer to the Hebrews says the man who despised Moses' law died without mercy, Jesus says the one who rejects Him rejects the One who sent Him, and the word He spoke will judge in the last day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe setting aside God's word is never a small thing, because the word set aside is the very word that will judge. Grace is not to be frustrated and Christ is not to be despised, and I hold that the safest response to His word is to receive it while there is time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G114; cancellation (literally or figuratively):--disannulling, put away.
BiblicalUsage: There is a disannulling of the commandment that went before, because it was weak and unprofitable, and Christ appeared once to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself. The word means cancellation, a setting aside that clears the way.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the old commandment was set aside so that a better hope could come in, and the sin it could not remove was put away by His blood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prepared; by implication, skilful; feminine plural the future; also treasure
BiblicalUsage: This word means prepared or ready, and it looks forward to a day that is coming. Vengeance and recompense are ready for the enemies of God, the decree against the Jews was prepared and published in every province, and Job calls on those who are ready to rouse up Leviathan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the future is not an accident waiting to happen, it is prepared, and the God who prepares judgment also prepares deliverance. Haman's decree and Mordecai's counter-decree were both ready on their day, and I hold that God's timing is never late.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Mordecai; Queen Esther; Haman; Job
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prepared
BiblicalUsage: Nebuchadnezzar told the three men that if they would not worship the image, they would be cast into the furnace that very hour, and he asked who was the God who could deliver them. The Aramaic word means ready or prepared, and the furnace was ready.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the king's question was answered by the fire itself, because the God he doubted walked in it with them.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, antique, i.e. venerable or splendid
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah says the merchandise of Tyre will be holiness to the LORD, and it will not be treasured up or laid by, but given to those who dwell before Him. The word means antique or venerable, something kept for its value.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that wealth kept for God stops being a treasure hoarded and becomes a provision for His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Athlai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Athlai was one of the sons of Bebai who had married a foreign wife, and he put her away when Ezra called the people back to the law. He appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Athlai's obedience cost him something real, and the record keeps his name because repentance is worth remembering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄθλος (a contest in the public lists); to contend in the competitive games:--strive.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says a man who strives for the mastery in the games is not crowned unless he strives lawfully, and the word is the athlete's word. It is the only place it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Christian race has rules, and the crown goes to the one who runs it God's way, not the fastest way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G118; a struggle (figuratively):--fight.
BiblicalUsage: The writer to the Hebrews tells his readers to remember the former days, when they endured a great fight of afflictions after they were illuminated. The word means a struggle, the contest itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that remembering past endurance is fuel for present faith, because the God who carried them through the fight has not changed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and probably a derivative of G5087 (meaning a penalty); not guilty:--innocent.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for innocent, not guilty, and it sounds twice in the trial of Jesus. Judas said he had betrayed innocent blood, and Pilate washed his hands and said he was innocent of the blood of this just person.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two confessions stand against each other: Judas knew what he had done and despaired, Pilate knew what he was doing and washed his hands anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a female donkey (from its docility)
BiblicalUsage: The she-ass is the humble animal of the Bible's great turning points, and Saul's story begins with his father's lost asses. Kish sent Saul to find them, and the search led him to Samuel and to the throne, and Balaam's ass saw the angel in the road and spoke.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God uses the lowliest things to steer the proudest lives, and a lost donkey can be the road to a kingdom. The ass that saw the angel and the asses that led Saul to Samuel both show that God steers by the humblest means, and I hold that no errand is too small for His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prepared
BiblicalUsage: The counter-decree that saved the Jews was published in every province, and the word means prepared or ready. The copies were made ready so that the Jews could defend themselves on the appointed day.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's deliverance is never improvised, it is prepared before the danger reaches us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G2372; to be spiritless, i.e. disheartened:--be dismayed.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children to anger, lest they be discouraged, and the word means to lose heart or spirit. It is the only place it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a child's spirit is a tender thing, and a father's harshness can break what only patience can build.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G820; to render infamous, i.e. (by implication) contemn or maltreat:--despise, dishonour, suffer shame, entreat shamefully.
BiblicalUsage: To dishonour is to treat as worthless, and the word cuts both ways in the New Testament. The apostles rejoiced that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name, the rich dishonour the poor in James's charge, the tenants dishonoured the vineyard owner's servants, and Jesus answered the charge of having a devil by saying, I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dishonour reveals what a person truly values, because the apostles counted shame for Christ an honour and the world counts honour for Christ a shame. The two scales will never agree, and I hold that God's weighing is the one that lasts.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; James, Brother of the Lord; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G820; infamy, i.e. (subjectively) comparative indignity, (objectively) disgrace:--dishonour, reproach, shame, vile.
BiblicalUsage: Dishonour is the word for shame and disgrace, and Paul sets it against glory at every turn. The body is sown in dishonour and raised in glory, the apostles served by honour and dishonour alike, God gave men over to vile affections, and in a great house there are vessels of honour and vessels of dishonour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel turns dishonour inside out: what is sown in shame is raised in glory, and the servants who bear both honour and dishonour are the ones God uses. The vessel's worth is decided by the Master's hand, and I hold that no one who belongs to Him is ever truly disgraced.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G820; used like G818, to maltreat:--handle shamefully.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to handle shamefully, and it appears in the parable of the vineyard, where the tenants wounded the owner's servant in the head and sent him away shamefully handled. It stands in the Textus Receptus at this verse, where other Greek texts read the related word for dishonour.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the tenants' shameful handling of the servant shows what rebellion does to every messenger God sends, and the parable ends with the stone the builders rejected.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5092; (negatively) unhonoured or (positively) dishonoured:--despised, without honour, less honourable (comparative degree).
BiblicalUsage: Without honour is the lot of the apostles in Paul's irony, we are fools for Christ's sake and ye are wise, we are weak and ye are strong, we are despised. Paul says the uncomely parts of the body receive more abundant honour, and Jesus said a prophet is not without honour except in his own country.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the upside-down honour of the kingdom is the test of whether we see as God sees. The despised apostles carried the gospel to the world, and I hold that the honour Christ gives is never the honour the world offers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a receptacle (for milk, i.e. pail; figuratively, breast)
BiblicalUsage: Job says the wicked man's breasts are full of milk, and the word is a pail or a breast, a vessel that holds and gives. It appears only here, in Job's picture of a man who prospers to the very end.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Job's point is sharp: prosperity can fill a man to the brim and still leave him empty before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sneezing
BiblicalUsage: The sneezing of Leviathan gives off light, and this is the word for that sneeze. It appears only here, in God's description of the creature no man can tame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is meant to humble us: even Leviathan's sneeze shines, and the God who made him is beyond our measuring.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G109; mist:--vapour.
BiblicalUsage: Vapour is the word for mist, and it appears in the signs of the last days and in the picture of a life. Peter quotes Joel that there will be blood and fire and vapour of smoke, and James asks what your life is, for it is even a vapour that appears for a little time and then vanishes away.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a vapour is the honest measure of my life, and the wonder is that God breathes eternity into something so brief.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; James, Brother of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and the base of G5114; uncut, i.e. (by implication) indivisible (an "atom" of time):-- moment.
BiblicalUsage: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump, the dead will be raised incorruptible, and this is the word for that indivisible instant. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the change will be faster than thought, and the trumpet will find the saints ready or not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5117; out of place, i.e. (figuratively) improper, injurious, wicked:--amiss, harm, unreasonable.
BiblicalUsage: Out of place is the word for what is wrong, harmful, or wicked. The thief on the cross said this man has done nothing amiss, Festus was told to come down and accuse Paul if there was any wickedness in him, the islanders first thought Paul was a murderer and then changed their minds, and Paul asks prayer for deliverance from unreasonable and wicked men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thief's confession is the key to the word: Christ had done nothing out of place, and every charge against Him fell apart. The world still calls good men wicked, and I hold that the cross is where the charge was answered once for all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atroth-Addar, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Atroth-addar was a town on the border of Ephraim, named twice as the boundary line was drawn from the Jordan up to the hill country. It marked where one tribe's land ended and another's began.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a boundary town matters because the land was God's gift measured out tribe by tribe, and every border in the record was drawn by His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atroth-beth-Joab, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Atroth-beth-Joab was a town of the sons of Salma, named once in the genealogy of Judah among the families of Bethlehem. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the town's place in the record ties it to Bethlehem's families, and the smallest places still belong to the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atroth-Shophan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Atroth-shophan was one of the towns the children of Gad built when they settled east of the Jordan, named once in the list of their cities. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the towns Gad built were homes for families who had chosen the far side of the river, and the record keeps their names.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to afflict
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means to afflict or grieve, and Darius uses it when he comes to the lions' den at dawn and cries out with a lamentable voice to Daniel. The king had fasted all night and could not sleep for grief over his servant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the king's grief shows what power cannot do: it could throw Daniel to the lions, but it could not save him from them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an (idolatrous) image
BiblicalUsage: This word names the idols, the carved images men worshipped, and the Bible follows them to their end. The Philistines cut off Saul's head and stripped his armour and sent word to the house of their idols, David's men burned the idols the Philistines left behind, Hosea says Israel made idols from their silver and gold, and Judah forsook the house of the LORD to serve groves and idols.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the idols always end the same way, stripped, burned, or abandoned, because they are the work of men's hands and cannot save. The house of God was forsaken for them, and I hold that every idol still asks for the worship that belongs to God alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to carve, i.e. fabricate or fashion; hence (in a bad sense) to worry, pain or anger
BiblicalUsage: To grieve or to pain is the sense here, and the word runs from prayer to sorrow. Jabez prayed that God would keep him from evil so that it might not grieve him, Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food because he was grieved for David, and the day of victory turned to mourning when the people heard the king was grieved for his son.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe grief is honest in the Bible, and it is never wasted when it is carried to God. Jabez asked to be kept from it, Jonathan felt it for his friend, and David's grief over Absalom shows that even a king's heart can break, and I hold that God meets the grieving where they are.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to fasten (or make firm), i.e. to close (the eyes)
BiblicalUsage: The proverb says a man who shuts his eyes to devise froward things, and moves his lips, brings evil to pass. The word is the closing of the eyes, the deliberate shutting out of light.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that evil begins with a shut eye, because the man who will not see good has already decided to do harm.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lean idly, i.e. to be indolent or slack
BiblicalUsage: The Danites told their brothers not to be slothful, but to arise and go up against Laish, for the land was very good and God had given it into their hand. The word means to lean idly, to slacken when action is needed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that sloth is not rest, it is a refusal to take what God has already given.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to separate; hence, to select, refuse, contract
BiblicalUsage: To withhold or take away is the sense, and the word turns on what is kept back. Esau cried that Jacob had supplanted him twice and taken away his blessing, God took of the Spirit on Moses and put it on the seventy elders, and the Preacher says he withheld not his heart from any joy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows both sides of taking: a brother's theft, God's generous sharing, and a king's refusal to deny himself anything. What is taken away in deceit God can give back in grace, and I hold that the Spirit shared with the elders is the pattern for all His gifts.
RelatedTopics: Blessing; Outpouring of the Spirit; Wisdom
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atsaljah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Azaliah was the father of Shaphan the scribe, and both passages name him the same way, as the man King Josiah sent to repair the house of the LORD. The book of the law was found during that work, and his son carried it to the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a father's name is remembered here because his son was in the room when the lost book was found, and the reform that followed began with a family that served the house of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bind fast, i.e. close (the eyes); intransitively, to be (causatively, make) powerful or numerous; to crunch the bones
BiblicalUsage: To be mighty or numerous is the sense, and the word follows Israel's growth and the rise of kingdoms. The children of Israel were fruitful and waxed exceeding mighty in Egypt, the people multiplied because the midwives feared God, Abimelech told Isaac to leave because he was much mightier than the Philistines, and the he-goat of Daniel's vision waxed very great and then was broken.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe might is a gift that turns on who holds it: Israel's might threatened Pharaoh, Isaac's might threatened Abimelech, and the goat's might broke at its height. God gives increase and He takes it away, and I hold that the only might that lasts is the one that fears Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to inclose; by analogy, to hold back; also to maintain, rule, assemble
BiblicalUsage: To restrain or shut up is the word, and it runs from the plague to the rain to the temple. Aaron stood between the dead and the living and the plague was stayed, Solomon prayed that heaven would be shut up when there was no rain, the king asked who could restrain power enough to build a house for God, and Asa prayed that no man would prevail against the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word belongs to God alone in the end, because only He can stay a plague, open the heavens, or hold back the proud. Men try to restrain what they cannot control, and I hold that the prayer of Asa is the right one: let not man prevail against Thee.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to store up
BiblicalUsage: To store up is to gather treasure into a house, and the word follows the treasures of kings and the storehouses of God. Hezekiah was told that all his treasures would be carried to Babylon, Amos says the violent store up robbery in their palaces, and Nehemiah set faithful treasurers over the storehouses of the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a treasure shows where the heart is, because Hezekiah's storehouse was emptied by pride and Nehemiah's was filled by faithfulness. What is stored for God is kept, and I hold that what is stored for self is already lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an assembly, especially on a festival or holiday
BiblicalUsage: A solemn assembly is a gathering called for worship, and the word appears at both ends of Israel's story. The law commands a solemn assembly on the seventh day of unleavened bread, Jehu called one to trap the worshippers of Baal, and the prophets say God hates the feasts and the solemn meetings when they are offered with iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the assembly is only as true as the hearts that gather in it, because God commanded the meeting and then rejected it when it became a show. Jehu's assembly was a trap, and I hold that God still sees the difference between a crowd and a congregation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (hired) workman
BiblicalUsage: The people complained that God did not see their fasting, while they exacted all their labours, and the word names the hired workmen they drove. It appears only here, in the fast God did not choose.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a fast that grinds the labourer is no fast at all, because God measures worship by mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the spine (as giving firmness to the body)
BiblicalUsage: The fat tail of the peace offering was burned on the altar, whole, and the word names the spine and the fat tail together. It appears only here, in the law of the offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the best part was God's portion, because the fat was His and the offering was made whole.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: indolent
BiblicalUsage: The sluggard is the Bible's portrait of laziness, and the proverbs paint him from every side. Go to the ant, thou sluggard, consider her ways and be wise, how long wilt thou sleep, the sluggard is as vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, and he hides his hand in his bosom and will not bring it to his mouth again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sluggard's trouble is not that he cannot work, it is that he will not, and the proverbs hold up the ant to shame him. A little sleep and a little slumber is all it takes to let poverty come like a robber, and I hold that diligence is the quiet virtue that keeps a household standing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atsel, the name of an Israelite, and of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Two bearers share this name, and the record keeps them apart. One is Azel the son of Eleasah, a Benjamite named in the family lists of Saul's house, and the other is a place, the valley of Azal, to which the people will flee in the day the LORD goes forth to fight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Azels show how one name can hold a family and a refuge at once, and the valley that shelters the fleeing is as real as the man who bore the name.
RelatedPeople: Azel, Son of Eleasah; King Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an extremity (Isaiah 41:9), also a noble
BiblicalUsage: The nobles of Israel saw God and ate and drank on the mountain, and the word names those chief men, and Isaiah says God took Israel from the ends of the earth and called them from its chief men. It means a noble or an extremity, the far edge or the high place.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the nobles who saw God and lived are the picture of grace: the chief men were not struck down, they were fed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (as abstractly) indolence
BiblicalUsage: Slothfulness is the word for the idleness that lets a house decay, and the proverb says slothfulness casts into a deep sleep while the idle soul suffers hunger. By much slothfulness the building decays, and through idleness of the hands the house drops through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a house falls the same way a soul does, not all at once but by small neglects, and the cure is to take up the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: indolence
BiblicalUsage: The virtuous woman looks well to the ways of her household and eats not the bread of idleness, and the word is the same idleness the proverbs warn against all through. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the worthy woman's strength is in her watching, because a household stands on the work no one sees.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Atsmon, a place near Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Azmon was a town on the southern border of the promised land, named three times as the boundary was drawn from the wilderness of Zin toward the river of Egypt. It marked the edge of the inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the border towns matter because the land was given with edges, and Azmon stood where the promise ended and the wilderness began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a idol; also, a pain or wound
BiblicalUsage: This word holds two meanings that meet in the heart: an idol and a sorrow. The psalm says the sorrows of those who hasten after another god will be multiplied, the same psalm says God heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds, the proverb says he that winks with the eye causes sorrow, and Job says he is afraid of all his sorrows.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two meanings are one warning, because the idol that promises comfort only multiplies sorrow, and the God who was forsaken for it is the only One who binds the wound. The sorrows of the idolater and the wounds of the broken are both healed in the same place, and I hold that He is near to both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a joint of the hand (i.e. knuckle); also (according to some) a party-wall (Ezekiel 41:8)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a joint of the hand, the knuckle, and it appears in two strange places. The false prophetesses sewed pillows to the armholes, and Ebed-melech told Jeremiah to put old rags under his armholes before they pulled him from the cistern.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the smallest joints of the body still matter to God, because He counts the rags under a prophet's arms.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bulwark, i.e. (figuratively) argument
BiblicalUsage: God calls the nations to bring forth their strong reasons, and the word means a bulwark or an argument, a defence set up like a wall. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God is not afraid of our arguments, because He invites the nations to bring their strongest case and watch it fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: powerful (specifically, a paw); by implication, numerous
BiblicalUsage: Mighty and numerous is the word for nations too strong to count, and it follows Israel into the land. Seven nations greater and mightier than Israel stood before them, the cities were great and fenced up to heaven, Amos says the mighty oppress the just and take a bribe, and Daniel says the king of fierce countenance will destroy wonderfully and will prosper and practise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe might is measured by God, not by numbers, because the nations greater than Israel fell before a people with no army of their own. The mighty who oppress the just will answer for it, and I hold that the power that looks unbreakable is the one God breaks first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: at this time, whether adverb, conjunction or expletive
BiblicalUsage: Now is the word that turns a sentence toward the present moment, and it carries some of the Bible's greatest turns. Jacob said, I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies, and now I am become two bands, Solomon said, now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side, Isaiah said the government will be ordered from henceforth even for ever, and Micah cried, now gather thyself in troops, O daughter of troops.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe now is the most honest word in the Bible, because it will not let me live in yesterday's mercies or tomorrow's promises. Jacob's now was a confession, Solomon's now was a rest, and I hold that God's now is always the moment to trust Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: thou and thee, or (plural) ye and you
BiblicalUsage: Thou is the word God and man speak to each other all through the Bible, and it is the most personal word in the language. The LORD said to Pharaoh, if thou refuse to let my people go, David said, but thou, O LORD, art a shield for me, and again, but thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel, and the psalm says, thou rulest the raging of the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thou is the word that makes God near, because it is spoken face to face, not about Him but to Him. Pharaoh heard it as a warning and David spoke it as a prayer, and I hold that the difference between the two is the whole difference between rebellion and faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Ἄτταλος (a king of Pergamus); Attaleia, a place in Pamphylia:--Attalia.
BiblicalUsage: Attalia was the port in Pamphylia where Paul and Barnabas stopped on their way back to Antioch after preaching in Perga. It appears only here, at the end of the first missionary journey.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the port matters because it marks the road home, and the journey that began with a sending ended with a return and a report.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Attai, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Three men bear the name Attai, and the record keeps each one in his own place. One was the son of Jarha the Egyptian, born to Sheshan's daughter, one was a Gadite captain who joined David at Ziklag, and one was the son of Rehoboam and Maachah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three Attais show how the record honours men in very different stations, a servant's son, a soldier, and a king's son, and God counts them all.
RelatedPeople: Attai, Son of Jarha; Attai the Gadite; Attai, Son of Rehoboam; King David; Rehoboam
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: venerable
BiblicalUsage: The Ancient of days is the title Daniel gives to God on His throne, and this Aramaic word means venerable, aged, enduring. Daniel saw the Ancient of days sit, His garment white as snow and His hair like pure wool, and the Son of man came to Him, and judgment was given to the saints of the most High.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Ancient of days is the comfort of every believer, because the God who was before all things will still be on the throne when all things end. The beasts rise and fall, but the Ancient of days remains, and I hold that His kingdom is the one that will never pass away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: venerable
BiblicalUsage: The Ancient of days is the title Daniel gives to God on His throne, and this Aramaic word means venerable, aged, enduring. Daniel saw the Ancient of days sit, His garment white as snow and His hair like pure wool, and the Son of man came to Him, and judgment was given to the saints of the most High.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Ancient of days is the comfort of every believer, because the God who was before all things will still be on the throne when all things end. The beasts rise and fall, but the Ancient of days remains, and I hold that His kingdom is the one that will never pass away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prepared, i.e. full grown; spoken only (in plural) of he-goats, or (figuratively) leaders of the people
BiblicalUsage: The he-goat is the leader of the flock, and the word follows it from Jacob's flocks to the judgment of the shepherds. Jacob saw the rams leaping on the cattle in his dream, Moses says Israel ate the fat of lambs and the rams of Bashan and goats, and Ezekiel says God will judge between the rams and the he-goats, between the fat cattle and the lean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the he-goat's story is about leadership, because the strong push the weak aside and God notices. The dream that made Jacob rich and the judgment that separates the rams are the same word, and I hold that the Chief Shepherd will sort His flock Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a fire-place, i.e. furnace
BiblicalUsage: The burning fiery furnace is the heart of Daniel's third chapter, and this word names it. Whoever would not worship the golden image would be cast into it, Nebuchadnezzar heated it seven times hotter in his rage, and then he came near to its mouth and called the three men out by name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the furnace is the Bible's plainest picture of what faith costs and what God does with it, because the fire that was meant to destroy them only burned their bonds. The fourth man in the fire was the difference, and I hold that God does not always keep His people out of the furnace, but He always goes in with them.
RelatedPeople: King Nebuchadnezzar; Shadrach; Meshach; Abednego; Daniel
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ledge or offset in a building
BiblicalUsage: The galleries of the temple were the ledges and passages that ran around the side chambers, and Ezekiel measured them as carefully as the rest of the house. The word appears only in his vision of the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the ledges of God's house were measured, because nothing in His dwelling is an afterthought.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from αὐχμός (probably from a base akin to that of G109) (dust, as dried by wind); properly, dirty, i.e. (by implication) obscure:--dark.
BiblicalUsage: Peter says we have a more sure word of prophecy, and we do well to take heed to it, as to a light that shines in a dark place, until the day dawn and the day star arise in our hearts. The word means murky or dim, the darkness the light shines into.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the dark place is where I live now, and the sure word is the lamp that keeps me from stumbling until the morning comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G827; to beam forth (figuratively):--shine.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ should shine unto them. The word is the beaming forth of that light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the light is always shining, and the blindness is the enemy's work, not the light's failure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a ray of light, i.e. (by implication) radiance, dawn:--break of day.
BiblicalUsage: After Paul raised Eutychus, he went up and broke bread and talked a long while, even till break of day, and so departed. The word means the dawn, the first ray of morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the dawn after a long night of preaching is a small picture of the resurrection morning, when the talking will give way to the seeing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Latin (" august "); Augustus, a title of the Roman emperor:--Augustus.
BiblicalUsage: Caesar Augustus decreed that all the world should be taxed, and his decree sent Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where Christ was born. The word is the emperor's title, and it appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the emperor's decree was God's instrument, because the man who ruled the world moved a young couple to the town where the Messiah had to be born.
RelatedPeople: Caesar Augustus; Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G109; a yard (as open to the wind); by implication, a mansion:--court, (sheep-)fold, hall, palace.
BiblicalUsage: The court or fold is the walled yard where the sheep are kept, and Jesus uses it for His flock and His Father's house. He says the thief enters not by the door into the sheepfold, and that He has other sheep which are not of this fold, and Peter followed Him into the high priest's palace and warmed himself by the fire in the courtyard.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fold is the picture of belonging: the sheep know the Shepherd's voice, the door is Christ Himself, and the other sheep are still being brought in. Peter denied Him in the courtyard of the same house, and I hold that the fold's door is still open to the one who denies and comes back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G836; to play the flute:--pipe.
BiblicalUsage: To pipe is to play the flute, and Jesus uses it for the children in the marketplace who piped and no one danced, and mourned and no one lamented. Paul says even lifeless things like the pipe give a distinct sound, or no one knows what is piped.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the pipers in the marketplace are still playing, and the question is still whether we will dance to the tune God is playing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G832; a flute-player:--minstrel, piper.
BiblicalUsage: The minstrels were already playing at Jairus's house when Jesus arrived, making a noise over the dead girl, and John says the voice of harpers and musicians and pipers will be heard no more in fallen Babylon. The word is the flute-player, the hired mourner.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the minstrels show the two ends of music: at Jairus's house the noise stopped when Life walked in, and in Babylon the music stops because judgment has come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G833; to pass the night (properly, in the open air):--abide, lodge.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there, and Luke says He spent the days teaching in the temple and the nights lodging on the Mount of Olives. The word means to spend the night in the open, to abide.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the nights on the mountain were the quiet half of His last week, and the city that would not receive Him by day could not keep Him by night.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G109; a flute (as blown):--pipe.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says even things without life, whether pipe or harp, give a distinction in their sounds, and if they do not, no one knows what is piped or harped. The word is the flute itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's point is plain: a message that cannot be understood is no message at all, and the church must speak so that people can hear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of the same as G109 (meaning a breeze, i.e. the morning air); properly, fresh, i.e. (adverb with ellipsis of G2250) to-morrow:--(to-)morrow, next day.
BiblicalUsage: Tomorrow is the word for the day that has not come, and the Bible treats it with both warning and patience. The rulers gathered on the morrow to judge Peter and John, James says to those who plan their business for tomorrow, ye know not what shall be on the morrow, Jesus says take no thought for the morrow, and Paul quotes the saying, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe tomorrow belongs to God, and the two errors are to presume on it and to despair of it. The rulers' tomorrow brought a bold witness, the merchants' tomorrow was a vapour, and I hold that the only safe plan for tomorrow is the one that says, if the Lord will.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; John the Apostle; James, Brother of the Lord; Paul; Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a (presumed) derivative of the same as G109 (meaning blown); rough (properly as a gale), i.e. (figuratively) severe:--austere.
BiblicalUsage: The wicked servant called his master an austere man, one who takes up what he did not lay down and reaps what he did not sow, and the master answered him out of his own mouth. The word means severe or exacting.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the servant's excuse condemned him, because he knew his master's character and still buried the talent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G842; self-satisfaction, i.e. (abstractly) contentedness, or (concretely) a competence:--contentment, sufficiency.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says godliness with contentment is great gain, and that God is able to make all grace abound so that believers, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work. The word means contentment, or a competence that needs nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that contentment is not having everything, it is needing nothing more than what God has already given.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G846 and G714; self-complacent, i.e. contented:--content.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he has learned, in whatsoever state he is, therewith to be content, and the word means self-sufficient in the Christian sense, satisfied because Christ supplies. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe contentment is learned, not born, and Paul learned it in need and in plenty alike.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G846 and the base of G2237; self-pleasing, i.e. arrogant:--self-willed.
BiblicalUsage: The self-willed are those who please themselves and despise government, and Peter says they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities. Paul says a bishop must not be self-willed, because the overseer is a steward of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that self-will is the root of every other sin on these lists, because it puts my pleasure above God's order.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G846 and the same as G140; self-chosen, i.e. (by implication) voluntary:--of own accord, willing of self.
BiblicalUsage: The Macedonians gave beyond their power, willing of themselves, and Titus accepted Paul's exhortation and went to Corinth of his own accord. The word means voluntary, chosen by oneself and not forced.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the freest giving is the giving no one demands, because it shows a heart already won.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G846 and an obsolete ἕντης (a worker); to act of oneself, i.e. (figuratively) dominate:--usurp authority over.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he does not permit a woman to teach or to usurp authority over a man, but to be in silence, and the word means to exercise authority or dominate. It appears only here, and it has been much debated.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's word here is about order in the church, not about worth, because the same letter honours women who labour in the gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G846 and G5495; self-handed, i.e. doing personally:--with … own hands.
BiblicalUsage: On the third day of the storm the sailors cast out the tackling of the ship with their own hands, and the word means with one's own hands, doing it personally. It appears only here.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sailors' own hands could not save the ship, and the lightening of it only proved how little was left in their control.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G846 and a derivative or G2632; self-condemned:--condemned of self.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the heretic, after the first and second admonition, is to be rejected, because he is subverted and sins, being condemned of himself. The word means self-condemned, judged by his own words.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a person who will not be corrected has already passed sentence on himself, and the church's rejection only names what he has done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G846 and the same as G3155; self-moved ("automatic"), i.e. spontaneous:--of own accord, of self.
BiblicalUsage: The earth brings forth fruit of herself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn, and the iron gate of the prison opened to Peter of its own accord. The word means of itself, without a hand to move it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the kingdom grows the same way in both verses: quietly, surely, and by a power no hand can see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G846 and G3700; self-seeing, i.e. an eye-witness:--eye-witness.
BiblicalUsage: Luke opens his Gospel by saying it came from those who were eyewitnesses from the very beginning. The word means someone who saw it with their own eyes, not someone who heard it second-hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Christian faith rests on what people actually saw, and Luke knew that mattered enough to say so in his first breath.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the particle αὖ (perhaps akin to the base of G109 through the idea of a baffling wind) (backward); the reflexive pronoun self, used (alone or in the compound G1438) of the third person, and (with the proper personal pronoun) of the other persons:--her, it(-self), one, the other, (mine) own, said, (self-), the) same, ((him-, my-, thy-)self, (your-)selves, she, that, their(-s), them(-selves), there(-at, - by, -in, -into, -of, -on, -with), they, (these) things, this (man), those, together, very, which. Compare G848.
BiblicalUsage: This is the plain pronoun behind he, she, it, they, them and himself — thousands of times over, it is the word that points back to someone already named. In John 1:3 all things were made by him, in John 3:16 God gave his Son for the world, and in Romans 8:29 we are conformed to the image of his Son. The word itself carries no meaning of its own; it borrows everything from the person it points to.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this little word quietly teaches me something large: Scripture is never vague about who did what. When it says he, it means a real person — Christ himself, God himself — and my faith rests on him, not on an idea.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: genitive (i.e. possessive) of G846, used as an adverb of location; properly, belonging to the same spot, i.e. in this (or that) place:--(t-)here.
BiblicalUsage: This is the possessive form of the same pronoun — his, its, theirs — used as an adverb of place, meaning belonging to the same spot. Paul left Priscilla and Aquila there at Ephesus, and Jesus told his disciples to sit there while he went to pray.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a word this small reminds me that God works in particular places, with particular people, not in abstractions.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb; to grow ("wax"), i.e. enlarge (literal or figurative, active or passive):--grow (up), (give the) increase.
BiblicalUsage: Paul planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the increase — that is the heart of this word. It is the growth of a plant, a child, a church, and a believer: Luke says the child Jesus grew, John says Christ must increase while he decreases, and Peter ends his letter by telling us to grow in grace. The growth is real, but it is never self-made.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe growth in the Christian life is God's work in me, not my achievement. My part is to plant and water faithfully; his part is the increase, and that takes the pressure off me and puts the glory where it belongs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G837; growth:--increase.
BiblicalUsage: This is the noun form of growth — the increase itself. Paul uses it of the body growing with the increase of God as it holds fast to the Head, and of the whole body growing as every part does its work.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a healthy church grows the way a body grows: joined to Christ, each part supplying what the others need.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perversity
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah says the Lord mingled a perverse spirit in the midst of Egypt, so that the nation staggered like a drunken man in his vomit. The word names a twisting of judgment until nothing is straight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one verse shows what happens when a nation turns from God: even its wisdom goes crooked.
