It is the word for the heavy burdens the Pharisees bind on men's shoulders, for the weightier matters of the law they leave undone, for the grievous wolves Paul says will enter the flock, and for John's plain word that God's commandments are not grievous.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's weight and man's weight are not the same, because His commandments are not grievous but the Pharisees' burdens are. The same word describes the wolves and the law's weightier matters, and I hold that we know a burden is from God when it is heavy with glory and not with guilt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G926 and G5092; highly valuable:--very precious.
BiblicalUsage: Barytimos means very precious, of great value, and it describes the alabaster box of very precious ointment poured on Jesus' head at Bethany.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the most precious thing in the room that night was not the ointment but the love that poured it, and the disciples who counted its price missed its point.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: iron (as cutting); by extension, an iron implement
BiblicalUsage: Barzel is iron, the metal that cuts and breaks and holds an edge. Moses promises a land whose stones are iron, Goliath's spearhead weighs six hundred shekels of iron, the proverb says iron sharpens iron and a man sharpens his friend, and the psalm says the Son will break the nations with a rod of iron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe iron is the Bible's picture of strength that can serve or crush, because the same metal arms a giant and sharpens a friend. God gives iron to a land He loves and a rod of iron to a Son He has anointed, and I hold that strength is only good when the hand that holds it belongs to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Barzillai, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Barzillai is the name of three Israelites, and the chief of them is Barzillai the Gileadite, the old man of eighty who brought beds and basins and food to David when he fled from Absalom, who refused the king's offer of a place in Jerusalem, and whom David remembered on his deathbed with kindness to his sons. A later Barzillai is named among those who returned from exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Barzillai is the picture of loyalty that asks for nothing, because he fed a fugitive king and went home to die in his own city. David never forgot it, and I hold that the kindness shown to a king in his lowest hour is the kindness God remembers longest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the balsam plant
BiblicalUsage: Basam is the balsam plant, the spice garden, and the beloved says he has come into his garden to gather myrrh and eat his honeycomb.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the spice garden is love's own picture, because what is planted in delight is gathered in delight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G928; torture:--torment.
BiblicalUsage: Basanismos is torment, and in Revelation it is the torment of the locusts that sting men for five months. It is the smoke of torment that rises forever from those who worship the beast, and the torment Babylon's merchants watch from afar when her judgment comes in one hour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe torment in Revelation is never meaningless pain, because every instance of it is judgment with a name and a reason. The locusts torment those without God's seal, the beast's worshippers are tormented for their worship, and Babylon is tormented for her sins, and I hold that the God who torments in judgment is the same God who warned us plainly so we could flee it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G928; a torturer:--tormentor.
BiblicalUsage: A basanistes is a torturer, a jailer who torments, and the unforgiving servant is delivered to the tormentors until he pays all that he owes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the tormentors in the parable are the end of unforgiveness, because the servant who would not forgive is given over to those who will not forgive him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G931; to torture:--pain, toil, torment, toss, vex.
BiblicalUsage: Basanizo means to torment, to torture, to toss as a ship is tossed by waves. The devils beg Jesus not to torment them before the time, the disciples' ship is tossed in the wind on the sea, the woman in travail is tormented in her labour, and the devil is cast into the lake of fire to be tormented day and night forever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word runs from the devils' fear to the devil's end, because the same torment they dreaded is the torment they will suffer. They knew the time was coming, and I hold that their begging proves what the lake of fire confirms: judgment is real, and it is forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps remotely from the same as G939 (through the notion of going to the bottom); a touch-stone, i.e. (by analogy) torture:--torment.
BiblicalUsage: Basanos is torment, the touchstone that tests and the pain that proves. They bring to Jesus all who are sick and tormented with diseases, and the rich man lifts up his eyes in hell, being in torments, and begs that his brothers be warned so they do not come into this place of torment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe torment in the Gospels is always a place you can still be saved from, because the sick are brought to Jesus to be healed and the rich man begs for his brothers while there is still time. His torment is the warning, and I hold that the warning is mercy while we are alive to hear it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flesh (from its freshness); by extension, body, person; also (by euphemistically) the pudenda of a man
BiblicalUsage: Basar is flesh, the body, the stuff we are made of. Adam calls Eve bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, God says His Spirit will not always strive with man because he is flesh, Isaiah says all flesh will see the glory of the Lord together, and Ezekiel promises God will take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe flesh is the Bible's word for our frailty and our hope at once, because the same flesh that fails is the flesh God promises to renew. He made us flesh, He came in flesh, and I hold that the God who gives a heart of flesh is the God who will raise our flesh in glory.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be fresh, i.e. full (rosy, (figuratively) cheerful); to announce (glad news)
BiblicalUsage: Basar as a verb means to bring good news, to publish glad tidings. Isaiah says how beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him that brings good tidings of peace, the Spirit anoints the servant to preach good tidings to the meek, the psalm says to show forth His salvation from day to day, and Nahum says the feet of him that brings good tidings stand on the mountains.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe good news is only good because of who carries it and what it says, and Isaiah's beautiful feet belong to the messenger of peace. The gospel was good tidings before the Gospels were written, and I hold that every preacher since has only been repeating the news that God has come to save.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to trample down
BiblicalUsage: Bashac means to trample down, and Amos uses it against those who tread upon the poor and take wheat from them, warning that the stone houses they build will not be theirs to live in.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that trampling the poor is trampling the image of God, and Amos says the house built on it will stand empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to boil up; hence, to be done in cooking; figuratively to ripen
BiblicalUsage: Bashal means to boil, to cook. It is the word for the Passover lamb that must be roasted, not boiled, for the kid that must not be boiled in its mother's milk, for the pot of pottage Elisha's servant sets before the sons of the prophets, and for the priests' servants who come with a fleshhook while the meat is boiling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cooking pot is where God's law meets the daily table, because He tells His people not only what to eat but how to cook it. The rules about boiling look small until you see what they guard, and I hold that a God who cares about the pot cares about the people who eat from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bashan (often with the article), a region East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Bashan is the rich land east of the Jordan, the kingdom of Og, whose cities and oaks and strong bulls are named again and again. Israel turns to fight Og at Edrei, takes all his cities and his land, and divides Bashan among the half-tribe of Manasseh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bashan stands in Scripture for strength that cannot save, because Og's bed was made of iron and his kingdom was still given into Israel's hand. The oaks are tall and the bulls are strong, and I hold that none of it matters when God has given the land to His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: boiled
BiblicalUsage: Bashel means boiled, and it describes the meat that must not be boiled at the Passover and the shoulder of the ram that is boiled for the Nazarite's offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the cooking of the offering is ordered by God, and the boiled shoulder is holy because He said so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G935; properly, royalty, i.e. (abstractly) rule, or (concretely) a realm (literally or figuratively):--kingdom, + reign.
BiblicalUsage: Basileia is the kingdom, the reign, the realm of a king. Jesus says the kingdom of heaven belongs to the poor in spirit, teaches us to pray for the kingdom to come, tells Nicodemus a man must be born again to see the kingdom of God, and John hears the seventh angel announce that the kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdom is not a place we build but a reign we enter, because Jesus says it belongs to the poor in spirit and comes to those who are born again. It is prayed for, it is preached, and one day it will be announced as finished, and I hold that every prayer for the kingdom to come is a prayer for the King to come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G934; a palace:--king's court.
BiblicalUsage: Basileion means a king's court, a palace, and Jesus uses it when He asks the crowds what they went into the wilderness to see, a man clothed in soft raiment, for those who wear soft clothing live in kings' houses.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jesus' question draws the line between the palace and the wilderness, because John wore camel's hair and lived where kings do not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G935; kingly (in nature):--royal.
BiblicalUsage: Basileios means royal, kingly, and Peter says believers are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe royal priesthood is the dignity God gives His people, because He makes those who were not a people into a nation of kings and priests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G935; to rule (literally or figuratively):--king, reign.
BiblicalUsage: Basileuo means to reign, to rule as a king. Gabriel says the Son will reign over the house of Jacob forever, Paul says Christ must reign until He has put all enemies under His feet, that those who receive grace will reign in life through Jesus Christ, and John hears that the Lord God omnipotent reigns.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reigning is the promise that makes every other promise sure, because a King who reigns forever cannot lose what He has won. Death reigned through Adam, grace reigns through Christ, and I hold that the reign of Jesus is the one reign that will never end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G939 (through the notion of a foundation of power); a sovereign (abstractly, relatively, or figuratively):--king.
BiblicalUsage: Basileus is a king, and the word follows Jesus from His birth to His cross to His return. The wise men ask where He is who is born King of the Jews, Jesus tells Pilate He was born to be a King and to bear witness to the truth, Pilate writes King of the Jews on the cross, and John sees Him coming with King of kings and Lord of lords written on His vesture and His thigh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the title King follows Jesus because it is true at every point of His life, and the men who used it as a charge against Him were telling the truth without knowing it. Pilate wrote it in mockery, the wise men spoke it in worship, and I hold that one day every knee will confess what the cross already declared.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G935; regal (in relation), i.e. (literally) belonging to (or befitting) the sovereign (as land, dress, or a courtier), or (figuratively) preeminent:--king's, nobleman, royal.
BiblicalUsage: Basilikos means royal, belonging to the king. It covers the nobleman whose son lies sick at Capernaum, the royal law of loving your neighbour as yourself, and the people of Tyre and Sidon who come to Herod because their country is nourished by the king's country.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the royal word shows how the kingdom touches every station, because a nobleman begs for his son, a law is called royal for its dignity, and a whole country lives by a king's favour. The nobleman's faith is the pattern, and I hold that the King who healed his son still answers the royal and the common alike.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine from G936; a queen:--queen.
BiblicalUsage: Basilissa is a queen, and it is the word for the queen of the south who came to hear Solomon's wisdom and will rise in judgment against this generation. It is also the word for the Ethiopian eunuch who serves Candace the queen of the Ethiopians, and for Babylon who sits a queen and says she will see no sorrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the queen of the south is the rebuke to every generation that has greater wisdom in front of it and will not hear, because she travelled to the ends of the earth for Solomon while this generation has Christ before them. Babylon calls herself a queen and falls in one hour, and I hold that the difference between the two queens is the difference between seeking wisdom and boasting in pride.
RelatedEvents: The Queen of Sheba Visits Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from βαίνω (to walk); a pace ("base"), i.e. (by implication) the foot:--foot.
BiblicalUsage: Basis means a step, the foot, and it appears once, when Peter takes the lame man by the right hand and his feet and ankle bones receive strength.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the lame man's feet are the proof of the miracle, because the feet that never walked are the first thing God makes strong.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: akin to G5335; to malign, i.e. (by extension) to fascinate (by false representations):--bewitch.
BiblicalUsage: Baskaino means to bewitch, to fascinate with false words, and Paul asks the Galatians who has bewitched them that they should not obey the truth, when Christ was plainly set forth crucified before their eyes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that bewitching is what false teaching does when it looks spiritual, and Paul's question is still the right one for anyone who has drifted from the plain gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps remotely derived from the base of G939 (through the idea of removal); to lift, literally or figuratively (endure, declare, sustain, receive, etc.):--bear, carry, take up.
BiblicalUsage: Bastazo means to lift, to bear, to carry a load. Jesus takes our infirmities and bears our sicknesses, Paul tells us to bear one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ, Jesus bears His own cross to Golgotha, and He says whoever does not bear his cross and come after Him cannot be His disciple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bearing is the shape of the Christian life, because Jesus bore our sicknesses first and then asks us to bear one another's burdens and our own cross. The load is real and the command is plain, and I hold that no one bears alone what Christ has already carried.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to babble; hence, to vociferate angrily
BiblicalUsage: Bata means to speak rashly, to babble out words without thinking. The law says a man who swears rashly with his lips is guilty when he knows it, the proverb says rash words are like the piercings of a sword while the tongue of the wise is health, and the psalm says Moses spoke unadvisedly with his lips at Meribah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rash words are the easiest sin and the hardest to take back, because a sword-thrust of a sentence cannot be unsaid. Moses himself spoke unadvisedly once, and I hold that his failure is our warning: even the meekest man must guard his mouth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: figuratively, to trust, be confident or sure
BiblicalUsage: Batach means to trust, to be confident, to lean on with assurance. Proverbs says to trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding, Isaiah says God keeps in perfect peace the mind that is stayed on Him because it trusts in Him, the psalm says it is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in man, and Jeremiah says blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe trust is the whole of faith in one word, because it is not agreeing that God is true but leaning on Him with all your weight. The man who trusts in man is cursed and the man who trusts in the Lord is blessed, and I hold that the difference is not the size of the trouble but the place of the trust.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to desist from labor
BiblicalUsage: Batel means to cease from labour, to stop working, and it appears once, when the grinders cease because they are few in the days of old age.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the ceasing grinders are old age itself, and the Preacher's picture is honest about what time does to us all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bath or Hebrew measure (as a means of division) of liquids
BiblicalUsage: Bath is a measure for liquids, the bath of the temple's great sea and of the offerings. Solomon's molten sea holds two thousand baths, the law fixes the bath as a tenth of a homer so that measures are honest, and Isaiah says ten acres of vineyard will yield one bath of wine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's measures are a sermon on honesty, because He fixes the bath and the ephah so that no man can cheat his neighbour with a false measure. The temple sea holds its thousands of baths by His order, and I hold that a God who measures wine cares about honest dealing in the market too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the daughter (i.e. city) of Rabbah
BiblicalUsage: Bath-rabbim means the daughter of many, the daughter of Rabbah, and it names the gate by the fishpools of Heshbon where the beloved's eyes are compared to still waters.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gate's name is kept because the Song delights in real places, and the eyes compared to those pools are praised for their stillness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bath-Sheba, the mother of Solomon
BiblicalUsage: Bathsheba is the wife of Uriah the Hittite whom David sees from his roof and takes. She is the mother of the child who dies and then of Solomon, and the queen mother who comes to David in his old age and to Solomon on his throne to plead for Adonijah's life and for her own place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bathsheba's name carries both the sin and the grace of the story, because the same woman who was taken in adultery becomes the mother of the king who builds the temple. God does not erase her, and I hold that her place in the genealogy of Christ is proof that grace writes names the world would rather forget.
RelatedPeople: Bathsheba; King David; King Solomon; Nathan; Uriah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bath-shua,
BiblicalUsage: Bath-shua is another name for Bathsheba, the mother of Solomon, named in the genealogy of David's sons born in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two names belong to one woman, and the chronicler's Bath-shua is David's Bathsheba, the mother of the king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: desolation
BiblicalUsage: Bathah means desolation, a waste place, and Isaiah says the vineyard that bears wild grapes will be laid waste, neither pruned nor dug, and briers and thorns will come up in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a laid-waste vineyard is the end of unfruitfulness, because God gives His vineyard every care and then judges it by its fruit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut in pieces
BiblicalUsage: Bathaq means to cut in pieces, and Ezekiel says the company gathered against unfaithful Jerusalem will stone her and dispatch her with their swords.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cutting is judgment in plain language, and Ezekiel leaves no soft words around what unfaithfulness earns.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to chop up
BiblicalUsage: Bathar means to cut in two, to divide, and Abram cuts the animals of the covenant in half and lays each piece against the other before the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the divided animals are the covenant itself, because God passes between the pieces and binds Himself to His promise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G899; a step, i.e. (figuratively) grade (of dignity):--degree.
BiblicalUsage: Bathmos is a step, a grade of standing, and Paul says deacons who have used the office well purchase to themselves a good degree and great boldness in the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that faithful service earns standing before God, and the good degree is the reward of deacons who serve well.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G901; profundity, i.e. (by implication) extent; (figuratively) mystery:--deep(-ness, things), depth.
BiblicalUsage: Bathos is depth, and it is the word for the deep water where Jesus tells Peter to launch out and let down his nets. It is also the word for the depth that cannot separate us from the love of God, for the depth of the riches of God's wisdom and knowledge that Paul cries out over, and for the depth of Christ's love that passes knowledge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe depth is the Bible's measure for what cannot be measured, because the love of God has a depth no line can sound and a height no ladder can reach. Paul bows his knees so we can comprehend it, and I hold that the deep things of God are not hidden from us but given to us by His Spirit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G901; to deepen:--deep.
BiblicalUsage: Bathyno means to dig deep, and Jesus says the wise builder digs deep and lays his foundation on the rock.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that digging deep is the work faith does before the storm comes, because a foundation laid on rock is the only one that stands when the flood beats on the house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G939; profound (as going down), literally or figuratively:--deep, very early.
BiblicalUsage: Bathys means deep, and it is the word for the deep well at Sychar where the Samaritan woman says Jesus has nothing to draw with. It is also the word for the women who come very early to the tomb, for Eutychus who sinks into a deep sleep while Paul preaches, and for the deep things of Satan the church at Thyatira is warned not to know.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe deep cuts both ways in this word, because the well is deep and the sleep is deep and the things of Satan are deep. The woman at the well found living water deeper than her well, and I hold that the deep things of God are the only deep things worth knowing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1324); a bath, or measure for liquids:--measure.
BiblicalUsage: Batos is the bush, the thorn-bush where Moses saw the burning bush, and also the bath, the measure for oil in the parable of the unjust steward. The same spelling carries both senses, and the burning bush is the famous one: Moses sees it, and the Lord calls him by name.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bush is the greater sense, because a bush that burns and is not consumed is God's own sign that He is present and holy, and the measure of oil is only a measure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1324); a bath, or measure for liquids:--measure.
BiblicalUsage: Batos is the bush, the thorn-bush where Moses saw the burning bush, and also the bath, the measure for oil in the parable of the unjust steward. The same spelling carries both senses, and the burning bush is the famous one: Moses sees it, and the Lord calls him by name.

Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a frog:--frog.
BiblicalUsage: Batrachos is a frog, and John sees three unclean spirits like frogs come out of the mouth of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the frogs are a fitting picture for lying spirits, because they come out of the mouths that lie and go out to gather the kings for battle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: figuratively, to finish, or (intransitively) stop
BiblicalUsage: Batsa means to cut off, to finish, to be greedy for gain. The proverb says the ways of everyone greedy of gain take away the life of its owners, he who is greedy of gain troubles his own house, Isaiah says the Lord will cut off the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and Habakkuk woes the man who covets an evil covetousness to his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word ties greed to cutting, because the greedy man cuts himself off from his own house and from God. He takes and he loses, and I hold that the covetousness Habakkuk woes is the same greed the proverb warns will cost a man his life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gather grapes; also to be isolated (i.e. inaccessible by height or fortification)
BiblicalUsage: Batsar means to be fenced, fortified, inaccessible, and also to gather grapes. The spies report cities great and fenced up to heaven, Caleb asks for the mountain with its fenced cities and giants, Nehemiah says Israel took strong cities and a fat land, and Jeremiah says the remnant of Israel will be gleaned as a vine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fenced city is the Bible's picture of a strength that is not strength, because the walls that frightened the spies fell before a God who keeps His promises. Caleb asked for the hardest mountain, and I hold that his courage is the answer to every report that says the walls are too high.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dough (as swelling by fermentation)
BiblicalUsage: Batseq is dough, the lump that rises, and it is the dough Israel carries out of Egypt in their kneading troughs and bakes into unleavened cakes because they were thrust out in haste.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the unleavened dough is the Exodus itself in a basket, because a people in a hurry has no time for bread to rise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dough (as swelling by fermentation)
BiblicalUsage: Batseq is dough, the lump that rises, and it is the dough Israel carries out of Egypt in their kneading troughs and bakes into unleavened cakes because they were thrust out in haste.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the unleavened dough is the Exodus itself in a basket, because a people in a hurry has no time for bread to rise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: clipped, i.e. the grape crop
BiblicalUsage: Batsiyr is the grape harvest, the vintage, the gathering of the grapes. The law promises the threshing will reach to the vintage and the vintage to the sowing time, Gideon says the gleaning of Ephraim is better than the vintage of Abiezer, Isaiah says the earth will be like the shaking of an olive tree and the gleaning of grapes when the vintage is done, and Micah says he is like the gleanings of the summer fruits when there is no cluster to eat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the vintage is the Bible's picture of a harvest that is both gift and judgment, because the same gathering that feeds a people in obedience leaves nothing when the land is judged. Gideon's gleaning honours Ephraim, and I hold that God counts the gleanings as carefully as He counts the harvest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Batsluth or Batslith, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bazluth is named among the Nethinim. They are the temple servants whose children returned from exile with Zerubbabel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the servants of the house are written down with the rest, and Bazluth's children are kept in the record because they belonged to the Lord's work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: inaccessible, i.e. lofty
BiblicalUsage: Batsowr means inaccessible, lofty, hard to reach, and Zechariah calls the cedars to howl because the mighty are spoiled and the forest of the vintage is come down.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the lofty cedars are the pride of Lebanon, and their fall is God's answer to everything that stands tall against Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: restraint (of rain), i.e. drought
BiblicalUsage: Batstsoreth is restraint, the holding back of rain, drought, and Jeremiah uses it for the drought that comes on Judah and for the tree planted by the waters that does not fear when the drought comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the drought tests what a tree is rooted in, because the tree by the waters does not fear the year of drought.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: desolation
BiblicalUsage: Battah means desolation, a waste place, and Isaiah says the flies and bees will come and rest in the desolate valleys and the holes of the rocks when Assyria comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that desolation is the land God gives over to judgment, and the valleys that once sang will lie empty until He restores them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Βάττος (a proverbial stammerer) and G3056; to stutter, i.e. (by implication) to prate tediously:--use vain repetitions.
BiblicalUsage: Battologeo means to use vain repetitions, to babble on like the heathen, and Jesus warns His disciples not to pray that way, thinking they will be heard for their much speaking.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God is not impressed by many words, and the prayer He hears is the one that means what it says.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: security
BiblicalUsage: Battuchoth means security, safety, and Job says the tabernacles of robbers prosper and those who provoke God are secure.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the security of the wicked is the hardest thing in Job to bear, because it looks as though provoking God costs nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bavvai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bavvai is named once. He is the ruler of half of Keilah who repairs another measure of the wall with his men.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the wall was built measure by measure by men like Bavvai, and every measure is remembered because every builder mattered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a house (in the greatest variation of applications, especially family, etc.)}
BiblicalUsage: Bayith is the Aramaic word for house, and it is the word for the house of God in the days of exile and return. Daniel goes to his house and tells his companions to seek mercies of the God of heaven, Daniel kneels in his house with his windows open toward Jerusalem, Zerubbabel and Jeshua rise up and build the house of God at Jerusalem, and Cyrus commands that the house be built in its place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the house in exile is the promise that God has not moved out, because Daniel prays toward a house that lies in ruins and the exiles come home to rebuild it. The house of God is the place where His people meet Him, and I hold that the God who answers Daniel in his house still answers His people in His house today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bajith, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bajith is a place in Moab, named once. The people go up to the high places to weep over the judgment coming on their land.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the weeping at Bajith is the sound of a nation that trusted in its high places and found them empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

The house of God is the place where His people meet Him, and I hold that the God who answers Daniel in his house still answers His people in His house today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plunder
BiblicalUsage: Baz is spoil, plunder, the prey taken in war. God says the little ones Israel feared would be a prey will go in and possess the land, Ezekiel says His flock became a prey because there was no shepherd, and Jeremiah says all who devour Israel will be devoured and all who spoil her will be spoiled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe spoil is the Bible's measure of who is really in charge, because the people who take the prey are the ones God has given the victory to, and the people who spoil Israel are the ones God will spoil in turn. The children Israel feared for are the ones God carries in, and I hold that no one who trusts Him ends as prey.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably to cleave
BiblicalUsage: Baza means to cleave, to cut off, and Isaiah uses it for the land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia whose ambassadors go by the sea in vessels of bulrushes, a nation scattered and peeled.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the scattered nation is still known to God, and Isaiah says a present will yet be brought to the Lord from that far land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to disesteem
BiblicalUsage: Bazah means to despise, to disesteem, to count as nothing. Esau despises his birthright for a bowl of pottage, Goliath disdains David when he sees he is only a youth, Isaiah says the Servant is despised and rejected of men, and Malachi says the priests despise God's name while they offer polluted bread on His altar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe despising is the sin that looks smallest and costs the most, because Esau sold his birthright for a meal and the priests sold God's honour for convenience. The Servant was despised and rejected, and I hold that the God men despise is the God who saves them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a flash of lightning
BiblicalUsage: Bazaq is a flash of lightning, and Ezekiel says the living creatures run and return as the appearance of a flash of lightning.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the flash is the glory of the creatures' movement, because they go where the Spirit goes and they go as fast as lightning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to disperse
BiblicalUsage: Bazar means to scatter, to disperse, and Daniel uses it for the king who scatters plunder among his followers, while the psalm says God scatters the people who delight in war.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God scatters the proud and their plunder alike, and the king who scatters spoil to buy loyalty will find it scattered again.

Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-ha-Emek, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Emek means house of the valley, and it is named once, on the border of Asher in Joshua 19:27, where the boundary turns toward the sunrising and reaches Zebulun and the valley of Jiphthah-el. A border town, known only by where the line ran.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the borders God set for his people were exact, and a valley town counted as much as a capital.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-ha-Etsel, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Ezel means house of narrowing, and Micah names it once, in Micah 1:11, in a lament over the towns of Judah: the inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth in the mourning of Beth-ezel. A place too hemmed in, too afraid, to come out and help — its name became its story.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Micah's picture still stings: fear can narrow a whole town until it will not move.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-ha-Ram, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Aram means place of the height, and it is named once, in Joshua 13:27, among the towns in the valley given to Gad — Beth-aram and Beth-nimrah and Succoth, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon. A town east of the Jordan, listed with its neighbours and left there.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the towns across the Jordan were still God's gift, even when they sat outside the land most people picture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-ha-Ram, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Haran means house of the joyful shouter, and it appears once, in Numbers 32:36, where the Gadites built Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran as fenced cities, with folds for sheep. A fortified town with a glad name, built by men settling down east of the Jordan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a fenced city with a joyful name is a good picture of settling into what God has given.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-ha-Jeshimoth, a town East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Jeshimoth means house of the desolation, and it sits at both ends of Israel's story east of the Jordan. Israel camped from Beth-jesimoth to Abel-shittim in Numbers 33:49, on the edge of the promised land, and Joshua 12:3 and Joshua 13:20 list it among the conquered towns. Long after, Ezekiel 25:9 names it again among the cities of Moab that God would open to judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a town called house of desolation, standing where Israel camped before crossing over, is a reminder that God brings his people through desolate places, not around them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-hag-Gilgal, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Gilgal means house of the wheel, and it appears once, in Nehemiah 12:29, where the singers gathered from the villages around Jerusalem — from Beth-gilgal among them — for the dedication of the wall. The name never stands as a single word in the Hebrew text; it comes as two words, house and Gilgal, joined together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe it is a small, glad note in Nehemiah's story: singers coming in from the villages to fill the city with praise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-hak-Kerem, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Haccerem means house of the vineyard, and it is named twice, in two very different moods. Jeremiah 6:1 tells Benjamin to set up a sign of fire in Beth-haccerem as the enemy comes, and Nehemiah 3:14 shows Malchiah, ruler of part of Beth-haccerem, repairing the dung gate in the rebuilding. A vineyard town that saw both alarm and repair.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the same town can stand in a warning and in a rebuilding, and God is in both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Beth-lechemite, or native of Bethlechem
BiblicalUsage: A Beth-lehemite is simply a man from Bethlehem, house of bread — and the word is famous because of who it describes. In 1 Samuel 16:18 a servant calls David a son of Jesse the Beth-lehemite, and in 1 Samuel 17:58 David answers Saul the same way. In 2 Samuel 21:19 the word marks Elhanan, a Beth-lehemite who slew the brother of Goliath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe it matters that David is introduced by his town before his throne: God chose a shepherd from Bethlehem, and the town's name went with him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-ham-Markaboth or Beth-Markaboth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Marcaboth means house of the chariots, and it is named twice, both times in lists of Simeon's towns. Joshua 19:5 counts it among the cities given to Simeon, and 1 Chronicles 4:31 lists it again as one of their cities until the reign of David. A chariot town, kept on the rolls of two different generations.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town named for chariots, kept quietly on Simeon's list, shows how much of Israel's story is ordinary towns held faithfully.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-ham-Merchak, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Hammerchaq means the remote house, and it appears once, in 2 Samuel 15:17, on the worst day of David's life: the king went forth, and all the people after him, and tarried in a place that was far off, fleeing from Absalom. The Hebrew is a house far away, and the English hides the name — but the place is where a fleeing king stopped to gather his people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a far-off house can hold a king's last stand, and David's pause there was not defeat but gathering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Beth-shimshite, or inhabitant of Bethshemesh
BiblicalUsage: A Beth-shemite is a man of Beth-shemesh, house of the sun — and the word is tied to the ark's return. In 1 Samuel 6:14 the cart carrying the ark came into the field of Joshua, a Beth-shemite, and stood there by a great stone. In 1 Samuel 6:18 the golden mice are counted for every Philistine city, down to the country villages of the Beth-shemites.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Beth-shemites remind me that God's ark can come home to an ordinary field, and ordinary men have to decide what to do with it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-hash-Shittah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Shittah means house of the acacia, and it is named once, in Judges 7:22, in the rout of Midian: the host fled to Beth-shittah, with Gideon's three hundred blowing their trumpets behind them. A grove town on the road the enemy ran, named only because they ran that way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the flight to Beth-shittah shows what God does with three hundred trumpets: the enemy runs, and even the road they take is remembered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Car, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Car means house of the ram, and it is named once, in 1 Samuel 7:11, as the limit of a victory: the men of Israel pursued the Philistines and smote them until they came under Beth-car. A place on the Philistine side of the line, remembered because Israel's pursuit stopped there.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God sets the limits of our victories too, and Beth-car is where this one ended.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-le-Aphrah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-le-Aphrah means house of dust, and Micah names it once, in Micah 1:10, with a word-play that is also a command: in the house of Aphrah, roll thyself in the dust. The town's name and the mourning fit each other exactly — dust for a house of dust.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Micah's pun is a sermon in a sentence: the town's name told the people what to do, and they did it in the dust.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Lebaoth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Lebaoth means house of lionesses, and it is named once, in Joshua 19:6, among Simeon's thirteen cities and their villages. No story, no battle — just a fierce name on a town list, kept beside Sharuhen.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that strength was part of the inheritance too, and a town called house of lionesses proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Lechem, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bethlehem means house of bread, and no town in Scripture carries more weight for its size. Rachel died and was buried on the way to Bethlehem in Genesis 35:19, and Ruth 1:1 opens with a famine driving Elimelech's family out of Bethlehem, then Ruth 1:19 brings Naomi and Ruth back to it. Micah 5:2 looks ahead and names Bethlehem Ephratah as the town from which the ruler of Israel would come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bethlehem is God's favourite kind of place: small, hungry, and chosen. The bread of life was born in the house of bread, and I hold that is no accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Maakah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Maachah means house of pressure, and it is named twice, both times around the siege of Abel. In 2 Samuel 20:14 Sheba's flight takes him through to Abel and to Beth-maachah, and in 2 Samuel 20:15 Joab's army besieges him in Abel of Beth-maachah, casting up a bank against the city. A northern town, caught in a rebellion it did not start.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Beth-maachah's name fits the siege: pressure, from outside and from within, until a wise woman talked the city out of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Millo, the name of two citadels
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Millo means house of the rampart, and it is named at Shechem, in the crowning of Abimelech. In Judges 9:6 all the men of Shechem and the house of Millo went and made Abimelech king by the oak at Shechem, and in Judges 9:20 Jotham's curse calls down fire on the house of Millo if they dealt falsely with Jerubbaal. The name never stands as a single word in the Hebrew text; it comes as two words, house and Millo, joined together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jotham's curse is the whole story of Beth-Millo: a crown made in a hurry, and a fire promised for the men who made it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Nimrah, a place east of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Nimrah means house of the leopard, and it is named twice, both times as a town of Gad east of the Jordan. Numbers 32:36 lists it among the fenced cities the Gadites built, with folds for sheep, and Joshua 13:27 sets it in the valley, in the rest of the kingdom of Sihon. A walled town with a wild name.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town named for a leopard, built with sheepfolds, is a good picture of Israel east of the Jordan: walled, watchful, and settled.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Patstsets, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Pazzez means house of dispersion, and it is named once, in Joshua 19:21, among the towns of Issachar — Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez. A town on a list, with a scattered name, and nothing more told about it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a town named for scattering had its place in the inheritance, and God did not lose track of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Peor, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Peor means house of Peor, and it is the landmark of the end of Moses' life. Israel abode in the valley over against Beth-peor in Deuteronomy 3:29, and Moses rehearsed the law there in Deuteronomy 4:46. Then Deuteronomy 34:6 says God buried Moses in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor, and no man knows his sepulchre to this day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Beth-peor is holy ground because of what happened across the valley from it: the law given, and the lawgiver buried by God's own hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Palet, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Palet means house of escape, and it is named twice, at the two ends of Judah's story. Joshua 15:27 lists it among the towns of southern Judah, and Nehemiah 11:26 names it again among the places where the returned exiles settled. A place of escape, given first and then given back.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town called house of escape, settled twice by God's people, is a small picture of the whole exile and return.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Rapha, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Rapha means house of healing, and he is named once, in 1 Chronicles 4:12: Eshton begat Beth-rapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah. A son of Eshton, a man in Judah's genealogy, with a name that sounds like a promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a man called house of healing, named once in a list, still carries his father's hope in his name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Rechob, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Rehob means house of the street, and it is named twice, at opposite ends of Israel's story. Judges 18:28 sets it in the valley by which Dan rebuilt Laish, far from Zidon, and 2 Samuel 10:6 shows the Ammonites hiring the Syrians of Beth-rehob to fight David. A road town, first a landmark for Dan, then a source of soldiers against David.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town on the road to Hamath could not stay neutral for long, and Beth-rehob did not try.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Shean or Beth-Shan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Shean means house of ease, and it is named where Israel's story turns darkest. Joshua 17:11 gives it to Manasseh, though the Canaanites still held it, and 1 Samuel 31:10 says the Philistines fastened Saul's body to the wall of Beth-shan after Gilboa. Then 1 Samuel 31:12 tells how the valiant men of Jabesh went all night and took the body of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Beth-shean shows both sides of the same wall: shame fastened to it, and loyalty that came in the night to take it down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Shemesh, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Shemesh means house of the sun, and it is the town where the ark came home. In 1 Samuel 6:12 the cows took the straight way to Beth-shemesh, lowing as they went, and the men of the town rejoiced to see the ark — but 1 Samuel 6:19 says the Lord smote the men of Beth-shemesh because they looked into the ark. Centuries later, 2 Kings 14:11 says Amaziah and Joash faced each other at Beth-shemesh, king against king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Beth-shemesh teaches me the same lesson twice: God's presence is a joy, and it is not a toy. The town rejoiced, then it looked too closely, and then kings fought there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Tappuach, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Tappuah means house of the apple, and it is named once, in Joshua 15:53, among the hill towns of Judah — Janum, Beth-tappuah, and Aphekah. An orchard town, named for its fruit, and left at that.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town named for apples, kept on Judah's list, is a reminder that God gave his people good land with good fruit in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Beth-Tsur, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Beth-Zur means house of the rock, and the name covers both a town and a man. Joshua 15:58 lists the town among Judah's hill cities, and 2 Chronicles 11:7 shows Rehoboam fortifying it. But 1 Chronicles 2:45 says Maon was the father of Beth-zur — the same name carried by a son of Maon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name meaning house of the rock fits both: a fortified town and a man in Judah's line, each set on something solid.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an egg (from its whiteness)
BiblicalUsage: An egg is a small, plain thing, and Scripture uses it four times, always as a picture of something easily taken. Deuteronomy 22:6 protects the nest with its eggs, Isaiah 10:14 pictures Assyria gathering the riches of the peoples as one gathers eggs left in a nest, and Job 39:14 watches the ostrich leave her eggs in the earth and warm them in the dust.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the egg in these verses is a warning and a comfort at once: what is small and unguarded is easily gathered, and God still tells his people to leave the nest alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bezek, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bezek means lightning, and it is the rallying ground of two different wars. Judges 1:4 says Judah slew ten thousand in Bezek, and Judges 1:5 says they found Adoni-bezek there, the lord of the town. Later, 1 Samuel 11:8 says Saul numbered Israel in Bezek before marching to save Jabesh — three hundred thousand men, counted at Bezek.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bezek is where Israel learned to count its strength: first in battle, then in muster, and both times the Lord delivered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wicked
BiblicalUsage: This is the Aramaic word for bad, and it appears once, in a letter of accusation. In Ezra 4:12 the king's enemies write that the Jews are building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up its walls. One word, used by enemies to describe Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the enemies' word says more about them than about the city: they called bad what God was rebuilding.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alarms
BiblicalUsage: Terrors is the word for alarms that God himself sends, and it appears twice, both times in a sufferer's mouth. Job 6:4 says the terrors of God set themselves in array against him, the arrows of the Almighty within him. Psalms 88:16 says the same thing from the pit: thy terrors have cut me off.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job and the psalmist are honest about something hard: the terrors they felt came from God's hand, and they still cried out to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably akin to G979 (through the idea of vital activity); force:--violence.
BiblicalUsage: Force is the word for violence, and Luke uses it three times, each time around the apostles in danger. In Acts 5:26 the captain brings the apostles without violence, fearing the people; in Acts 21:35 Paul is carried by the soldiers for the violence of the crowd; and in Acts 27:41 the ship breaks apart under the violence of the waves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Luke keeps showing me the same thing: the gospel moves through violence without using it, and God keeps his servants in the middle of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G970; violent:--mighty.
BiblicalUsage: Violent is the word for mighty force, and it appears once, at Pentecost. In Acts 2:2 a sound came from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. The Spirit arrived like weather — sudden, loud, and impossible to ignore.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mighty wind is the right picture for the Spirit: he does not slip in quietly when he comes to fill a house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G971; a forcer, i.e. (figuratively) energetic:--violent.
BiblicalUsage: The violent are the forceful ones, and the word appears once, in a hard saying of Jesus. In Matthew 11:12 he says the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force. Not violence against others, but the eager, pressing energy of people crowding into the kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus is describing hunger, not harm: the kingdom is taken by people who press in because they cannot stay away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G970; to force, i.e. (reflexively) to crowd oneself (into), or (passively) to be seized:--press, suffer violence.
BiblicalUsage: To force one's way in is the word for pressing, crowding, seizing — and it appears twice, both times about the kingdom. In Matthew 11:12 Jesus says the kingdom suffereth violence, and in Luke 16:16 he says every man presseth into it since the days of John. The same pressing, from two Gospels.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pressing is the point: the kingdom is not entered by drifting, but by people who mean to get in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a diminutive of G975; a booklet:--little book.
BiblicalUsage: The little book is the small scroll in the angel's hand in Revelation 10, and John is told to take it and eat it. In Revelation 10:2 the mighty angel holds the little book open, in Revelation 10:9 John takes it and eats it, and in Revelation 10:10 it is sweet in his mouth and bitter in his belly. The word is the diminutive of book — a little book with a great message. Note: the text spells it βιβλαρίδιον, with the letters in a different order from the dictionary form, but it is the same word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little book is the whole prophetic calling in miniature: sweet to receive, bitter to carry, and not to be left unread.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a diminutive of G976; a roll:--bill, book, scroll, writing.
BiblicalUsage: A book in the New Testament is a scroll, a roll of writing — and the word covers everything from a bill of divorcement to the book of life. In Matthew 19:7 the Pharisees ask about Moses' writing of divorcement, in Luke 4:17 the book of Isaiah is handed to Jesus in the synagogue, in John 20:30 John says many other signs are not written in this book, and in Revelation 5:1 John sees a book sealed with seven seals in the Father's hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the book in Revelation is the one that matters most: sealed until the Lamb takes it, and then opened for the whole world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, the inner bark of the papyrus plant, i.e. (by implication) a sheet or scroll of writing:--book.
BiblicalUsage: The book is the written record, and the word opens the New Testament itself: the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, in Matthew 1:1. Luke 3:4 quotes the book of the words of Isaiah, Philippians 4:3 says the fellow-labourers' names are in the book of life, and Revelation 20:15 warns that whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the book of life is the record that decides everything, and I hold that my name is there because Christ wrote it, not because I earned it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a reduplicated and prolonged form of an obsolete primary verb (perhaps causative of G1006); to eat:--eat.
BiblicalUsage: To eat is the word for devouring, and it appears once, in the gathering after the feeding of the five thousand. In John 6:13 they filled twelve baskets with the fragments of the five barley loaves, which remained over and above unto them that had eaten. One word, for the crowd that ate and left twelve baskets behind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the twelve baskets are the point: Jesus feeds more than enough, and nothing is wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bidkar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bidkar means with a stab, and he is named once, as Jehu's captain. In 2 Kings 9:25 Jehu tells Bidkar to take up Joram's body and cast it in the field of Naboth the Jezreelite, remembering how they rode together when the Lord laid this burden on Ahab. A captain carrying out a king's sentence on the very ground where Naboth died.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bidkar's single verse is a reminder that God's word against Ahab waited years, and then fell in a day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bigtha, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Bigtha means in the wine-press, and he is named once, among the seven chamberlains of King Ahasuerus. In Esther 1:10, on the seventh day of the feast, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he commanded Bigtha and six others to bring Queen Vashti before him. A court servant, called on a day of wine and pride.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bigtha's one verse opens the whole book of Esther: a king's command, a queen's refusal, and God moving behind it all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bigthan or Bigthana, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Bigthan means in their wine-press, and he is one of the two chamberlains who plotted against the king. In Esther 2:21 Bigthan and Teresh sought to lay hand on King Ahasuerus, and Mordecai told it. In Esther 6:2 the record is read back to the king: it was found written that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh. The plot failed because a faithful man spoke up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bigthan's story is Mordecai's story too: a quiet warning, written down, and remembered on the very night it mattered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bigvai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bigvai means in my bodies, and he is the head of a family that came home from exile. Ezra 2:14 counts the children of Bigvai, two thousand fifty and six, and Nehemiah 7:19 counts them again. Ezra 8:14 names Uthai and Zabbud, of the sons of Bigvai, coming up with Ezra — seventy males, returning to the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the children of Bigvai are the return in miniature: counted twice, named by family, and home at last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the first-fruits of the crop
BiblicalUsage: Firstfruits is the first of the crop, brought to God before any of it is eaten. Exodus 23:19 commands the first of the firstfruits to be brought into the house of the Lord, Exodus 34:22 ties it to the feast of weeks, Leviticus 23:17 describes the two wave loaves baked with leaven, and Nehemiah 10:35 shows the returned exiles promising to bring the firstfruits of their ground year by year.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe firstfruits is the whole gospel of giving in one word: God gets the first, not the leftover, because the first belongs to him and the rest is blessed by it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the early fig
BiblicalUsage: The firstripe fig is the early fruit, the first sweet thing of the season — and both prophets use it to say what Israel should have been. Hosea 9:10 says God found Israel like grapes in the wilderness and saw their fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree, before they went to Baal-peor. Micah 7:1 longs for the firstripe fruit and finds none: his soul desired the firstripe fig, and there was none to eat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the firstripe fig is a picture of promise kept and promise lost: Israel was meant to be the first sweet fruit, and instead the tree was empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a young she-camel
BiblicalUsage: A young she-camel is the picture Jeremiah uses for Judah running after other gods. In Jeremiah 2:23 God says, see thy way in the valley, know what thou hast done: thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways. A young camel, fast and restless, crossing and recrossing its own tracks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the young camel is a hard picture of my own wandering: swift, restless, and always running the wrong way until God calls me back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bikri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bichri means youthful, and his name is remembered because of his son. In 2 Samuel 20:1 Sheba the son of Bichri blew a trumpet and said, we have no part in David, and in 2 Samuel 20:2 every man of Israel went up from after David and followed him. In 2 Samuel 20:21 a wise woman of Abel tells Joab that Sheba's head will be thrown over the wall, and the rebellion ends.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bichri's name survives as a warning: a father's name can be carried into a rebellion, and a son's trumpet can split a kingdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: except, without, besides
BiblicalUsage: Apart from, except, without — this is the word for the line that leaves God alone on one side of it. In Genesis 41:16 Joseph says it is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace, and in Genesis 41:44 Pharaoh says without Joseph no man shall lift up his hand in Egypt. In Isaiah 43:11 God says beside me there is no saviour, and in Isaiah 45:6, that there is none beside me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line the whole Bible draws: apart from God there is no saviour, no answer, and no peace — and I hold that line with both hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bilam, a Mesopotamian prophet; also a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Balaam means not of the people, and he is the prophet hired to curse Israel who could only bless them. In Numbers 22:5 Balak sends for Balaam the son of Beor, and in Numbers 22:12 God tells him not to go, for the people are blessed. In Numbers 24:10 Balak's anger is kindled because Balaam has blessed them three times — and Joshua 13:22 ends the story plainly: Balaam the soothsayer did the children of Israel slay with the sword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Balaam is the proof that no curse can stick where God has blessed, and the warning that a man can speak God's words and still love the wages of unrighteousness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bildad, one of Job's friends
BiblicalUsage: Bildad means confusing love, and he is the second of Job's three friends. Job 2:11 brings him with Eliphaz and Zophar when they hear of Job's trouble, and then he speaks three times — Job 8:1, Job 18:1, and Job 25:1 — each speech shorter and harder than the last, until he has nothing left but God's dominion and the smallness of man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bildad shows me how a friend can be right about God's greatness and wrong about his suffering friend, both at once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bilgah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Bilgah means cheerfulness, and the name belongs to two priests in two different centuries. In 1 Chronicles 24:14 Bilgah takes the fifteenth course of priests in David's ordering, in Nehemiah 12:5 a Bilgah comes up with Zerubbabel, and in Nehemiah 12:18 Shammua stands for Bilgah in the days of Joiakim. One name, two priests, both serving at the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name meaning cheerfulness, carried by priests across the exile, is a small sign that worship outlasts every ruin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bilgai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bilgai means my cheerfulness, and he is named once, among the priests who sealed the covenant. Nehemiah 10:8 lists him with Maaziah and Shemaiah: these were the priests. One verse, one name on a sealed promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a signature on the covenant is an act of faith, and Bilgai's is one of the quiet ones.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bilhah, the name of one of Jacob's concubines; also of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bilhah means troubled, and she is Rachel's handmaid, given to Jacob as a wife, and the mother of Dan and Naphtali. Genesis 29:29 says Laban gave Bilhah to Rachel, Genesis 30:3 shows Rachel giving her to Jacob so that she might have children by her, Genesis 35:22 records Reuben going in to her, and Genesis 35:25 lists Dan and Naphtali as the sons of Bilhah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bilhah's story is one of the hardest in Genesis: a woman used by others, named troubled, and still the mother of two tribes of Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bilhan, the name of an Edomite and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bilhan means their decrepitude, and the name belongs to two men who must not be mixed up. Genesis 36:27 makes him a son of Ezer the Horite, the father of Akan — the Horite Akan of Genesis 36, not Achan of Joshua 7 — and 1 Chronicles 1:42 repeats the line. Then 1 Chronicles 7:10 names a different Bilhan, a Benjamite, the son of Jediael, whose sons are listed after him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Bilhans are a warning to read slowly: same name, different men, and the difference matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bilshan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bilshan means in slander, and he is named twice, both times in the same list. Ezra 2:2 counts him among the men who came up with Zerubbabel, and Nehemiah 7:7 counts him again in the same return. A man who came home from exile, named in two copies of one list.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bilshan's double listing is the return in miniature: the same names, counted twice, because coming home mattered enough to record twice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a failure of, i.e. (used only as a negative particle, usually with a prepositional prefix) not, except, without, unless, besides, because not, until, etc.
BiblicalUsage: Not, except, without, unless — this is the small word that draws the lines of the whole Bible, and it appears over a hundred times. In Genesis 3:11 God asks, who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat? In Exodus 20:20 Moses says fear not, for God is come to prove you. In Amos 3:3 the prophet asks, can two walk together, except they be agreed? And in Deuteronomy 12:23 the law says, only be sure that thou eat not the blood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this little word carries the whole weight of obedience: not, except, unless — the lines God draws are the lines that keep his people alive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bimhal, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bimhal means in circumcision, and he is named once, in 1 Chronicles 7:33, among the sons of Japhlet, a descendant of Asher: Pasach, and Bimhal, and Ashvath. One name in a genealogy, and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a name in a genealogy is enough: God kept the sons of Asher, and Bimhal among them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bina or Binah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Binea means fountain, and he is a descendant of Jonathan, named twice in the same line. In 1 Chronicles 8:37 Moza begat Binea, and Rapha was his son, and in 1 Chronicles 9:43 the same line is given again, with Rephaiah in place of Rapha. A man in Saul's family, kept on the record in two chapters.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the double record is deliberate: Jonathan's line mattered to the Chronicler, and Binea's fountain-name runs through it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Binnui, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Binnui means built up, and the name belongs to several Levites in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah. Ezra 10:30 names a Binnui among those who put away foreign wives, Nehemiah 3:24 shows Binnui the son of Henadad repairing another piece of the wall, and Nehemiah 10:9 lists Binnui among the Levites who sealed the covenant. Note that the Hebrew text numbers the covenant verse one higher than the King James text does.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name meaning built up, carried by men who rebuilt the wall and sealed the covenant, is a name that fits its owners.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a structure
BiblicalUsage: A structure is the word for a building, and it appears once, in Ezekiel's measuring of the temple. In Ezekiel 41:13 he measured the house, an hundred cubits long, and the separate place, and the building, with the walls thereof, an hundred cubits long. A measured building, in a measured house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the measuring matters: God counts the cubits of his house, and nothing about it is careless.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Binjamin, youngest son of Jacob; also the tribe descended from him, and its territory
BiblicalUsage: Benjamin means son of the right hand, and he is Jacob's youngest, Rachel's last child, Joseph's full brother. Genesis 35:18 says his dying mother called him Ben-oni, son of my sorrow, but his father called him Benjamin. Genesis 42:4 shows Jacob refusing to send him to Egypt, Genesis 43:29 shows Joseph blessing him at the sight of him, and Deuteronomy 33:12 calls him the beloved of the Lord, who shall dwell in safety by him.
