TheologicalSignificance: I believe Benjamin's story is the story of a name changed at birth: sorrow to right hand, and the beloved of the Lord dwelling in safety.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {an edifice}
BiblicalUsage: This is the Aramaic word for a building, and it appears once, in the questioning of the builders. In Ezra 5:4 the king's officers ask, what are the names of the men that make this building? The temple going up again, and the empire wanting names.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is still asked of every building for God: who is making it, and by whose leave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {an edifice}
BiblicalUsage: This is the Aramaic word for a building, and it appears once, in the questioning of the builders. In Ezra 5:4 the king's officers ask, what are the names of the men that make this building? The temple going up again, and the empire wanting names.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is still asked of every building for God: who is making it, and by whose leave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G979; to spend existence:--live.
BiblicalUsage: To live out the rest of one's life is the word for spending existence — and it appears once, in Peter's call to a changed life. In 1 Peter 4:2 he says the believer should no longer live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God. A short word for a whole remaining life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter's one use says it all: the time left is to be lived to God's will, not to men's lusts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word; life, i.e. (literally) the present state of existence; by implication, the means of livelihood:--good, life, living.
BiblicalUsage: Life here is not the soul's life but the life of this world — what a man lives on, and what he lives for. In Luke 8:14 the seed is choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of this life, in Luke 15:12 the prodigal asks for the portion of goods that falleth to him, in Luke 21:4 the widow casts in all the living that she had, and in 1 John 2:16 the pride of life is named as not of the Father.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a warning about the wrong kind of life: the living that chokes, the pride that is not of the Father, and the widow who gave it all away anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G980; living (properly, the act, by implication, the mode):--manner of life.
BiblicalUsage: Manner of life is the word for how a man has lived from his youth, and it appears once, in Paul's defence. In Acts 26:4 Paul says his manner of life from his youth, which was at the first among his own nation at Jerusalem, know all the Jews. A whole life, offered as evidence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's manner of life is the best defence he could give: not an argument, but a life the Jews had watched since he was young.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G980; relating to the present existence:--of (pertaining to, things that pertain to) this life.
BiblicalUsage: Things of this life are the everyday affairs — food, drink, business, lawsuits — and the word warns twice about them. In Luke 21:34 Jesus says take heed, lest your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness and cares of this life. In 1 Corinthians 6:3 Paul asks, know ye not that we shall judge angels? how much more things that pertain to this life? And in 1 Corinthians 6:4 he tells them to set the least esteemed to judge such things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cares of this life are the quiet danger: they do not kill faith in a day, they overcharge the heart until the day comes unawares.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a split, i.e. a wide level valley between mountains}
BiblicalUsage: A plain is a wide valley between mountains, and this Aramaic word appears once, in the setting of the golden image. In Daniel 3:1 Nebuchadnezzar set up the image in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. A wide, flat place, chosen so that everyone could see the idol.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the plain of Dura is the point: idolatry loves an open space where everyone can see it and no one can hide from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a split, i.e. a wide level valley between mountains
BiblicalUsage: A valley is a wide, level place between mountains, and the word runs through the whole story. In Genesis 11:2 men journeying from the east found a plain in the land of Shinar and dwelt there, building Babel. In Deuteronomy 8:7 God promises a good land, with valleys and hills. In Isaiah 40:4 every valley shall be exalted, and in Ezekiel 37:1 the Lord sets the prophet down in the midst of a valley full of dry bones.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the valley in Ezekiel is the promise for every valley: God sets his prophet down in the middle of the dry bones, and the bones live.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, examination, i.e. (by implication) punishment
BiblicalUsage: Punishment after examination is the meaning of this word, and it appears once, in the law of the bondmaid. In Leviticus 19:20, if a man lies with a bondmaid betrothed to another and not redeemed, she shall be scourged — punishment, but not death, because the case was examined and her standing was different. One word for a measured penalty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the examined punishment shows a God who judges the case, not just the act — and that is mercy inside the law.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Birsha, a king of Gomorrah
BiblicalUsage: Birsha means with iniquity, and he is named once, as the king of Gomorrah. In Genesis 14:2 he made war with Bera king of Sodom and three other kings against Chedorlaomer. A king in the first war of Genesis, named and gone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a king called with iniquity, ruling Gomorrah, is a name that tells the end of the story before it happens.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: food
BiblicalUsage: Food is the word for meat, cakes, a meal dressed for someone — and all three uses are in the same dark story. In 2 Samuel 13:5 Jonadab tells Amnon to ask Tamar to dress him meat, in 2 Samuel 13:7 David sends Tamar to Amnon's house to dress him meat, and in 2 Samuel 13:10 Amnon tells Tamar to bring the meat into the chamber. A meal made with care, used as a trap.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the food in this story is a warning: even a sister's cooking can be turned to evil when the heart asking for it is already rotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Birzoth, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Birzoth means in leanness, and the name is given once, in 1 Chronicles 7:31, among the children of Asher: Malchiel, who is the father of Birzavith, in the line of Beriah. One name in a genealogy, and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a name given once in Asher's line is still kept by God, and brief mention is not small worth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bishlam, a Persian
BiblicalUsage: Bishlam means in peace, and he is named once, as one of the men who wrote against the rebuilding. In Ezra 4:7, in the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel wrote a letter against Jerusalem, and the writing was in the Syrian tongue. A man named in peace, writing a letter of opposition.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bishlam's letter is the pattern of every opposition to God's work: it arrives in an official tongue, with official names, and it still fails.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: trust
BiblicalUsage: Confidence is the word here, and it appears once, in one of Isaiah's plainest sentences. In Isaiah 30:15 the Lord says, in returning and rest shall ye be saved, in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength — and ye would not. Trust offered, and refused.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one verse is the whole argument of Isaiah in a sentence: strength is in quiet confidence, and the people would not have it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bithron, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Bithron means division or ravine, and it is named once, as the ground Abner's men crossed. In 2 Samuel 2:29 Abner and his men walked all that night through the plain, and passed over Jordan, and went through all Bithron, and came to Mahanaim. A district in the Jordan valley, crossed in the dark after a battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bithron's one verse is a picture of retreat after defeat: a long night's walk through divided ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bithjah, an Egyptian woman
BiblicalUsage: Bithiah means daughter of Jehovah, and she is named once, in 1 Chronicles 4:18: Mered took Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh to wife, and she bare Miriam and Shammai and Ishbah. An Egyptian princess, married into Judah, and given a name that claims the Lord as her father.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bithiah's name is the gospel in a genealogy: Pharaoh's daughter, called daughter of Jehovah, and written into Judah's line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Bithynia, a region of Asia:--Bithynia.
BiblicalUsage: Bithynia is a region in the north of Asia Minor, and it is named twice, once by a closed door and once by an open letter. In Acts 16:7 Paul and his company assayed to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit suffered them not. In 1 Peter 1:1 Peter writes to the strangers scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia — the same region, now full of believers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bithynia is the proof that a closed door is not a closed future: the Spirit said no to Paul, and the gospel still reached Bithynia.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a swamp
BiblicalUsage: A swamp is the word for marshy ground, and it appears three times, always where water and dry land meet. Job 8:11 asks, can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water? Job 40:21 says the behemoth lies under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed and fens. And Ezekiel 47:11 says the miry places of the healing river shall not be healed, but given to salt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the swamp in Ezekiel is the sober note in a hopeful chapter: even the river of life leaves some miry places, and not everything is healed yet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fortress
BiblicalUsage: A stronghold is the word for a fortress, and it appears once, in a promise to prisoners. In Zechariah 9:12 the Lord says, turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I declare that I will render double unto thee. A fortress for people who have nothing left but hope.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe prisoners of hope is one of the finest names in Scripture, and the stronghold is where they are told to run.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: trust
BiblicalUsage: Trust is the word for confidence, and it appears three times, twice in the same taunt. In 2 Kings 18:19 the Rabshakeh asks Hezekiah, what confidence is this wherein thou trustest? Isaiah 36:4 repeats the question word for word. And Ecclesiastes 9:4 answers from the other side: to him that is joined to all the living there is hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Rabshakeh's question is still asked of every believer, and the answer is the same one Hezekiah gave: my confidence is the Lord, and he has not failed yet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: oh that!; with leave, or if it please
BiblicalUsage: Oh that, if it please, pray excuse me — this is the word for an entreaty, and it appears twelve times, always on the lips of someone asking for something hard. In Exodus 4:10 Moses says, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, and in Exodus 4:13 he says, O my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send. In Judges 6:15 Gideon says, Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? And in 1 Kings 3:17 the woman before Solomon begins, O my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this little word is the sound of honest prayer: not demanding, but pleading — and God answers pleading.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to separate mentally (or distinguish), i.e.(generally) understand
BiblicalUsage: To understand is the word for discerning, separating one thing from another in the mind — and it appears over a hundred and sixty times. Proverbs 1:2 says the proverbs are to know wisdom and instruction, to perceive the words of understanding. Proverbs 2:5 promises, then shalt thou understand the fear of the Lord. Daniel 1:17 says God gave the four children skill in all learning and wisdom, and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams. And Daniel 9:22 shows Gabriel coming to give Daniel skill and understanding.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe understanding is not cleverness but sight: the fear of the Lord opens the eyes, and Daniel's understanding came because God gave it, not because he took it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {understanding}
BiblicalUsage: Understanding is the Aramaic word for discernment, and it appears once, in Daniel's praise of God. In Daniel 2:21 Daniel says God changeth the times and the seasons, he setteth up kings and removeth kings, and he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding. One verse, and it gives understanding its source.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this verse is the whole doctrine of wisdom in a sentence: God gives it, to whom he will, when he will.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {understanding}
BiblicalUsage: Understanding is the Aramaic word for discernment, and it appears once, in Daniel's praise of God. In Daniel 2:21 Daniel says God changeth the times and the seasons, he setteth up kings and removeth kings, and he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding. One verse, and it gives understanding its source.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this verse is the whole doctrine of wisdom in a sentence: God gives it, to whom he will, when he will.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a palace
BiblicalUsage: A castle or citadel is what this Aramaic word means, and it appears once, in the finding of the decree. In Ezra 6:2 there was found at Achmetha, in the palace that is in the province of the Medes, a roll, and therein was a record thus written. The king's decree, found in the palace archive, and the temple rebuilding saved by it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the roll in the palace is God's providence in a drawer: a record, kept and found, at the very hour it was needed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a castle or palace
BiblicalUsage: A palace is the word for a castle, a citadel, a temple — and it is the setting of the whole book of Esther. In Esther 1:2 Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Shushan the palace. In Esther 2:5 Mordecai dwelt in Shushan the palace. In Nehemiah 1:1 Nehemiah was in Shushan the palace when the news from Jerusalem came, and in Daniel 8:2 Daniel saw his vision while he was at Shushan in the palace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Shushan the palace is where God hides his people in plain sight: a Jew in the citadel, a cupbearer at court, and a kingdom turned by their faithfulness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fortress
BiblicalUsage: A fortress is the word for a fortified place, and it appears twice, both times in the reign of a good king building up Judah. In 2 Chronicles 17:12 Jehoshaphat waxed great exceedingly, and built in Judah castles and cities of store. In 2 Chronicles 27:4 Jotham built cities in the mountains of Judah, and in the forests he built castles and towers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the castles of Jehoshaphat and Jotham are a picture of wise strength: build the walls while there is peace, so they stand when there is war.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a palace (i.e. large house)
BiblicalUsage: A palace is the word for a great house, and all three uses are in Esther, around the king's feast and Haman's fall. In Esther 1:5 the king made a feast in the court of the garden of the king's palace. In Esther 7:7 the king arose in his wrath from the banquet and went into the palace garden, and in Esther 7:8 he returned from the palace garden to the place of the banquet, and found Haman fallen on the bed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the palace garden in Esther is where the story turns: the king walks out in wrath, and walks back in to find Haman fallen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Biztha, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Biztha means booty, and he is named once, among the seven chamberlains of King Ahasuerus. In Esther 1:10, on the seventh day of the feast, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas to bring Queen Vashti before him. A court servant, called on a day of wine and pride.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Biztha's one verse opens the whole book of Esther: a king's command, a queen's refusal, and God moving behind it all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bizjothjah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bizjothjah means contempt of Jehovah, and it is named once, in Joshua 15:28, among the towns of southern Judah near Beersheba — Hazar-shual, and Beer-sheba, and Bizjothjah. A town with a hard name, kept on Judah's list.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town named contempt of Jehovah, kept on the inheritance list, is a reminder that God gives his people towns whose names they must live down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: booty
BiblicalUsage: Booty is the word for spoil, plunder, prey — and it appears ten times, mostly in war. In Daniel 11:24 a king shall scatter among his followers the prey and spoil and riches. In Esther 9:10 the Jews slew the sons of Haman, but on the spoil laid they not their hand. And in Nehemiah 4:4 the prayer is to give the enemies for a prey in the land of captivity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spoil in Esther is the point: the Jews took their deliverance and left the plunder, and that restraint is the victory.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: disesteem
BiblicalUsage: Contempt is the word for disesteem, and it appears once, in the princes' warning to the king. In Esther 1:18 the princes say that if Vashti's deed comes abroad, there will arise too much contempt and wrath — the whole empire's wives despising their husbands. One word, for a court's fear of a bad example.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the princes' fear says more about their marriages than about Vashti: a kingdom afraid of contempt is a kingdom already rotting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G984; injurious:--hurtful.
BiblicalUsage: Hurtful is the word for injurious, and it appears once, in Paul's warning about riches. In 1 Timothy 6:9 they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. One word, for the lusts that drown.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's word is exact: hurtful lusts do not merely wound, they drown.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; properly, to hinder, i.e. (by implication) to injure:--hurt.
BiblicalUsage: To hurt is the word for hindering, injuring — and it appears twice, both times in a promise of protection. In Luke 4:35 the devil comes out of the man and hurts him not. In Mark 16:18 Jesus says his disciples shall take up serpents, and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses belong together: the devil could not hurt the man, and the poison could not hurt the disciple, because the Lord stood between.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G989; to vilify; specially, to speak impiously:--(speak) blaspheme(-er, -mously, -my), defame, rail on, revile, speak evil.
BiblicalUsage: To blaspheme is to speak evil against God, to vilify him with words — and the word appears thirty-four times. In Matthew 9:3 the scribes say within themselves, this man blasphemeth, when Jesus forgives sins. In Matthew 26:65 the high priest rends his clothes and says, he hath spoken blasphemy. In Luke 12:10 Jesus warns that blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven. And in Acts 13:45 the Jews contradict Paul and blaspheme.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe blasphemy is the sin of calling God's work evil, and the scribes and the high priest show me how easily religious men do it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G989; vilification (especially against God):--blasphemy, evil speaking, railing.
BiblicalUsage: Blasphemy is the word for vilification, evil speaking, railing — against God and against men. In Matthew 12:31 Jesus says all manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men, but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven. In Matthew 15:19 blasphemies come out of the heart, with murders and adulteries. In Ephesians 4:31 Paul says let all bitterness and clamour and evil speaking be put away from you, and in Colossians 3:8 he says put off all these: anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul puts blasphemy beside anger and malice for a reason: evil speaking against God and evil speaking against men grow from the same root.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G984 and G5345; scurrilious, i.e. calumnious (against men), or (specially) impious (against God):--blasphemer(-mous), railing.
BiblicalUsage: A blasphemer is the person who speaks evil against God, and the word appears four times. In 1 Timothy 1:13 Paul says he was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious — but he obtained mercy. In Acts 6:11 men are set up to say they heard Stephen speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God. And in 2 Timothy 3:2 Paul lists blasphemers among the lovers of their own selves in the last days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's own past is the hope in this word: he was a blasphemer, and he obtained mercy, because he did it ignorantly in unbelief.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from βλαστός (a sprout); to germinate; by implication, to yield fruit:--bring forth, bud, spring (up).
BiblicalUsage: To spring up is the word for a seed germinating, budding, bringing forth — and it appears four times. In Matthew 13:26 the blade springs up and brings forth fruit, in Mark 4:27 the seed springs and grows up, he knows not how, in James 5:18 the earth brings forth her fruit after Elijah's prayer, and in Hebrews 9:4 Aaron's rod that budded is kept in the ark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the budding rod is the picture I keep coming back to: dead wood, in the ark, that blossomed — because God gives life where there is none.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps the same as the base of G985; Blastus, an officer of Herod Agrippa:--Blastus.
BiblicalUsage: Blastus is named once, as the chamberlain of Herod Agrippa. In Acts 12:20 Herod was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon, and they came with one accord, having made Blastus the king's chamberlain their friend, and desired peace, because their country was nourished by the king's country. A court official, used as a bridge to peace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Blastus is a small picture of how the world works: the cities needed the king's food, so they befriended the king's chamberlain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G991; vision (properly concrete; by implication, abstract):--seeing.
BiblicalUsage: Seeing is the word for what the eyes take in, day after day — and it appears once, in the torment of Lot. In 2 Peter 2:8 the just man dwelling among the wicked, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds. One word, for the daily wearing-down of a righteous man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lot's torment is the warning in this word: what we see every day shapes the soul, even when we do not join in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to look at (literally or figuratively):--behold, beware, lie, look (on, to), perceive, regard, see, sight, take heed. Compare G3700.
BiblicalUsage: To see is the word for looking, perceiving, taking heed — and it appears over a hundred times. In Matthew 5:28 Jesus says whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart. In Matthew 7:3 he asks why we behold the mote in our brother's eye. In John 1:29 John says, behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world. And in Hebrews 11:1 faith is the evidence of things not seen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two lookings are the whole Christian life: the look that lusts, and the look that beholds the Lamb — and faith is the sight of what cannot be seen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G906; fit to be cast (i.e. applied):--must be put.
BiblicalUsage: Must be put is the word for fit to be cast, applied — and it appears once, in Jesus' saying about new wine. In Luke 5:38 new wine must be put into new bottles, and both are preserved. One word, for the vessel that fits the wine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the new bottle is the point: new wine needs a new vessel, and the gospel needs a heart made new to hold it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Boaz, the ancestor of David; also the name of a pillar in front of the temple
BiblicalUsage: Boaz means fleetness, and he is the kinsman-redeemer of Ruth, the ancestor of David. In Ruth 2:1 he is introduced as a mighty man of wealth, of the kindred of Elimelech. In Ruth 2:8 he tells Ruth to abide by his maidens and glean in his field. In Ruth 4:9 he buys all that was Elimelech's before the elders, and takes Ruth to wife. And 1 Kings 7:21 names the other Boaz: the left pillar of Solomon's temple, set up and called Boaz.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Boaz is the picture of Christ in the Old Testament: a redeemer with the wealth to pay, the will to do it, and the welcome for a foreigner who had nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cistern
BiblicalUsage: A cistern is a pit for holding water, and this word appears three times, in thirst and in idolatry. In 2 Samuel 23:15 David longs for water from the well of Bethlehem, and in 2 Samuel 23:16 his mighty men break through the Philistines to draw it. In Jeremiah 2:13 God says his people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the broken cistern is one of the saddest pictures in the Bible: men digging their own water-holes while the fountain stands open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: stink-weed or any other noxious or useless plant
BiblicalUsage: Stinkweed is the word for a noxious, useless plant, and it appears once, in Job's oath. In Job 31:40 Job says, let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley — and the words of Job are ended. A curse on his own fields, if he has done what he is accused of.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's stinkweed is the mark of a clear conscience: he is willing to let his fields grow weeds if he has lied.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1123 and H7266); sons of commotion; Boanerges, an epithet of two of the apostles:--Boanerges.
BiblicalUsage: Boanerges means sons of thunder, and it is the name Jesus gave to James and John, the sons of Zebedee. In Mark 3:17 he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, the sons of thunder. The word is spelled Βοανηργές in the Greek text, with a different vowel from the dictionary form, but it is the same name. Two fishermen, given a thunder-name by their Master.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thunder-name fits: James and John were zealous, quick, and loud — and Jesus kept them, thunder and all, and made apostles of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a prolonged form of a primary verb; to halloo, i.e. shout (for help or in a tumultuous way):--cry.
BiblicalUsage: To cry out is the word for shouting for help, and it appears twelve times. In Luke 3:4 the voice of one crying in the wilderness is Isaiah's word, and in John 1:23 John the Baptist takes it for himself. In Luke 18:38 the blind man cries, Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me. And in Mark 15:34 Jesus cries with a loud voice on the cross, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cry in this word is the whole range of prayer: the herald's shout, the blind man's plea, and the Saviour's forsaken cry — and God hears them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {an immature grape}
BiblicalUsage: Sour grapes are unripe grapes, and the word is famous for a proverb God rejects. In Isaiah 18:5 the sour grape is ripening in the flower, before the harvest. In Jeremiah 31:29 the proverb says the fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge — and in Jeremiah 31:30 God answers, every one shall die for his own iniquity. Ezekiel 18:2 quotes the same proverb and gives the same answer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hates the sour-grape proverb because it blames the fathers for the children's sin, and he will have each man answer for his own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: trial
BiblicalUsage: A trial is the word for a testing, a tried stone — and it appears once, in the cornerstone promise. In Isaiah 28:16 the Lord says, behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste. One word, for the stone that has been tested and holds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tried stone is Christ: tested, precious, sure — and the one who believes on him shall not make haste.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G994; a halloo, i.e. call (for aid, etc.):--cry.
BiblicalUsage: A cry is the word for a call for aid, and it appears once, in the cry of the unpaid labourers. In James 5:4 the hire of the labourers who reaped your fields, kept back by fraud, crieth, and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. One word, for wages that cry to heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cry of unpaid wages still reaches the ears of the Lord of sabaoth, and the rich who keep them back will answer for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G998; aid; specially, a rope or chain for frapping a vessel:--help.
BiblicalUsage: Help is the word for aid — and for the ropes used to undergird a ship in a storm. In Acts 27:17 the sailors used helps, undergirding the ship, fearing they would fall into the quicksands. In Hebrews 4:16 the same word is turned to grace: let us come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two helps belong together: sailors undergirding a ship, and sinners finding grace to help — both in time of need.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G998; to aid or relieve:--help, succor.
BiblicalUsage: To help is the word for aiding, succouring — and it appears eight times, mostly in cries for help. In Matthew 15:25 the woman of Canaan worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me. In Mark 9:22 the father of the possessed boy says, if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us, and in Mark 9:24 he cries, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. And in Hebrews 2:18 Jesus is able to succour them that are tempted, because he himself suffered being tempted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the father's cry is the prayer I pray most: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief — and the Helper who was tempted himself answers it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G995 and theo (to run); a succorer:--helper.
BiblicalUsage: A helper is the word for a succourer, and it appears once, in a confession of trust. In Hebrews 13:6 the writer says, so that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me. One word, for the Lord who stands beside.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the boldness in this verse comes from the Helper: I will not fear what man can do, because the Lord is my helper.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: treacheries
BiblicalUsage: Treacheries is the word for treacherous behaviour, and it appears once, in Zephaniah's charge against Jerusalem's leaders. In Zephaniah 3:4 her prophets are light and treacherous persons, her priests have polluted the sanctuary and done violence to the law. One word, for prophets who cannot be trusted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Zephaniah's charge is the test of every prophet: light and treacherous, or faithful and true — and the city suffers either way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: thumb, Bohan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bohan means thumb, and he is a Reubenite who set a boundary stone between Judah and Benjamin. In Joshua 15:6 the border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben, and in Joshua 18:17 the boundary descended to the same stone. A man remembered only by the stone that bears his name — a mark of division between two tribes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stone of Bohan is a small picture of God's order: even a boundary stone gets a name, and the tribes knew where they stood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: white scurf
BiblicalUsage: A freckled spot is the word for a harmless white scurf on the skin, and it appears once, in the priest's examination. In Leviticus 13:39 the priest shall look, and if the bright spots in the skin be darkish white, it is a freckled spot that groweth in the skin, and he is clean. One word, for a spot that looks like leprosy and is not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the freckled spot is a mercy in the law: not every mark is uncleanness, and the priest is told to look twice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the thumb of the hand or great toe of the foot
BiblicalUsage: The thumb is the word for the thumb of the hand and the great toe of the foot, always used of both together. In Exodus 29:20 the blood is put on the thumb of Aaron's right hand and the great toe of his right foot, and in Leviticus 8:23 Moses does the same at the consecration. In Judges 1:6 Adoni-bezek's thumbs and great toes are cut off, and in Judges 1:7 he says seventy kings gathered their meat under his table with their thumbs cut off.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thumb and the toe in the consecration are the point: the priest's hands and feet both belong to God, from the tip of the ear to the great toe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a whitish spot on the skin
BiblicalUsage: A bright spot is the word for a white patch on the skin, and it appears eleven times, all in the law of leprosy. In Leviticus 13:2 a man with a rising, a scab, or a bright spot is brought to Aaron the priest. In Leviticus 13:4 the priest shuts up the plague seven days if the bright spot is white in the skin. In Leviticus 13:19 a bright spot after a boil is examined the same way, and in Leviticus 14:56 the law is summed up for the rising, the scab, and the bright spot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bright spot shows how careful God is with his people: the priest looks, waits seven days, and looks again before he calls anything unclean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a vacuity, i.e. (superficially) an undistinguishable ruin
BiblicalUsage: Without form is the word for emptiness, a void, a waste — and it appears three times, in the beginning and in two judgments. In Genesis 1:2 the earth was without form, and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep. In Isaiah 34:11 God stretches out upon Edom the line of confusion and the stones of emptiness. And in Jeremiah 4:23 the prophet says, I beheld the earth, and, lo, it was without form, and void, and the heavens, and they had no light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the void in Genesis is the promise inside the judgment: the earth was without form, and then God spoke, and form came. What is empty in his hands does not stay empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bokeru, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bocheru means firstborn, and he is named twice, in the same line of Benjamin. In 1 Chronicles 8:38 Azel had six sons, and Bocheru is named among them, and in 1 Chronicles 9:44 the same six sons are listed again. A Benjamite, kept on the record in two chapters.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a firstborn named twice in Benjamin's line is still kept by God, and the double record is no accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bo-kim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bochim means weeping, and it is the place where Israel wept. In Judges 2:1 the angel of the Lord comes up to Bochim and says, I will never break my covenant with you — but you have not obeyed my voice. In Judges 2:5 the people lifted up their voice and wept there, and they called the name of that place Bochim.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bochim is named for the right thing: they wept because they had disobeyed, and the weeping was the beginning of the way back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G906; a throw (as a measure of distance):--cast.
BiblicalUsage: A stone's cast is the word for a throw, a measure of distance — and it appears once, in Gethsemane. In Luke 22:41 Jesus was withdrawn from his disciples about a stone's cast, and kneeled down, and prayed. One word, for the small distance between the Lord and his friends on the hardest night.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stone's cast is the distance of prayer: near enough to be with them, far enough to be alone with the Father.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G906; a missile, i.e. javelin:--dart.
BiblicalUsage: A dart is the word for a missile, a javelin — and the noun itself never stands alone in the New Testament text. The sounding of the deep in the shipwreck story uses the verb form instead, the heaving of the lead, and the noun is known only from the lexicon, not from a verse of its own. I say so plainly, because a word with no verse should not be given one.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that an honest gap is better than a borrowed verse: this word has no passage of its own, and I will not pretend otherwise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1002; to heave the lead:--sound.
BiblicalUsage: To sound is the word for heaving the lead, and it appears once, in the shipwreck. In Acts 27:28 they sounded, and found it twenty fathoms, and when they had gone a little further, they sounded again, and found it fifteen fathoms. The lead going down in the dark, measuring the water under a breaking ship.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sounding is a picture of faith in a storm: you cannot see the bottom, so you let down the lead and measure what you can.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G939; properly, a stand, i.e. (specially) an altar:--altar.
BiblicalUsage: An altar is the word for a stand, a raised place for sacrifice — and it appears once, in Athens. In Acts 17:23 Paul says, as I passed by and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. One altar, built for a god its makers did not know.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the unknown god's altar is Paul's open door: they knew they were missing someone, and he told them who.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1162); Booz, (i.e. Boaz), an Israelite:--Booz.
BiblicalUsage: Booz is the Greek form of Boaz, the kinsman-redeemer of Ruth and the ancestor of David. In Matthew 1:5 Salmon begat Booz of Rachab, and Booz begat Obed of Ruth, in the genealogy of Jesus. In Luke 3:32 Booz stands in the same line, the son of Salmon, in the genealogy that runs back to Adam. The Greek text spells the name Βόες, a different form from the dictionary spelling, but it is the same man. For his story, see the study on Boaz.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Greek spelling changes nothing: the redeemer of Ruth is in the line of Christ, by whatever letters his name is written.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, dawn (as the break of day); generally, morning
BiblicalUsage: Morning is the word for the break of day, and it appears nearly two hundred times. In Genesis 1:5 the evening and the morning were the first day. In Exodus 14:24 the Lord looked through the pillar of fire in the morning watch and troubled the Egyptians. In Psalms 30:5 weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. And in Lamentations 3:23 God's mercies are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the morning in Lamentations is the promise I live on: his mercies are new every morning, and no night, however long, outlasts them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vegetable lye (from its cleansing); used as a soap for washing, or a flux for metals
BiblicalUsage: Lye is the word for potash, the alkali used to cleanse and to smelt — and it appears twice. In Isaiah 1:25 God says, I will turn my hand upon thee, and purely purge away thy dross, and take away all thy tin. In Job 9:30 Job says, if I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean — and the word for the cleansing is lye, the strong soap of the ancient world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lye in Isaiah is a hard mercy: God purges away the dross himself, because no washing of mine could do it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vegetable lye (from its cleansing); used as a soap for washing, or a flux for metals
BiblicalUsage: Lye is the word for potash, the alkali used to cleanse and to smelt — and it appears twice. In Isaiah 1:25 God says, I will turn my hand upon thee, and purely purge away thy dross, and take away all thy tin. In Job 9:30 Job says, if I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean — and the word for the cleansing is lye, the strong soap of the ancient world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lye in Isaiah is a hard mercy: God purges away the dross himself, because no washing of mine could do it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; mud:--mire.
BiblicalUsage: Mire is the word for mud, and it appears once, in Peter's proverb about the false teachers. In 2 Peter 2:22 it has happened unto them according to the true proverb, the dog is turned to his own vomit again, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire. One word, for the mud a washed sow runs back to.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mire is the warning in the proverb: washing without a new nature only makes the return to the mud certain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vegetable alkali
BiblicalUsage: Soap is the word for lye, the alkali used in washing — and it appears twice, both times about a washing that does not work. In Jeremiah 2:22 God says, though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me. In Malachi 3:2 the Lord is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap, and who may abide the day of his coming?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the soap in Jeremiah is the point: no washing of mine can take away the mark of sin — only the Refiner can, and he comes with fire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; the north (properly, wind):--north.
BiblicalUsage: The north is the word for the north wind, the quarter of the cold — and it appears twice, both times in the gathering of God's people. In Luke 13:29 they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and sit down in the kingdom of God. In Revelation 21:13 the holy city has gates on the north, three gates, and on the south three gates. The Greek text spells it βορρᾶς, without the rough breathing of the dictionary form, but it is the same word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the north gate is the promise: they come from every quarter, north included, and sit down in the kingdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: shame (the feeling and the condition, as well as its cause); by implication (specifically) an idol
BiblicalUsage: Shame is the word for the feeling and the condition and its cause — and it appears thirty times. In Isaiah 54:4 God says, fear not, for thou shalt not be ashamed, neither be thou confounded. In Jeremiah 3:25 the people lie down in their shame, and their confusion covereth them. In Psalms 69:19 the psalmist says, thou hast known my reproach, and my shame, and my dishonour. And in Habakkuk 2:10 the violent man has consulted shame to his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shame in Isaiah is the promise and the shame in Jeremiah is the warning: God takes away the shame of his people, and he leaves the shame on the house that chose it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: shamefulness
BiblicalUsage: Shamefulness is the word for shame, and it appears once, in Hosea's word about the calf of Bethel. In Hosea 10:6 the calf of Beth-aven shall be carried into Assyria for a present to king Jareb, and Ephraim shall receive shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel. One word, for the shame of an idol carried off as a present.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shame in Hosea is exact: Israel's god was carried away as a gift, and the shame was all that was left.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb (compare G977, G1016); to pasture; by extension to, fodder; reflexively, to graze:--feed, keep.
BiblicalUsage: To feed is the word for pasturing, tending a flock — and it appears nine times. In Matthew 8:30 a herd of swine was feeding on the mountain when the demons begged to enter them. In Luke 15:15 the prodigal joins himself to a citizen who sends him into the fields to feed swine. In John 21:15 Jesus says, feed my lambs, and in John 21:17 he says it again, feed my sheep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the feeding in John is the whole charge of the ministry: the risen Lord does not ask Peter for a plan, he asks him to feed the sheep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bosmath, the name of a wife of Esau, and of a daughter of Solomon
BiblicalUsage: Bashemath means spice, and the name belongs to two women who must not be mixed up. In Genesis 26:34 Esau takes Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite to wife, and in Genesis 36:3 and Genesis 36:4 another Bashemath, the daughter of Ishmael, bears Reuel to Esau. Then 1 Kings 4:15 names a different Basmath, the daughter of Solomon, who married Ahimaaz, one of his officers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Bashemaths are a warning to read slowly: two wives of Esau with one name, and a daughter of Solomon with the same name again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1160); Bosor (i.e. Beor), a Moabite:--Bosor.
BiblicalUsage: Bosor is the Greek form of Beor, the father of Balaam — and it appears once, in Peter's charge against the false teachers. In 2 Peter 2:15 they have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness. One verse, for the prophet who loved the pay.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Balaam's way is still the way of the false teacher: the right way forsaken, for wages.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1006; herbage (as if for grazing):--herb.
BiblicalUsage: Herb is the word for herbage, the green growth that feeds the flocks — and it appears once, in the picture of the fruitful earth. In Hebrews 6:7 the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God. One word, for the ground that drinks the rain and bears fruit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the herb in Hebrews is the test of the soil: the rain falls on all the ground, but only the ground that bears fruit receives the blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only in plural) a pistachio-nut (from its form)
BiblicalUsage: Pistachio nuts are the delicacy Jacob sends to Egypt, and the word appears once, in his parting gift. In Genesis 43:11 Jacob says, take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds. A father's present, sent with his sons to a ruler he does not know is his own son.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the nuts in Jacob's gift are a father's hope in a basket: the best of the land, sent to soften a stranger's heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: akin to G900; a hole (in the ground); specially, a cistern:--ditch, pit.
BiblicalUsage: A ditch is the word for a pit, a hole in the ground — and it appears three times, twice in the same warning. In Matthew 15:14 Jesus says, if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch, and in Luke 6:39 he says it again. In Matthew 12:11 he asks, what man shall there be among you, that shall have one sheep, and if it fall into a pit on the sabbath day, will he not lay hold on it, and lift it out?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ditch is the warning and the pit is the mercy: the blind fall in together, and the shepherd lifts the sheep out even on the sabbath.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a bunch (of grapes):--(vine) cluster (of the vine).
BiblicalUsage: A cluster is the word for a bunch of grapes, and it appears once, in the harvest of wrath. In Revelation 14:18 the angel cries with a loud voice to him that had the sharp sickle, thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, for her grapes are fully ripe. One word, for the vintage of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the clusters in Revelation are ripe for a reason: the vine of the earth has had its season, and the sickle comes when it is fully ripe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mud (as whitish clay)
BiblicalUsage: Mire is the word for mud, whitish clay — and it appears once, in the taunt against Zedekiah. In Jeremiah 38:22 the women left in the king's house shall say, thy friends have set thee on, and have prevailed against thee: thy feet are sunk in the mire, and they are turned away back. One word, for a king stuck in the mud while his friends leave.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mire in Jeremiah is the end of bad counsel: the king's feet sink, and the friends who set him on are gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Botscath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bozkath means rocky height, and it is named twice, as a town of Judah and as a mother's home. In Joshua 15:39 it is listed among the lowland towns of Judah, and in 2 Kings 22:1 Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath is named as the mother of Josiah, the king who found the book of the law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bozkath is remembered for a mother: Jedidah of Boscath, whose son Josiah turned the kingdom back to the book.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Botsrah, a place in Edom
BiblicalUsage: Bozrah means sheepfold or fortress, and it is a town of Edom, named eight times. In Genesis 36:33 Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead, and 1 Chronicles 1:44 repeats the king-list. In Isaiah 63:1 the Lord comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah, and in Jeremiah 49:13 God swears that Bozrah shall become a desolation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bozrah holds both ends of Edom's story: kings crowned there, and the Lord coming from there in judgment, with dyed garments.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an enclosure, i.e. sheep fold
BiblicalUsage: A sheepfold is the word for an enclosure, a fold for the flock — and it appears once, in a promise of gathering. In Micah 2:12 the Lord says, I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee, and I will surely gather the remnant of Israel, and put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold. The fold is the picture, and the gathering is the promise. This is a different word from the town of Bozrah, though the English spells them alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sheep of Bozrah is one of the tenderest pictures in the prophets: the remnant gathered, put together, safe in the fold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1014; volition, i.e. (objectively) advice, or (by implication) purpose:--+ advise, counsel, will.
BiblicalUsage: Counsel is the word for purpose, will, resolve — God's and man's. In Acts 2:23 Jesus was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God. In Acts 4:28 the rulers did whatsoever God's hand and counsel determined before to be done. In Ephesians 1:11 we are predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will. And in Hebrews 6:17 God, willing to show the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the counsel of God is the anchor of my hope: what he determined before, he does, and his counsel cannot be broken by any counsel of men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1014; a resolve:--purpose, will.
BiblicalUsage: Will is the word for a resolve, a purpose settled — and it appears three times. In Romans 9:19 Paul asks, who hath resisted his will? In Acts 27:43 the centurion, willing to save Paul, kept the soldiers from killing the prisoners. And in 1 Peter 4:3 Peter says the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the will in Romans is the question and the will in Acts is the answer: who resists God's will, and yet a centurion's will saved Paul's life — God works through both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1012; to advise, i.e. (reflexively) deliberate, or (by implication) resolve:--consult, take counsel, determine, be minded, purpose.
BiblicalUsage: To take counsel is the word for deliberating, resolving — and it appears in the middle voice, as a man counselling with himself. In Luke 14:31 a king going to war sitteth down first and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand. In John 11:53 the chief priests took counsel together to put Jesus to death. And in 2 Corinthians 1:17 Paul asks, when I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? The Greek text spells the word βουλεύομαι, the middle form, where the dictionary gives the active form, but it is the same word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three counsels are a warning and a pattern: the king counts the cost, the priests plot a murder, and Paul asks whether his own mind was steady — and only one of the three was right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1011; an adviser, i.e. (specially) a councillor or member of the Jewish Sanhedrin:--counsellor.
BiblicalUsage: A counsellor is a member of the council, the Sanhedrin — and the word appears twice, both times for Joseph of Arimathea. In Mark 15:43 Joseph of Arimathea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came and went in boldly unto Pilate and craved the body of Jesus. In Luke 23:50 the same is said again: Joseph, a counsellor, a good man, and a just.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joseph's boldness is the model for a man in power: he waited for the kingdom, and when the hour came he went in boldly and asked for the body.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a primary verb; to "will," i.e. (reflexively) be willing:--be disposed, minded, intend, list, (be, of own) will (-ing). Compare G2309.
BiblicalUsage: To will is the word for being willing, intending, disposed — and it appears thirty-seven times. In James 1:18 of his own will begat he us with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures. In 2 Peter 3:9 the Lord is not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. In Hebrews 6:17 God, willing more abundantly to show the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath. And in Acts 27:43 the centurion, willing to save Paul, commanded them which could swim to cast themselves first into the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the willing in James and Peter is the heart of the gospel: God willed to beget us by his word, and he is not willing that any should perish.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; a hillock:--hill.
BiblicalUsage: A hill is a hillock, a rise in the ground — and it appears twice, in a promise and in a warning. In Luke 3:5 Isaiah's word is quoted: every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low. In Luke 23:30 Jesus says, then shall they begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hills in Luke are the two ends of the story: brought low when the way is prepared, and called on for cover when the judgment comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G1006; an ox (as grazing), i.e. an animal of that species ("beef"):--ox.
BiblicalUsage: An ox is the working animal of the farm, and it appears seven times, mostly in Jesus' sabbath arguments. In Luke 13:15 the Lord says, doth not each one of you on the sabbath loose his ox or his ass from the stall, and lead him away to watering? In Luke 14:5 he asks which of you shall have an ass or an ox fallen into a pit, and will not straightway pull him out on the sabbath day? And in 1 Corinthians 9:9 Paul quotes the law, thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ox in these verses is God's argument for mercy: if you would water your ox on the sabbath, you can heal a man on it too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to go or come (in a wide variety of applications)
BiblicalUsage: To come is the word for going in, entering, arriving — and it is the commonest verb of movement in the Old Testament, over two thousand times. In Genesis 7:1 the Lord says to Noah, come thou and all thy house into the ark. In Genesis 19:1 the two angels came to Sodom at even, and Lot sat in the gate. In 1 Samuel 17:45 David says to Goliath, thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield, but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts. And in 2 Samuel 7:18 David went in, and sat before the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the comings in this word are the whole story of faith: Noah coming into the ark, David coming to Goliath in the Lord's name, and David coming in to sit before the Lord — and I come the same way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cattle-tender
BiblicalUsage: A herdsman is the word for a cattle-tender, and it appears once, in Amos's defence of his calling. In Amos 7:14 Amos says, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son, but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit — and then the Lord took him as he followed the flock and said, go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Amos's herdsman is the pattern of God's prophets: not a prophet's son, but a man taken from the flock to speak to the nation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pit hole (especially one used as a cistern or a prison)
BiblicalUsage: A pit is the word for a hole in the ground, a cistern, a prison — and it appears sixty-two times. In Genesis 37:20 Joseph's brothers say, come, let us slay him, and cast him into some pit. In Psalms 40:2 David says, he brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock. And in Jeremiah 38:6 they take Jeremiah and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah, and Jeremiah sinks down in the mire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pit in the Psalms is the promise for every pit: he brought me up out of it, and set my feet upon a rock — and he does the same for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Botsets, a rock near Michmash
BiblicalUsage: Bozez is one of the two sharp rocks at the pass of Michmash, named in the account of Jonathan's climb to the Philistine garrison. The name marks the steep ground Jonathan had to cross, a crag on one side of the passage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God remembers the very rocks His people climbed, and Bozez is proof that no part of the story is too small to be named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from βραβεύς (an umpire of uncertain derivation); an award (of arbitration), i.e. (specially) a prize in the public games:--prize.
BiblicalUsage: The word brabeîon is a prize in the public games. You meet it in 1 Corinthians, where it does exactly what it sounds like it should do.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that brabeîon shows God wastes no words — every word He gives, including this one, belongs where it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G1017; to arbitrate, i.e. (genitive case) to govern (figuratively, prevail):--rule.
BiblicalUsage: brabeúō — to arbitrate, to rule — turns up in its single occurrence in Colossians. It is a small word, and it stays in its own lane.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, brabeúō is a small window into how precisely God speaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, comparative of G1024, but apparently in the sense of βράσσω (to wield); the arm, i.e. (figuratively) strength:--arm.
BiblicalUsage: In Acts we find brachíōn, the word for the arm, and by figure, strength. Plainly used, and no mystery about what it means.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe brachíōn is worth a moment of attention, and I think you will see why when you read the verse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; short (of time, place, quantity, or number):--few words, little (space, while).
BiblicalUsage: brachýs is simply short, of time, place, or number. Scripture uses it in Acts, and the context leaves nothing to guess at.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that brachýs is no exception: no word in Scripture is filler.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1021; to delay:--be slack, tarry.
BiblicalUsage: Here is bradýnō, the word for to delay, to tarry. It turns up in 1 Timothy, and the meaning is as plain as the word is short.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that bradýnō is small but not slight: to delay, to tarry is part of the picture too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1021 and a prolonged form of G4126; to sail slowly:--sail slowly.
BiblicalUsage: bradyploéō means to sail slowly. It appears once, in Acts among them, and that use is enough to fix its sense.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bradyploéō, little-used as it is, earns its place in Scripture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; slow; figuratively, dull:--slow.
BiblicalUsage: The word bradýs is slow, and by figure, dull. You meet it in James, where it does exactly what it sounds like it should do.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that bradýs shows God wastes no words — every word He gives, including this one, belongs where it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1021; tardiness:--slackness.
BiblicalUsage: bradýtēs — tardiness, slackness — turns up in its single occurrence in 2 Peter. It is a small word, and it stays in its own lane.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, bradýtēs is a small window into how precisely God speaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to moisten (especially by a shower):--(send) rain, wash.
BiblicalUsage: In James we find bréchō, the word for to moisten, to send rain. Plainly used, and no mystery about what it means.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bréchō is worth a moment of attention, and I think you will see why when you read the verse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; an infant (properly, unborn) literally or figuratively:--babe, (young) child, infant.
BiblicalUsage: bréphos covers an infant, a babe, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people would. You find it 8 times, in 1 Peter among other places, and each time it is doing the same steady work. It is a word you understand best by watching where it goes, not by guessing at it.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple: an infant, a babe is part of how God speaks to us, and bréphos is the word He chose for it. That is reason enough to learn it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1026; rain:--rain.
BiblicalUsage: Here is brochḗ, the word for rain. It turns up in Matthew, and the meaning is as plain as the word is short.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that brochḗ is small but not slight: rain is part of the picture too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a noose:--snare.
BiblicalUsage: bróchos means a noose, a snare. It appears once, in 1 Corinthians among them, and that use is enough to fix its sense.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bróchos, little-used as it is, earns its place in Scripture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G977; food (literally or figuratively), especially (ceremonially) articles allowed or forbidden by the Jewish law:--meat, victuals.
BiblicalUsage: Scripture uses brōma for food, meat. Across its 15 occurrences the word stays true to that sense, whether it stands in 1 Corinthians or in 1 Timothy. That steadiness is what makes it worth knowing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that brōma proves nothing in Scripture is filler. Food, meat turns up again and again because God wants it noticed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: akin to βρέμω (to roar); thunder:--thunder(-ing).
BiblicalUsage: brontḗ means thunder, and the Bible means it plainly. It occurs 11 times in the New Testament, in John and Mark and elsewhere, and none of those places bends the word out of shape. What it says in one place is what it says in all of them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe brontḗ earns its place. Thunder is the kind of thing God repeats because His people need to hear it more than once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1035; eatable:--meat.
BiblicalUsage: In Luke we find brṓsimos, the word for eatable, food. Plainly used, and no mystery about what it means.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe brṓsimos is worth a moment of attention, and I think you will see why when you read the verse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G977; (abstractly) eating (literally or figuratively); by extension (concretely) food (literally or figuratively):--eating, food, meat.
BiblicalUsage: brōsis is simply eating, and by extension, food. Scripture uses it in 1 Corinthians, and the context leaves nothing to guess at.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that brōsis is no exception: no word in Scripture is filler.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to grate the teeth (in pain or rage):--gnash.
BiblicalUsage: Here is brýchō, the word for to gnash the teeth. It turns up in Acts, and the meaning is as plain as the word is short.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that brýchō is small but not slight: to gnash the teeth is part of the picture too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1031; a grating (of the teeth):--gnashing.
BiblicalUsage: brygmós covers the gnashing of teeth, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people would. You find it 7 times, in Luke among other places, and each time it is doing the same steady work. It is a word you understand best by watching where it goes, not by guessing at it.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple: the gnashing of teeth is part of how God speaks to us, and brygmós is the word He chose for it. That is reason enough to learn it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to swell out, i.e. (by implication) to gush:--send forth.
BiblicalUsage: The word brýō is to swell out, to gush forth. You meet it in James, where it does exactly what it sounds like it should do.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that brýō shows God wastes no words — every word He gives, including this one, belongs where it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bunni or Buni, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bunni stands among the Levites who cried to the LORD when the people returned to the law, and his name turns up again among those who sealed the covenant and in the line of Hashabiah. He belongs to the generation that rebuilt worship after the exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God keeps the names of faithful Levites, and Bunni is remembered because he stood and prayed with his people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bukki, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Bukki is the name of two Israelites: Bukki the son of Jogli, a prince of Dan who helped divide the land, and Bukki the son of Abishua, a priest in Aaron's line and an ancestor of Ezra. The name covers a prince and a priest, two very different callings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God uses both princes and priests, and Bukki's two bearers show that one name can serve Him in more than one way.
RelatedPeople: Bukki, Son of Jogli; Bukki, Son of Abishua
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bukkijah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bukkiah was a son of Heman, one of the singers set apart for the service of song in the house of the LORD, and the sixth lot of the musicians fell to him with his sons and brethren. He belongs to the choirs David organized for worship.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts singers among His servants, and Bukkiah's place in the lots shows that music in worship is ordered, not accidental.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to trample (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Take bûwç at face value and you have it: to trample. The word appears 12 times, and Ezekiel and Isaiah show it in use without any need for a clever reading. Scripture is not hiding the meaning here; it is stating it.
TheologicalSignificance: My conviction is that bûwç is not a footnote. To trample sits at the heart of how God deals with His people, and the word keeps pointing there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to involve (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: bûwk means to involve, to entangle. It appears 3 times, in Esther among them, and that use is enough to fix its sense.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bûwk, little-used as it is, earns its place in Scripture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bul, the eighth Hebrew month
BiblicalUsage: Bul is the eighth month of the Hebrew year, the month in which Solomon's temple was finished in the eleventh year of his reign. The name marks the completion of the house, finished throughout all its parts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God finishes what He starts, and Bul is the month that says so: the house was done, down to the last detail.
