TheologicalSignificance: I believe seven times passing over a king is God's clock, not man's: the grass eats the king until the king learns who rules, and the times pass only when God says they have passed enough. Seven times is not a sentence without an end — it ends when the king lifts his eyes to heaven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to slide by, i.e. (by implication) to hasten away, pass on, spring up, pierce or change
BiblicalUsage: Chalaph means to change, to alter, to pass through. Laban changed Jacob's wages ten times, the law forbids changing a dedicated beast for another, Jael's hammer passed through Sisera's temples, and Samuel told Saul to go on forward from Tabor to the plain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe change is the word of this root in every direction: wages changed by a cheat, a vow that must not be changed, a hammer that passes through, and a road that goes forward. God changes what He will, and forbids what He will not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a part
BiblicalUsage: Chalaq means a part, a portion. The enemies of Jerusalem warned the king that if the city were rebuilt he would have no portion beyond the river, and Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar twice that his portion would be with the beasts of the field.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a portion is what is left when everything else is taken: the king's portion beyond the river, and the king's portion with the beasts. God decides the portion, and the portion decides the man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: smooth (especially of tongue)
BiblicalUsage: Chalaq means smooth — smooth skin, and smooth words. Jacob said he was a smooth man beside his hairy brother, the strange woman's mouth is smoother than oil, a flattering mouth works ruin, and God promises there will be no more flattering divination in Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe smooth is the most dangerous word in Proverbs: smooth skin nearly cost Jacob his blessing, and a smooth mouth costs a man his soul. God promises an end to flattery, and that is a promise worth holding.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chalak, a mountain of Idumaea
BiblicalUsage: Halak is a mountain of Edom, named twice as the boundary of the conquest — from the mount Halak, that goes up to Seir, to Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon, the land Joshua took. It is the southern edge of the land Joshua measured out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a mountain can be a border: Halak is where the promised land stops going south, and God measures His gift by mountains.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be smooth (figuratively); by implication (as smooth stones were used for lots) to apportion or separate
BiblicalUsage: Chalaq means to divide, to share out. Abram divided his force by night and smote the kings, Pharaoh said he would divide the spoil, the land was divided for an inheritance by number, and God divided the sun and moon and stars to all the nations under heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dividing is God's work and man's temptation in turn: He divides the land for His people and the lights for the nations, and Pharaoh divides the spoil for himself. The difference is whose hand holds the knife.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something very smooth; i.e. a treacherous spot; figuratively, blandishment
BiblicalUsage: Chalaqlaqqah means slippery places, and by extension flattery. The psalmist prays his enemies' way will be dark and slippery, Jeremiah says the prophets' way will be slippery in the darkness, and Daniel says the vile king will obtain the kingdom by flatteries, and many will cleave to him with flatteries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe slippery ground and smooth words are the same danger: the prophets slip in the dark, and the king slips into the kingdom on flattery. God makes the way slippery for those who make it smooth for themselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flattery
BiblicalUsage: Chalaqqah is flattery, and it appears once: those who do wickedly against the covenant will be corrupted by flatteries, but the people who know their God will be strong and do exploits.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe flattery corrupts the covenant-breaker and cannot touch the one who knows his God — that is the whole verse in one line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to prostrate; by implication, to overthrow, decay
BiblicalUsage: Chalash means to weaken, to overthrow, to cut down. Joshua discomfited Amalek with the edge of the sword, Job says man dies and wastes away, and Isaiah taunts the fallen morning star: how are you cut down to the ground, you who weakened the nations?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe weakening is the end of every proud strength: Amalek weakened, man wasted away, and the star that weakened nations was cut down to the ground. The sword discomfits, the grave wastes, and pride falls — all by the same word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to snatch at
BiblicalUsage: Chalat means to snatch at, to catch hastily — and it appears once, when Ben-Hadad's men caught at Ahab's word of mercy and seized on it as a promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe desperate men catch at any word of life, and Ahab's careless word was caught before he could take it back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the loins (as the seat of vigor)
BiblicalUsage: Chalats means the loins, the seat of strength. God told Jacob kings would come out of his loins, Solomon said the son from his father's loins would build the house, and Job said if his loins had not blessed him — warmed with the fleece of his sheep — he would be condemned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the loins carry the promise and the proof together: kings come from them, temples are built by them, and Job's loins blessed him because he clothed the poor. Strength in the loins is for giving, not for keeping.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pull off; hence (intensively) to strip, (reflex.) to depart; by implication, to deliver, equip (for fight); present, strengthen
BiblicalUsage: Chalats means to pull off, to strip away, and to pass over armed. The priest commands the leprous stones to be taken away, Moses arms men for war against Midian, the tribes pass over armed before their brothers, and forty thousand prepared for war passed over to the plains of Jericho.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe stripping and arming are two sides of one word: the house is stripped of its plague, and the men are armed for the war. God takes away what defiles and puts on what defends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G5465; hail:--hail.
BiblicalUsage: Chalaza is hail, and in Revelation it falls three times. Hail and fire mingled with blood came at the first trumpet, lightnings and earthquake and great hail when the temple opened, and a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent, at the last bowl.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hail in Revelation is the old plague grown to the size of judgment: stones like talents falling on men who will not repent, and still they blaspheme God. The hail grows heavier through the book, and the hearts grow harder with it.
RelatedEvents: The Seven Trumpets; The Seven Bowls
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: writhing (in childbirth); by implication, terror
BiblicalUsage: Chalchalah is writhing, like a woman in childbirth, and by extension terror. Isaiah's loins are filled with pain and pangs take hold on him, great pain comes on Ethiopia when the sword falls on Egypt, and Nineveh's heart melts, knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God uses birth pangs for judgment on purpose: the pain that brings forth life is the pain that announces death to the proud city. Isaiah writhes, Ethiopia writhes, and Nineveh writhes — and the pangs never bring forth what the proud expected.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chalchul, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Halhul was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once with Beth-zur and Gedor. It sits in the hill country list of Joshua 15, among the towns Judah inherited.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hill towns are kept for a reason: Judah's inheritance ran over hills as well as valleys, and Halhul is on the list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew or (H3778); a Chaldæan (i.e. Kasdi), or native or the region of the lower Euphrates:--Chaldæan.
BiblicalUsage: Chaldaios is a Chaldean, a man of Chaldea — and it appears once, when Stephen says Abraham came out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Haran.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Chaldeans are named once so we remember where Abraham started: God called a man out of Chaldea, and the calling never stopped.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G5465 through the idea of reducing the strength; difficult, i.e. dangerous, or (by implication) furious:--fierce, perilous.
BiblicalUsage: Chalepos means fierce, difficult, perilous — the two demoniacs were exceeding fierce, so no man could pass that way, and Paul warns that in the last days perilous times will come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fierce men and perilous times are the same word, and the same warning: some roads cannot be passed without Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G5469 and the reduplicated form of G71; to be a bit-leader, i.e. to curb (figuratively):--bridle.
BiblicalUsage: Chalinagogeo means to bridle, to hold with a bit. James says the man who seems religious but bridles not his tongue deceives his own heart, and the man who offends not in word is able also to bridle the whole body.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tongue is the horse and the bridle is the test: hold the tongue, and the whole body follows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5465; a curb or head-stall (as curbing the spirit):--bit, bridle.
BiblicalUsage: Chalinos is a bit, a bridle. James says we put bits in the horses' mouths to turn about their whole body, and John sees blood come out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bit is small and the body is large, and that is the whole of James's point — and the winepress is the warning of what happens when no one holds the reins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chali, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hali was a town in the portion of Asher, named once on the border list — Helkath, Hali, Beten, and Achshaph. It is one of the border towns that marked where Asher's land ran.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the border towns are kept for a reason: Asher's land was measured town by town, and Hali is on the list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a trinket (as polished)
BiblicalUsage: Chaliy is a trinket, an ornament of fine gold. A wise reprover on an obedient ear is like an earring of gold, and the joints of the beloved's thighs are like jewels, the work of a cunning workman.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wise words are ornaments: a reproof that lands well is worth more than gold in the ear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a flute (as perforated)
BiblicalUsage: Chaliyl is a flute, a pipe. A company of prophets came down with psaltery and tabret and pipe and harp, the people piped with pipes when Solomon was anointed, Isaiah counts the pipe among the feasts of the careless, and Jeremiah's heart sounds for Moab like pipes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pipe plays for both joy and mourning in Scripture: it sounds at an anointing and at a funeral, and God hears both kinds. Music is not holy or unholy by itself — it is holy or unholy by the heart that plays it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literal for a profaned thing; used (interj.) far be it!
BiblicalUsage: Chaliylah is the Bible's strongest refusal — far be it, God forbid. Abraham says, that be far from Thee to slay the righteous with the wicked; the tribes say, God forbid that we should rebel against the LORD; God says to Eli, be it far from Me; and Joab says, far be it from me that I should swallow up or destroy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe far be it is the word for a line that must not be crossed: Abraham draws it for God, the tribes draw it for themselves, and God draws it for Eli. Some things are simply far from us, and far from Him.
RelatedEvents: The Altar by the Jordan; Sheba's Rebellion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alternation
BiblicalUsage: Chaliyphah means a change — of raiment, of shifts, of turns. Joseph gave each brother changes of raiment and Benjamin five, Samson wagered thirty changes of garments on his riddle, Solomon sent ten thousand men a month to Lebanon by courses, and Naaman carried ten changes of raiment to the king of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe changes of clothing are changes of fortune in this word: Joseph's gift, Samson's wager, Solomon's courses, and Naaman's payment. God changes the garments of His people, and He changes their fortunes with them.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Samson; King Solomon
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Naaman Healed of Leprosy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: spoil
BiblicalUsage: Chaliytsah is spoil, armour stripped from the fallen. Samson went down to Ashkelon and took their spoil to pay his wager, and Abner told Asahel to take one of the young men and take his armour instead of chasing him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe spoil is the wage of war, and both verses show men reaching for it instead of reaching for what matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5475 and perhaps G1491; copper-like, i.e. "chalcedony":--chalcedony.
BiblicalUsage: Chalkedon is chalcedony, a copper-like stone, and it appears once: the third foundation of the wall of the New Jerusalem was chalcedony, set among jasper and sapphire and the other precious stones.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the foundations of God's city are named stone by stone, and chalcedony is kept among them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5475; coppery:--brass.
BiblicalUsage: Chalkeos means coppery, made of brass — and the word itself is a spelling puzzle. The Greek text behind the King James spells it chalkous, and it stands once, in the idols of gold and silver and brass that men worshipped and would not repent of.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe brass idols are the saddest kind: men make gods of metal and then worship what their own hands made.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5475; a copper-worker or brazier:--coppersmith.
BiblicalUsage: Chalkeus is a coppersmith, a worker in brass — and it appears once, in Paul's warning: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil, and the Lord will reward him according to his works.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a trade is not a character, and Alexander is the proof: he worked in brass and did evil, and Paul leaves him to the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: diminutive from G5475; a copper dish:--brazen vessel.
BiblicalUsage: Chalkion is a copper dish, a brazen vessel — and it appears once, in the washings of the Pharisees, who would not eat without washing, and kept the washing of cups and pots and brazen vessels and tables.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the copper dish is the picture of religion that washes the outside and never touches the inside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a compound of G5475 and G3030 (in the implied mean of whiteness or brilliancy); burnished copper, an alloy of copper (or gold) and silver having a brilliant lustre:--fine brass.
BiblicalUsage: Chalkolibanon is fine brass, brass refined in a furnace — and it appears twice, both times of Christ: His feet like fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace, and the Son of God whose feet are like fine brass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe feet like fine brass are feet that have been through the fire and cannot be burned — and they are coming to walk among the churches.
RelatedEvents: John's Vision of the Risen Christ on Patmos; The Letter to the Church in Thyatira
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G5465 through the idea of hollowing out as a vessel (this metal being chiefly used for that purpose); copper (the substance, or some implement or coin made of it):--brass, money.
BiblicalUsage: Chalkos is brass — and in the Gospels it means money. Jesus told the twelve to provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in their purses, and to take nothing for the journey save a staff only, no scrip, no bread, no money in their purses.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brass in the purse is the test of the mission: go without it, and see who provides.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cake (as usually punctured)
BiblicalUsage: Challah is a cake, usually unleavened and punctured. It is set out for the consecration of Aaron, baked for the meat offering, carried in the basket of the Nazarite, and dealt out by David to every man and woman of Israel when the ark came home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a cake in Scripture is never only a cake: it is consecration, offering, vow, and homecoming in turn. God feeds His people with the same bread He is offered.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flint
BiblicalUsage: Challamiysh is flint, the hardest rock. God brought water out of the rock of flint for thirsty Israel, Job says man puts his hand upon the rock and overturns mountains, the psalm says the flint was turned into a fountain of waters, and the Servant set His face like a flint.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe flint is the Bible's picture of two things at once: the rock that gives water when God strikes it, and the face that will not turn aside. Hardness is a curse in one verse and a calling in the other.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably purslain
BiblicalUsage: Challamuwth is probably purslain, a tasteless plant — and it appears once, when Job asks whether what is unsavoury can be eaten without salt, or whether there is any taste in the white of an egg.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's tasteless plant is his whole complaint in one bite: life with no salt in it, and no one to season it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: smooth
BiblicalUsage: Challaq means smooth, and it appears once, in Isaiah's charge against idolaters: among the smooth stones of the stream is your portion, and to them you have poured drink offerings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe smooth stones make smooth gods, and a portion among stones is the poorest inheritance of all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: frail
BiblicalUsage: Challash means frail, weak — and it appears once, in Joel's call to war: beat your plowshares into swords, and let the weak say, I am strong.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the weak saying I am strong is not boasting — it is the only honest thing left to say when God calls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a window (as perforated)
BiblicalUsage: Challown is a window, and it frames four escapes. Noah opened the window of the ark after forty days, Rahab let the spies down by a cord through the window, the mother of Sisera looked out at a window waiting for a chariot that never came, and Michal let David down through a window to save his life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a window in Scripture is either a way out or a way of watching: Noah looked out on a new world, Rahab let men down to safety, Michal let a king down to safety, and Sisera's mother watched for a son who was already dead. Four windows, and only the watching one ends in grief.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; The Walls of Jericho
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: smooth
BiblicalUsage: Challuq means smooth, and it appears once: David chose five smooth stones out of the brook and put them in his shepherd's bag before he faced Goliath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe smooth stones are God's answer to bronze armour: five from a brook, and one was enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dream
BiblicalUsage: Chalowm is a dream. God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, He says He will speak to a prophet in a dream, the law warns that a dreamer of dreams may still be a false prophet, and Gideon's enemy dreamed of a cake of barley bread tumbling into the camp.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dreams are God's speech and the devil's counterfeit in turn: He speaks to Abimelech to stop a sin, He speaks to prophets to guide a people, and He lets a Midianite dream the defeat before it happens. The test is never the dream — it is the God who sent it.
RelatedEvents: Abraham and Abimelech; Miriam and Aaron Oppose Moses
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, surviving; by implication (collectively) orphans
BiblicalUsage: Chalowph means the surviving, the left behind — the orphans, the perishing. The proverb says to open your mouth for the dumb, in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dumb and the perishing are the test of a mouth: speak for those who cannot speak, or your own words are worth nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a distribution
BiblicalUsage: Chaluqqah is a distribution, a division — and it appears once, when Josiah kept the Passover and the Levites stood in the holy place according to the divisions of the families.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe order is worship too: every family in its division, every Levite in his place, and the Passover kept as it was written.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: defeat
BiblicalUsage: Chaluwshah is defeat, being overcome — and it appears once, when Moses heard the noise in the camp and said it was not the voice of them that shout for mastery, nor the voice of them that cry for being overcome.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Moses could tell the difference by ear: the camp was singing to a calf, and neither victory nor defeat sounds like that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hot
BiblicalUsage: Cham means hot, warm. The Gibeonites showed bread they had taken hot from their houses, now dry and mouldy, and Elihu asks how garments are warm when God quiets the earth by the south wind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hot bread and warm garments are the small mercies of the road, and the Gibeonites' lie is the warning that even bread can be a deceit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cham, a son of Noah; also (as a patronymic) his descendants or their country
BiblicalUsage: Ham was the second son of Noah, named with Shem and Japheth among those who went out of the ark. He saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside, and his name became the name of Egypt — the tabernacles of Ham, where God smote the firstborn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ham's story is the warning that seeing and telling are different sins: he saw, and then he told, and the telling is what the story remembers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hot
BiblicalUsage: Cham means hot, warm. The Gibeonites showed bread they had taken hot from their houses, now dry and mouldy, and Elihu asks how garments are warm when God quiets the earth by the south wind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hot bread and warm garments are the small mercies of the road, and the Gibeonites' lie is the warning that even bread can be a deceit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: violence; by implication, wrong; by meton. unjust gain
BiblicalUsage: Chamac is violence, wrong, unjust gain. The earth was filled with violence before the flood, the law forbids putting your hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness, a false witness rises up to testify what is wrong, and the cruelty done to Jerubbaal's seventy sons came home on Abimelech.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe violence in this word is not only the sword: it is the false witness, the unrighteous hand, and the cruelty that comes home. God drowned the violent earth, and He will drown the violent tongue too.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; Abimelech's Rise and Fall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be violent; by implication, to maltreat
BiblicalUsage: Chamac means to be violent, to maltreat, to wrong. Job's vine shakes off its unripe grape, Wisdom says the sinner wrongs his own soul, Jeremiah says Jerusalem's skirts are violently uncovered for the greatness of her iniquity, and Lamentations says God violently took away His tabernacle like a garden.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe violence turns on its maker in this word: the sinner wrongs his own soul, the city is uncovered for her own iniquity, and even God's tabernacle is taken violently when His people will not listen. The violent vine shakes off its own grape, and the violent city is stripped by its own sin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to delight in
BiblicalUsage: Chamad means to delight in, to desire, to covet. Every tree in the garden was pleasant to the sight, the commandment says you shall not covet your neighbour's house or wife or field, and Achan said, when I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, then I coveted them and took them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe desire is the hinge of the whole story: the trees were pleasant and the command was plain, and Achan's eye went from seeing to coveting to taking in one verse. What you delight in, you will in the end obey.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Ten Commandments; The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb perhaps from the base of G5490 through the idea of a fissure in the soil; earthward, i.e. prostrate:--on (to) the ground.
BiblicalUsage: Chamai means on the ground, to the ground. Jesus spat on the ground and made clay to open blind eyes, and the soldiers who came to arrest Him went backward and fell to the ground at His word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ground is where Jesus does His work: clay for blind eyes, and strong men fallen flat at the sound of His name.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Man Born Blind; The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to commiserate; by implication, to spare
BiblicalUsage: Chamal is the word for sparing someone when you could destroy them, and it runs both ways in Scripture. Saul spared Agag and the best of the sheep when God had said destroy them all, and Pharaoh's daughter had compassion on the baby Moses in the bulrushes and spared his life. Nathan's parable turns on the same word: the rich man had no pity and would not spare his own flock, taking the poor man's lamb instead. Most often it is God who spares, or refuses to spare, and the word carries the weight of a decision, not a passing feeling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word shows me that mercy is a choice with consequences, not a soft mood. Saul's sparing looked kind and cost him the kingdom, while God's sparing in Malachi falls on those who fear Him and serve Him. I hold that true pity never overrules what God has said is right, and that is why I want my compassion shaped by His word rather than by my feelings in the moment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be hot (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Chamam is plain physical warmth, and Scripture uses it for bodies, fires, and company alike. David in his old age could not get warm, so his servants sought a young woman to lie beside him and give him heat. Elisha lay upon the dead child until the child's flesh waxed warm, and the Teacher in Ecclesiastes says two lying together have heat while one alone cannot get warm. Isaiah turns the same warmth into mockery: the idol-maker burns part of his wood, warms himself by it, and then bows to the rest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe warmth in the Bible is nearly always something shared or given, never hoarded. A fire warms the hands that made an idol out of it, yet the same heat raised a dead child when a prophet stretched himself over him. I hold that God made warmth to be passed from one person to another, and the loneliest picture in Scripture is a man who cannot get warm alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to wrap; hence, to depart (i.e. turn about)
BiblicalUsage: Chamaq is turning away, withdrawing, and it appears only twice. In the Song the beloved has withdrawn and gone, and the one who seeks him cannot find him. Jeremiah uses it of a backsliding daughter who goes about, turning this way and that instead of coming home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a warning in miniature: turning away from the one you love leaves you calling into silence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wine
BiblicalUsage: Chamar is the Aramaic word for wine, and it shows up at two very different tables. Belshazzar drank wine before a thousand of his lords and praised gods of gold and silver from the temple vessels, on the very night his kingdom fell. In Ezra the same wine is listed among the supplies the king orders for the temple, given day by day without fail for the burnt offerings of the God of heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wine itself is neither holy nor cursed in these verses; what matters is the table it is poured at. At Belshazzar's feast it sealed a kingdom's judgment, and at the rebuilt temple it served worship. I hold that God gives good gifts to be used in His service, and the same gift turns to shame the moment it is lifted against Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to boil up; hence, to ferment (with scum); to glow (with redness); to smear with pitch
BiblicalUsage: Chamar is boiling up, foaming, churning inside. Moses' mother daubed the little ark with pitch to seal it, Job says his face is foul with weeping, and the psalm pictures waters that roar and are troubled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word catches what grief and fear feel like from the inside: a pot coming to the boil that will not settle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tax a fifth
BiblicalUsage: Chamash appears once, in Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh: take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven plenteous years.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one verse is enough to show Joseph's wisdom: prepare in plenty for the famine you can see coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chamath-Rabbah
BiblicalUsage: Hamath the great stands in Amos as a measuring stick for Israel's pride. The prophet tells the people at ease in Zion to go and look at Hamath, and at Calneh and Gath, and ask whether those kingdoms are any better than theirs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God names real cities when He argues with His people, because a real place is harder to argue away than an idea.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chamath-Tsobah
BiblicalUsage: Hamath-zobah is named once, as a city Solomon went up against and prevailed over, in the account of his building and his borders. The name joins two places into one: Hamath, the great northern city, and Zobah, the Aramean kingdom beside it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a single-verse town matters, because it marks how far the kingdom God promised actually reached under Solomon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chamath, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Hamath was the great city of upper Syria on the Orontes, and its name became the shorthand for Israel's northern border. The spies searched the land as far as Hamath, the promised land is described as reaching to the entering in of Hamath, and Solomon's feast at the temple drew people from Hamath all the way to the river of Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hamath matters because God drew Israel's borders with real places, and the city's name keeps turning up wherever the land's edges are described. The promise was not vague, and neither was its map.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chamathite or native of Chamath
BiblicalUsage: The Hamathite is one of the families descended from Canaan, listed among the peoples who spread abroad after the flood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the table of nations is there to remind me that every people, even one named in a single line, comes from the same first family.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: five
BiblicalUsage: Chamesh is simply the number five, and it counts everything from years to kings. Seth lived a hundred and five years and begat Enos, Joseph tells his brothers five years of famine remain, Israel reached the wilderness of Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month, and five Amorite kings joined together against Gibeon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is nothing mystical to find in the number itself; Scripture counts with it the way any family counts years and loaves. What matters is not the five but what God does with the five, whether years of famine or kings gathered for battle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ferment, (figuratively) extortion
BiblicalUsage: Chamets is leaven, the fermented lump that makes bread rise, and the law is blunt about it: for seven days no leavened bread is to be eaten, and no leaven at all is to be burned in any offering made by fire. The Passover bread is unleavened because Israel left in haste, and Amos later turns the word back on a people who offer leavened thanksgiving while their hearts are far from God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe leaven is the Bible's picture of how a little spreads through the whole lump, for good or for ill. God commanded it out of the Passover house so that Israel would remember the haste of their deliverance. I hold that what I allow to ferment in my own life will not stay small, and that is why the command is so absolute.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ferment, (figuratively) extortion
BiblicalUsage: Chamets is leaven, the fermented lump that makes bread rise, and the law is blunt about it: for seven days no leavened bread is to be eaten, and no leaven at all is to be burned in any offering made by fire. The Passover bread is unleavened because Israel left in haste, and Amos later turns the word back on a people who offer leavened thanksgiving while their hearts are far from God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe leaven is the Bible's picture of how a little spreads through the whole lump, for good or for ill. God commanded it out of the Passover house so that Israel would remember the haste of their deliverance. I hold that what I allow to ferment in my own life will not stay small, and that is why the command is so absolute.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fifty
BiblicalUsage: Chamishshiym is the number fifty, and it measures arks, cities, years, and men. The ark was fifty cubits broad, Abraham pleaded for Sodom if fifty righteous could be found there, the fiftieth year is hallowed as jubile with liberty proclaimed through the land, and the Levites entered the service of the tabernacle from thirty years old until fifty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fifty in Scripture is a working number, not a secret code: the breadth of a boat, the age a man stops carrying the tabernacle, the year debts are cancelled. God counts plainly, and the jubile shows me His counting always bends toward freedom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fifth; also a fifth
BiblicalUsage: Chamiyshiy is the fifth, the ordinal, and it marks days, portions, and offerings. The evening and the morning were the fifth day, Joseph set the fifth part of Egypt's increase for Pharaoh, a man who harmed a holy thing adds the fifth part to his amends, and on the fifth day Shelumiel brought his offering for Simeon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fifth part teaches me that making things right costs more than the damage done. Restitution adds a fifth on top, because repentance is not only repaying what was taken but honouring the one it was taken from.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: seasoned, i.e. salt provender
BiblicalUsage: Chamiyts appears once, in the picture of a restored land: the oxen and young asses that ear the ground shall eat clean, seasoned provender, winnowed with the shovel and the fan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the cattle's fodder is part of God's promise: when He heals His people, the land feeds them well.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: heat; by implication, the sun
BiblicalUsage: Chammah is the heat of the sun itself, and Scripture sets it beside God's glory. The sun shall be ashamed when the LORD of hosts reigns in Zion, and in the day He binds up His people's breach the light of the sun shall be sevenfold. Job went mourning without the sun, and the psalm says of the sun's circuit that there is nothing hid from its heat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sun is the one light no one can hide from, and that is why the prophets use it to picture God's day. Its heat finds everything, and so will His reign. I hold that the same sun that scorches a mourning Job will one day shine sevenfold on a healed people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sun-pillar
BiblicalUsage: Chamman is the sun-pillar, the standing image set up for idol worship, and every mention of it is a mention of its destruction. God warns He will cut down the images, Isaiah says the day is coming when men will not look to the altars the work of their hands, Josiah broke the images down and made dust of them, and Ezekiel sees the altars laid desolate with the sun-images broken.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sun-images show how quickly worship of the Creator slides into worship of the creation. Men set up a pillar to the sun and then bowed to their own work. I hold that God will not share His glory with a statue, and every one of these verses ends with the image in pieces.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chammath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hammath is a name that points two ways at once. Joshua lists it among the fenced cities of Naphtali, a place with walls and a territory. Chronicles names Hemath as the father of the house of Rechab, so the same spelling also belongs to a man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the double use is worth stating plainly rather than smoothing over: one Hammath is a walled town, the other is a father, and the text does not confuse them even if the spelling is the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chammath-Dor, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hammoth-dor, the hot springs of Dor, was a Levitical city in Naphtali, given with its suburbs as a city of refuge for the slayer. Joshua lists it among the cities given to the Levites out of Naphtali, with pasture land around it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a city of refuge with hot springs in its name is a small mercy worth noticing: God gave His priests a home, and the pursued a place to run.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chammon, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hammon is the name of two towns, and Scripture keeps them apart by their tribes. One stands in Asher near great Zidon, and the other in Naphtali was given to the Levites out of the half tribe of Manasseh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe two towns sharing a name is a reminder to read the map, not just the word: the same warm springs can water two different inheritances.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chammuel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hamuel is named once, in the genealogy of Simeon: Hamuel the son of Mishma, whose son was Zacchur and whose grandson was Shimei. He sits four generations down from Simeon, in the line that stayed in the south.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogies keep men like Hamuel on the record for a reason: God counts the quiet names in a family, not only the famous ones.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wrapping, i.e. drawers
BiblicalUsage: Chammuwq is the curve, and it appears once, in the praise of the beloved: the joints of her thighs are like jewels, the work of a cunning workman.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the craftsman's eye is the point here: beauty in the Song is measured, not gushed over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a heap
BiblicalUsage: Chamorah is a heap, and it appears once, in Samson's own boast: with the jawbone of an ass, heaps upon heaps, with the jaw of an ass have I slain a thousand men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wordplay is the point: Samson piles the dead in heaps and names his heap after the ass's jaw that made it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chamor, a Canaanite
BiblicalUsage: Hamor was the Hivite prince of Shechem, and his name is bound to the darkest chapter in Jacob's family. His son Shechem seized Dinah, and Hamor came to Jacob to arrange the marriage, offering intermarriage and shared land. The sons of Jacob answered deceitfully, and on the third day Simeon and Levi slew Hamor and Shechem and took Dinah out of the house, and Joshua later notes the ground Jacob bought from the children of Hamor, where Joseph's bones were buried.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hamor's story is a hard one to sit with, because a father tried to settle his son's violence with a bargain, and the field he sold became the burial place of Joseph. I hold that no treaty can cover what was done to Dinah, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise.
RelatedPeople: Jacob; Shechem, Son of Hamor; Dinah; Joseph, Son of Jacob
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a male ass (from its dun red)
BiblicalUsage: Chamowr is the male ass, the working animal of the whole Bible. Abraham saddled his ass and took Isaac toward Moriah, the tenth commandment forbids coveting a neighbour's ass, Samson found a fresh jawbone and slew a thousand men with it, and Zechariah promises a king coming lowly and riding upon an ass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ass is the Bible's picture of ordinary service carrying extraordinary weight. It bears Abraham's wood, Samson's weapon, and at last the King Himself into Jerusalem. I hold that God delights to use the lowly and the overlooked, and this animal proves it from Genesis to Zechariah.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Ten Commandments
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mother-in-law
BiblicalUsage: Chamowth is a mother-in-law, and Ruth's story is the reason the word feels warm. Ruth clung to Naomi after Orpah kissed her and went back, Boaz praised Ruth for all she had done for her mother-in-law since her husband died, and Naomi herself took up the planning for Ruth's future, saying she would seek rest for her. Micah shows the other side: in a broken house, a daughter-in-law rises against her mother-in-law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Naomi and Ruth redeem the word from every joke about mothers-in-law. Loyalty made them family twice over, by marriage and then by choice. I hold that Micah's warning is the shadow of it: when a house forgets God, even the closest bonds turn against each other.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, violent; by implication, a robber
BiblicalUsage: Chamowts appears once, in Isaiah's call to learn to do well: seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single verse is enough: God names the oppressor only to tell His people to stand against him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chamran, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Chamran, whom the King James renders Amram, is named once, as a son of Dishon the Horite, a descendant of Esau. Chronicles places him among the sons of Dishon, beside Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this Amram must be kept apart from Amram the father of Moses: the names match, the men do not, and the genealogy is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: staunch, i.e. able-bodied soldiers
BiblicalUsage: Chamush describes men harnessed for battle, arrayed by fives, and it marks Israel on the move. God led the children of Israel out of Egypt harnessed, the armed men of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh passed before their brethren into the land, and they crossed the Jordan harnessed before the LORD. Gideon, told to go down to the host, heard the enemy talking in their camp.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows that Israel did not wander unarmed into the promise: God ordered them like an army, five by five, before they had fought a single battle. I hold that readiness is part of faith, and the crossing of the Jordan proves it.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Crossing the Jordan
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chamul, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hamul was the younger son of Pharez, Judah's son by Tamar, and his name turns up wherever Judah's line is counted. He went down into Egypt with Jacob's family, his sons became the family of the Hamulites in the wilderness census, and Chronicles counts him among the sons of Pharez.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hamul's quiet place in three censuses is the point: God keeps the line of Judah by name, generation after generation, even for a younger son.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chamulite (collectively) or descendants of Chamul
BiblicalUsage: The Hamulites are the descendants of Hamul, counted in the wilderness census as a family of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a clan is how a man's name outlives him: Hanoch's sons became a counted family of Reuben.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chamutal or Chamital, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Hamutal was the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah and a wife of Josiah, and her name is tied to the last kings of Judah. Her son Jehoahaz reigned three months in Jerusalem, and her son Zedekiah reigned eleven years before the city fell.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hamutal's story is a mother's grief written in the margins of a kingdom's fall: she gave Judah two kings, and both reigns ended in exile. I hold that God still names her, even when the kingdom her sons ruled is gone.
RelatedPeople: King Josiah; Jehoahaz, King of Judah; Zedekiah, King of Judah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3667); Chanaan (i.e. Kenaan), the early name of Palestine:--Chanaan.
BiblicalUsage: Chanaan is the Greek spelling of Canaan, the early name of the land of Palestine, and it appears in Stephen's defence and in Paul's sermon. Stephen tells how a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and Paul, preaching at Pisidian Antioch, tells how God destroyed seven nations in the land of Chanaan and divided their land to Israel by lot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name matters because both speeches are histories: Stephen and Paul each retell the same story of a land promised, taken, and given. The Greek spelling is only a doorway into the Hebrew Canaan, and the land itself is the thread that runs through both sermons.
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; Paul Preaches at Pisidian Antioch
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5477; a Chanaanæan (i.e. Kenaanite), or native of gentile Palestine:--of Canaan.
BiblicalUsage: A Chanaanaean is a native of gentile Palestine, and the word appears once, in the story of the woman of Canaan who came to Jesus crying for her daughter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe her faith is the point of the name: a Gentile from the old land of Canaan is the one who will not take no for an answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to incline; by implication, to decline (of the slanting rays of evening); specifically, to pitch a tent; gen. to encamp (for abode or siege)
BiblicalUsage: Chanah is pitching camp, and the wilderness is full of it. Israel encamped before Pi-hahiroth by the sea, and wherever the cloud abode, there the children of Israel pitched their tents. After the Jordan they encamped at Gilgal and kept the passover, and the psalmist says that though a host should encamp against him, his heart shall not fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe encamping is the Bible's picture of a people who live by God's leading and not their own map. They pitched where the cloud stopped and moved when it lifted. I hold that my own life works the same way: I camp where He puts me, and I do not fear the host camped across the valley.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Circumcision and Passover at Gilgal
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to narrow; figuratively, to initiate or discipline
BiblicalUsage: Chanak is training up and dedicating, and it covers houses, children, and temples. A man who has built a new house and not dedicated it may go home from battle, a child is trained in the way he should go, and Solomon dedicated the house of the LORD with twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dedication is the first use of anything: a house, a child, a temple is given to God before it is used for anything else. Proverbs puts the same truth in a parent's hands, and I hold that what is trained toward God early is the thing that does not depart from Him late.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chanamel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hanameel was the son of Shallum, Jeremiah's uncle, and his name is tied to the field at Anathoth. He came to Jeremiah in the prison court saying buy my field, for the right of redemption is yours. Jeremiah bought it, weighed the silver, and gave the evidence of the purchase to Baruch before the witnesses.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hanameel's field is the most hopeful purchase in the Bible: Jeremiah bought land in a country about to fall, because God had said houses and fields would be possessed again. The cousin who sold it did not know it, but his field became a sermon.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah Buys the Field at Anathoth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps the aphis or plantlouse
BiblicalUsage: Chanamal appears once, in the psalm of Israel's history: God destroyed their vines with hail, and their sycamore trees with frost.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single verse is enough to show that even the weather answers to God when He judges.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chananel, probably an Israelite, from whom a tower of Jerusalem was named
BiblicalUsage: Hananeel is not a man but a tower, the tower of Jerusalem that marks the city's edges in promise and in rebuilding. Jeremiah says the city shall be built to the LORD from the tower of Hananeel to the gate of the corner, Eliashib the priest built from the sheep gate even to the tower of Hananeel, and Zechariah sees the city lifted up from Benjamin's gate to the tower of Hananeel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a tower named God has favoured is the right landmark for a city God promised to rebuild. The same tower appears in the promise, in the rebuilding, and in the last vision, and I hold that God finishes what He measures out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to favor or (causatively) to entreat
BiblicalUsage: Chanan in Aramaic is showing favour, and in Daniel it is a king being told to show mercy and a prophet caught praying for it. Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar to break off his sins by showing mercy to the poor, and later Daniel is found making supplication before his God, which is what sends him to the lions.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses belong together: mercy shown to the poor, and mercy sought from God, are the same word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chanan, the name of seven Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hanan is a name carried by seven Israelites, and Scripture keeps them apart by their fathers and their work. One Hanan is counted among the sons of Shashak in Benjamin, another is among the Nethinim who returned with Zerubbabel, and another is Hanan the son of Igdaliah, whose chamber in the temple held the sons of the Rechabites.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe seven men sharing one name is a reminder that God counts servants, not only leaders: a Nethinim, a Benjamite, and a temple chamber-keeper are all on the record by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to bend or stoop in kindness to an inferior; to favor, bestow; causatively to implore (i.e. move to favor by petition)
BiblicalUsage: Chanan is bending down in kindness to someone below you, and it is the verb behind grace itself. God tells Moses He will be gracious to whom He will be gracious, Jacob tells Esau the children are the ones God has graciously given him, Solomon prays that God will hear His people when they turn and make supplication, and the blessing on Israel asks the LORD to be gracious unto thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the verb the whole gospel stands on: God stoops. He does not wait for us to climb to Him; He bends down in kindness to the inferior, and that is grace. I hold that every prayer for favour in Scripture is answered by a God who has already promised to be gracious to whom He will be gracious.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chanani, the name of six Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hanani is a name carried by six Israelites, and the sharpest of them is the father of the prophet Jehu. The word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet Jehoshaphat and rebuke him, and another Hanani, a son of Heman, is counted among the musicians of the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hanani's line shows both sides of God's house: a father who raised a prophet, and a son who sang in the temple. The prophet's rebuke and the musician's song both belong to the same family of service.
RelatedPeople: Hanani, Father of Jehu the Prophet; Jehu, Son of Hanani
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chananjah, the name of thirteen Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hananiah is a name carried by thirteen Israelites, and three of them could not be more different. One is Hananiah of Judah, whom the Babylonians renamed Shadrach; one is Hananiah the son of Azur, the prophet who broke Jeremiah's yoke and promised peace within two years; and one is a Hananiah who repaired the wall of Jerusalem beside the apothecaries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three Hananiahs are a warning against judging a man by his name alone: one stood in the fire and would not bow, one spoke peace when God had said judgment, and one quietly rebuilt a wall. I hold that God knows which Hananiah is which, and so must I.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be narrow; by implication, to throttle, or (reflex.) to choke oneself to death (by a rope)
BiblicalUsage: Chanaq is throttling, choking, and it appears twice, both times in death. Ahithophel, seeing his counsel was not followed, saddled his ass, went home, put his household in order, and hanged himself. Nahum pictures the lion that tore enough for his whelps and strangled for his lionesses, and then says God is against it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is as blunt as the acts it names: counsel refused ends in a rope, and a lion's strength ends under God's judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to spice; by implication, to embalm; also to ripen
KeyPassages: Genesis 50:2; Genesis 50:3; Genesis 50:26; Song of Solomon 2:13
BiblicalUsage: Chanat is ripening and embalming, and it spans a burial and a springtime. Joseph commanded the physicians to embalm his father, and they fulfilled forty days for him while Egypt mourned. At the last, Joseph himself was embalmed and put in a coffin in Egypt. In the Song the same word ripens figs: the fig tree puts forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give a good smell.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one word holding both embalming and ripening says something true about the whole Bible: death is prepared for, and life ripens after it. Joseph's body was kept for the exodus, and the fig tree ripens for the summer. I hold that God ripens what He has kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chanes, a place in Egypt
BiblicalUsage: Hanes is a place in Egypt, named once, where the princes of rebellious Judah sent their ambassadors looking for help that would shame them. Isaiah says the princes were at Zoan and the ambassadors came to Hanes, and the help they sought would only bring shame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single mention is the point: Judah's princes went to Hanes for safety, and Isaiah names the town so the failure has an address.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: soiled (i.e. with sin), impious
BiblicalUsage: Chaneph is the impious, the soiled, the hypocrite, and it is always a condition of the heart before it is an act. Isaiah says every one is an hypocrite and an evildoer, and God sends Assyria against a hypocritical nation. Job says the hypocrite's hope shall perish, and that a hypocrite shall not come before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hypocrite's danger is not that he sins but that he hides it under religion. Job knew the difference: the hypocrite hopes in his own standing, and that hope perishes. I hold that God sees the soil on the heart no washing can hide, and the only cure is the honesty Job finally learned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: soiled (i.e. with sin), impious
BiblicalUsage: Chaneph is the impious, the soiled, the hypocrite, and it is always a condition of the heart before it is an act. Isaiah says every one is an hypocrite and an evildoer, and God sends Assyria against a hypocritical nation. Job says the hypocrite's hope shall perish, and that a hypocrite shall not come before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hypocrite's danger is not that he sins but that he hides it under religion. Job knew the difference: the hypocrite hopes in his own standing, and that hope perishes. I hold that God sees the soil on the heart no washing can hide, and the only cure is the honesty Job finally learned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: initiated; i.e. practiced
BiblicalUsage: Chaniyk appears once: when Abram heard his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued to Dan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a quiet commendation: Abram's household was trained before it was ever needed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: graciousness
BiblicalUsage: Chaniynah appears once, in God's sentence on a people who served other gods: there will I not show you favour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word cuts deepest because it is the absence of grace: a people told plainly that favour is withheld.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lance (for thrusting, like pitching a tent)
BiblicalUsage: Chaniyth is the spear, the thrusting lance, and it is the weapon of the mighty men. There was no smith in Israel because the Philistines would not let the Hebrews make swords or spears. Jashobeam lifted up his spear against three hundred slain at one time, and the man who touches thorns must be fenced with iron and the staff of a spear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spear in these verses is less about the weapon than about who holds it. Israel had no smith and no spears until God gave them men who could lift one against three hundred. I hold that the weapon matters far less than the hand God puts it in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Channah, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Hannah was the wife of Elkanah and the mother of Samuel, and her name means grace. She was loved and yet childless, and she prayed in the temple so long and so silently that Eli thought she was drunken. She spoke in her heart, only her lips moved, and then she prayed the prayer that begins my heart rejoiceth in the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hannah's prayer is the model of praying when no one can hear the words: she did not perform her grief, she poured it out before the LORD, and He remembered her. I hold that God hears the prayer spoken only in the heart, and Hannah proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Channathon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Channathon is a place in Palestine, named once, as a border town of Zebulun, where the border compassed to it and turned toward the north. Joshua draws the line of Zebulun past it on the way to the valley of Jiphthah-el.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a border town named once belongs on the map God drew, because the inheritance was measured town by town.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Channiel, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hanniel is a name carried by two Israelites. One is a son of Ulla in Asher, and the other is Hanniel the son of Ephod, the prince of Manasseh who helped divide the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Hanniels show how the same name can sit in a genealogy and in a commission: one is counted, the other is sent to divide the inheritance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: supplication
BiblicalUsage: Channowth is supplication, and it appears once, in the psalmist's darkest question: hath God forgotten to be gracious?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is itself the supplication: a man asking whether God has forgotten grace is already reaching for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: gracious
BiblicalUsage: Channuwn is gracious, and it is the word God uses about Himself more than any other. The LORD passed by Moses and proclaimed Himself merciful and gracious, longsuffering and abundant in goodness. Nehemiah's prayer calls Him a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful. Joel tells the people to rend their hearts and turn, for He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and Jonah quotes the same words back to God, angry that grace would reach Nineveh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the hinge of the whole Bible: God is gracious before we are anything else, and every prophet quotes His own description of Himself. Jonah resented it, Joel preached it, and Nehemiah prayed it. I hold that God's grace is not His mood but His name, and He will not deny it.
RelatedEvents: Moses Sees God's Glory and the Second Tablets
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chanokite (collectively) or descendants of Chanok
BiblicalUsage: The Hanochites are the descendants of Hanoch, counted among the families of Reuben in the wilderness census.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the family name is the record: a son of Reuben becomes a clan, and the clan is counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chanok, an antediluvian patriach
BiblicalUsage: Chanok is a name carried by three men, and the greatest of them is Enoch the son of Jared, who walked with God and was not, for God took him. Another is Enoch the son of Cain, for whom Cain named the first city. The third is Hanoch the son of Reuben, counted among the heads of Israel's families in Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three must be kept apart, because only one walked with God and was taken: the son of Cain got a city named for him, and the son of Reuben got a clan, but Enoch the son of Jared got God Himself. I hold that walking with God is the only distinction that finally matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: consecration
BiblicalUsage: Chanukka in Aramaic is dedication, and Daniel uses it for the wrong kind. Nebuchadnezzar gathered the princes and rulers to the dedication of the golden image he had set up, and they stood before it. Ezra uses the same word for the right kind: the children of Israel kept the dedication of the house of God with joy, offering a hundred bullocks and two hundred rams.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two dedications stand as a warning and a pattern. One image is dedicated by a king who demands worship, and the other house is dedicated by a people who offer joyfully. I hold that what is dedicated tells you who is worshipped, and the difference between the two could not be sharper.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: initiation, i.e. consecration
BiblicalUsage: Chanukkah is the dedication of the altar and the house, and it always comes with offerings. The princes offered at the dedication of the altar, and this was the dedication after the altar was anointed. Solomon kept the dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days, and at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem the Levites were sought out to keep it with gladness and thanksgiving.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dedication in Scripture is never a ribbon-cutting but a giving: the altar is dedicated by what is laid on it, and the wall by the songs sung over it. I hold that God receives a house the way He receives a sacrifice, by what His people bring to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: impiety
BiblicalUsage: Chanuphah is profaneness, and it appears once, in God's charge against the prophets: from the prophets of Jerusalem is profaneness gone forth into all the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a warning that corruption spreads from the pulpit outward, not the other way round.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chanun, the name of an Ammonite and of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hanun is a name carried by an Ammonite king and two Israelites. Hanun the son of Nahash became king after his father, and David sent servants to comfort him, but his princes shamed the messengers and brought war on Ammon. Another Hanun, the son of Zalaph, repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Hanuns are the two ways a man can answer kindness: one shamed the messengers and lost a war, and the other took up a trowel and rebuilt a wall. I hold that how I receive mercy decides what I build next.
RelatedPeople: Hanun, Son of Nahash; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a vault or cell (with an arch); by implication, a prison
BiblicalUsage: Chanuwth is a vault or cell, and it appears once, when Jeremiah was put into the dungeon and into the cabins, and remained there many days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cells were small and the suffering was not: a prophet kept in the dark for speaking the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pure
BiblicalUsage: Chaph is pure, clean, and it appears once, in Elihu's report of Job's claim: I am clean without transgression, I am innocent, and there is no iniquity in me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single verse shows how dangerous a true word can be when it is used to defend a false case.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to cover, i.e. (in a sinister sense) to act covertly
BiblicalUsage: Chapha is acting covertly, and it appears once: the children of Israel did secretly those things that were not right against the LORD their God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single verse names the root of Israel's fall: sin done in secret, as if God could not see it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cover; by implication, to veil, to encase, protect
BiblicalUsage: Chaphah is covering, and it covers heads in grief and faces in judgment. David went up the ascent of Olivet weeping with his head covered, Haman hasted to his house mourning with his head covered, and when the king's word went out they covered Haman's face. In the temple the same word covers the house itself: Solomon overlaid the house with gold, and the beams and posts and doors were covered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe covering in Scripture is never neutral: David covers his head in sorrow, Haman covers his in shame, and God covers His house in gold. What covers a man tells you what has happened to him. I hold that the only covering that does not shame is the one God provides, and these verses show me all three kinds side by side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to pry into; by implication, to delve, to explore
BiblicalUsage: Chaphar is digging and prying into, and it is the work of wells and spies alike. Abraham gave seven ewe lambs as a witness that he had digged a well, Isaac digged again the wells his father's servants had digged, and when the Nile turned to blood all the Egyptians digged round about the river for water. In Deuteronomy the people ask to send men to search out the land before they go up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe digging is the Bible's picture of patient work: a well is not found by wishing, and a land is not known by hearsay. Abraham dug, Isaac re-dug, and Egypt dug in desperation. I hold that God gives water to diggers, and knowledge to those who search.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chapharajim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hapharaim is a place in Palestine, named once, among the towns of Issachar. Joshua lists it between Shion and Anaharath, in the portion that fell to Issachar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a town named once still belongs on the map: the inheritance was counted town by town, and none was too small to record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to seek; causatively, to conceal oneself (i.e. let be sought), or mask
BiblicalUsage: Chaphas is seeking out and disguising, and it does both in the same breath. Saul tells his men to take knowledge of all the lurking places where David hides, and to search him out through all the thousands of Judah. The same Saul disguises himself to visit the medium at Endor, a prophet disguises himself with ashes to wait for the king, and Josiah disguises himself to fight at Megiddo.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows two kinds of seeking: Saul seeking David to kill him, and men disguising themselves to hide what they are doing. Both end badly. I hold that a man who must disguise himself to do a thing already knows it should not be done.
RelatedEvents: Saul Consults the Medium at Endor
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to spread loose; figuratively, to manumit
BiblicalUsage: Chaphash appears once, in the law of the bondmaid betrothed to a husband and not at all redeemed: freedom was not given her, and the case is judged with mercy rather than death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single verse shows God's law making room for a woman with no freedom of her own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to start up suddenly, i.e. (by implication) to hasten away, to fear
BiblicalUsage: Chaphaz is starting up suddenly in haste or fear, and it runs through battles and prayers. Saul went on one side of the mountain and David on the other, in haste, and the Syrians fled so fast the whole way to Jordan was full of garments and vessels cast away in their haste. Moses tells Israel not to tremble or be terrified, and the psalmist confesses he said in his haste that he was cut off from before God's eyes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe haste in Scripture is nearly always fear wearing a fast coat. Armies throw away their goods to run faster, and a praying man says things in haste he later regrets. I hold that God does not hurry His people, and the verse that steadies me most is the one where the hasty confession is followed by God's hearing.
