Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to blush; figuratively, to be ashamed, disappointed; causatively, to shame, reproach
BiblicalUsage: Chapher is blushing with shame, and it is the colour of judgment and of grace. Fear not, says Isaiah, for thou shalt not be ashamed, and thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth. Jeremiah pictures the mother of seven languishing, ashamed and confounded, and Job says his friends were confounded because they had hoped and came and were ashamed. Isaiah warns Israel they shall be ashamed of the oaks they desired.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shame in the Bible is a true feeling with a false master. The prophets use it to describe judgment, and then God promises to take it away. I hold that the shame God removes is not denied but forgiven, and the promise to forget the shame of youth is one I cling to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pleased with
BiblicalUsage: Chaphets is being pleased with, delighting in, desiring, and it describes God's pleasure and man's. The Lord whom ye seek shall suddenly come to His temple, even the messenger of the covenant whom ye delight in. Nehemiah prays for the servants who desire to fear God's name, the psalm says God has no pleasure in wickedness, and asks what man is he that desireth life and loveth many days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe delight is the test of the heart: what I delight in is what I worship, whether it is the messenger of the covenant or a long life. God has no pleasure in wickedness, and neither should I. I hold that praying like Nehemiah, to be counted among those who desire to fear His name, is the right desire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pleased with
BiblicalUsage: Chaphets is being pleased with, delighting in, desiring, and it describes God's pleasure and man's. The Lord whom ye seek shall suddenly come to His temple, even the messenger of the covenant whom ye delight in. Nehemiah prays for the servants who desire to fear God's name, the psalm says God has no pleasure in wickedness, and asks what man is he that desireth life and loveth many days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe delight is the test of the heart: what I delight in is what I worship, whether it is the messenger of the covenant or a long life. God has no pleasure in wickedness, and neither should I. I hold that praying like Nehemiah, to be counted among those who desire to fear His name, is the right desire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a burrower, i.e. probably a rat
BiblicalUsage: Chaphor is the burrower, the mole, and it appears once: in that day a man shall cast his idols of silver and gold to the moles and to the bats.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is deliberate: idols made to be worshipped end up in the dark with the creatures that never see the sun.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to carve; by implication, to delineate; also to entrench
BiblicalUsage: Chaqah is carving and delineating, and it is used for beauty and for idolatry alike. Solomon carved cherubims and palm trees and open flowers on the temple doors and overlaid them with gold. Ezekiel saw every form of creeping things and abominable beasts pourtrayed on the wall of the temple, and Aholibah saw images of the Chaldeans pourtrayed with vermilion. Job says God set a print upon the heels of his feet.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe carving shows what a people love: Solomon carved heaven's creatures in gold, and apostate Israel carved creeping things on the wall. The same skill serves worship or idolatry. I hold that my own hands will carve something, and the question is only what image I am tracing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to hack, i.e. engrave (Judges 5:14, to be a scribe simply); by implication, to enact (laws being cut in stone or metal tablets in primitive times) or (gen.) prescribe
BiblicalUsage: Chaqaq is engraving, cutting a law or a picture into something that lasts. The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come. Isaiah is told to write the vision in a table and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever. Ezekiel is told to pourtray the city of Jerusalem upon a tile, and Moses says Gad provided the first part for himself, because there, in a portion of the lawgiver, was he seated.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe engraving is the Bible's answer to forgetting: what is cut into stone or written in a book outlasts the men who made it. The lawgiver's portion and the prophet's tablet both say the same thing. I hold that God's word is not spoken into the air but engraved, so that the time to come can still read it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to penetrate; hence, to examine intimately
BiblicalUsage: Chaqar is penetrating examination, searching a matter to the bottom. Jonathan says he will sound his father about David, and show it to him. The law commands that when a rumour of idolatry is heard, the people shall enquire and make search and ask diligently. The Preacher sought out and set in order many proverbs, and the princes of Ammon accused David's servants of coming to search out the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe searching is a duty, not a suspicion: God commands His people to enquire diligently before they judge a city, and Jonathan sounds his own father before he trusts him. I hold that a hasty judgment is a sin, and the Bible's remedy is always the same: search it out first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chakupha, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Hakupha is named twice, among the children of the Nethinim who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. Ezra and Nehemiah both count his children in the returning families.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts the servants as carefully as the priests: Hakupha's family is on the return list by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5463; cheerfulness, i.e. calm delight:--gladness, X greatly, (X be exceeding) joy(-ful, -fully, -fulness, -ous).
BiblicalUsage: Chara is joy, and the New Testament ties it to fellowship and to faith that holds. John writes so that our joy may be full, Peter says believers rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory though they do not see Christ, Paul tells the Thessalonians they are his glory and joy, and he calls himself a helper of the Corinthians' joy, not a lord over their faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe joy in the New Testament is never a private mood but a shared possession: John's joy is full when his readers walk in the light, and Paul's joy is a church standing firm. I hold that joy is the fruit of faith, not its precondition, and it grows precisely where it is shared.
RelatedPeople: John the Apostle; Simon Peter; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to demolish
BiblicalUsage: Charab appears once, in the letter against Jerusalem: search the book of the records, and you will find that this city is a rebellious city, hurtful unto kings, and that they have moved sedition within the same of old time.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows how enemies quote history: the charge is true in part, and that is what makes it dangerous.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to parch (through drought) i.e. (by analogy,) to desolate, destroy, kill
BiblicalUsage: Charab is laying waste, desolating, and it is the word of Assyria's trail and of God's judgment alike. The kings of Assyria have destroyed the nations and cast their gods into the fire, Ezekiel says the cities shall be laid waste and the high places desolate, Amos hears that the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the cities that are inhabited shall be laid waste.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe desolation in Scripture is never the last word, but it is a true word: empires waste nations, and God wastes the altars His people built to false gods. I hold that the same God who lays waste also promises to rebuild, and I read these verses with both halves in view.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a desert
BiblicalUsage: Charabah is dry ground, and it is the ground God makes where there was only water. All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died in the flood. Moses stretched out his hand and the LORD caused the sea to go back, and the waters were a wall while Israel went on dry ground. The priests stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and Elijah and Elisha went over on dry ground when the waters parted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dry ground is one of the Bible's great miracles precisely because it is so ordinary: God does not give His people wings, He gives them a path. The flood drowned the dry land, and the sea and the river opened to make it again. I hold that the God who makes dry ground in the middle of a sea can make a way through anything I face.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; The Exodus and the Red Sea; Crossing the Jordan
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: parching heat
BiblicalUsage: Charabown is parching heat, drought, and it appears once: day and night thy hand was heavy upon me, and my moisture is turned into the drought of summer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the most honest description of unconfessed sin in the Bible: it dries a man out from the inside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shudder with terror; hence, to fear; also to hasten (with anxiety)
BiblicalUsage: Charad is trembling with terror, and it follows Saul through his whole story. The people followed him trembling, the earth quaked and there was a very great trembling when Jonathan attacked, Saul was afraid and his heart greatly trembled when he saw the Philistines, and all the guests of Adonijah were afraid and rose up and went every man his way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe trembling is the body's confession when the heart will not make one. Saul trembled before Philistines and before a medium, and Adonijah's guests trembled when they heard Solomon was king. I hold that the fear of God is the only trembling that steadies a man, and Saul's story shows what happens when it is missing.
RelatedEvents: Saul Consults the Medium at Endor
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charadah, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Haradah is a place in the desert, named twice, as one of the stations where Israel encamped on the way from Mount Hor. Numbers lists it between Libnah and Makheloth on the march through the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a desert station named only in the marching list still matters: God led them stage by stage, and every camp is on the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fear, anxiety
BiblicalUsage: Charadah is fear and anxiety, the trembling that takes hold of the whole body. Isaac trembled very exceedingly when Esau came in and he knew the blessing had gone to Jacob. Elisha asks the Shunammite what can be done for her, since she has been careful for them with all this care. Daniel's companions fled to hide themselves when a great quaking fell upon them, and Isaiah says fearfulness affrighted him and the night of his pleasure turned to fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe anxiety in Scripture is not a modern invention: Isaac trembled, Isaiah's heart panted, and a whole company fled from a vision they could not bear. The Shunammite's carefulness is the same word turned toward kindness. I hold that fear is honest, and the Bible's answer is not to deny it but to bring it to the God who steadies trembling hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to leap suddenly, i.e. (by implication) to be dismayed
BiblicalUsage: Charag appears once: the strangers shall fade away, and be afraid out of their close places.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the close places are the last hiding spots: enemies driven out of them have nowhere left to run.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G5482; a scratch or etching, i.e. stamp (as a badge of servitude), or sculptured figure (statue):--graven, mark.
BiblicalUsage: Charagma is a stamp, an etching, a mark, and it carries the weight of belonging. Paul tells the Athenians that the Godhead is not like gold or silver or stone, graven by art and man's device. In Revelation the mark is the beast's: he causes all to receive a mark in their right hand or in their foreheads, and those who worship the beast and receive his mark drink the wine of God's wrath. The beast and the false prophet who deceived them that had the mark are cast into the lake of fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mark is the Bible's picture of allegiance made visible: every person bears someone's stamp. Paul says God cannot be stamped by human art, and John says the beast stamps his followers. I hold that the only safe mark is the one God puts on His own, and I want to be sure whose stamp I carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to glow or grow warm; figuratively (usually) to blaze up, of anger, zeal, jealousy
BiblicalUsage: Charah is burning anger, and it kindles in God and in men alike. The Spirit of God came upon Saul and his anger was kindled greatly when he heard the men of Jabesh, and Samuel was grieved when God repented that He had made Saul king. Saul was very wroth when the women sang that David had slain his ten thousands, and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzza when he put his hand to the ark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe anger in these verses is a fire that reveals what a man loves: Saul's anger flares at a song, Samuel's at a rejected king, God's at a careless hand on holy things. I hold that not all burning is sin, but the burning that guards my own pride always is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to scorch
BiblicalUsage: Charak is scorching, and it appears once, in the proof of the deliverance: upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the whole miracle in one line: the fire did not even leave a smell.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to braid (i.e. to entangle or snare) or catch (game) in a net
BiblicalUsage: Charak is catching game in a net and roasting it, and it appears once: the slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting, but the substance of a diligent man is precious.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the proverb is a small economics lesson: the lazy man cannot even finish what he started.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G5482; a graver (the tool or the person), i.e. (by implication) engraving (("character"), the figure stamped, i.e. an exact copy or (figuratively) representation):--express image.
BiblicalUsage: Charakter appears once, and it carries the whole of Christology: the Son is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of His person, upholding all things by the word of His power.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is exact on purpose: Christ is not a copy of God but the stamp itself, the same image pressed into flesh.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to seclude; specifically (by a ban) to devote to religious uses (especially destruction); physical and reflexive, to be blunt as to the nose
BiblicalUsage: Charam is devoting to destruction under the ban, and it is the hardest word in the Old Testament. God commanded Saul to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they have, and then sent him to utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites. Solomon laid tribute on the Canaanites Israel could not utterly destroy, and the Simeonites smote the tents of Ham and destroyed them utterly in the days of Hezekiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word must be read with its whole weight, not softened away: God devoted Amalek to destruction, and Saul's failure to do it cost him the kingdom. I hold that the ban belongs to God's judgment, not to man's anger, and the difference is everything. I do not get to devote what God has not devoted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charan, the name of a man and also of a place
BiblicalUsage: Charan is both a man and a place, and the place is the one Scripture keeps returning to. Terah took Abram and Lot and Sarai and went forth to go to Canaan, and they came unto Haran and dwelt there, until Abram departed out of Haran as the LORD had spoken, at seventy-five years old, and took Sarai his wife and Lot and all their substance. Haran also names Terah's son, the father of Lot, who died before his father in Ur.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Haran is the halfway house of faith: Terah stopped there on the way to Canaan and died there, and Abram had to leave it to follow God. I hold that the place between the call and the promise is the most dangerous ground of all, because it is easy to settle there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pull off, i.e. (by implication) to expose (as by stripping); specifically, to betroth (as if a surrender); figuratively, to carp at, i.e. defame; to spend the winter
BiblicalUsage: Charaph is reproaching, defying, taunting, and Goliath is its loudest voice. I defy the armies of Israel this day, he said, and David answered by asking who this uncircumcised Philistine is that he should defy the armies of the living God. David came in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied. Centuries later Sennacherib wrote letters to rail on the LORD God of Israel the same way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe defiance is always aimed past the people at God Himself: Goliath defied the armies, but David heard the defiance of the living God. The same is true of Sennacherib's letters. I hold that God answers reproach, and the valley of Elah is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to grate the teeth
BiblicalUsage: Charaq is grating the teeth, and it is always the sound of enemies. Job says his enemy gnasheth upon him with his teeth, the psalm pictures hypocritical mockers in feasts gnashing upon the righteous, the wicked plotteth against the just and gnasheth upon him, and the wicked shall see the righteous honoured and gnash with his teeth and melt away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gnashing of teeth is the Bible's sound for hatred that cannot act: the teeth grind because the hands are tied. Job heard it, the psalmists heard it, and the last verse promises it ends in melting away. I hold that God hears the grinding too, and He will answer it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to glow, i.e. literally (to melt, burn, dry up) or figuratively (to show or incite passion)
BiblicalUsage: Charar is burning, glowing, drying up, and it is the heat of judgment and of sickness. The vine wood is cast into the fire, both ends devoured and the midst burned, and the pot is set to boil until the bones are burned. The bellows are burned and the founder melteth in vain, and Job says his skin is black upon him and his bones are burned with heat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the burning in these verses is thorough: fire takes the ends and the middle, the bones and the skin. Jeremiah's founder melts in vain because the wicked are not plucked away. I hold that fire in the Bible always tests what it touches, and what is left after it is what was real.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fabricator or any material
BiblicalUsage: Charash is the craftsman, the fabricator, the man who works material with his hands. There was no smith in Israel because the Philistines would not let the Hebrews make swords or spears. David tells Solomon there are workmen in abundance, hewers and workers of stone and timber and all manner of cunning men, and the money for the temple repair went to the artificers and builders to buy hewn stone and timber.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the craftsman in Scripture is never a background figure: God gave Bezalel skill, and He gave David workmen in abundance to build His house. The Philistines knew it too, and took the smiths away first. I hold that skill is a gift from God, and a people without craftsmen is a people who cannot build.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to scratch, i.e. (by implication) to engrave, plough; hence (from the use of tools) to fabricate (of any material); figuratively, to devise (in a bad sense); hence (from the idea of secrecy) to be silent, to let alone; hence (by implication) to be deaf (as an accompaniment of dumbness)
BiblicalUsage: Charash covers ploughing, engraving, and keeping silent, and the same root does all three. Elijah found Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, Samuel warns that a king will set men to ear his ground and make his instruments of war, Absalom tells Tamar to hold her peace, and Israel begs Samuel not to cease crying to the LORD, not to keep silent for them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three uses are one picture: the plough cuts a furrow, the engraver cuts a line, and silence cuts off speech. Elisha was ploughing when his life changed, and Tamar was told to be silent when hers broke. I hold that God speaks into all three, whether He calls a ploughman or hears a cry that will not be silent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mechanics, the name of a valley in Jerusalem
BiblicalUsage: Charashim is the valley of craftsmen, named once, in the genealogy of Judah, where the sons of Meonothai were craftsmen and the valley took their name. The valley kept the trade of the family that lived there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a valley named for its workers is a small honour: the craftsmen's trade became the land's name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to engrave
BiblicalUsage: Charath appears once, and it is the highest use of engraving in the Bible: the tables were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse settles who the author is: the law was not only spoken by God but engraved by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the loin (as the seat of strength)
BiblicalUsage: Charats is the loin, the seat of strength, and it appears once, in Belshazzar's terror: his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows fear undoing a king at the very place of his strength: the loins give way before the knees do.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to point sharply, i.e. (literally) to wound; figuratively, to be alert, to decide
BiblicalUsage: Charats is pointing sharply, deciding, decreeing, and it runs from a dog's tongue to the end of the age. Against Israel not a dog shall move his tongue, says God before the last plague. Isaiah says the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness, and Daniel hears that desolations are determined unto the end of the war, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is about God's decisions standing firm: what He decrees is cut sharp and cannot be moved, whether it is a dog's tongue held still or a desolation determined to the end. I hold that the same sharpness that judges also protects, and Israel's safety in Egypt proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from χαράσσω (to sharpen to a point; akin to G1125 through the idea of scratching); a stake, i.e. (by implication) a palisade or rampart (military mound for circumvallation in a siege):--trench.
BiblicalUsage: Charax is a palisade, a trench, a sharpened stake, and it appears once, in Jesus' weeping over Jerusalem: thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single verse is a prophecy with a date on it: the trench Jesus described is the one Rome would dig.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charbona or Charbonah, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Harbona is a chamberlain of King Ahasuerus, and his two mentions frame the whole book of Esther. He is named among the seven who served in the king's presence when the king was merry with wine, and it is Harbonah who points to the gallows fifty cubits high that Haman made for Mordecai, and the king says hang him thereon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Harbona's second mention is the turn of the story: the servant who fetched wine now points at the gallows, and the gallows built for Mordecai takes Haman instead. I hold that God turns the instruments of the wicked back on their makers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charchas, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Harhas is named once, as the keeper of the wardrobe and the grandfather of Shallum, the husband of Huldah the prophetess, to whom the priests went when the book of the law was found. His grandson Shallum married the woman who spoke God's word to King Josiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single mention is enough to place him: a keeper of robes whose granddaughter-in-law spoke the word of God to a king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fever (as hot)
BiblicalUsage: Charchur is fever, burning heat, and it appears once, among the curses of the covenant: the LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list is deliberate: fever is named among the judgments that pursue a people who break the covenant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charchur, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Harhur is named twice, among the children of the Nethinim who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. Both lists place his family among the temple servants who came back to serve.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the return list is a roll call of the lowly: Harhur's family came home with the priests and the singers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a potsherd, i.e. (by implication) a pottery; the name of a gate at Jerusalem
BiblicalUsage: Charcuth is a potsherd, and it names a gate: Jeremiah is sent to the valley of Hinnom by the entry of the east gate, the potsherd gate, to proclaim the words God will tell him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gate's name fits the message: a broken potsherd of a city, proclaimed at a gate named for broken pots.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah Breaks the Flask at Topheth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: parched or ruined
BiblicalUsage: Chareb is parched, dry, ruined, and it describes both land and bread. The land that was desolate shall become like the garden of Eden, and the waste cities shall be fenced and inhabited. Haggai asks whether it is time to dwell in cieled houses while God's house lies waste, Jeremiah hears that the desolate streets shall hear joy again, and the law gives the dry meat offering to all the sons of Aaron alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds ruin and restoration in the same breath: the same land called desolate is promised to become Eden. Haggai's rebuke and Ezekiel's promise belong together. I hold that God wastes what His people neglect and restores what they return to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fearful; also reverential
BiblicalUsage: Chared is trembling, fearful and reverential at once, and it is the trembling God looks for. Every one that trembled at the words of the God of Israel assembled to Ezra, God says He will look to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit and trembleth at His word, and the same promise is given to those who tremble at His word when their brethren cast them out. Eli sat by the wayside with his heart trembling for the ark of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this trembling is the opposite of Saul's fear: it is not the shaking of a man afraid of his enemies but the reverence of a man who has heard God speak. Eli trembled for the ark, Ezra's company trembled at the word. I hold that God looks for this trembling, and He says so Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the leaping insect, i.e. a locust
BiblicalUsage: Charegol is the leaping insect, the beetle, and it appears once, among the clean creatures Israel may eat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a small reminder that God's law reaches even to the insects, and nothing is too small for His ordering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chareph, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hareph is named once, as the father of Beth-gader, in the genealogy of Caleb. Chronicles counts him among the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one line can carry a father's whole legacy: Hareph's son became a town's name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: arid
BiblicalUsage: Charer is arid, parched, and it appears once: the man who trusts in man shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a picture of a life without God: dry ground, salt land, and no good coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: excrements of doves {or a vegetable}
BiblicalUsage: Charey-yowniym is dove's dung, and it appears twice, both times in a siege. In Samaria the famine was so great that the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung sold for five pieces of silver, and Rabshakeh taunted the men on the wall that they would eat their own dung and drink their own water with the besiegers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is there to show how far a siege can bring a city: when even dung is sold for silver, the famine has done its work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charhajah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Harhaiah is named once, as a goldsmith and the father of Uzziel, who repaired the wall of Jerusalem beside the apothecaries. His son worked the wall next to Hananiah of the apothecaries, and they fortified it to the broad wall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the goldsmith's son rebuilding a wall is the whole return from exile in miniature: every trade took up the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charim, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Harim is a name carried by several men, and the clearest is the priest whose course fell third in David's ordering. The children of Harim returned from exile a thousand and seventeen, Malchijah the son of Harim repaired a portion of the wall, and the third lot of the priests came forth to Harim.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three mentions show one family across the whole story: a priestly course under David, a returning family under Zerubbabel, and a wall-builder under Nehemiah. I hold that God keeps a family through exile the same way He kept its course.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: accusative case of G5485 as preposition; through favor of, i.e. on account of:--be-(for) cause of, for sake of, +…fore, X reproachfully.
BiblicalUsage: Charin is a small preposition, through favour of, on account of, for the sake of, and it carries the reason for things. Her sins are forgiven, for she loved much, and for this cause Paul bows his knees unto the Father. Cain slew his brother because his own works were evil and his brother's righteous.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word does heavy work: it tells me why forgiveness came, why Paul knelt, and why the first murder happened.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5483; a (divine) gratuity, i.e. deliverance (from danger or passion); (specially), a (spiritual) endowment, i.e. (subjectively) religious qualification, or (objectively) miraculous faculty:--(free) gift.
BiblicalUsage: Charisma is a free gift of grace, and Paul uses it for both the gifts of the Spirit and the gift of salvation itself. There are diversities of gifts but the same Spirit, to another faith and to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit. The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Peter says every man should minister the gift he has received, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word will not let me earn what God gives: a gift is a gift, whether it is healing or eternal life. Paul puts the Spirit's gifts and salvation under the same word on purpose. I hold that the right response to a gift is stewardship, and Peter says so plainly: minister it to one another.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5485; to grace, i.e. indue with special honor:--make accepted, be highly favoured.
BiblicalUsage: Charitoo is to grace, to make accepted, to highly favour, and it appears twice, both times of grace given. God hath made us accepted in the beloved, to the praise of the glory of His grace. And the angel said to Mary, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses are one doctrine: the favour Mary received is the same favour every believer receives in the Beloved.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chariph, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hariph is named twice, once among the returning exiles, whose children numbered a hundred and twelve, and once among those who sealed the covenant. Nehemiah counts his children in the return, and then records his name on the sealed covenant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two mentions are a small testimony: a family that came back, and then signed its name to the covenant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ploughing or its season
BiblicalUsage: Chariysh is ploughing, or its season, and it marks the farmer's year. Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest. Joseph tells his brothers five years remain in which there shall neither be earing nor harvest, and Samuel warns that a king will set men to ear his ground and reap his harvest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ploughing season is the Bible's picture of ordinary work under God's ordering: even in earing time and harvest, the Sabbath stands. Joseph's famine took away both earing and harvest, and Samuel's king would take the ploughmen for himself. I hold that work is God's gift, and rest is His command, and neither may swallow the other.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quiet, i.e. sultry (as feminine noun, the sirocco or hot east wind)
BiblicalUsage: Chariyshiy is the sultry, quiet heat, the sirocco, and it appears once: God prepared a vehement east wind, and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, so that he fainted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the east wind is God's answer to a prophet who wanted shade on his own terms.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, cut out (or hollow), i.e. (by implication) a pocket
BiblicalUsage: Chariyt is a pocket, a bag, a purse, and it appears twice, both times holding what men value. Naaman bound two talents of silver in two bags and laid them on his servants, and Isaiah lists the crisping pins among the finery of the daughters of Zion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is small and the lesson is plain: what a man carries in his pocket shows what he trusts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, incisure or (passively) incised; hence, a threshing-sledge (with sharp teeth); also a slice (as cut)
BiblicalUsage: Chariyts is a threshing-sledge with sharp teeth, and also the cheeses it resembles, and it appears in David's hands twice over. Jesse sends ten cheeses to the captain of David's brethren, and David later puts the Ammonites under saws and under harrows of iron and makes them pass through the brickkiln.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a reminder that David carried cheese before he carried a crown, and the same hands did both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G5485; to grant as a favor, i.e. gratuitously, in kindness, pardon or rescue:--deliver, (frankly) forgive, (freely) give, grant.
BiblicalUsage: Charizomai is granting as a favour, forgiving freely, and it is the verb of grace in action. Paul tells the Corinthians to forgive the repentant man and comfort him, lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. The crowd desired a murderer to be granted unto them instead of the Holy One. Paul says we have received the things that are freely given to us of God, and he forgave for the Corinthians' sakes in the person of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forgiveness is never earned but always granted: the same word that gives a murderer to a crowd gives forgiveness to a brother. Paul forgives because God freely gave, and I am told to do the same. I hold that grace I will not pass on is grace I have not understood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charnepher, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Harnepher is named once, as a son of Zophah, in the genealogy of Asher. Chronicles lists him among the sons of Zophah, beside Suah, Beri, and Imrah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy keeps even the briefest names: Harnepher is counted among his brethren of Asher.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Charodite, or inhabitant of Charod
BiblicalUsage: A Harodite is an inhabitant of Harod, and the word appears once, in the list of David's mighty men: Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mighty men are named by their towns on purpose: a man's home is part of his honour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charosheth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Harosheth of the Gentiles was the home of Sisera, captain of Jabin's host, with nine hundred chariots of iron. The LORD sold Israel into Jabin's hand, Sisera gathered his chariots from Harosheth to the river Kishon, and Barak pursued them back to Harosheth until not a man was left.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Harosheth is the measure of the victory: nine hundred iron chariots gathered there, and none came back. The place that launched the oppression became the place the pursuit ended.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mechanical work
BiblicalUsage: Charosheth is mechanical work, the skilled cutting of stone and carving of timber for the tabernacle, given to Bezalel and his workmen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word honours the hands: God filled men with skill to cut stone and carve wood for His house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a burning of anger
BiblicalUsage: Charown is the burning of anger, and it is almost always God's. Samuel tells Saul the LORD has done this to him because he did not execute God's fierce wrath upon Amalek. Hezekiah makes a covenant that God's fierce wrath may turn away, Moses is told to hang the heads of the people so the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away, and the law promises that when the cursed thing is removed, the LORD will turn from the fierceness of His anger.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the burning anger of God is not like man's temper: it has a cause, a cure, and an end. It burns against Amalek and against the cursed thing, and it turns away when His people obey. I hold that the fierceness of His anger is the other side of His mercy, and both are real.
RelatedEvents: Saul Consults the Medium at Endor
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2771); Charrhan (i.e. Charan), a place in Mesopotamia:--Charran.
BiblicalUsage: Charran is the Greek spelling of Haran, the place in Mesopotamia where Abraham dwelt before God brought him into the land of promise. Stephen tells the council that the God of glory appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia before he dwelt in Charran, and that from Charran, when his father was dead, God removed him into the land where they now dwelt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Stephen names Charran because it is the halfway place again: Abraham stopped there, and God moved him on. The Greek spelling is only the doorway; the story is the same one Genesis tells.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charsha, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Harsha is named twice, among the children of the Nethinim who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. His children are counted in both return lists, Ezra's and Nehemiah's.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe exile did not erase the servants: Harsha's children are counted among those who came back to rebuild.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G5482; a sheet ("chart") of writing-material (as to be scribbled over):--paper.
BiblicalUsage: Chartes is a sheet of writing material, paper, and it appears once, in John's refusal of it: having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink, but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe John preferred a face to a page, and the verse is a small defence of being together over merely writing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a horoscopist (as drawing magical lines or circles)}
BiblicalUsage: Chartom is the magician, the horoscopist who draws magical lines and circles, and Daniel's whole book is their undoing. The Chaldeans say no king has asked such things at any magician or astrologer or Chaldean, Daniel says the secret cannot be shown by the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, or the soothsayers, and the magicians come in and cannot make the dream known. Nebuchadnezzar himself calls Belteshazzar the master of the magicians.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the magicians are in the book to fail: they are summoned four times and they fail four times, and Daniel succeeds because the God in heaven reveals secrets. I hold that every human art that claims to read the future is a poor copy of prophecy, and Babylon proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a horoscopist (as drawing magical lines or circles)}
BiblicalUsage: Chartom is the magician, the horoscopist who draws magical lines and circles, and Daniel's whole book is their undoing. The Chaldeans say no king has asked such things at any magician or astrologer or Chaldean, Daniel says the secret cannot be shown by the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, or the soothsayers, and the magicians come in and cannot make the dream known. Nebuchadnezzar himself calls Belteshazzar the master of the magicians.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the magicians are in the book to fail: they are summoned four times and they fail four times, and Daniel succeeds because the God in heaven reveals secrets. I hold that every human art that claims to read the future is a poor copy of prophecy, and Babylon proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sour grape (as sharp in taste)
BiblicalUsage: Chartsan is a sour grape, the husk, and it appears once, in the law of the Nazarite: all the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows how thorough consecration is: not even the husk of a grape is allowed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fetter; figuratively, a pain
BiblicalUsage: Chartsubbah is a fetter, a band, and it appears twice, once as a chain to be broken and once as a chain the wicked do not feel. Isaiah's chosen fast is to loose the bands of wickedness and undo the heavy burdens, and the psalm says of the prosperous wicked that there are no bands in their death, but their strength is firm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses are one warning: the bands God wants loosed are the ones the wicked never feel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, pointed, i.e. a bramble or other thorny weed
BiblicalUsage: Charuwl is the bramble, the thorny weed, the nettle, and it grows where men are broken or judged. The outcasts bray among the bushes and gather under the nettles, the sluggard's field is grown over with thorns and nettles have covered it, and Moab shall become the breeding of nettles and saltpits and a perpetual desolation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe nettles are the Bible's picture of neglect: a field left alone grows thorns, and a nation left to itself becomes a nettle-bed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charumaph, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Harumaph is named once, as the father of Jedaiah, who repaired the wall of Jerusalem over against his own house. Jedaiah worked the stretch in front of his own door, and his father's name is kept on the record of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the detail is the devotion: Jedaiah repaired the stretch of wall in front of his own front door.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Charuphite or inhabitant of Charuph (or Chariph)
BiblicalUsage: A Haruphite is an inhabitant of Haruph, and the word appears once, among the mighty men who came to David at Ziklag: Shephatiah the Haruphite.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the roll call at Ziklag names towns for a reason: Shephatiah's home is part of his standing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Charuts, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Haruz is named once, as the father of Meshullemeth, the mother of Amon king of Judah, a man of Jotbah. His daughter married into the royal house, and his name is kept in the record of Amon's reign.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a grandfather's name in a king's record is no accident: Haruz is there because God counts the family behind the throne.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, incised or (active) incisive; hence (as noun masculine or feminine) a trench (as dug), gold (as mined), a threshing-sledge (having sharp teeth); (figuratively) determination; also eager
BiblicalUsage: Charuwts is sharp, incisive, a threshing instrument, a trench, a decision, and it cuts in every use. Damascus threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron, the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument but beaten out with a staff, the multitudes stand in the valley of decision, and Daniel hears that the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is sharp on purpose: threshing separates grain from chaff, and decision separates the peoples in the valley. Isaiah's farmer knows which tool fits which seed, and God knows which judgment fits which nation. I hold that God's sharpness is never careless, and the threshing floor is where the harvest is proved.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; Prophecy; Day of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, pierced, i.e. a bead of pearl, gems or jewels (as strung)
BiblicalUsage: Charuwz is a bead, a pearl, a jewel strung on a thread, and it appears once: thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels, thy neck with chains of gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a lover's praise in a craftsman's words: beauty described bead by bead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to restrain or (reflex.) refrain; by implication, to refuse, spare, preserve; to observe
BiblicalUsage: Chasak is restraining, holding back, sparing, and it is God's hand on the edge of sin and of judgment. God tells Abimelech He withheld him from sinning against Him, and He tells Abraham he has not withheld his son, his only son, from God. David blesses the LORD who kept His servant from evil, and Ezra says God has punished us less than our iniquities deserve.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe withholding is one of God's kindest works: He held Abimelech back from a sin he did not know he was committing, and He held Abraham's knife back from Isaac. I hold that the times God restrains me are the times I most need Him, and Ezra's prayer shows the other side: He punishes less than we deserve, and that is mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to strip off, i.e. generally to make naked (for exertion or in disgrace), to drain away or bail up (a liquid)
BiblicalUsage: Chasaph is stripping off, making bare, and it is used for God's arm and for a city's shame alike. The LORD hath made bare His holy arm in the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see His salvation. To rebellious Jerusalem God says He will discover her skirts upon her face, that her shame may appear. Ezekiel sets his face toward the siege with his arm uncovered, and Babylon is told to make bare the leg and uncover the thigh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe baring is the Bible's picture of exposure: God's bare arm saves, and a city's bared shame condemns. The same verb does both, and the difference is whose arm is bared and why. I hold that God uncovers what must be seen, whether it is His salvation or our sin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to regard
BiblicalUsage: Chashab in Aramaic is to regard, to reckon, and it appears once, in Nebuchadnezzar's confession: all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing, and He doeth according to His will in the army of heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a humbled king saying men are reputed as nothing is the whole book of Daniel in one verse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to plait or interpenetrate, i.e. (literally) to weave or (generally) to fabricate; figuratively, to plot or contrive (usually in a malicious sense); hence (from the mental effort) to think, regard, value, compute
BiblicalUsage: Chashab is weaving thoughts together, devising, reckoning, accounting, and it is the commonest verb for thinking in the Bible. Joseph tells his brothers they thought evil against him, but God meant it unto good. Eli thought Hannah had been drunken because she prayed in her heart. In Solomon's days silver was nothing accounted of, and the Tyrian craftsman sent for the temple was skilful to grave any manner of graving.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows that thoughts are weavings: Joseph's brothers wove evil and God wove good from the same thread, Eli wove a wrong conclusion from a silent prayer, and a king's craftsman wove gold into a temple. I hold that God is the master weaver, and my own thoughts are only threads until He sets them in His pattern.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Hannah; Eli; King Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chashnah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hashabnah is named once, among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day. Nehemiah lists him among the sealers, between Rehum and Maaseiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name on a sealed covenant is a promise kept on paper: he signed, and the record kept his signature.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chashabnejah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hashabniah is a name carried by two men in Nehemiah's day. One is the father of Hattush, who repaired the wall beside Jedaiah, and the other is a Levite who stood on the stairs and called the people to bless the LORD their God for ever and ever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Hashabniahs show the two works of the return: one man's son rebuilt the wall, and the other called the people to bless the God who brought them home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chashabjah, the name of nine Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hashabiah is a name carried by nine Israelites, and three of them show the Levites' three works. One is a son of Jeduthun who prophesied with a harp to give thanks, one is the son of Kemuel who ruled the Levites under David, and one is a chief of the Levites who gave passover offerings under Josiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three Hashabiahs are the Levites in miniature: a musician, a ruler, and a giver, all serving the same house. I hold that God gives different Levites different work, and the house needs all three.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be necessary (from the idea of convenience) or (transitively) to need
BiblicalUsage: Chashach is needing, being necessary, and it appears twice, once as a refusal and once as a supply. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego tell the king they are not careful to answer him, they do not need to defend themselves. And the king's decree orders that what the priests need for the burnt offerings be given them day by day without fail.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses are one picture: men who need no defence before a king, and priests whose needs are met without fail.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hush or keep quiet
BiblicalUsage: Chashah is keeping quiet, holding one's peace, and it is a silence that can be wisdom or cowardice. The king of Israel asks why they sit still and take not Ramoth from the king of Syria, the sons of the prophets tell Elisha to hold his peace because his master will be taken, the Preacher says there is a time to keep silence and a time to speak, and God says He has long time holden His peace and been still.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe silence in Scripture is never empty: a king's stillness loses a city, a prophet's stillness guards a grief, and God's stillness is patience before He cries like a travailing woman. I hold that knowing when to keep silence is a gift, and the Preacher is right that it has its time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be dark (as withholding light); transitively, to darken
BiblicalUsage: Chashak is being dark, darkening, and it is the plague and the prophecy alike. The locusts covered the face of the whole earth so that the land was darkened, God makes the day dark with night and turns the shadow of death into morning, He will cause the sun to go down at noon and darken the earth in the clear day, and the Preacher says the sun and the light shall be darkened before the evil days come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe darkness in these verses is always God's doing, whether plague or prophecy: He darkens the land of Egypt and He darkens the noon of Israel's judgment. I hold that the God who makes the day dark is the same God who turns the shadow of death into morning, and the Preacher's warning is to remember Him before the light fails.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to weaken, i.e. crush
BiblicalUsage: Chashal is weakening, crushing, and it appears once, in the image of the fourth kingdom: as iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things, so shall it break in pieces and bruise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a warning in iron: the kingdom that crushes everything will itself be broken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to make (intrans. be) unsteady, i.e. weak
BiblicalUsage: Chashal is being unsteady, weak, feeble, and it appears once: Amalek smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is why God remembers Amalek: they struck the weak at the back of the line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cling, i.e. join, (figuratively) to love, delight in; elliptically; to deliver
BiblicalUsage: Chashaq is clinging, joining, loving, delighting in, and it holds both God's love and a builder's hooks. The LORD did not set His love upon Israel because they were many, for they were the fewest of all people, and He had a delight in their fathers to love them. The same word names the hooks of the pillars in the tabernacle court, and all that Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem and Lebanon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word joins what it touches: God clings to a people He chose when they were fewest, and silver hooks join the pillars of His court. Solomon's desires and God's delight are the same verb, and the difference is the object. I hold that love in the Bible is a clinging, not a feeling, and God clings to His people first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dry grass
BiblicalUsage: Chashash is dry grass, stubble, and it appears twice, both times burning. As the fire devoureth the stubble and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be rottenness. And the wicked conceive chaff and bring forth stubble, and their breath as fire shall devour them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe stubble is the Bible's picture of a life with no root: it burns fast, because there is nothing in it to last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chasbaddanah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hashbadana is named once, standing beside Ezra the scribe on the pulpit of wood when the law was read to the people. He stood on Ezra's left hand with the others who upheld the reading of the law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe standing beside Ezra on the day the law was read is honour enough: his name is on the platform where the book was opened.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: necessity
BiblicalUsage: Chashchuwth is necessity, what is needful, and it appears once: whatsoever more shall be needful for the house of thy God, bestow it out of the king's treasure house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a king's open purse for God's house: whatever is needful, take it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: darkness; figuratively, misery
BiblicalUsage: Chashekah is darkness, and figuratively misery, and it falls on Abram and on the wicked alike. A horror of great darkness fell upon Abram as the sun went down, and God made His covenant with him in it. Isaiah says the rebellious shall look to the earth and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish, and be driven to darkness. The psalm says the wicked walk on in darkness, and yet the darkness hideth not from God, for the night shineth as the day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe darkness in these verses is both a place God meets men and a place men hide from Him: Abram's horror came with a covenant, and the wicked's darkness comes with no hiding at all. I hold that the same darkness that terrifies one man comforts another, because God is in it either way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably bronze or polished spectrum metal
BiblicalUsage: Chashmal is amber, polished bronze, and it appears three times, always in the vision of God's glory. Out of the midst of the fire came the colour of amber, and from the appearance of His loins upward and downward was as the appearance of fire with brightness, as the colour of amber.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is kept for glory alone: it never describes anything but the brightness around the throne.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wealthy
BiblicalUsage: Chashman is wealthy, a prince, and it appears once: princes shall come out of Egypt, and Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a promise that reaches past Israel: the princes of Egypt will come, and Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chasmonah, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Hashmonah shows up only as a stop on the wilderness march, named twice as Israel pitches there and then moves on to Moseroth. The name means fatness, but the text gives no story about the place, only its place in the long list of camps.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts the unremarkable stops too. Hashmonah has no event attached to it, yet it is written down, and that tells me no stage of the journey is forgotten by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dark (figuratively, i.e. obscure)
BiblicalUsage: This word means dark in the sense of obscure or low, and its one appearance sets the diligent man against mean men, the low and unnoticed. Diligence lifts a man to stand before kings, while obscurity is where the careless stay.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God sees the diligent even when men call them obscure, and He is the one who brings them before kings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the dark
BiblicalUsage: The Aramaic word for darkness appears when Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar that God reveals deep and secret things and knows what is in the darkness. Darkness hides nothing from Him, and the light dwells with Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no secret of mine is hidden from God, and that is comfort rather than threat, because the God who sees the darkness also brings light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a combination or gathering, i.e. of watery clouds
BiblicalUsage: This is a gathering or mass of watery clouds, and David uses it in his song of deliverance when God comes down wrapped in darkness, dark waters and thick clouds of the skies. The word paints the storm God rides in to rescue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is not kept out by the storm clouds; He comes through them to deliver His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chashshub, the name of two or three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hashub names more than one man, and each is named for faithful work rather than fame. One is a Merarite Levite chief in the Jerusalem lists, another repairs the wall by the tower of the furnaces, and another stands among those who seal the covenant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God records the repairers and the sealers by name. Hashub's work was walls and covenants, and that is the kind of faithfulness God remembers.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Israel Renews the Covenant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cashubah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hashubah is listed among the sons of Zerubbabel, one name in the line of David after the exile. He is named only here, with no deed attached, and his place in the genealogy is the whole of his record.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in the line of David is never wasted ink. Hashubah belongs to the family through which God kept His promise, and that is enough to matter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chashum, the name of two or three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hashum heads a family of 223 exiles who return with Zerubbabel, and the name turns up again beside Ezra as the law is read and among those who seal the covenant. The same name covers a family head, a listener at the reading, and a sealer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the returning families in His record from the journey home to the reading of the law. Hashum's name follows the whole arc of the return.
RelatedEvents: Ezra Reads the Law; Israel Renews the Covenant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: attached, i.e. a fence-rail or rod connecting the posts or pillars
BiblicalUsage: These are the fillets, the silver rods that bind the pillars of the tabernacle court together. They are small pieces, hooks and rods of silver, yet without them the pillars do not stand as one enclosure.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God cares about the bindings as much as the pillars, and the small silver rods that hold His house together are worth naming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, drawn off, i.e. separated; hence, a small company (as divided from the rest)
BiblicalUsage: The word means a small flock, a little company drawn off from the rest, and Israel looks like two little flocks of kids pitched against the Syrians who fill the country. The picture is deliberate: tiny Israel against a host.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God delights to give the victory to the little flock, so that no one mistakes whose battle it was.
RelatedPeople: King Ahab; Ben-Hadad II, King of Syria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a form of an obsolete primary χάω (to "gape" or "yawn"); a "chasm" or vacancy (impassable interval):--gulf.
BiblicalUsage: A chasm is a gaping, impassable interval, and Jesus uses it for the great gulf fixed between the rich man in torment and Lazarus in Abraham's bosom. No one can pass from one side to the other.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus meant the gulf to be taken seriously: the choices of this life fix where we stand in the next, and no crossing is made after death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chasupha, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Hasupha heads a family of Nethinim, the temple servants who return from exile in the first caravan. The name means stripped, and the family is listed in both the Ezra and Nehemiah registers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God honours the servants by name, not only the priests and princes. Hasupha's family kept the temple running, and their return is recorded twice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an offence, or a sacrifice for it
BiblicalUsage: This word is both the offence and the offering for it, sin and sin offering in one. Abimelech calls what Abraham brought on his kingdom a great sin, Moses confronts Aaron over the great sin of the calf, and Jeroboam is charged with making Israel sin a great sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the double meaning is the gospel in miniature: the sin and the offering for the sin share one word, because God meets the offence with the sacrifice. Sin is never named without the remedy standing beside it, and that is why I trust Him with my own.
RelatedEvents: Abraham and Abimelech; The Golden Calf; Fall of Samaria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to miss; hence (figuratively and generally) to sin; by inference, to forfeit, lack, expiate, repent, (causatively) lead astray, condemn
BiblicalUsage: To sin is first of all to miss, to miss the mark and the way. Joseph calls adultery sin against God, Moses tells Israel they have sinned a great sin at the calf, David confesses to Nathan that he has sinned against the LORD, and Daniel owns the same sin for the whole people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sin is missing the mark God set, not merely breaking a rule, and that is why confession is the way back. David's plain words still show the pattern: name it before God, and He puts it away.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; King David; Daniel
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; David and Bathsheba
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to chop or carve wood
BiblicalUsage: To hew is to cut wood, and the word follows the axe from the forest to the altar. A man goes into the wood to hew, the Gibeonites are made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and Ezekiel looks ahead to a day when no wood will need cutting because the weapons themselves will burn.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the hewing of wood belongs to God, whether it is daily labour or the service of the altar. The Gibeonites' low work was still work for the LORD, and I believe no honest labour is beneath Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to stop
BiblicalUsage: The word means to hold in or restrain, and God uses it of Himself when He says He will refrain for His name's sake, that He cut not off His people. He holds back the anger they deserved.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's restraint is mercy at work, and the only reason I am not cut off is that He holds Himself back for His name's sake.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to clutch; hence, to seize as a prisoner
BiblicalUsage: To catch or seize is the word for the Benjamites lying in wait to catch wives from the daughters of Shiloh as they come out to dance. It is a snatching, sudden and planned, and the text leaves the ugliness of it standing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this verse shows how far Israel had fallen when every man did what was right in his own eyes, and seizing a wife could be planned in the open.
RelatedEvents: The Levite's Concubine and the War against Benjamin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: concretely, crushed; also afraid; abstractly, terror
BiblicalUsage: This word is fear and terror, and also the shattering that fear brings. God puts the fear and dread of man on every beast after the flood, Hannah sings that the bows of the mighty are broken, Isaiah warns that Ephraim will be broken, and Leviathan is described as made without fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fear belongs in its right place: beasts fear man, the mighty are broken, and only Leviathan fears nothing. The fear of the LORD is the one fear that steadies a man instead of shattering him.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; Calling of Samuel; The Sign to Ahaz
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lay hold of; especially to pick up fire
BiblicalUsage: To take up is the word for snatching up coals, and it carries fire in every use. Isaiah pictures a broken vessel with no sherd left to take fire from the hearth, Proverbs asks whether a man can take fire in his bosom unburned, and the same coals are heaped on an enemy's head by kindness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fire is the right picture for this word, because what we take up either burns us or blesses us. Kindness that heaps coals on an enemy's head is fire put to its proper use.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to cut off, i.e. (figuratively) to decree
BiblicalUsage: The word means to cut off or decree, and it stands at the head of Daniel's seventy weeks, determined upon his people and the holy city. The time is cut out and marked, not left open.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's decrees are measured out in advance, and the seventy weeks show He keeps His timetable even when His people cannot see it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to swathe
BiblicalUsage: To swathe is to wrap a newborn child, and Jerusalem is pictured as a baby whose navel was not cut and who was not swaddled at all on the day she was born. The picture is of a child nobody cared for.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this verse is meant to break the heart: Jerusalem was abandoned at birth, and everything God did for her afterwards was pure grace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to seal
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is to seal, and the king seals the stone over the lions' den with his own signet and the signets of his lords, so that nothing may be changed concerning Daniel. The seal is meant to lock the sentence in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the king's seal could not hold what God had decided, and the stone sealed by men became the door God opened in the morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to close up; especially to seal
BiblicalUsage: To seal is to close up with a mark of authority, and Scripture uses it for books and for decrees. Daniel is told to seal the book until the time of the end, the king's order against the Jews is sealed with his ring, and Jeremiah seals the evidence of the field he buys as a sign of hope.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a seal is a promise made visible: what God seals is kept, and what men seal against His people cannot stand. Jeremiah sealing a deed in a doomed city is faith holding the paper while the siege goes on.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah Buys the Field at Anathoth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a relative by marriage (especially through the bride); figuratively, a circumcised child (as a species of religious espousal)
BiblicalUsage: This word is the son-in-law, the bridegroom, the husband joined by marriage. Lot warns his sons-in-law to flee Sodom, Zipporah calls Moses a bloody husband at the circumcision, and Isaiah and Joel both dress the bridegroom in joy for the wedding day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marriage language runs deeper than the wedding day: God uses the bridegroom to picture His own joy over His people. The husband in these verses is bound by covenant, not by convenience, and that is how I understand His love for us.
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; The Burning Bush
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
