Definition: to give (a daughter) away in marriage; hence (generally) to contract affinity by marriage
BiblicalUsage: To make a marriage alliance is the word for becoming a son-in-law, and it shapes kings and nations alike. Jethro brings Zipporah back to Moses his son-in-law, Saul offers his daughter to David, Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh, and the law forbids marriages that would turn Israel after other gods.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that marriage alliances are never only personal: they bind houses and they bind hearts to gods. The law draws the line where it does because whom we marry shapes whom we worship.
RelatedEvents: Jethro's Advice; David and Jonathan's Covenant Friendship; Solomon's Dream at Gibeon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to clutch
BiblicalUsage: To seize or snatch away is Job's word for God taking away, when no one can hinder Him or ask what He is doing. It is the language of a power that answers to no one.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job is right that God cannot be stopped or questioned, and my comfort is that the hand which seizes is the hand of a Father.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to force a passage, as by burglary; figuratively, with oars
BiblicalUsage: To dig or row is to force a passage, and the word is used for digging through a wall and for rowing against the sea. Ezekiel digs through the temple wall to see the hidden idols, digs again to carry out his baggage in the sight of the people, the sailors row hard to bring the ship to land, and Amos warns that no digging into hell escapes God's hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is no passage God cannot follow: through walls, through the sea, or down into hell itself. The diggers and rowers in these verses are all trying to get somewhere, and God is already there.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel Carries Out His Baggage; Jonah and Nineveh
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dismay
BiblicalUsage: This word is dismay, sheer terror, and Job throws it at his friends when they see his casting down and are afraid. They came to comfort and ended up dismayed by what they saw.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job names something true about suffering: it dismays even the friends, and only God is not frightened by it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chathath, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hathath is the son of Othniel and grandson of Kenaz, named in the genealogy of Judah. His name means fearful, the same spelling as the word for dismay, but here it belongs to a man, not a feeling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God puts even a fearful name in the record of His people without shame. Hathath stands among the sons of Othniel, and his name is kept with theirs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to prostrate; hence, to break down, either (literally) by violence, or (figuratively) by confusion and fear
BiblicalUsage: To be dismayed is to be broken down by fear, and the Bible answers it with the same command again and again. Joshua is told not to be dismayed, David tells Solomon to fear not nor be dismayed, Jeremiah is promised deliverance from captivity, and Judah is told the battle is not theirs but God's.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cure for dismay is not courage I work up but the presence God promises. Every one of these verses pairs the command not to fear with the reason: the LORD is with us, and the battle is His.
RelatedEvents: Joshua Commissioned to Lead Israel; Jehoshaphat's Victory by Prayer and Praise
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: terror
BiblicalUsage: Terror is the word for the fears that come with old age, when a man is afraid of what is high and fears are in the way. The Preacher lists it among the signs that the long home is near.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Preacher is honest about the fears of age, and the answer is to remember the Creator before those days come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a swathing cloth (figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: A swaddling-band is the cloth that wraps a newborn, and God uses it for the sea itself, making the cloud its garment and thick darkness its swaddling-band. The sea is pictured as an infant in His hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sea is no wild power loose in the world; God wrapped it at birth, and it stays within the bands He set.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wedding
BiblicalUsage: A wedding is the word for the day of espousals, and the daughters of Zion are called to behold King Solomon with the crown his mother crowned him with on the day of his wedding, the day of the gladness of his heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wedding day is meant to be glad, and Solomon's crown shows that marriage is crowned with joy, not only duty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an offence
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is simply sin, and Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar to break off his sins by righteousness and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. The counsel is plain: stop the sin and start the mercy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's counsel still stands: breaking off sin by righteousness is the way back to peace, and mercy to the poor is part of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatipha, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Hatipha heads a family of Nethinim, the temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. The name means seized, and the family is listed in both registers of the return.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God kept the temple servants on the rolls beside the priests. Hatipha's family came home to serve, and their name is written down twice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatita, a temple porter
BiblicalUsage: Hatita heads a family of Levitical porters, the gatekeepers who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. The name means exploring, and the family stands guard at the doors in both lists.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gatekeepers matter to God as much as the singers and the priests. Hatita's family kept the doors, and the house was safe because of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut or carve (wood, stone or other material); by implication, to hew, split, square, quarry, engrave
BiblicalUsage: To hew is to cut stone or wood with force, and the word cuts both ways in Scripture. God tells His people to look to the rock from which they were hewn, yet they hewed out broken cisterns that hold no water, Wisdom hews out seven pillars for her house, and God hews the people by the prophets.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same cutting can build or expose: Wisdom's hewn pillars stand, while broken cisterns show what men make when they cut away from God. I want to be hewn from the rock, not by my own hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut or split in two; to halve
BiblicalUsage: To divide is to cut in two, and the word marks the turning points of the story. Jacob divides his household into two bands before meeting Esau, Elijah's mantle divides the Jordan, Gideon divides three hundred men into three companies, and Moses commands the prey of Midian to be divided in two.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God works through divisions that men make in fear and faith alike. Jacob divided out of fear, Elijah out of power, and God honoured both, because He is the one who parts the waters.
RelatedEvents: Jacob Meets Esau Again; Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire; Gideon's Victory over Midian; War against Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to shear or cut close; figuratively, to be severe
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means urgent or harsh, and it describes a king's decree in both places: Daniel asks why the decree is so hasty, and the furnace is heated because the king's commandment was urgent. Haste and heat go together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a hasty king's decree cannot outrun God's timing, and the urgent furnace only showed that God was already standing in it.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-Addar, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-addar, the enclosure of glory, is named once as a point on the southern border of Canaan, where the boundary turns from Akrabbim toward Kadesh-barnea and on to Azmon. It marks the edge of the land God was giving Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the border towns matter to God, because the promise was drawn on a real map with real names. Hazar-addar sits on the line He set.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-Susah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-susah, the horse village, is listed among the cities allotted to Simeon in the far south of Judah. It is named once, in the allotment list, with no story of its own.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the allotment lists are promises kept in writing. Hazar-susah was given a name and a tribe, and that is the record of God's provision.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-Susim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-susim, the village of horses, is named among the Simeonite cities held until the reign of David. The list places it beside Beth-marcaboth and Beth-birei, towns of the same southern country.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the towns of the small tribes too. Hazar-susim belonged to Simeon, and Simeon's cities are named in full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-Enan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-enan, the village of fountains, stands on the north-east border of Canaan, named in the border law of Numbers and again in Ezekiel's vision of the land divided among the tribes. The same name marks the boundary in the law and in the promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the border God drew in the wilderness is the border He keeps in the vision. Hazar-enan is still there when Ezekiel looks ahead, and God's boundaries do not move.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-Enon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-enon, the village of springs, is named in Ezekiel's vision as a point on the northern border, the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath. It is the same border town as Hazar-enan under a slightly different spelling.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God names the springs on the border of the promised land, and the vision of the new boundaries is as exact as the old ones.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-Gaddah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-gaddah, the village of good fortune, is listed among the towns of southern Judah, beside Heshmon and Beth-palet. It is named once, in the allotment, with nothing more said of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the quiet towns of Judah are part of the inheritance too. Hazar-gaddah has no story, but it has a place in the land God gave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-hat-Tikon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-hatticon, the middle court, is named in Ezekiel's vision on the northern border, between Damascus and Hamath, by the coast of Hauran. It is a border marker in the land as God draws it for the future.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's future map is drawn with the same care as the old one. Hazar-hatticon sits in the middle of the border, and the middle is His too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsar-Shual, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazar-shual, the jackal village, is a town of southern Judah that turns up in Joshua's allotment, in Simeon's list, and again among the towns settled after the return from exile. The same name serves two tribes and two eras.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a town that outlasts the exile is a small proof of God's keeping. Hazar-shual was settled before the captivity and settled again after it.
RelatedTopics: Ancient Israel; History; Exile and Return
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to trumpet, i.e. blow on that instrument
BiblicalUsage: To sound the trumpet is the work of the priests, and the word follows the ark and the temple through Israel's worship. Priests blow the trumpets before the ark as it comes to Jerusalem, a hundred and twenty priests sound at the dedication of Solomon's temple, and the trumpeters sound again when Hezekiah restores worship.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the trumpet is the sound of God's presence arriving among His people. It is blown at the ark, at the temple, and at the restoration, and each time it says the same thing: God is here, and worship has begun.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem; Building of Solomon's Temple; Hezekiah Restores Worship and Keeps Passover
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsarmaveth, a place in Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Hazarmaveth, the village of death, is the third son of Joktan in the table of nations, named in Genesis and again in the Chronicles genealogy. He founded a people of southern Arabia that became a province and a trading centre.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God tracks the nations from the beginning, even a son of Joktan whose name means death. Hazarmaveth is in the record because every nation comes from Noah's sons.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something cutting; hence, gravel (as grit); an arrow
BiblicalUsage: Gravel is grit under the teeth, and both verses use it for what is hard to bear. Jeremiah says his teeth are broken with gravel stones, and Proverbs says the bread of deceit is sweet at first but leaves the mouth filled with gravel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God lets us taste the gravel so we learn the difference between sweet lies and true bread.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to chop into, pierce or sever; hence, to curtail, to distribute (into ranks); to shoot an arrow
BiblicalUsage: This word cuts and divides: it shoots arrows, it shares out into ranks, and it cuts a life short. The song of Deborah hears the noise of archers at the watering places, the locusts march out in bands with no king, and Job asks what pleasure a man has in his house when his months are cut off.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God sets the bands and the boundaries: the locusts march in order without a king, and a man's months are numbered by a hand greater than his own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a yard (as inclosed by a fence); also a hamlet (as similarly surrounded with walls)
BiblicalUsage: A court is an enclosed yard, and the word stretches from the tabernacle to the king's house. The court of the tabernacle is hung with fine linen, Solomon builds the inner court of the temple with hewn stone and cedar, the people make booths in the courts of the house of God, and Esther stands in the inner court of the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the court is where the people meet God and where the queen risks her life to meet the king. Both courts are enclosed, and both are entered only on the terms of the one who owns them.
RelatedPeople: Moses; King Solomon; Queen Esther; Nehemiah
RelatedEvents: The Tabernacle Is Built; Building of Solomon's Temple; Ezra Reads the Law; Esther Saves Her People
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatserim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazerim is named once, as the villages where the Avims dwelt as far as Azzah, until the Caphtorims destroyed them and dwelt in their place. It is a place remembered only by who lived there and who took it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God records the peoples who came and went before Israel, because the land's story did not start with us. Hazerim belongs to the Avims and the Caphtorims before it belongs to anyone else.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat of Sihon and Og
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatseroth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazeroth is a camp on the wilderness march, named as the place Israel abides after the craving at Kibroth-hattaavah, the place they leave when Miriam and Aaron oppose Moses, and a stop on the long list of the journey. It is a camp of complaint and of opposition.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God does not hide the ugly camps. Hazeroth is where the people craved and where Miriam spoke against Moses, and the march went on anyway.
RelatedEvents: The Quail and the Craving at Kibroth-hattaavah; Miriam and Aaron Oppose Moses
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsetson-tamar, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazezon-tamar, the place of palm trees, is named twice and both times war comes to it. The kings smite the Amorites there in Abram's day, and a great multitude gathers there against Jehoshaphat, the same place called En-gedi.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a place of palms can be a place of battle, and God defends His people in both. Hazezon-tamar saw Abram rescue Lot and Jehoshaphat pray, and the victories belong to the same God.
RelatedEvents: Abram Rescues Lot; Jehoshaphat's Victory by Prayer and Praise
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chatsi-ham-Menachtite or descendant of Chatsi-ham-Menuchoth
BiblicalUsage: This is the half of the Manahethites, a clan division listed among the sons of Salma with Bethlehem and the Netophathites. The name marks a family split in two, half reckoned here and half elsewhere.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts half-clans as carefully as whole tribes, and no family is too small to be named in the line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsi-ham-Menuchoth, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Half of the Manahethites is listed among the sons of Shobal, father of Kirjath-jearim, beside Haroeh. It is a clan name, a people reckoned by halves, with its resting place in the genealogy of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the half of a clan is still a people to God. The Manahethites are named in their halves, and neither half is lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: grass; also a leek (collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Grass is the Bible's picture of how quickly flesh fades. Ahab sends Obadiah to find grass to save the horses in the drought, the enemies of Judah are like grass of the field and grass on the housetops, and Isaiah cries that all flesh is grass while the word of our God stands for ever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the grass teaches me my place: I wither and fade, and only God's word stands. That is not a hard word to me, because the standing word is the one that saves.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: grass; also a leek (collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Grass is the Bible's picture of how quickly flesh fades. Ahab sends Obadiah to find grass to save the horses in the drought, the enemies of Judah are like grass of the field and grass on the housetops, and Isaiah cries that all flesh is grass while the word of our God stands for ever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the grass teaches me my place: I wither and fade, and only God's word stands. That is not a hard word to me, because the standing word is the one that saves.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a trumpet (from its sundered or quavering note)
BiblicalUsage: The trumpet is the instrument of worship and of war, and it sounds at every great moment. All Israel brings up the ark with trumpets and shouting, the priests sound at the dedication of the temple, Phinehas carries the trumpets into the war against Midian, and the priests sound again when the foundation of the second temple is laid.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the trumpet belongs to God in worship and in battle alike. It calls the people to praise and it calls them to war, and in both cases it is God's sound, not man's.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem; Building of Solomon's Temple; War against Midian; Rebuilding of the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: new Chatsor, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hazor, the new Hazor, is listed among the towns of southern Judah, beside Hadattah and Kerioth. It shares its name with the great northern Hazor but is a different town, named once in the allotment.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that two towns can share a name and still be two towns to God. This Hazor is Judah's, and it is counted in Judah's inheritance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chatsor, the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine and of one in Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Hazor is the great northern city, head of all the kingdoms of Canaan, whose king Jabin gathers the northern kings against Joshua. Joshua takes it and burns it, and centuries later Solomon rebuilds it as one of his fortified cities.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hazor shows both sides of God's dealing with a city: taken and burned under Joshua, then rebuilt under Solomon. The same stones serve judgement and then serve the kingdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the middle (of the night)
BiblicalUsage: Midnight is the middle of the night, and it is the hour God chooses for His great acts. He goes out into Egypt about midnight to strike the firstborn, the mighty are taken away at midnight without hand, and the psalmist rises at midnight to give thanks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe midnight belongs to God as much as midday. He judges at midnight and He is praised at midnight, and the dark hour is His hour too.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Plagues; The Death of the Firstborn
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an offence (sometimes habitual sinfulness), and its penalty, occasion, sacrifice, or expiation; also (concretely) an offender
BiblicalUsage: This word is sin in its full weight: the offence, its guilt, its penalty, and the offering that answers it. Sin lies at Cain's door like a crouching beast, Moses pleads to make atonement for Israel's great sin, Solomon prays for forgiveness when the people turn back, and Isaiah's sin is purged by the coal from the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sin is not a small mistake but a weight that needs an altar. The coal that touches Isaiah's lips is the answer to every verse here: God provides the purging He demands.
RelatedEvents: Cain Murders Abel; The Golden Calf; Building of Solomon's Temple; Isaiah's Vision and Call
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an offence (sometimes habitual sinfulness), and its penalty, occasion, sacrifice, or expiation; also (concretely) an offender
BiblicalUsage: This word is sin in its full weight: the offence, its guilt, its penalty, and the offering that answers it. Sin lies at Cain's door like a crouching beast, Moses pleads to make atonement for Israel's great sin, Solomon prays for forgiveness when the people turn back, and Isaiah's sin is purged by the coal from the altar.

Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a criminal, or one accounted guilty
BiblicalUsage: A sinner is one accounted guilty, reckoned as an offender before God. The men of Sodom are sinners before the LORD exceedingly, Saul is sent to destroy the sinners the Amalekites, Isaiah warns that sinners will be destroyed together, and the censers of Korah's sinners are hammered into a covering for the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Bible never softens the word sinner, and that is why grace is so startling. The censers of guilty men become the altar's covering, and judgement itself is turned into a sign.
RelatedEvents: Abram and Lot Part Ways; Anointing of Saul as King; Korah's Rebellion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an expiation
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is the sin offering, and at the dedication of the house of God the returned exiles offer twelve he goats for a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe. The offering covers the whole people at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the twelve goats show that the whole of Israel needed covering, and God provided one offering for every tribe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chattil, one of 'Solomon's servants'
BiblicalUsage: Hattil heads a family of Solomon's servants who return from exile with Zerubbabel, listed among the children of Shephatiah and Pochereth. The family is named in both registers of the return.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the servants of Solomon's house were not forgotten in the exile. Hattil's family came home, and their name is written in both lists.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chattush, the name of four or five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hattush names more than one man, and each is named for his place in the work. One is a son of Shechaniah in the line of David, another comes up with Ezra from Babylon, and another repairs the wall of Jerusalem by his own house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the same name straight across the generations. Hattush in the genealogy, Hattush on the journey, and Hattush on the wall are all part of one story of return.
RelatedEvents: Ezra's Journey to Jerusalem; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a carving; hence, a tapestry (as figured)
BiblicalUsage: This is carved work, the tapestry with which the strange woman decks her bed, coverings of tapestry with fine linen of Egypt. The word is the decoration of a bed made for sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the warning here is plain: sin dresses its bed beautifully, and the carving is the trap.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to show
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is to show or declare, and the whole second chapter of Daniel turns on it. The Chaldeans ask the king to tell them the dream so they can show the interpretation, they confess no man can show the king's matter, and Daniel asks for time so that he can show the interpretation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the chapter proves that only God can show what men cannot. The wise men of Babylon could not declare the dream, and Daniel could, because the God of heaven reveals secrets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dell or crevice (as if pierced in the earth)
BiblicalUsage: This word is to hide or lurk, and it describes Israel in a strait, hiding in caves and thickets and rocks and high places and pits when the Philistines press them. The whole people goes to ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hiding places of Israel show what fear does to a people, and Saul's unlawful sacrifice grew out of that same fear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to live; by implication (intensively) to declare or show
BiblicalUsage: To declare or show is the word for speaking out what one has seen. Eliphaz promises to show Job what he has seen, Elihu is afraid at first to show his opinion and then insists on showing it, and the psalm says day unto day utters speech and night unto night shows knowledge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gives us things to declare, and silence is not always humility. Elihu waited out of respect, but the heavens never wait: they declare God's glory every day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to blanch (as with shame)
BiblicalUsage: To grow pale is to blanch with shame, and God promises that Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale. The shame that whitened his face will be taken away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God removes the shame that makes His people pale, and the house of Jacob will not blush before its enemies again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chavilah, the name of two or three eastern regions; also perhaps of two men
BiblicalUsage: Havilah is a land, and it is also two men. The land of Havilah is where gold lies, compassed by the river Pison; Havilah the son of Cush and Havilah the son of Joktan are both named in the table of nations; and Saul smites the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one name can hold a land and two men without confusion, because God keeps the record straight. Havilah's gold, Havilah's sons, and Havilah's border are all His.
RelatedPeople: Havilah, Son of Cush; Havilah, Son of Joktan
RelatedEvents: Creation; Anointing of Saul as King
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chavran, a region East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Hauran is named in Ezekiel's vision as a borderland of the restored land, lying between Damascus and Hamath on the north and measured again on the east side. It marks the edge of the country God draws for His people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God draws the borders of the restored land with the same care as the first. Hauran is on the map He gives Ezekiel, and the promise is drawn in full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: by implication, an encampment or village
BiblicalUsage: A havvah is an encampment or village, a small town taken and named. Jair the son of Manasseh takes the small towns and calls them Havoth-jair, the towns of Jair are counted in Joshua's allotment of Bashan, and Solomon's officer holds the towns of Jair in Gilead.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gives His people towns to name, and the naming is part of the taking. Jair called the villages after his own name, and the land remembered it.
RelatedEvents: Reuben and Gad Settle East of the Jordan
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chavvah (or Eve), the first woman
BiblicalUsage: Eve is the first woman, named by Adam after the fall because she is the mother of all living. She conceives and bears Cain and says she has gotten a man from the LORD, and her name carries the whole story of life after the fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Eve's name is hope spoken in the middle of judgement: mother of all living, named when death had just entered the world. Life goes on because God said it would.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hamlets of Jair, a region of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Havoth-jair, the villages of Jair, are the towns Jair the son of Manasseh took and named after himself. They are counted in the settlement east of Jordan, in the record of the conquest, and again in the days of Jair the judge, whose thirty sons rode on thirty colts and held thirty cities.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the villages of Jair outlasted Jair himself, and the name stayed on the land. What God gives His people to name, He lets them keep.
RelatedEvents: Reuben and Gad Settle East of the Jordan; The Defeat of Sihon and Og; Jair, Judge of Israel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alive; also (as noun in plural) life
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is the living, those who live, and Daniel uses it for the living God against the dead idols of Babylon. The secret is revealed to Daniel for the sake of the living, the living are to know that the Most High rules, Nebuchadnezzar blesses Him that lives for ever, and Darius cries to Daniel as the servant of the living God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the living God is the point of every one of these verses. The gods of Babylon cannot speak or save, but the living God reveals, rules, and delivers, and that is why Daniel's God is still the God I pray to.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; King Nebuchadnezzar; Darius the Mede
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling; Daniel in the Lions' Den
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alive; also (as noun in plural) life
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is the living, those who live, and Daniel uses it for the living God against the dead idols of Babylon. The secret is revealed to Daniel for the sake of the living, the living are to know that the Most High rules, Nebuchadnezzar blesses Him that lives for ever, and Darius cries to Daniel as the servant of the living God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the living God is the point of every one of these verses. The gods of Babylon cannot speak or save, but the living God reveals, rules, and delivers, and that is why Daniel's God is still the God I pray to.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; King Nebuchadnezzar; Darius the Mede
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling; Daniel in the Lions' Den
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to live
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is to live, and in Daniel it is the court greeting, O king, live for ever. The Chaldeans say it to Nebuchadnezzar, the accusers say it before the furnace, the queen says it to Belshazzar, and Daniel says it to Darius from the lions' den.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the greeting is truer than the courtiers knew: kings are wished life for ever, but only God lives for ever. Daniel says the words to a king in a den and walks out alive, because the living God keeps His servants.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall; Daniel in the Lions' Den
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to live, whether literally or figuratively; causatively, to revive
BiblicalUsage: To live, to revive, to come alive again is the word for God's power over death. The widow's child revives at Elijah's prayer, a dead man revives when he touches Elisha's bones, the dry bones live and stand as an exceeding great army, and Jacob lives seventeen years in Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the God who revives the dead child and the dry bones is the same God who gives me life. Revival is not a metaphor here: breath returns, bones stand, and the dead get up.
RelatedPeople: Elijah; Elisha; Ezekiel; Joseph, Son of Jacob
RelatedEvents: Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath; A Dead Man Revived by Elisha's Bones; The Valley of Dry Bones; Joseph and His Brothers
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to live; causatively to revive
BiblicalUsage: To live is the word at the edges of life and death. Pharaoh orders the sons killed and the daughters left to live, God promises that the bitten Israelite who looks on the serpent shall live, Adam is kept from the tree of life lest he live for ever, and the manslayer flees to a city that he might live.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe life is God's to give and to guard: He spares the daughters, He heals the bitten, He bars the tree, and He shelters the slayer. Every one of these verses turns on who decides who lives.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian; The Bronze Serpent; The Fall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vigorous
BiblicalUsage: This word means lively or vigorous, and the midwives use it of the Hebrew women, who are lively and delivered before the midwives come. The liveliness of the mothers is the excuse that saves the babies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God used the strength of the mothers to defeat Pharaoh's order, and the midwives' plain words hid His deliverance in plain sight.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an army, or strength
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is strength, might, and an army, and it gathers around the kings of Babylon. The herald cries mightily to the peoples and nations, the most mighty men of the army bind the three friends, Nebuchadnezzar learns that God does His will in the army of heaven, and Belshazzar cries aloud to bring in the wise men of his kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there are two armies in Daniel and only one of them rules. The army of Babylon binds and burns, but the army of heaven does God's will, and no one can stay His hand.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an army, or strength
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is strength, might, and an army, and it gathers around the kings of Babylon. The herald cries mightily to the peoples and nations, the most mighty men of the army bind the three friends, Nebuchadnezzar learns that God does His will in the army of heaven, and Belshazzar cries aloud to bring in the wise men of his kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there are two armies in Daniel and only one of them rules. The army of Babylon binds and burns, but the army of heaven does God's will, and no one can stay His hand.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wall
BiblicalUsage: This is a wall, and Ezekiel uses it for the false prophets' work: one builds up a wall and others daub it with untempered mortar, while they say Peace and there is no peace. The wall looks finished and holds nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a wall daubed with lies will fall when the storm comes, and God is the one who brings the storm.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: life
BiblicalUsage: This word is a lifetime, a living, and it describes the ten concubines David shuts up after Absalom's rebellion, fed but never visited, living in widowhood until the day of their death. Their whole remaining life is summed in one word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this verse is one of the saddest in David's story: women shut up for the rest of their lives because of a son's sin, and God records it without looking away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chazael, a king of Syria
BiblicalUsage: Hazael is the king of Syria whom God tells Elijah to anoint, and his life is written in violence from the start. The king of Syria sends him to Elisha to ask whether he will recover, and the next morning Hazael spreads a wet cloth over the king's face and reigns in his stead.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hazael shows that God raises up even cruel kings to do His judgements. Elijah anoints him at God's command, and Elisha weeps over what he will do to Israel.
RelatedPeople: Elijah; Elisha; Hazael, King of Syria
RelatedEvents: Elijah at Horeb: The Still Small Voice; Elisha and Hazael at Damascus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gaze upon; mentally to dream, be usual (i.e. seem)
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is to see, to behold, and it carries the visions of Daniel. The king sees a great image whose brightness is terrible, he sees a stone cut out without hands smite it, and he sees four men loose in the furnace, the fourth like the Son of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what Nebuchadnezzar saw is what God wanted him to see: an image that falls and a fourth man in the fire. Seeing is the gift here, and God gives it to a pagan king.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gaze at; mentally to perceive, contemplate (with pleasure); specifically, to have a vision of
BiblicalUsage: To see is to perceive with understanding, and the word is used for seeing men and seeing God. Jethro tells Moses to provide able men who fear God, the nobles of Israel see God and eat and drink, and Amos writes the words he saw concerning Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe seeing in the Bible is never only with the eyes: the nobles see God and live, and the prophet sees a word before he speaks it. God shows Himself to those He calls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strong (usu. in a bad sense, hard, bold, violent)
BiblicalUsage: This word is strength, the strong and mighty hand, and it is always God's hand in these verses. Pharaoh lets Israel go by a strong hand and drives them out by a strong hand, the nations hear of God's strong hand and stretched out arm, and Moses shows all that mighty hand in the sight of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the strong hand is the whole story of the Exodus in one phrase: God does not persuade Pharaoh, He overpowers him. His strength is what sets His people free.
RelatedEvents: Moses and Aaron Confront Pharaoh; Building of Solomon's Temple; The Death of Moses
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fasten upon; hence, to seize, be strong (figuratively, courageous, causatively strengthen, cure, help, repair, fortify), obstinate; to bind, restrain, conquer
BiblicalUsage: To be strong is the command given to leaders at the hard moments. Joshua is told to be strong and of a good courage because the LORD is with him, David tells Solomon to be strong and do the work of the temple, and Hezekiah tells Judah to be strong and courageous because there are more with us than with the king of Assyria.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength in the Bible is borrowed, never owned: Joshua borrows it from God's presence, Solomon from God's promise, and Hezekiah from God's numbers. I am strong only when I am not alone.
RelatedPeople: Joshua; King David; King Solomon; King Hezekiah
RelatedEvents: Joshua Commissioned to Lead Israel; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chazajah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hazaiah is named in the list of the sons of Judah who dwell in Jerusalem after the return, the son of Adaiah in the line of Shiloni. He is named once, in the register of those who resettle the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts the resettlers of Jerusalem by name, and Hazaiah's single mention is the record of a family that came home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the breast (as most seen in front)
BiblicalUsage: The breast is the wave offering, the priest's portion of the sacrifice. Moses takes the breast of the ram of Aaron's consecration and waves it before the LORD, the law gives the breast to Aaron and his sons, and the wave breast is eaten in a clean place by the priest's household.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God feeds His priests from His own altar. The breast waved before Him comes back as their due, and worship and provision are one act.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: powerful
BiblicalUsage: This word means strong or loud, and it is used for a sound that grows and for a house that grows. The trumpet sounds long and waxes louder and louder at Sinai, and David waxes stronger and stronger while the house of Saul waxes weaker.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God makes His voice louder at Sinai and His king stronger in the war, and both grow because He is behind them.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; David Becomes King
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chaziel, a Levite
BiblicalUsage: Haziel is named among the sons of Shimei, a Levite, with Shelomith and Haran, three chiefs of the fathers of Laadan. He is named once, in the ordering of the Levites under David.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Levites are ordered by name because their service is ordered by God. Haziel's place among the chiefs of Laadan is his part in the worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hog (perhaps as penned)
BiblicalUsage: The swine is unclean because it divides the hoof yet does not chew the cud, and the law forbids eating its flesh or touching its carcase. Isaiah turns the same animal into a charge against rebels who eat swine's flesh among the graves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the swine teaches that looking clean is not being clean: the divided hoof is not enough, and God judges the whole animal. The rebels who eat it have chosen the unclean on purpose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a flash of lightning
BiblicalUsage: This word is the lightning of the thunder, the flash that comes with the storm. God makes a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning, He asks Job who divided a watercourse for the overflowing waters or a way for the lightning, and Zechariah tells Israel to ask the LORD for rain and He will make bright clouds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lightning belongs to God the way the rain does: He decrees its path and no one else does. The same God who flashes the sky gives the showers to the field.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chazo, a nephew of Abraham
BiblicalUsage: Hazo is a son of Nahor by his wife Milcah, named among the eight children Milcah bore, and his brother Chesed is named beside him. He is a nephew of Abraham, and his name means vision.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hazo matters because his family is the family God chose Abraham out of. Nahor's sons are named so that we can see the kin Abraham left behind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sight (mentally), i.e. a dream, revelation, or oracle
BiblicalUsage: A vision is what God shows, and the word marks the times when He speaks. In Samuel's day there is no open vision and the word of the LORD is precious, Daniel is given understanding in all visions and dreams, and a vision appears to him in the third year of Belshazzar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a vision is God's initiative, not man's invention: it is precious when it is rare, and it is given to the faithful when it comes. Daniel receives visions because he resolved to be faithful first.
RelatedEvents: Calling of Samuel; Daniel's Resolve in Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a view
BiblicalUsage: This word is a view or appearance, and Nebuchadnezzar uses it for the great tree of his dream, whose height reaches to heaven and whose sight is to the end of all the earth. Daniel repeats the same words when he interprets it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tree's great sight is the pride of the king, and the sight that reaches to the ends of the earth is the pride God cuts down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a revelation
BiblicalUsage: This word is a revelation, a vision written down, and it is named as a source for the acts of Solomon: the rest of his deeds are written in the book of Nathan the prophet, in the prophecy of Ahijah, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps more books than the one we hold, and the visions of Iddo are a reminder that Solomon's story was seen by seers as well as written by kings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a look; hence (figuratively) striking appearance, revelation, or (by implication) compact
BiblicalUsage: A vision or a look is the word for what the prophets see, and it is grievous wherever it falls. Daniel considers the he goat that comes from the west, Isaiah is told a grievous vision of treachery and spoiling, and the covenant with death is disannulled when the overflowing scourge passes through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prophets' visions are not comforts but warnings, and the grievous vision is grievous because it is true. God shows His prophets the treachery so they can name it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rope (as twisted), especially a measuring line; by implication, a district or inheritance (as measured); or a noose (as of cords); figuratively, a company (as if tied together); also a throe (especially of parturition); also ruin
BiblicalUsage: A cord is a rope, a measuring line, and a company bound together, and the word stretches across all three. Saul meets a company of prophets coming down from the high place, David measures the Moabites with a line, and Amos warns Amaziah that his land will be divided by line.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the line measures what God has decided: it gives the prophets their company, the Moabites their judgement, and Amaziah his loss. The cord that binds can also be the cord that divides.
RelatedEvents: Anointing of Saul as King; Amos and Amaziah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheber, the name of a Kenite and of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Heber names two different men, and they must not be folded into one. Heber the Kenite pitches his tent by Kedesh, and Sisera flees to the tent of Jael his wife; Heber the son of Beriah is a son of Asher who goes down into Egypt with Jacob.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the two Hebers straight, and so must I: one is the Kenite whose tent ends Sisera's flight, and the other is a son of Asher in the house of Jacob.
RelatedPeople: Heber, the Kenite; Heber, Son of Beriah; Jael
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a society; also a spell
BiblicalUsage: This word is a society and also a spell, and the two meanings meet in the company a man keeps. The law forbids the charmer who binds with spells, Babylon trusts in the multitude of her sorceries and enchantments, and Proverbs contrasts a corner of the housetop with a wide house shared with a brawling woman.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the company we keep is a kind of spell: the charmer binds with words, and a quarrelsome house binds with strife. The law forbids the one and wisdom warns against the other, because both take hold of a man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: association
BiblicalUsage: This is a company or association, and Elihu charges Job with going in company with the workers of iniquity and walking with wicked men. The company a man walks with is the charge against him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Elihu is wrong about Job, but right about company: the people we walk with shape the road we are on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chebrite (collectively) or descendants of Cheber
BiblicalUsage: The Heberites are the family of Heber the son of Beriah, counted in the second census of Israel in the wilderness. The clan takes its name from its father, and the name is the record of the family.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts families in the wilderness as carefully as He counts tribes, and the Heberites are named because they belong.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chebron, a place in Palestine, also the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hebron is a city and also a man, and the name means association. Hebron the son of Kohath is named through Mareshah the father of Hebron, David's sons are born to him in Hebron the city, and all Israel gathers to David at Hebron to make him king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hebron is where the promise becomes a throne: David's sons are born there and Israel crowns him there, and the city of association becomes the city of the king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chebronite (collectively), an inhabitant of Chebron
BiblicalUsage: The Hebronites are the family of Hebron the son of Kohath, counted among the families of the Kohathites, and Jerijah their chief is sought out in the fortieth year of David among mighty men of valour at Jazer of Gilead. The clan serves and the clan fights.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gives the Levites both service and strength: the Hebronites keep the holy things and their chief is found among mighty men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a concealment
BiblicalUsage: This is a hiding place, and Habakkuk uses it for the hiding of God's power: His brightness is as the light, He has horns coming out of His hand, and there is the hiding of His power. The power is real even where it is hidden.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's power is most hidden where it is most present, and the brightness that blinds is the same hand that hides.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chesed, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Chesed is the name of two men, and neither must be confused with the word for steadfast love, which is spelled the same. Chesed the son of Nahor is named among the children Milcah bore, and the father of Solomon's officer Ben-hesed is named in the list of the king's commissaries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is kept straight by the record itself: Nahor's son and the officer's father are two men, and the steadfast love of God is a different word with the same letters. I will not fold them into one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strength
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is strength or might, and it belongs to kings who forget where it came from. God gives Nebuchadnezzar a kingdom, power, and strength, and glory, and the king then boasts that Babylon was built by the might of his power.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the king's strength was given and the king's boast was stolen: the might of his power was God's gift, and God took back the praise.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lack; hence, destitution
BiblicalUsage: This is want or lack, and it describes the poor who flee into the wilderness for want and famine, and the man who hastens to be rich and does not consider that poverty shall come upon him. Want follows the hasty and the hungry alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe want is the end of haste: the man who rushes to be rich does not see the poverty coming, and God sees it plainly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: deficiency
BiblicalUsage: This is deficiency, what is wanting, and the Preacher says that which is crooked cannot be made straight, and that which is wanting cannot be numbered. The lack itself cannot be counted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Preacher is right that some lacks cannot be numbered or straightened, and only God can supply what is wanting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rest, i.e. the state of the dead
BiblicalUsage: This is the world, the land of the living, and Hezekiah uses it from his sickbed when he says he will not see the LORD in the land of the living and will behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world. The world is the place of the living.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hezekiah's fear was that sickness would take him out of the land of the living, and God's answer was fifteen more years in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prickly plant
BiblicalUsage: A thorn or brier is the picture of the best of men in a corrupt age and of the slothful man's way. Micah says the best of them is as a brier and the most upright sharper than a thorn hedge, and Proverbs says the slothful man's way is as a hedge of thorns.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thorn is the right picture for both: the best of a corrupt age still pricks, and the slothful man's road is blocked by his own making.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an apartment (usually literal)
BiblicalUsage: A chamber is an inner room, and the word is used for rooms where secrets are spoken and deeds are done. Bathsheba goes into the king's chamber to plead for Solomon, Elisha tells the king of Israel the words spoken in the enemy's bedchamber, and Ish-bosheth is slain on his bed in his bedchamber.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no chamber is private from God: the plea in the chamber is heard, the words in the bedchamber are told, and the murder in the bedchamber is avenged. The inner room is His too.
RelatedEvents: Solomon's Succession and Adonijah; Elisha at Dothan; David Becomes King
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {rejoicing}
BiblicalUsage: This is joy, gladness, and it is named at the dedication of the house of God, when the children of Israel, the priests, and the Levites kept the dedication with joy. The house is finished and the joy is the offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe joy belongs at the dedication, because the house God gives back is worth celebrating.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {rejoicing}
BiblicalUsage: This is joy, gladness, and it is named at the dedication of the house of God, when the children of Israel, the priests, and the Levites kept the dedication with joy. The house is finished and the joy is the offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe joy belongs at the dedication, because the house God gives back is worth celebrating.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a form of the same as G5490; a lip (as a pouring place); figuratively, a margin (of water):--lip, shore.
BiblicalUsage: A lip is the edge of the mouth, and also the edge of the sea, the shore. Peter says to refrain the lips from guile, Hebrews calls praise the fruit of the lips giving thanks, Jesus charges a people who honour Him with their lips while their heart is far, and Abraham's seed is numbered like the sand on the sea shore.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lip is where the heart shows itself: lips can honour God while the heart is far, and lips can offer praise that pleases Him. God counts the sand on the shore, and He hears every lip.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G5494 and G4482; a storm-runlet, i.e. winter-torrent:--brook.
BiblicalUsage: A winter torrent is a brook that runs full in the rainy season, and Jesus crosses the brook Cedron with His disciples on the way to the garden. The brook is named once, at the edge of the arrest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brook Cedron is part of the road to the cross: Jesus crosses the winter water to the garden where He will be taken, and He crosses it willingly.
RelatedEvents: The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G5494; to storm, i.e. (passively) to labor under a gale:--be tossed with tempest.
BiblicalUsage: To be tossed with tempest is the word for the ship on the way to Rome, exceedingly tossed, so that the next day they lighten the ship. The storm does the tossing and the sailors can only throw cargo overboard.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tossing is the storm, not the end: the ship is lightened and Paul is kept, and God brings them all safe to land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of χέω (to pour; akin to the base of 5490 through the idea of a channel), meaning a storm (as pouring rain); by implication, the rainy season, i.e. winter:--tempest, foul weather, winter.
BiblicalUsage: Winter is the rainy season, the time of storm and cold, and it is the season Jesus warns about and Paul sails through. Pray that your flight is not in winter, John notes that the feast of dedication came in winter, the storm takes sun and stars away for many days, and Paul tells Timothy to come before winter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe winter in the Bible is the hard season God still rules: the flight, the feast, the storm, and the journey are all His. He keeps His people through the cold, and the winter does not last for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from the base of G5494 in the sense of its congener the base of G5490 (through the idea of hollowness for grasping); the hand (literally or figuratively (power); especially (by Hebraism) a means or instrument):--hand.
BiblicalUsage: The hand is the instrument of power and of touch, and it is everywhere in the New Testament. The eye cannot say to the hand that it has no need of it, Peter tells us to humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, Thomas is told to behold the hands of the risen Christ, and Jesus shows His hands and feet to the disciples.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hand of God is both mighty and pierced: it humbles us and it saves us, and the risen hands still bear the marks. My hand has its place in the body, and His hand has me.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Appears to Thomas; Jesus Appears to the Disciples on Easter Evening
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5497; to be a hand-leader, i.e. to guide (a blind person):--lead by the hand.
BiblicalUsage: To lead by the hand is the word for Saul after the light on the Damascus road: he rises from the earth blind, and they lead him by the hand into Damascus. Paul tells the same story again in Jerusalem, led by the hand of those with him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the proud persecutor had to be led like a child, and that is how God begins His work in him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5495 and a reduplicated form of G71; a hand-leader, i.e. personal conductor (of a blind person):--some to lead by the hand.
BiblicalUsage: One who leads by the hand is what Elymas becomes when the hand of the Lord blinds him on Cyprus: he goes about seeking someone to lead him by the hand. The sorcerer who would lead others astray must be led himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God turns the tables on Elymas: the man who blinded others with sorcery is blinded and must be led by the hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a compound of G5495 and G1125; something hand-written ("chirograph"), i.e. a manuscript (specially, a legal document or bond (figuratively)):--handwriting.
BiblicalUsage: A handwriting is a written bond, the record of ordinances against us, and Paul says Christ blotted it out, took it out of the way, and nailed it to His cross. The debt is cancelled by the nailing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the handwriting against me is nailed to the cross, and there is nothing left for the accuser to read.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: irregular comparative of G2556; from an obsolete equivalent χέρης (of uncertain derivation); more evil or aggravated (physically, mentally or morally):--sorer, worse.
BiblicalUsage: Worse is the word for the second state being worse than the first. Jesus warns the healed man lest a worse thing come upon him, the unclean spirit returns with seven worse than himself, Peter warns that the latter end is worse than the beginning for those who turn back, and Hebrews asks how much sorer punishment belongs to those who tread the Son of God under foot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe worse is a real direction, not only a word: turning back after knowing the truth leaves a man worse than before. The warning is meant to keep me from going back.
RelatedEvents: The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5495 and a derivative of G4160; manufactured, i.e. of human construction:--made by (make with) hands.
BiblicalUsage: Made with hands is the word for every temple men build, and the New Testament sets it against the one God made. The Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, God does not dwell in temples made with hands, Christ did not enter holy places made with hands but heaven itself, and the false witnesses charge Jesus with destroying the temple made with hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is too great for a house made with hands, and that is good news. He dwells in heaven itself and appears for us there, not in a building we can lock, and the temple He wants is a people.
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; Paul at Athens; Jesus Before the Sanhedrin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G5495 and τείνω (to stretch); to be a hand-reacher or voter (by raising the hand), i.e. (generally) to select or appoint:--choose, ordain.
BiblicalUsage: To appoint by stretching out the hand is the word for choosing elders and messengers. Paul and Barnabas ordain elders in every church with prayer and fasting, and the churches choose a brother to travel with Paul in the grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stretched-out hand is the church's way of choosing: elders are appointed by the people and commended to the Lord, and the choice is made in prayer.
RelatedEvents: The Return Journey and the Appointment of Elders
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, the palate or inside of the mouth; hence, the mouth itself (as the organ of speech, taste and kissing)
BiblicalUsage: The palate is the mouth that tastes, and the word is used for tasting words and for the tongue that will not move. The ear tries words as the mouth tastes meat, Ezekiel's tongue cleaves to the roof of his mouth so he cannot reprove, and Hosea is told to set the trumpet to his mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mouth is the place where truth is tasted and spoken: Job tastes words the way the mouth tastes meat. Ezekiel's silence is itself a judgement on a rebellious house, and Hosea's trumpet shows the mouth is also where warning is sounded.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelah, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Helah is one of the two wives of Ashur the father of Tekoa, and her sons are Zereth, Jezoar, and Ethnan. She is named only in the genealogy of Judah, as the mother of three sons.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God names the mothers in the genealogy as well as the fathers. Helah's sons are counted, and her name stands at the head of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, disease; hence, rust
BiblicalUsage: This word is disease and rust, the scum that will not leave the pot. Jerusalem is the bloody city, the pot whose scum is in it and will not come out, and the pot is set empty on the coals so the filthiness may be molten and the scum consumed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rust in the pot is the sin that will not wash out, and God sets the empty pot on the fire to burn it away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelbah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Helbah is named once, among the towns Asher fails to drive out, beside Accho and Zidon and Ahlab and Achzib and Aphik and Rehob. The town stays in Canaanite hands, and the failure is recorded.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God records the towns Israel did not take as honestly as the towns they did. Helbah stands as a witness to an unfinished conquest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: galbanam, an odorous gum (as if fatty)
BiblicalUsage: Galbanum is one of the sweet spices of the holy incense, taken with stacte and onycha and pure frankincense, each of like weight. It is a resin that burns sweet before the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God names the ingredients of His incense because worship is exact: every spice in its measure, and the smell rises as He commanded.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelbon, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Helbon is named in the lament over Tyre as the source of the wine Damascus trades, the wine of Helbon with white wool. It is a place known for its vineyards, named once in the trade list of the nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts the wine of Helbon among the riches of Tyre, and the lament over the city names what it traded before it fell.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheldai, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Heldai names two men of the return. One is the Netophathite captain of the twelfth course, of Othniel, with twenty-four thousand in his course, and the other is one of the captives come from Babylon who brings gold for the crown of Joshua.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Heldais show the same name serving in the army and in the temple: a captain under David and a giver under Zerubbabel, both counted by God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheleb, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Heleb the son of Baanah, a Netophathite, is named among David's mighty men. He is listed once, in the roll of the thirty, with no deed attached to his name.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the roll of the mighty men is a roll of the faithful, and Heleb's name among them is his honour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fat, whether literally or figuratively; hence, the richest or choice part
BiblicalUsage: Fat is the best part, the portion that belongs to God on the altar. The priest's servant demands the fat before it is burned, Samuel says obedience is better than the fat of rams, Moses sings of the fat of lambs and the fat of kidneys of wheat, and Abel brings the fat of the firstlings of his flock.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fat is the best because God asks for the best: Abel gives it, Samuel says obedience beats it, and the song remembers it. The best belongs to God first, and obedience is the best of the best.
RelatedEvents: Calling of Samuel; Anointing of Saul as King; Cain Murders Abel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheled, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite is named among David's mighty men, in the list of those who gather to David at Hebron. He is the same man as Heleb, the name spelled with a different letter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the mighty men straight even when the spelling changes. Heled and Heleb are one man, and his place among David's men is sure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: life (as a fleeting portion of time); hence, the world (as transient)
BiblicalUsage: This word is a lifetime, the span of a man's days, and also the world men live in. Zophar promises that Job's age will be clearer than the noonday, the men of the world have their portion in this life, the psalmist counts his age as nothing before God, the inhabitants of the world are called to hear, and the psalm asks God to remember how short our time is.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my lifetime is short and my portion is in this world only if I choose it there. The psalms count our days as nothing before God, and that is why I want my portion in Him, not in the world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wretch, i.e. unfortunate
BiblicalUsage: This word is the poor and helpless, the ones the wicked hunt. The wicked sits in the lurking places with his eyes set against the poor, he crouches so the poor may fall by his strong ones, and the poor commits himself to God, who is the helper of the fatherless.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is the helper of the helpless in this psalm, and the poor who commits himself to Him is not left alone. The wicked crouches, but God sees it and will requite it with His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelem, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Helem is the same man as Heldai, named among those who bring gold from Babylon for the crown of Joshua, and the crowns are kept in the temple as a memorial to Helem and Tobijah and Jedaiah and Hen. His name is on the memorial.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God keeps the givers' names on the crown: Helem's gift is remembered in the temple, and the memorial is still there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dream
BiblicalUsage: A dream is the word for the visions of the night that trouble kings. The Chaldeans ask Nebuchadnezzar to tell them the dream so they can show it, the king demands the dream itself, Daniel says there is a God in heaven who reveals the dream, and Nebuchadnezzar sees a dream that makes him afraid.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dreams in Daniel are God's letters to a pagan king, and only God can read them. The wise men cannot show the dream, and Daniel can, because the God of heaven reveals secrets.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheleph, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Heleph is named once, as a point on the border of Naphtali, from Heleph and Allon to Zaanannim and Adami and Nekeb and Jabneel, down to the Jordan. It marks the edge of the tribe's land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the borders of Naphtali are drawn by God with named points, and Heleph is one of them. The land is measured and the measurement is kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, exchange; hence (as preposition) instead of
