BiblicalUsage: This word means in exchange for, and it is used for the Levites' portion: God gives them the tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in exchange for the service of the tabernacle, and they eat it as their reward for that service.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God pays His servants with an inheritance: the tithe is the exchange for the service, and the service is the exchange for the tithe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelek, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Helek is a son of Gilead, named in the census of Manasseh as the father of the Helekites, and again in the lot of the rest of Manasseh's children. The clan takes its name from him, and the name is the record of the family.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Helekites are counted because Helek is counted, and God keeps the families of Manasseh in full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, smoothness (of the tongue); also an allotment
BiblicalUsage: A portion is a share, a lot, and the word is used for the shares men claim and the share God gives. David says the part of those who stay with the stuff is the same as those who fight, Israel cries that it has no portion in David, Sheba cries that it has no part in David, and Levi has no part nor inheritance because the LORD is his inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the portion that matters is the one God gives: men fight over shares in David, but Levi's share is the LORD Himself. I want the portion that cannot be taken away.
RelatedEvents: David Recovers Ziklag; The Kingdom Divides; Sheba's Rebellion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelets, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Helez the Pelonite, also called the Paltite, is one of David's mighty men and the captain of the seventh course, of the children of Ephraim, with twenty-four thousand in his course. He is named in the roll of the thirty and in the order of the captains.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Helez shows that a mighty man is also an ordered man: he fights in the thirty and he commands in his month, and both are service to the king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelon, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Helon is the father of Eliab, prince of the children of Zebulun, named in the numbering of Israel, in the offering of the princes, and over the host of Zebulun when Israel leaves Sinai. He is named only as the father of a prince.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the father of a prince is worth naming, because the prince is known by his father's name. Helon's name rides with Eliab's in every list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, smoothness; figuratively, flattery; also an allotment
BiblicalUsage: A field is a portion of ground, and the word marks the ground where the stories turn. Joram and Ahaziah meet Jehu in the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite, Joram's body is cast in the portion of Naboth's field, Ruth lights on a part of the field belonging to Boaz, and David stands in a parcel of ground full of barley against the Philistines.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God writes His judgements and His mercies on the same kind of ground: Naboth's field is the place of murder and of vengeance, and Boaz's field is the place of gleaning and of grace. The field is His either way.
RelatedEvents: Jehu's Purge of Ahab's House; Ruth's Loyalty; David Becomes King
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelkath Hats-tsurim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Helkath-hazzurim, the field of sharp swords, is named for a single fight at Gibeon, where Abner's men and Joab's men caught each other by the head and thrust their swords into each other's sides, and fell down together. The place takes its name from the swords.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the field of sharp swords is a warning written in the ground: the house of Saul and the house of David fought each other to the death, and the place remembers it.
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; David's War with the House of Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelkath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Helkath is a city of Asher, named on the border of the tribe and again as a city given to the Levites with its suburbs. It is a border town that becomes a Levites' town.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a border town given to the Levites is a border kept holy. Helkath belongs to Asher and to the Levites, and the gift is the point.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelkai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Helkai is named once, as the head of the priestly house of Meraioth in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua. He is one name in the list of the priests who return and serve.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the priests are counted house by house, and Helkai's house is one of them. The return is recorded in names, not only in numbers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chelkite or descendant of Chelek
BiblicalUsage: The Helekites are the family of Helek the son of Gilead, counted in the second census of Israel in the wilderness. The name is the clan's name, taken from its father.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the clan is counted because the father is counted, and the Helekites belong to Manasseh by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a trinket
BiblicalUsage: This is a trinket, a jewel, and Hosea uses it for the earrings and jewels Israel decks herself with to go after her lovers and forget the LORD. The jewels are the ornaments of adultery.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the jewels show how far Israel had gone: she dressed herself for her lovers with the gifts God gave her, and forgot the Giver.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: curdled milk or cheese
BiblicalUsage: Curds and butter are the food of guests and of children, and the word follows the table through the Bible. Abraham sets butter and milk before his visitors under the tree, Moses sings of butter of kine and milk of sheep, the child Immanuel eats butter and honey, and butter is brought to David and his people hungry in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe butter on the table is God's provision in its simplest form: Abraham feeds strangers, the song remembers plenty, and the child eats what the land gives. The table is His.
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Absalom's Rebellion; The Sign to Ahaz
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: anger
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is rage or fury, and it is Nebuchadnezzar's word in both verses: in his rage and fury he commands the three friends brought before him, and then he is full of fury and his face changes against them. The king's rage heats the furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the king's fury only shows who is really in charge: he heats the furnace seven times hotter, and God walks in it with them.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: heat; figuratively, anger, poison (from its fever)
BiblicalUsage: Wrath is heat, fury, and poison, and the word burns through the Bible. Josiah hears that great is the wrath of the LORD kindled against Judah, the king's wrath is pacified when Haman is hanged, Phinehas turns God's wrath away from Israel, and Josiah's men hear again that the wrath of the LORD is poured out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's wrath is real and it can be turned: Phinehas turns it away by zeal, and the king's wrath is pacified by justice. Wrath that can be turned is wrath that still leaves room for mercy.
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law; Esther Saves Her People; Israel's Sin at Peor and Phinehas
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bitumen (as rising to the surface)
BiblicalUsage: Slime is bitumen, the sticky pitch of the ancient world, and it holds the bricks of Babel together, fills the pits where the kings of Sodom fall, and daubs the ark of bulrushes that carries Moses. The same slime builds a tower and saves a baby.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the slime shows that God uses the same stuff for judgement and for rescue: the pits swallow kings and the pitch keeps the ark afloat.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Abram Rescues Lot; Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: delight
BiblicalUsage: A precious thing is what is desired, and the word is used for the desire of Israel, the desire of women, the desire of all nations, and the goodly raiment Rebekah puts on Jacob. The desire of Israel rests on Saul, the king of the north regards no god but his own will, the nations' desire will come to fill the house, and Rebekah dresses her younger son in his brother's clothes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe desire is the test of every heart here: Israel desires a king, the king of the north desires only himself, and God promises that the desire of all nations will come. What we desire shows whom we worship.
RelatedEvents: Anointing of Saul as King; Jacob Receives Isaac's Blessing; Rebuilding of the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chemdan, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Hemdan is a son of Dishon the Horite, named among the children of Dishon with Eshban and Ithran and Cheran. He is a Horite chief in the genealogy of Edom, and he is not Achan of Joshua chapter seven, who is a different man altogether.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Horites are kept in the record because Edom's story matters to God, and Hemdan's name stands among the chiefs of Seir.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: delight
BiblicalUsage: Desirable is the word for what men want and what God takes away. The women lament for the pleasant fields and the fruitful vine, the sisters dote on desirable young men in blue, and Amos warns that the pleasant vineyards men plant will not be drunk from.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the desirable things in these verses are all taken away, because they were wanted more than God. The pleasant fields are lamented, the desirable young men are a snare, and the vineyard is planted in vain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wine (as fermenting)
BiblicalUsage: This is wine, the foaming blood of the grape, and Moses sings that Israel drank the pure blood of the grape along with the butter and the fat and the milk. The wine is part of the plenty God gave.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the blood of the grape in the song is the picture of God's plenty: the land gives wine as well as bread, and the gift is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a skin bottle (as tied up)
BiblicalUsage: A bottle is a skin for water, and it carries the story of Hagar and the warning of Habakkuk. Abraham gives Hagar a bottle of water and sends her away, God opens her eyes to a well and she fills the bottle again, and Habakkuk curses the man who puts his bottle to his neighbour to make him drunk.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bottle is small and the lesson is large: God fills the bottle Hagar thought was empty, and He judges the man who uses his bottle to shame his neighbour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: commiseration
BiblicalUsage: Chemlah is pity that moves a hand to help, and it appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis the angels take hold of Lot because the Lord is merciful to him, and in Isaiah the Lord redeems His people in His love and His pity, bearing them Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's pity is never cold feeling but rescue in motion, and that is how He has dealt with me too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chen, a figurative name for an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hen is named once, in Zechariah, among the men whose names are set on the crown laid up as a memorial in the temple of the Lord. His name sits beside Helem, Tobijah and Jedaiah, men who had come from the exile bringing silver and gold for the crowning of Joshua the high priest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a single name kept in the temple record matters, because God remembers the men who honour His house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: graciousness, i.e. subjective (kindness, favor) or objective (beauty)
BiblicalUsage: Chen is favour, the grace that makes someone welcome in another's eyes, and it runs through the whole story of Scripture. Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord, Moses found grace before God, Ruth found grace in the eyes of Boaz, and Proverbs says the wise find favour and good understanding with God and men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe grace is the thread that holds the Bible together, because every blessing in it begins with God choosing to look on someone with favour. I hold that we never earn it, we only receive it, and that is why Noah, Moses and Ruth all stand where they stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chenadad, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Henadad is the name of a Levite whose sons are remembered for honest work on God's house. In Ezra they stand over the workmen of the house of God, and in Nehemiah his son Binnui repairs a stretch of the wall and is named again among the men who sealed the covenant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that faithful work done quietly for God's house is never wasted, even when the only record of it is a name on a list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chepher, a place in Palestine; also the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Chepher is both a place and a man's name, and the two uses sit side by side in the record. Joshua lists a king of Hepher among the kings he struck down, Solomon's officer Ben-hesed governs the land of Hepher, and a man named Hepher appears in the families of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name reminds me that places and people share one story in Scripture, and that God works through towns and families alike.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something covert, i.e. a trick
BiblicalUsage: Chephes is a secret plot, a trick worked out in the dark, and it stands only once in the Psalms. There the wicked search out iniquities and accomplish a diligent search, scheming together while the heart within them runs deep.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that no scheme is ever hidden from God, and that is my comfort when evil is plotted out of sight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pleasure; hence (abstractly) desire; concretely, a valuable thing; hence (by extension) a matter (as something in mind)
BiblicalUsage: Chephets is pleasure and desire, what a person delights in or longs for, and Scripture uses it for both God and man. Samuel tells Saul that the Lord delights in obedience more than in burnt offering, Ecclesiastes warns of days when a man finds no pleasure in them, and the psalmist says God's works are sought out by all who have pleasure in them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what we delight in shows what we worship, so I ask God to make my pleasure His pleasure. My position is simple: a heart that delights in obedience will never be far from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chephrite (collectively) or descendants of Chepher
BiblicalUsage: The Chephrites are the descendants of Hepher, named once in the census of Numbers as a family of Manasseh. They stand in the long count of the tribes on the plains of Moab, one household among the thousands being numbered before the land is divided.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts households as well as heroes, and no family is lost in His numbering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheptsi-bah, a fanciful name for Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chephzibah is the name of Hezekiah's wife, the mother of Manasseh, and it is also the new name God gives His land. In Kings she appears only as a name in the royal line, but in Isaiah the Lord says the land shall no more be called desolate, it shall be called Hephzibah, for the Lord delights in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God renames what was desolate with delight, and that is the hope I hold for every life He has claimed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an enactment, a resolution
BiblicalUsage: Cheqeq is a decree, a resolution set down by those in power, and it carries a warning wherever it appears. Isaiah pronounces woe on rulers who decree unrighteous decrees, and in Deborah's song the tribes are divided by great searchings of heart over whether to come to the battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a decree is only as good as the heart behind it, and unjust laws are no laws at all before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: examination, enumeration, deliberation
BiblicalUsage: Cheqer is searching, the patient work of looking into a matter until its depth is found, and Job and the proverbs both use it of God. Job asks whether searching can find out God, and the proverb says the heart of kings is unsearchable, while Isaiah says there is no searching of God's understanding.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God invites our searching but is never exhausted by it, and that is why the search itself is worship. My position is that a God we could fully map would be too small to trust.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of a presumed derivative apparently from the base of G5490 through the idea of deficiency; a widow (as lacking a husband), literally or figuratively:--widow.
BiblicalUsage: Chera is a widow, a woman left without her husband, and the New Testament returns to her again and again. Paul tells the unmarried and widows how to live, Timothy is told to honour widows indeed, the apostles appoint deacons because widows are being neglected, and James says pure religion visits the fatherless and widows in their affliction.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe how a church treats its widows shows what it really believes about God, because He calls Himself the defender of the widow. I hold that care for the lonely is not an extra in the faith but the proof of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: excrement
BiblicalUsage: Chere is dung, and it stands once, in the mouth of Rabshakeh at the siege of Jerusalem. He taunts the men on the wall that they will eat their own dung and drink their own urine with him, a crude threat meant to break their spirit before the Assyrian army.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Bible does not clean up the words of God's enemies, and their filth only shows the darkness they serve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: drought; also a cutting instrument (from its destructive effect), as a knife, sword, or other sharp implement
BiblicalUsage: Chereb is the sword, the cutting blade that stands for war, judgment and God's own word of power throughout the Old Testament. A flaming sword guards the way to the tree of life, Moses commands the Levites to take the sword through the camp, the captain of the Lord's host meets Joshua with a drawn sword, and David faces Goliath trusting not in a sword but in the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sword in Scripture always asks whose side we are on, because the same blade can defend or destroy. I hold that God's sword cuts true, and that is why David's trust was in the Lord and not in his own weapon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheres, a mountain in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Heres is a mountain in Palestine, named once, where the Amorites held on after the rest of the land was taken. The house of Joseph pressed them and they stayed in Mount Heres, in Aijalon and in Shaalbim, until Israel grew strong enough to put them to tribute.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the record keeps even the unfinished battles, because God's people did not conquer everything at once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the itch; the sun
BiblicalUsage: Cheres is a word with two faces, the sun and the itch, and both show up in its few appearances. In Deuteronomy it is the itch of Egypt laid on the disobedient, in Job it is the sun God commands not to rise, and in Judges it marks the time before the sun was up and before the sun went down.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a single word can carry both judgment and the turning of the day, and that is how rich the language of Scripture is. I believe God writes both meanings into one word on purpose, so that I remember His judgments and His mercies come from the same hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a net, i.e. (by analogy) lattice
BiblicalUsage: Cherek is a lattice, the openwork screen through which a lover watches, and it appears once in the Song of Songs. The beloved stands behind the wall looking through the windows, showing himself through the lattice, close at hand yet still partly hidden.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is honest about love, which sees truly even when it does not yet see fully.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: physical (as shutting in) a net (either literally or figuratively); usually a doomed object; abstractly extermination
BiblicalUsage: Cherem is a thing devoted to God for destruction, set apart so completely that no one may take it for himself. Jericho is made a curse and its spoil is forbidden, Achan takes of the accursed thing and brings trouble on Israel, and Saul keeps the spoil of the devoted Amalekites against the Lord's command.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cherem teaches me that what God has devoted is not mine to keep, and taking it is never a small sin. My position is that obedience is proved exactly where the prize looks worth keeping.
RelatedEvents: The Walls of Jericho; The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a piece of pottery
BiblicalUsage: Cheres is a potsherd, a broken piece of pottery, and Scripture uses it for both judgment and lowly suffering. Isaiah says a nation can be broken as a potter's vessel is broken, Jeremiah is told to take a potter's earthen bottle, Ezekiel breaks the sherds of a cup, and Job takes a potsherd to scrape himself as he sits in the ashes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God breaks what is proud and keeps what is broken, because a potsherd in His hand can still serve. I hold that Job scraping his sores with a shard is one of the truest pictures of suffering in the Bible.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheresh, a Levite
BiblicalUsage: Cheresh is a Levite named once, among the Levites who dwelt in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He stands in the list of the men who served at the house of God, a single name kept among the singers and gatekeepers of the restored city.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a name kept in the service of God's house is honour enough, even when nothing else is recorded of the man.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: deaf (whether literally or spiritual)
BiblicalUsage: Cheresh means deaf, whether the ear is shut or the heart is, and the Bible holds both meanings together. God asks Moses who makes the dumb or the deaf, the law forbids cursing the deaf, Isaiah promises the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and the psalmist says he was as a deaf man who heard not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the God who made the ear can open it, and the day the deaf hear is the day His healing is shown. I hold that spiritual deafness is the deeper danger, because it refuses to hear what God has said.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: magical craft; also silence
BiblicalUsage: Cheresh covers silence, secrecy and the craftsman's skill, three uses of one root that meet in the text. The spies go into Jericho secretly, Isaiah names the cunning artificer among the leaders taken away, and the valley of craftsmen is named for the workmen who lived there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe quiet work and secret counsel both have their place, and Scripture marks the difference between hiding for God and hiding from Him. I hold that the craftsman's quiet skill and the spy's quiet errand both serve God when the heart behind them is true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a chisel or graver; also a style for writing
BiblicalUsage: Cheret is a graving tool, a chisel for cutting words into hard material, and it appears in two very different scenes. Aaron fashions the golden calf with a graving tool, and Isaiah is told to write upon a great roll with a man's pen, the same kind of engraving turned to God's message.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the same tool can carve an idol or write God's word, and the difference is always the hand and the heart behind it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chereth, a thicket in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hereth is a thicket in Judah, named once, where David hid while Saul hunted him. The prophet Gad told David not to stay in the hold but to go into the land of Judah, and David came and remained in the forest of Hareth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God leads His people out of hiding and into the open, even when the open looks more dangerous than the thicket.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sickle (as cutting)
BiblicalUsage: Chermesh is a sickle, the curved blade for cutting grain, and the law uses it to mark the harvest and its limits. The firstfruits are counted from the day the sickle is first put to the standing corn, and a neighbour may pluck ears with his hand but must not move a sickle into his standing corn.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sickle in the law is about both provision and restraint, because God gives generously and still sets a boundary.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chermon, a mount of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hermon is the high mountain of the north, the snowy peak that marks the edge of the promised land. Moses names it among the borders Israel took from the Amorite kings, Joshua's conquests reach to its slopes, and the psalm says the dew of Hermon falls on the mountains of Zion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mountain that stood at the border reminds me that God's blessings run down from high places to His people below. I hold that Hermon is a picture of refreshment, because its dew falls where the Lord commands the blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hermons, i.e. its peaks
BiblicalUsage: The Hermons are the peaks of Mount Hermon, named once in the psalmist's cry from the land of Jordan. He remembers God from the hill Mizar and from the Hermonites, his soul cast down within him while the waves of trouble go over his head.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a man can remember God's mountain even when he is far from it, and memory itself becomes a kind of prayer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plural of Hebrew origin (H3742); "cherubim" (i.e. cherubs or kerubim):--cherubims.
BiblicalUsage: Cherubim is the Greek plural of the Hebrew word for the cherubs, and in the New Testament it stands only once, in Hebrews. There the cherubim of glory shadow the mercy seat above the ark, the place where God met His people, and the writer passes over them because his point is the better covenant that has come. The Greek text spells the word with a different ending than the dictionary form, so the verse is cited as a spelling variant rather than an exact match.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cherubim still point me to the mercy seat, where God meets sinners in mercy rather than in judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contumely, disgrace, the pudenda
BiblicalUsage: Cherpah is reproach, the shame laid on a person or a people, and Scripture shows God both sending it and taking it away. Rachel says God has taken away her reproach, David asks who will take away the reproach of Israel, Nehemiah calls the people to rebuild so they will be a reproach no more, and the psalmist lays his own reproach before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is the one who removes reproach, and no shame I carry is beyond His taking away. I hold that the cross is where every reproach ends, because Christ bore ours there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheshbon, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Heshbon is a city east of the Jordan, the royal city of Sihon king of the Amorites, and it marks Israel's first conquests on the way to the promised land. Israel dwelt in Heshbon and its villages, Moses names it in the charge to take the land, and Isaiah hears Heshbon crying out under the judgment on Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Heshbon reminds me that God gives His people ground to stand on, one city at a time, before the whole land is theirs.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat of Sihon and Og
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, contrivance; by implication, intelligence
BiblicalUsage: Cheshbown is the reckoning, the account a person makes when he searches a matter out to the end, and Ecclesiastes is its only home. The preacher applies his heart to seek out wisdom and the reason of things, counts one by one to find the account, and warns that in the grave there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the search for the true account of things is the work of a wise life. I hold that only God keeps the final reckoning straight, and His account is the one that will stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a belt or strap (as being interlaced)
BiblicalUsage: Chesheb is the woven band of the ephod, the curious girdle that bound the high priest's garments together. Exodus describes it as the work of the ephod itself, of gold and blue and purple and scarlet, and Leviticus shows Moses girding Aaron with it when he dresses him for the priesthood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the band that held the priest's garments together pictures how God holds His servants together for His service. I hold that nothing about the priest's dress was decoration alone, because every thread pointed to holiness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: delight
BiblicalUsage: Chesheq is delight, the longing a heart sets on something it wants, and it is used both of kings and of the fearful. Solomon finishes the house of the Lord and all his desire, the chronicler lists all that Solomon desired to build, and Isaiah turns the phrase over to terror, where the night of pleasure becomes fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe delight is a test of the heart, because what I long for most is what I truly serve. I hold that Solomon's desires built much and cost much, and that is the warning in the word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: darkness
BiblicalUsage: Cheshkah is darkness, and it stands once, in the psalm where David says God made darkness His secret place. The clouds and thick darkness round about Him are not His absence but His covering, the pavilion in which He hides Himself from sight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is present in the darkness as surely as in the light, and that is my comfort when I cannot see Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheshmon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Heshmon is a town in the south of Judah, named once in the long list of the cities given to the tribe. It stands among the cities of the wilderness edge, a small name kept in the record of the inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the smallest town in Judah's portion was given by God's own hand, and no part of the inheritance is too small to be recorded.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a crime or its penalty
BiblicalUsage: Chete is a crime and its penalty, the sin counted against a person and the punishment it brings, and the prophets and kings both use it this way. Daniel confesses that for their sins Jerusalem has become a reproach, Deuteronomy warns that a grudging heart toward the poor will be sin, the chronicler says every man shall die for his own sin, and Jehu is charged with the sins of Jeroboam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe chete is honest about sin: it is not only a mistake but a debt that must be paid. I hold that this is why the cross matters, because there the penalty fell on Christ instead of on us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cheth, an aboriginal Canaanite
BiblicalUsage: Heth is the ancestor of the Hittites, a son of Canaan named in the table of nations, and his children become the people Israel must deal with for centuries. Abraham speaks to the sons of Heth when he buys the burial cave for Sarah, and the chronicler traces the same line in the genealogy of the nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sons of Heth show how the nations around Israel were real neighbours with real claims, not faceless enemies. I hold that Abraham dealing fairly with them is a model for how God's people treat those outside the covenant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, rapine; figuratively, robbery
BiblicalUsage: Chetheph is robbery, lying in wait like a hunter for prey, and it stands once in the proverbs. There the strange woman lies in wait as for a prey and increases the transgressors among men, a single word that turns a seduction into a robbery.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that sin rarely announces itself as theft, and that is why the warning is given in a single sharp word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chethlon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hethlon is a place on the northern border of the land, named twice in Ezekiel's vision of the restored borders. The boundary runs by the way of Hethlon to the entering of Hamath, a fixed point on the edge of the land God promises to His people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the borders in Ezekiel are God's promise drawn on a map, and Hethlon marks how exact His promises are.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a piercer, i.e. an arrow; by implication, a wound; figuratively, (of God) thunderbolt; the shaft of a spear
BiblicalUsage: Chets is an arrow, a piercer, and Scripture uses it for warfare, for children and for God's own judgment. The psalmist says children are as arrows in the hand of a mighty man, Elisha tells Joash to take bow and arrows and calls the arrow the Lord's deliverance, and David's song says God sent out arrows and scattered His enemies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe children as arrows is one of the tenderest pictures in the Bible, because arrows are made to fly far. I hold that God's arrows never miss, and that is why David could sing of them in his deliverance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the bosom (as comprised between the arms)
BiblicalUsage: Chetsen is the bosom, the fold of the garment between the arms, and it stands once in a psalm about a harvest that fails. The reaper does not fill his hand, nor he that binds sheaves his bosom, because the blessing of the Lord is not on the work of the wicked.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a harvest without God's blessing leaves the bosom empty, and that is the psalm's quiet warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the half or middle
BiblicalUsage: Chetsiy is the half, the middle of a thing, and it appears in the most famous judgment of Solomon. The king calls for the living child to be divided in two, the queen of Sheba says the half of Solomon's wisdom was not told her, the tabernacle has a half curtain left over, and the chronicler counts the half tribe of Manasseh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the half in Solomon's judgment shows what a mother's love is, because she would rather lose the whole than see the child cut in two. I hold that God's wisdom is never half told, and the queen's words are the honest confession of everyone who meets it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chetsro, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hezro is one of David's mighty men, named in both lists of the thirty. He is called Hezro the Carmelite, and he stands among the warriors who fought at David's side through the long war with the house of Saul.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that men like Hezro are remembered because they stood faithful in the hard years, and God keeps the names of the faithful.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chetsron, the name of a place in Palestine; also of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hezron is the name of two men in the genealogies, one the son of Reuben and one the son of Pharez, and both lines run toward David. Reuben's son Hezron is counted in the family that went down to Egypt, Pharez's son Hezron stands in the line of Judah, and Ruth's genealogy ends with Hezron among the fathers of David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the double Hezron shows how carefully God keeps the lines that lead to the king, and no link in the chain is left out.
RelatedPeople: Hezron, Son of Pharez; Hezron, Son of Reuben
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chetsronite or (collectively) descendants of Chetsron
BiblicalUsage: The Hezronites are the descendants of Hezron, named in the census of Numbers as a family of Reuben and a family of Judah. They stand in the count of the tribes on the plains of Moab, two households sharing one ancestor's name.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts families by name, and the census is His way of saying every household belongs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an army; also (by analogy,) an intrenchment
BiblicalUsage: Cheyl is an army and also a rampart, the host that marches and the wall that defends, and the histories use both senses. David smites the host of Hadarezer, the Syrians come against Judah with a great host, and Jezebel is thrown down by the wall of Jezreel where the dogs eat her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same word for an army and a wall reminds me that God's people are both defended and sent, and neither is safe without Him. I hold that the wall and the host both belong to the Lord, and He is the defence behind each one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an intrenchment
BiblicalUsage: Cheylah is a rampart, a defensive wall, and it stands once in the psalm that walks around Zion. The singer is told to mark well her bulwarks and consider her palaces, so that the strength of the city can be told to the generation following.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ramparts of Zion are worth marking because they are God's own defences, and the church still walks round them today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chelam, a place East of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Helam is a place east of the Jordan where David met the Syrians in battle. Hadarezer gathered his army at Helam, David crossed the Jordan and arrayed against them there, and the Syrians fled before Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Helam is a reminder that God fights for His people even far from home, across the river and on foreign ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the bosom (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Cheyq is the bosom, the fold of the garment close to the heart, and Scripture uses it for tenderness and for danger together. A mother lays the living child in her bosom, the poor man's lamb lies in his bosom and eats of his morsel, Naomi lays the child in her bosom, and the proverb asks whether a man can take fire in his bosom and not be burned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bosom is where love keeps what it cherishes, and the proverb is right that fire kept there will burn. I hold that what I hold closest to my heart will either warm me or wound me, and I must choose what I carry there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an animal
BiblicalUsage: Cheyva is the Aramaic word for a beast, an animal, and Daniel uses it in the visions of the kingdoms. The beasts of the field are given into Nebuchadnezzar's hand, the great tree shelters the beasts beneath it, and the king himself is told he will dwell with the beasts of the field until he knows that the Most High rules.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the beast in Daniel shows how low a proud king can fall, and how high God lifts those who humble themselves. I hold that every kingdom that forgets God becomes a beast, and only His kingdom endures.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: help
BiblicalUsage: Chezeq is help and strength, and it stands once, in the first verse of the psalm where David calls the Lord his strength. The word is the cry of a man who has found his help in God alone, and it opens a psalm of deliverance from every enemy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength is not something I find in myself but Someone I run to, and David's first word in the psalm is mine too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sight
BiblicalUsage: Chezev is a sight, a vision seen in the night, and Daniel uses it for the revelations God gives in dreams. The secret is revealed to Daniel in a night vision, Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by the visions of his head on his bed, and Daniel himself has a dream and visions in the first year of Belshazzar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still speaks through visions in the way He chooses, and Daniel shows me to receive them with humility and prayer. I hold that the test of any vision is whether it agrees with God's word, because dreams can deceive but He cannot.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chezir, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hezir is the name of two Israelites, one the head of the seventeenth course of priests and one a man who sealed the covenant after the exile. The priest Hezir stands in David's ordering of the temple service, and the later Hezir stands among the leaders who put their names to the sealed promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a name on the covenant is a serious thing, and Hezir's signature is a picture of a people binding themselves to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prevailing power
BiblicalUsage: Chezqah is prevailing power, the strength that holds its ground, and the histories use it of kings who grow strong. Rehoboam strengthens himself when his kingdom is established, Uzziah is strengthened until his heart is lifted up, Isaiah is told to speak with a strong hand, and Daniel foresees a king who will stir up all against the realm of Grecia.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength that forgets God turns to pride, and that is the warning written into this word. I hold that prevailing power is only safe in a hand that stays humble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chezjon, a Syrian
BiblicalUsage: Hezion is a Syrian named once, as the father of Tabrimmon and the grandfather of Ben-hadad. Asa king of Judah sends silver and gold to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon the son of Hezion, asking him to break his league with Baasha and come to Judah's aid.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a name buried in a genealogy shows how God weaves the nations around His people into His story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mast
BiblicalUsage: Chibbel is a mast, the tall pole of a ship, and it stands once in the proverb about the drunkard. The man who drinks too much lies down in the midst of the sea, or as one who lies on the top of a mast, swaying and senseless above the waves.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the mast is a warning in a single picture, because drunkenness leaves a man with nowhere steady to stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a clasping of the hands (in idleness)
BiblicalUsage: Chibbuq is the folding of the hands, the clasp of idle arms, and both proverbs that use it say the same thing. A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep, and poverty comes as one that travelleth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that idleness is not rest, and the folded hands in these proverbs are the picture of a life slipping away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the Chiddekel (or Tigris) river
BiblicalUsage: Hiddekel is the Tigris, one of the four rivers of Eden, and it appears again at the end of Daniel's visions. In Genesis it flows east of Assyria out of the garden, and in Daniel the prophet stands by the bank of the great river when the man clothed in linen appears to him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the river that watered Eden still runs through the visions, because God's story is one river from beginning to end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5507 and G757; the commander of a thousand soldiers ("chiliarch"; i.e. colonel:--(chief, high) captain.
BiblicalUsage: Chiliarchos is the commander of a thousand, the chief captain, and the New Testament uses it for the officers who carry out orders. The chief captain at Jerusalem takes Paul with soldiers and chains, the captain with his officers takes Jesus in the garden, Herod's chief captains sit at his birthday feast, and the captains of the earth hide themselves in the day of wrath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows how earthly power works: it takes orders and it takes prisoners, but it cannot hold the One it arrests. I hold that every captain in these passages is small beside the King they stand against.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5507; one thousand ("chiliad"):--thousand.
BiblicalUsage: Chilias is a thousand, a counted multitude, and the New Testament uses it for crowds, armies and angels alike. Three and twenty thousand fall in one day in the wilderness, the number of believers grows to about five thousand, a king counts ten thousand against twenty thousand, and the angels round the throne are ten thousand times ten thousand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thousands in Scripture are never just numbers, because each one is a soul God counts. I hold that the angels round the throne show how small our crowds are beside His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plural of uncertain affinity; a thousand:--thousand.
BiblicalUsage: Chilioi is a thousand, and its most famous use is Peter's word that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years. John hears the witnesses prophesy a thousand two hundred and threescore days, the woman is fed in the wilderness for the same thousand days, and the blood runs to the horse bridles for a thousand and six hundred furlongs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter's thousand years teaches me patience, because God's slowness is not His absence. I hold that the thousand in Revelation is God's measure, not man's, and that is why I trust His timing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chilhijah, the name of eight Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hilkiah is the high priest who found the book of the law in the house of the Lord, and his name marks the turning point of Josiah's reign. In Kings he tells Shaphan that he has found the book, and in Chronicles he gives it to be read before the king, so that the whole nation hears what it had lost.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the finding of the book is the hinge of the whole story, because a nation that had lost God's word found it again. I hold that Hilkiah's discovery is still the pattern: revival begins when the book is opened.
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: gratis, i.e. devoid of cost, reason or advantage
BiblicalUsage: Chinnam means freely, without cost or without cause, and it cuts both ways in Scripture. The servant goes out free for nothing, David is slain without a cause, God tells Satan that Job is destroyed without cause, and the psalmist says his enemies hide a net for him without cause.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds two truths together: God's gifts come freely, and His people suffer innocently. I hold that both are true of Christ, who gave freely and was hated without a cause.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wheat
BiblicalUsage: Chinta is the Aramaic word for wheat, and it appears in the supplies ordered for the restored temple. The king's letter provides wheat for the priests and their offerings, and Ezra's commission lists a hundred measures of wheat among the gifts for the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wheat in these lists is provision with a purpose, because God feeds His people so that they can worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps akin to the base of G5490 (G5465) or G5494 (as descending or empty); snow:--snow.
BiblicalUsage: Chion is snow, and the New Testament uses it only for whiteness that shines. The angel at the empty tomb has raiment white as snow, and John's vision of the risen Christ shows a head and hairs white like wool, as white as snow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the snow in these visions is not cold but clean, the colour of a purity no earth can make, and the white at the tomb and on the throne is the same white because the risen Christ is the pure one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Chios, an island in the Mediterranean:--Chios.
BiblicalUsage: Chios is an island in the Aegean, named once in the record of Paul's journey to Jerusalem. The ship comes to Chios on the third day out from Miletus, a single stop on the long voyage that ends with Paul's arrest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small stops on Paul's journey matter, because the gospel travelled one harbour at a time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hasty flight
BiblicalUsage: Chippazown is hasty flight, the hurried leaving of a place, and it belongs to the Passover and the exodus. Israel eats the lamb in haste with loins girded and staff in hand, the bread of affliction is eaten because they came out of Egypt in haste, and Isaiah promises the return will not be in haste because the Lord will go before them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the haste of the exodus and the calm of the return belong together, because the same Lord hurries His people out and leads them home in peace. I hold that God is never rushed, even when His people must be.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a contrivance, i.e. actual (a warlike machine) or mental (a machination)
BiblicalUsage: Chishshabown is a contrivance, a device worked out by a cunning mind, and it appears as both a weapon and a warning. Uzziah's engines of war are invented by cunning men to shoot arrows from the towers, and Ecclesiastes says God made man upright but they have sought out many inventions.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word warns me that ingenuity is a gift that can build a tower of defence or a maze of sin, and every invention is judged by the heart that made it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: conjoined, i.e. a wheel-spoke or rod connecting the hub with the rim
BiblicalUsage: Chishshuq is a spoke, the rod that joins the hub of a wheel to its rim, and it stands once in the description of Solomon's temple. The wheels of the ten bases are made like a chariot wheel, with their axletrees, felloes, spokes and naves all cast in one piece.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the spokes of the temple were made with care, because nothing in God's house is careless work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: combined, i.e. the nave or hub of a wheel (as holding the spokes together)
BiblicalUsage: Chishshur is the nave, the hub of a wheel that holds the spokes together, and it stands once beside its fellow in the same verse. The wheels of the temple bases have their naves as well as their spokes, each part cast as one with the whole, so the wheel turns true.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hub is the quiet centre that holds the work together, and the temple needed its hidden parts as much as its gold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (H3801); a tunic or shirt:--clothes, coat, garment.
BiblicalUsage: Chiton is a tunic, the close garment worn under the outer robe, and the Gospels use it for generosity, for sharing and for the cross. Jesus says to give your coat as well as your cloak to the man who sues you, John the Baptist says the man with two coats should share with him who has none, and the soldiers gamble over the seamless coat of Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the coat in these sayings is the test of a generous heart, because it is the garment closest to the skin. I hold that Christ's seamless coat, gambled for at the cross, shows how far men will go to take what He wore.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an arrow
BiblicalUsage: Chitstsiy is an arrow, and it flies through the friendship of David and Jonathan. Jonathan shoots his arrows beyond the lad as a signal to David, telling him by their fall whether to flee or stay, and later Jehu draws a bow and an arrow finds Jehoram between the arms.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jonathan's arrows are the picture of a friendship that risks everything to warn a friend. I hold that a true friend shoots his arrows for you, not at you, and that is what Jonathan did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fear
BiblicalUsage: Chittah is terror, the dread that falls on whole cities, and it stands once in the story of Jacob. After the slaughter at Shechem, the terror of God falls on the cities round about, so that they do not pursue the sons of Jacob as they journey on.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the terror of God is His protection as well as His judgment, because it kept Jacob's family alive on the road, and the God who terrifies our enemies is the same God who keeps His promise to us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wheat, whether the grain or the plant
BiblicalUsage: Chittah is wheat, the grain of the harvest, and it appears at the turning points of three stories. Ruth gleans through the wheat harvest, the men of Beth-shemesh are reaping their wheat harvest when the ark returns, and Solomon gives Hiram twenty thousand measures of wheat for his household.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wheat in the Bible is always provision on the way to something more, because Ruth's harvest leads to a home and the ark's return leads to worship. I hold that God feeds His people in the middle of their story, not only at the end of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chittite, or descendant of Cheth
BiblicalUsage: Chittiy is a Hittite, a descendant of Heth, and the name follows Israel from the promise to the monarchy. God lists the Hittites among the peoples of the land He will give Abraham, Ahimelech the Hittite stands with David in the wilderness, and Uriah the Hittite is the man whose wife David takes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Hittites remind me that the peoples of the land were never abstractions, and Uriah's name is the rebuke that will not go away. I hold that David's sin against one Hittite is remembered because God counts every person, even the foreigner.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Uriah the Hittite; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fear
BiblicalUsage: Chittiyth is terror, the dread that a great power spreads, and Ezekiel uses it only of Tyre and Egypt. Tyre was a terror in the sea, and the slain of Egypt go down to the pit with the terror they spread in the land of the living.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the terror of the great powers is real but short-lived, because God brings every terror to the pit. I hold that no empire's fear outlasts God's judgment on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: swathed, i.e. a bandage
BiblicalUsage: Chittuwl is a bandage, a swathing cloth for a wound, and it stands once in the judgment on Pharaoh. God says Pharaoh's arm is broken and shall not be bound up, given no bandage to be healed, because the strength of Egypt will not be restored.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a wound God refuses to bandage is a judgment, and Egypt's broken arm is the picture of a power He will not heal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: white
BiblicalUsage: Chivvar is white, and it stands once, in Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days. His garment is white as snow and the hair of His head is like pure wool, and the throne itself is like fiery flame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the white in Daniel's vision is the colour of a holiness no man can approach on his own, and the Ancient of Days is still on His throne, so His whiteness is my hope and not my fear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chivvite, one of the aboriginal tribes of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chivviy is a Hivite, one of the peoples of Canaan, and the name runs from the promise to the conquest. God promises Moses a land of Hivites, the law lists them among the nations to be driven out, and the kings of the Hivites gather with the rest to fight Joshua.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Hivites show that God's promise always had an enemy to face, and the conquest was a real war against real peoples. I hold that the God who promised the land also gave the victory for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chiel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hiel is the Bethelite who rebuilt Jericho in the days of Ahab, and the cost of it is the whole story. He laid its foundation in his firstborn Abiram and set up its gates in his youngest son Segub, exactly as the Lord had spoken by Joshua the son of Nun.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hiel's story is the warning that God's words outlive the centuries, and a curse spoken long ago still falls true. I hold that rebuilding what God has cursed is never a small thing, whatever it costs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a puzzle, hence, a trick, conundrum, sententious maxim
BiblicalUsage: Chiydah is a riddle, a hard question put to test a person's wisdom, and it appears in the stories of Samson, Solomon and Daniel. Samson puts forth his riddle at the wedding feast, the queen of Sheba comes to prove Solomon with hard questions, and Daniel foresees a king of fierce countenance who understands dark sentences.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe riddles in Scripture are not games but tests, and the wise are shown by how they answer. I hold that the hardest question of all is the one God puts to us, and only His wisdom answers it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a throe (expectant of childbirth)
BiblicalUsage: Chiyl is a throe, the pang of a woman in labour, and the prophets use it for the terror of nations. The inhabitants of Palestina are in pangs at the news of Israel, Zion is told to be in pain as a woman that travaileth, Jerusalem is seized with pangs, and fear takes hold in Zion as pain takes a woman in travail.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is honest about judgment, because it comes on a people the way labour comes on suddenly and cannot be stopped. I hold that the same God who sends the pang is the one who delivers through it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chilen, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hilen is a town in Judah given to the sons of Aaron as a city of refuge. It stands in the list of the cities where a man who slew his neighbour unawares could flee and live, one of the safe places set aside in the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cities of refuge show God's heart for the one who never meant to kill, and Hilen is one of those mercies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: beauty
BiblicalUsage: Chiyn is beauty, the comely proportion of a thing, and it stands once in God's speech about leviathan. The Lord says He will not conceal the creature's parts, nor his power, nor his comely proportion, as if even the strength of the sea beast has a beauty worth naming.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God delights in the beauty of what He made, even in creatures that frighten us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chirah, an Adullamite
BiblicalUsage: Hirah is the Adullamite, the friend of Judah, named twice in the story of Judah and Tamar. He goes down with Judah to the sheep shearing, and he is the one Judah sends with the kid to redeem the pledge he left with Tamar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hirah is the friend who stands beside Judah in his worst chapter, and God keeps the names of friends as well as kings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chiram or Chirom, the name of two Tyrians
BiblicalUsage: Hiram is the name of two Tyrians, a king and a craftsman, and the books keep them distinct. Hiram king of Tyre sends his servants to Solomon and supplies timber for the temple, while Hiram the craftsman comes out of Tyre to cast the bronze work and finishes all the work for the house of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Hirams show how God uses both a king's friendship and a craftsman's hands to build His house. I hold that the craftsman's Hiram is the one I love most, because his work is still standing in the record.
RelatedPeople: Hiram, King of Tyre; Hiram, Craftsman of Tyre
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a hurry; hence (adverb) quickly
BiblicalUsage: Chiysh is quickly, in a hurry, and it stands once in the psalm about the shortness of life. The days of our years are threescore years and ten, and it is soon cut off, and we fly away, a single word for how fast a life goes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is meant to make me count my days, because a life flies away faster than I think.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a hurry; hence (adverb) quickly
BiblicalUsage: Chiysh is quickly, in a hurry, and it stands once in the psalm about the shortness of life. The days of our years are threescore years and ten, and it is soon cut off, and we fly away, a single word for how fast a life goes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is meant to make me count my days, because a life flies away faster than I think.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, the (outer) wall side; hence, exterior; figuratively, secular (as opposed to sacred)
BiblicalUsage: Chiytsown is the outer side, the exterior, and it marks the boundary between the holy and the common. The temple has carvings in the inner house and the outer, the king's entry is taken away from the outer way, Haman waits in the outward court, and Ezekiel measures the outward court of the new temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the outer places matter because they are where ordinary people stand before God, and He has always made room there. I hold that the God who dwells in the inner place still meets His people in the outer court.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chizki, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hizki is a Benjamite named once, among the sons of Elpaal in the genealogy of Benjamin. He stands in the long list of the families that settled Jerusalem, a single name kept in the record of the tribe.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God keeps the names of the families who came home, even when their story is only a line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chizkijah, a king of Judah, also the name of two other Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hezekiah is the king of Judah who restored the worship of the Lord and prayed his way through invasion and sickness. He begins to reign at twenty-five and does what is right in the sight of the Lord, he opens the doors of the temple and keeps the Passover, and when Sennacherib's letter comes he spreads it before the Lord and prays.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hezekiah is the king I would hold up to any leader, because he took his trouble to God before he took it to any man. I hold that his prayer over the letter is the pattern for every crisis: spread it out before the Lord and leave it there.
RelatedEvents: Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Hezekiah Restores Worship and Keeps Passover
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a revelation, expectation by dream
BiblicalUsage: Chizzayown is a revelation, a vision seen by night or by the prophets, and it carries the weight of God's word. Nathan speaks to David according to all this vision, Isaiah's burden is the valley of vision, Eliphaz is troubled by thoughts from the visions of the night, and Joel promises that young men shall see visions when the Spirit is poured out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a true vision always agrees with God's word, because He does not contradict Himself in the night. I hold that Joel's promise is still open, and the Spirit still opens eyes to see what God is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a military cloak:--robe.
BiblicalUsage: Chlamys is a military cloak, a robe, and the Gospels use it only for the robe put on Jesus in His suffering. The soldiers strip Him and put on Him a scarlet robe, and then they take the robe off Him again and lead Him away to be crucified.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scarlet robe is mockery dressed as majesty, and Christ wore their scorn so that I could wear His righteousness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative probably of G5491; to throw out the lip, i.e. jeer at:--mock.
BiblicalUsage: Chleuazo is to mock, to throw out the lip at someone, and it stands once, in Athens. When Paul speaks of the resurrection of the dead, some mock, while others say they will hear him again, and the gospel divides the crowd on the spot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the resurrection has always divided hearers, and mockery is the oldest answer to it, yet the gospel is still worth preaching to the mockers in Athens and everywhere else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from χλίω (to warm); tepid:--lukewarm.
BiblicalUsage: Chliaros is lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, and it stands once, in the letter to Laodicea. The Lord says He knows their works, that they are neither cold nor hot, and because they are lukewarm He will spue them out of His mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lukewarmness is the most dangerous state a church can be in, because it feels safe while it is sick, and the Lord's threat is mercy in disguise, since He would rather we were cold and honest than warm and self-deceived.
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Laodicea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of apparently a primary word; "green"; Chloë, a Christian female:--Chloe.
BiblicalUsage: Chloe is a Christian woman in Corinth, named once, because her household told Paul the truth about the church. It was declared to Paul by them which are of the house of Chloe that there were contentions among the believers, and her name is the reason the first letter to the Corinthians was written.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chloe's household did the church a service by telling the truth, because a church cannot be healed until its divisions are named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G5514; greenish, i.e. verdant, dun-colored:--green, pale.
BiblicalUsage: Chloros is green, the colour of fresh growth, and in Revelation it turns pale with death. The crowds sit on the green grass to be fed, the pale horse rides out with Death on its back, the hail burns up all green grass, and the locusts are told to hurt not the grass of the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same green can mean life in the feeding of the five thousand and judgment in the trumpets, and the difference is God's hand in it. I hold that the grass of the field is in His keeping either way, and He spares what He chooses.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a cherisher, i.e. the bosom
BiblicalUsage: Chob is the bosom, the fold where a thing is hidden close to the heart, and it stands once in Job's defence. He says if he covered his transgressions as Adam did, by hiding his iniquity in his bosom, then let his accusers judge him, but he will not hide what he has done.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bosom is where we hide what we are ashamed of, and Job's refusal to hide is the honest way, because confession is the only cure for a sin carried in the bosom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chobab, father-in-law of Moses
BiblicalUsage: Hobab is the son of Reuel and the father-in-law of Moses, and he is asked to travel with Israel because he knows the wilderness. Moses pleads with him to come and be their eyes in the desert, and generations later Heber the Kenite, of the children of Hobab, pitches his tent by the oak in Zaanannim when Deborah and Barak fight Sisera.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hobab's story is about a man from outside Israel who is invited in, and God uses outsiders more often than we think. I hold that Moses asking for his help is no weakness, because God gives His people guides from unexpected places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sailor
BiblicalUsage: Chobel is a sailor, a man who works the ropes of a ship, and the prophets use it for Tyre's proud fleet and Jonah's flight. The sailors of Tyre are the wise men of her ships, her pilots are the princes of the sea, and when the storm rises the shipmaster finds Jonah asleep below and wakes him to call on his God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sailors in these stories know the sea better than the prophets know their duty, and that is the rebuke in Jonah. I hold that God sends storms to wake His sleeping servants, and He uses sailors to do it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a joint
BiblicalUsage: Chobereth is a coupling, a joint that holds two things together, and it belongs to the tabernacle curtains. The loops of blue on the edge of one curtain are coupled to the loops on the edge of the other, so that the whole covering hangs as one, and the workmen repeat the coupling exactly as commanded.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the couplings of the tabernacle are a picture of the church, many pieces held together by God's own design. I hold that the joints no one sees are the ones that hold the whole together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chosah, an Israelite; also a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hosah is both a man and a place, a gatekeeper of the temple and a town on the border of Asher. The Levite Hosah stands with Obed-edom at the doors of the house of God, his sons keep the gates in David's ordering, and the town of Hosah marks the coast where the border of Asher turns to the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a gatekeeper's name is worth keeping, because the doors of God's house are kept by faithful men. I hold that Hosah's two uses show how one name can serve both the temple and the land.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wealth
BiblicalUsage: Chocen is wealth, the treasure a person piles up, and the prophets and proverbs weigh it against what lasts. The prophets of Jerusalem devour souls and take treasure, Jeremiah says God will give all the wealth of the city into the enemy's hand, Isaiah says the fear of the Lord is the true treasure, and the proverb says the house of the righteous holds much treasure.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wealth in these verses is always tested, and the only treasure that survives the test is the fear of the Lord. I hold that a full house without God is poorer than an empty one with Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: poverty
BiblicalUsage: Choser is lack, the want of all things, and it is the curse of a people who forsake God.
