BiblicalUsage: Freedom here is the liberty of a woman who is a slave, promised to a man but not yet redeemed. The law says she must not be put to death as an adulteress, because she was not free. The word appears once, in a law that protects someone who has no power of her own.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this single verse shows the heart of God's law: it bends toward the one who cannot defend herself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chuppah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Huppah is the head of the thirteenth course of priests in David's ordering of the temple service. His name appears once, in the list of the twenty-four courses. He is remembered because his course kept its turn, week after week, in the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Huppah matters because faithful service is often a turn kept, not a deed remembered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a canopy
BiblicalUsage: A canopy is a covering spread over something precious, and Isaiah says God will spread a canopy over every dwelling place of Mount Zion. Joel calls the bridegroom out of his chamber and the bride out of her closet, and the psalm pictures the sun coming out of his chamber like a bridegroom. The word holds marriage and shelter in the same breath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the canopy is God's picture of covering: He spreads Himself over His people the way a bridegroom's chamber shelters a wedding. The sun itself is described as a bridegroom, and the point is joy, not duty. I hold that God means His presence to feel like a covering, not a cage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chuppim, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Huppim is one of Benjamin's sons who goes down into Egypt with Jacob's household. His name returns in the chronicle of Benjamin's sons, in a list of men who became heads of families. Nothing more is told of him, and the lists are all that remain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Huppim is remembered because God counts the sons who go down into Egypt, and every name in the household matters to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {an enactment; hence, an appointment (of time, space, quantity, labor or usage)}
BiblicalUsage: A statute is an appointment God sets in place, and Abraham kept God's statutes long before Sinai. The Passover is called a statute forever, the fat and the blood are forbidden by a statute forever, and the second Passover keeps its appointed time. The word marks what God has fixed, not what men have agreed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe statutes show that God's commands are not suggestions; they are appointments He keeps. Abraham obeyed before the law was written, and Israel was told to keep the Passover forever, because God does not change His appointments. My position is that a statute is a promise in command form: God binds Himself to what He has appointed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chukkok or Chukok, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hukkok is a town on the border of Naphtali, given to the Levites as a city of their inheritance. The name appears twice, once in the border list and once in the list of Levitical towns. It is a boundary town, and its place in the record is a place on the map.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hukkok matters because even a border town is part of the inheritance, and God gives His servants a place in the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chushathite or descendant of Chushah
BiblicalUsage: A Hushathite is a descendant of Hushah, and the name belongs to warriors: Sibbecai kills a giant, and Mebunnai stands among David's mighty men. The word appears only in battle lists, attached to men who fought the Philistines. It is a family name worn into war.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Hushathites show that God uses families, not just individuals, and a name can carry a fighting tradition. Sibbecai's victory is told in a single line, and that is enough. I hold that faithfulness in battle is often a family matter, passed from father to son.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, perhaps to tie, i.e. (figuratively and reflexively) to owe, or (by implication) to forfeit
BiblicalUsage: To owe here is to be in debt, and the steward fears that if Daniel's face looks worse than the other young men's, the king will hold him to account. The word appears once, in the mouth of a frightened servant who owes the king an explanation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the steward's fear shows how heavy a debt can feel, and Daniel's faith answers it by trusting God with the outcome.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to cover, i.e. (figuratively) to compassionate
BiblicalUsage: To pity is to spare what you could destroy, and Joseph tells his brothers not to regard their stuff, because all Egypt is before them. God tells Israel not to pity the idols of the nations, and David's eye spares Saul in the cave. Jonah learns the same lesson last: God pities Nineveh, and the prophet must learn to pity what God pities.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pity is the test of whether we have understood God's mercy, because we are quick to spare ourselves and slow to spare others. David spared the man who hunted him, and God spared the city Jonah wanted judged. My position is that a heart that cannot pity has not yet learned how much it has been pitied.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; King David; Jonah; Moses
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to tie a knot, i.e. (figuratively) to propound a riddle
BiblicalUsage: To pose a riddle is to tie a knot in words, and Samson ties one for the Philistines at his wedding feast: out of the eater came forth meat. Ezekiel is told to put forth a riddle to the house of Israel, and the riddle is a parable of eagles and vines. The word is used for a puzzle that hides a truth until it is untied.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe riddles in Scripture are not games; they are truths wrapped so that only the willing will unwrap them. Samson's riddle cost him his wife and his secret, and Ezekiel's riddle carried a judgment. I hold that God speaks in riddles to those who will listen closely, and plainly to those who will not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a circle
BiblicalUsage: The circle is the vault of the heavens, and Isaiah says God sits upon the circle of the earth while men are as grasshoppers. Job's friend says God walks on the circle of heaven, beyond our sight. Wisdom says she was there when God set a compass upon the face of the deep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the circle tells us two things at once: God is above it all, and He was there before it began. The earth is a circle under His feet, and wisdom was beside Him when He drew it. My position is that a God who can sit on the circle of the earth is a God big enough to hold my life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a circle
BiblicalUsage: The circle is the vault of the heavens, and Isaiah says God sits upon the circle of the earth while men are as grasshoppers. Job's friend says God walks on the circle of heaven, beyond our sight. Wisdom says she was there when God set a compass upon the face of the deep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the circle tells us two things at once: God is above it all, and He was there before it began. The earth is a circle under His feet, and wisdom was beside Him when He drew it. My position is that a God who can sit on the circle of the earth is a God big enough to hold my life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chul, a son of Aram; also the region settled by him
BiblicalUsage: Hul is a son of Aram, named in the table of nations, and the region settled by his descendants carries his name. The name appears twice, both times in lists of the sons of Shem. Nothing is told of his life, and the land is his only memorial.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hul is remembered because the nations themselves are part of God's story, and every people has a place in His book.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to twist or whirl (in a circular or spiral manner), i.e. (specifically) to dance, to writhe in pain (especially of parturition) or fear; figuratively, to wait, to pervert
BiblicalUsage: To wait is to stay in place until the time comes, and Noah waits seven more days before he sends the dove out again. The nations will tremble when they hear of Israel, and a woman in labour writhes before she brings forth. Saul is sorely wounded by the archers, and the same word that means waiting also means writhing in pain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe waiting and writhing belong to the same word because waiting in Scripture is never passive. Noah waits and watches, the nations tremble and wait, and the woman labours toward a birth. My position is that God uses waiting to do His deepest work, and the pain of it is often the sign that something is being born.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sunburnt or swarthy (blackish)
BiblicalUsage: Brown is the colour of the flock Jacob bargains for, the dark and speckled sheep that will be his wages. Laban agrees, and then removes the brown cattle from the flock before Jacob can claim them. Jacob sets the brown sheep apart, and the word appears only in this one bargain, four times in four verses.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brown sheep matter because Jacob's wages depended on them, and God made the bargain work for the man who was cheated. Laban tried to take the brown ones away, and God gave them back. I hold that God sees the cheated bargain and settles it His own way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chupham, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hupham is a son of Benjamin, named in the census in the wilderness as the head of the family of the Huphamites. His name appears once, in the count of Israel's fighting men. The family that carries his name is counted among the tribes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hupham is remembered because the census counts every family, and no household is too small for God's numbering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chuphamite or descendant of Chupham
BiblicalUsage: A Huphamite is a descendant of Hupham, and the name appears once, in the wilderness census. The family is counted with Benjamin's tribe, and that is all the record says.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Huphamites matter because God counts families, not only famous men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: white linen
BiblicalUsage: White linen is the cloth of the palace, and the court of Ahasuerus hangs white and blue curtains for the king's feast. Mordecai leaves the king's presence in royal apparel of blue and white, and the linen marks the honour of the moment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe white linen in Esther shows how quickly God can turn a death sentence into a royal procession.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chur, the name of four Israelites and one Midianite
BiblicalUsage: Hur is the name of several men, and the two clearest are the one who goes up the hill with Moses while Joshua fights Amalek below and the king of Midian killed in the war with the Midianites. Aaron and Hur stand with Moses on the hill, and the other Hur dies with the kings of Midian. The name is the same, and the men are not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hur shows how one name can hold two very different stories: a man who stands with Moses on the hill, and a king who falls in judgment. The first Hur is the one I want to be like.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: white linen
BiblicalUsage: White linen is the cloth of the palace, and the court of Ahasuerus hangs white and blue curtains for the king's feast. Mordecai leaves the king's presence in royal apparel of blue and white, and the linen marks the honour of the moment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe white linen in Esther shows how quickly God can turn a death sentence into a royal procession.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Churam, the name of an Israelite and two Syrians
BiblicalUsage: Huram is the name of a Benjamite in the genealogies and of the king of Tyre who sends cedar and craftsmen to Solomon. The Benjamite appears once in a list, and the king appears in the letters and the building of the temple. The name covers a nobody and a king, and both are remembered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Huram of Tyre matters because a foreign king helped build God's house, and God uses outsiders for His work. The other Huram matters because God counts the Benjamites too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Churai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hurai is one of David's mighty men, named in the list of the warriors who stood with him. Nothing more is said of him, and his deeds are not recorded. He stands in the list because he stood with David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hurai is remembered because standing with David was itself the deed, and God records loyalty.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Churi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Huri is a Gadite, named once as the father of Abihail in the genealogy of Gad. His name appears in a single line, and no deed is attached to it. He is a link in a chain, and the chain is the point.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Huri matters because a genealogy is a chain of real people, and every link holds the next one up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hurry; figuratively, to be eager with excitement or enjoyment
BiblicalUsage: To hurry is to move fast because the matter is urgent: the tribes promise to go armed before Israel until the land is won, and Moses says vengeance is coming in the day their foot shall slide. The ambush hurries against Gibeah, and Jonathan's lad hurries to fetch the arrow. The word is speed with a purpose behind it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hurry in Scripture is usually God's people moving to obey, or God's judgment moving to arrive. The tribes hurried to keep a promise, and the lad hurried to serve his master. I hold that speed is good when the direction is right, and dangerous when it is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chushah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hushah is named once, as the father of Ezer in the genealogy of Judah. Nothing else is said of him, and his son's name is all that follows. He is a name in a list, and the list is his memorial.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hushah is remembered because Judah's line is God's line, and every father in it counts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chusham, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Husham is a king of Edom, from the land of Teman, who reigns after Jobab and before Hadad. His name appears twice, once in the list of Edomite kings and once in the chronicle that copies it. He rules a kingdom outside Israel, and the record keeps his reign.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Husham matters because God records the kings of Edom too, and no kingdom stands outside His knowledge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chushai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hushai is David's friend, the Archite who meets him on the Mount of Olives when Absalom has taken Jerusalem. David sends him back to defeat Ahithophel's counsel, and his advice saves David's life. He also appears as the father of Baana, one of Solomon's officers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hushai shows that loyalty in dark days is worth more than cleverness in easy ones. Ahithophel's counsel was better, and Hushai's was worse, yet God used the worse counsel to save David.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chushim, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Hushim is the name of three Israelites: a son of Dan who goes down into Egypt, a son of Aher in Benjamin's line, and a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hushim. The name appears in lists only, with no story for any of the three. Each one is counted in his father's household.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hushim matters because three men share one name and God counts all three, and no one is lost in a crowd.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a string; by implication, a measuring tape
BiblicalUsage: A thread is the smallest thing worth counting: Abram swears he will not take so much as a thread from the king of Sodom, and Rahab ties a scarlet thread in her window. Samson snaps new ropes like a thread, and the temple pillars are measured in lines of brass. The word runs from a refusal to a rescue to a measurement.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thread shows how God uses small things to hold great ones. Abram's thread is integrity, Rahab's thread is salvation, and Samson's thread is strength broken. My position is that the scarlet thread is the picture I keep: a thin red line, and a whole household saved by it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

BiblicalUsage: A thread is the smallest thing worth counting: Abram swears he will not take so much as a thread from the king of Sodom, and Rahab ties a scarlet thread in her window. Definition: properly, separate by a wall, i.e. outside, outdoors
BiblicalUsage: Outside is where the unclean is carried, where the Passover lamb may not be taken, and where Noah pitches the ark within and without. The word marks the boundary between what belongs inside and what must go out, and the camp's purity depends on keeping it. Outside is not always punishment: it is also where the work is done and the waste is burned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the line between inside and outside matters because holiness is a real boundary, not a feeling. The camp kept its purity by sending out what defiled it, and the ark was sealed inside and out. I hold that the gospel reverses the direction in the best way: Christ went outside the gate so that the unclean could come in.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; The Passover
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the 22nd, 14th and an obsolete letter (G4742 as a cross) of the Greek alphabet (intermediate between the 5th and 6th), used as numbers; denoting respectively 600, 60 and 6; 666 as a numeral:--six hundred threescore and six.
BiblicalUsage: These three letters are the old way of writing six hundred threescore and six, the number of the beast. The Greek text behind the audit spells the number out in words, while other ancient copies write it as three letters, chi, xi, and stigma. The letters stand for a number, and the number stands for a man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the number matters less than what it points to: a human system that demands worship, and a God who has already numbered its days.
RelatedEvents: The Beasts from the Sea and the Land
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (providential) turn (of affairs)
BiblicalUsage: A turn of affairs is a change God brings about, and the division of the kingdom happens because the cause is from the LORD. The word appears once, in the verse that explains why Rehoboam would not listen. The turning is not an accident; it is God's doing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God turns the affairs of nations, even through a foolish king's stubbornness, and His purposes are never derailed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sibbecai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Sibbecai is the Hushathite who kills Saph, one of the giants of the Philistines, in the battle at Gob. His name appears in the list of David's mighty men and in the account of the giant wars. He is a warrior remembered for a single killing that mattered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sibbecai shows that God gives ordinary warriors extraordinary victories, and one giant falls at a time.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an ear of grain
BiblicalUsage: Shibboleth is an ear of grain, and it becomes a password at the fords of Jordan: the men of Ephraim cannot say it, and forty-two thousand fall. The word is a test of belonging, and the test is in the tongue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shibboleth shows that words reveal where we come from, and God hears what our speech says about our hearts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sibrajim, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Sibraim is a place on the northern border of the promised land, named once in Ezekiel's vision of the borders. It stands between Hamath and Damascus, on the line God draws for the restored land. The name is a boundary marker in a prophecy of return.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sibraim matters because God draws the borders of His people's future, and no part of the promise is left vague.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sismai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Sismai is a descendant of Jerahmeel in Judah's line, named once in the genealogy. His father is Eleasah and his son is Shallum, and the chain runs through him. Nothing more is told of his life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sismai is remembered because the chain of Judah matters, and every link in it is held by God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an (idolatrous) booth
BiblicalUsage: Siccuth is the idolatrous booth Israel carried in the wilderness, the shrine of their star god. Amos names it in the judgment against a people who worshipped what they had made. The name appears once, and the sin it names is the reason for the exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Siccuth shows how quickly worship goes wrong when people build their own gods, and Amos names it plainly so no one can miss it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: silliness
BiblicalUsage: Folly is the opposite of wisdom, and the Preacher gives his heart to know it: madness and folly, and the difference between them. He tries wine and wisdom and folly together, and finds the same end waiting for them all. The word appears only in Ecclesiastes, and it carries the book's verdict on a life without God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe folly is not stupidity; it is wisdom without God, and the Preacher proves it by trying everything. He had the wealth and the wisdom to test it all, and his verdict stands. My position is that folly ends where it began — in vanity — and only the fear of God gives wisdom its meaning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Silla, a place in Jerusalem
BiblicalUsage: Silla is the place where Joash is struck down by his servants, in the house of Millo on the way down to Silla. The name appears once, as the road where a king's life ends. Joash, who repaired the temple as a boy, dies by conspiracy as a man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Silla is a sober reminder that a good beginning does not guarantee a good end, and kings need God to the last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prickle (as if pendulous)
BiblicalUsage: A brier is a prickling thorn, and God tells Ezekiel not to fear the briers and thorns among whom he must speak. The house of Israel will no longer be a pricking brier to God's people, and the word carries the sting with it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God warns His prophets about the briers because He knows the work will hurt, and He sends them anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sippai, a Philistine
BiblicalUsage: Sippai is a giant of the Philistines, killed by Sibbecai the Hushathite in the war at Gezer. His name appears once, in the account of the giants who fell to David's men. He is remembered because he fell.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sippai matters because the giants kept coming, and God's men kept meeting them, one at a time.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wainscot
BiblicalUsage: The wainscot is the cedar panelling that covers the inside of the temple, from floor to ceiling. Solomon builds the house with cedar within, and the panelling hides the stone behind beauty. The word appears once, in the building of the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cedar panelling shows that God is honoured by beauty in His house, and nothing in it is left bare.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sirah, a cistern so-called
BiblicalUsage: Sirah is the well from which Joab sends messengers to bring Abner back to Hebron, where Joab kills him. The name appears once, as the place of a murder dressed up as a summons. Abner walks back trusting the message, and the well is the last place of his peace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sirah shows how revenge dresses itself as business, and Joab's murder of Abner is the deed that stains his whole career.
RelatedEvents: David's War with the House of Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a coat of mail
BiblicalUsage: A coat of mail is the armour of the horseman, and Jeremiah tells Egypt to harness the horses and put on the coats of mail. Babylon is told to bend the bow and lift up the coat of mail, and the armour is part of the judgment on both nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe armour in Jeremiah is a picture of trust in the wrong things, because no coat of mail can stand against the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sithri, an Israelite,
BiblicalUsage: Zithri is a son of Uzziel, named once in the genealogy of the Levites before the Exodus. He is a cousin of Aaron and Moses, and his name stands in the record of the family that will carry the priesthood. Nothing more is told of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Zithri is remembered because the priestly line is counted before it is called, and God knows His servants by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sia or Siaha, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Sia, also called Siaha, is one of the Nethinim, the temple servants who return from exile with Zerubbabel. His name appears twice, once in each list of the returning exiles. He belongs to the servants whose names are kept because they came home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sia matters because the temple servants are named, and the lowest service in God's house is remembered.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sisera, the name of a Canaanitish king and of one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Sisera is the captain of Jabin's army, with nine hundred chariots of iron, and he oppresses Israel for twenty years. Deborah and Barak defeat him, and he flees to the tent of Jael, where a tent peg ends his life. Samuel reminds Israel of him generations later, as a warning of what happens when they forget God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sisera shows that no army, however iron its chariots, can stand against the God who fights for His people. The captain who terrified Israel dies in a woman's tent, and the song that follows is a song of deliverance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sichon, an Amoritish king
BiblicalUsage: Sihon is the Amorite king whose land Israel asks to pass through, and who refuses and fights instead. Israel defeats him and takes his cities, from Heshbon to the border, and Moses retells the victory as proof that God fights for His people. The name stands for the first kingdom that falls before Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sihon matters because he is the first king who learns that refusing God's people is refusing God. The victory at Heshbon is told and retold because it proves the promise is real.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat of Sihon and Og
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: scoria
BiblicalUsage: Dross is the scum that rises when silver is refined, and the psalm says God puts away the wicked like dross. Proverbs says take away the dross from the silver, and a vessel comes forth for the finer. Isaiah says Judah's silver has become dross, and Ezekiel says the whole house of Israel has become dross in the furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dross is the Bible's picture of what refining removes, and every believer knows the furnace. God does not throw away the silver; He takes away the dross so the silver can shine. My position is that the fire is not God's anger at His people — it is His care for them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sin the name of an Egyptian town and (probably) desert adjoining
BiblicalUsage: Sin is the wilderness between Elim and Sinai, where Israel comes on the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt. The whole congregation murmurs there for bread, and God gives them manna. The name appears in the journey lists as a stage on the way to the mountain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wilderness of Sin matters because it is where God feeds a murmuring people, and His provision does not wait for their gratitude.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sinai, mountain of Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Sinai is the mountain where God gives the law, and Israel comes to it in the third month after leaving Egypt. The LORD tells Moses to be ready, because on the third day He will come down in the sight of all the people. The name is the mountain of the covenant, and everything after it is measured from it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sinai is where God becomes Israel's God in covenant, and the mountain still defines what it means to belong to Him. The law was given on a mountain that burned, and the gospel was finished on a hill where a cross stood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Sinite, or descendant of one of the sons of Canaan
BiblicalUsage: A Sinite is a descendant of Canaan, named in the table of nations among the sons of Ham. The name appears twice, both times in lists of the peoples who filled the land. The Sinites are one of the peoples Israel will later meet in Canaan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Sinites matter because the table of nations names the peoples God knows, even those who will oppose His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sinim, a distant Oriental region
BiblicalUsage: Sinim is a distant land, named once, as the place from which God's people will come home. Some say it is China, and some say it is the south, and Isaiah does not say. The point is the distance: they will come from far away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sinim shows that God's gathering reaches to the ends of the earth, and no distance is too far for His people to come home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pot; also a thorn (as springing up rapidly); by implication, a hook
BiblicalUsage: A pot is the vessel of the kitchen and the temple: Israel remembers the flesh pots of Egypt, and the temple is furnished with pots of brass. Elisha purifies a pot of poisonous pottage for the sons of the prophets, and the same word names the thorn that springs up fast. The pot holds what feeds a household, and what poisons it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pot is the picture of ordinary life, where God provides and where poison creeps in. Israel missed the pots of Egypt more than they trusted the God who fed them, and Elisha's meal shows that God can cleanse what is poisoned. I hold that God cares about the kitchen as much as the temple, because His people live in both.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sivan, the third Hebrew month
BiblicalUsage: Sivan is the third month of the Hebrew year, and the king's scribes write Mordecai's decree in it. The month appears once, as the date on a law that saves a people. The timing matters: the decree goes out in time for the Jews to defend themselves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sivan matters because God works on a calendar, and the decree that saves His people is dated, not vague.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: potation, concretely (wine), or abstractly (carousal)
BiblicalUsage: Strong drink is wine drunk to excess, and the law calls the stubborn son a glutton and a drunkard. Hosea says the princes love shame more than their drink, Isaiah says the wine is mixed with water, and Nahum says the drunkards will be devoured like stubble. The word is not wine itself; it is wine abused.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Bible never condemns the gift, but it always condemns the abuse of it. Strong drink makes a man stubborn, shameful, and dull to God, and the prophets name it plainly. My position is that drunkenness is a small sin with a large harvest, and the harvest is always judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a copse
BiblicalUsage: A thicket is a tangle of brush, and Jeremiah says the destroyer of nations has gone up from his thicket like a lion. The word appears once, and the picture is of danger crouched and hidden.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thicket shows that judgment can wait out of sight, and the day it rises is the day it is too late to run.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a load (figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: A burden is a load laid on the shoulders, and Isaiah says the yoke of the oppressor will be broken as in the day of Midian. The burden will be taken from the shoulder and the yoke from the neck, and the Assyrian's burden will be removed from God's people. The word is the weight of oppression, and the promise is that God lifts it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God knows the weight His people carry, and He does not leave the burden where it is. The yoke breaks because the anointing breaks it, and the oppressor's load falls off. I hold that every burden God lifts is proof that He sees, and that He acts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something surrounding the person, i.e. a shield
BiblicalUsage: A shield is what surrounds a person, and the psalm says God's truth will be your shield and buckler. The word appears once, and it pictures protection that wraps around on every side.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's truth is not a wall in front of us but a shield around us, and that is why the psalmist can rest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a (black) tile (or tessara) for laying borders with
BiblicalUsage: A pavement of coloured stone is what the palace court is laid with, and the feast of Ahasuerus is spread over red and blue and white and black marble. The word appears once, in the description of a king's wealth. The pavement is the floor of a feast that ends in a queen's fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pavement shows how rich the world can look, and how little it protects the people who walk on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dungeon (as surrounded by walls)
BiblicalUsage: The prison is the round house where Joseph is put after Potiphar's wife lies about him, and the LORD is with him there. The keeper commits all the prisoners to Joseph's hand, and whatever he does prospers. The word appears only in Joseph's story, and it is the place where God is with the innocent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prison shows that God's presence is not limited to palaces, and Joseph's faithfulness in a cell is the same as his faithfulness in a house. The LORD was with Joseph in the pit and in the prison, and the promotion came when God chose. I hold that the darkest rooms in the Bible are often where God does His best work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hut (as of entwined boughs); also a lair
BiblicalUsage: A covert is a hiding place: the lion waits in his covert for the poor, and God hides His people in His pavilion in the time of trouble. Jeremiah says the LORD has forsaken His covert, and the psalm says God's tabernacle is in Salem. The word is a lair for a predator and a shelter for the hunted, and the difference is who is hiding.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the covert shows two kinds of hiding: the wicked hiding to strike, and the righteous hiding to be kept. God hides His people in His own pavilion, and that is the only hiding place that saves. I hold that the safest covert in the world is the presence of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a kind of locust (from its destructiveness)
BiblicalUsage: The bald locust is one of the clean insects Israel may eat, named once in the law of clean and unclean. The word is a kind of locust, and the law lists it among the flying creeping things that go on four feet. It appears once, and it is there because God names what His people may eat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a locust in the law shows that God cares about the details of His people's daily life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a military mound, i.e. rampart of besiegers
BiblicalUsage: A siege mound is the ramp an army builds against a walled city, and Joab's men build one against Abel while a wise woman saves the city. Sennacherib is told he will not build a mound against Jerusalem, and Jeremiah says to build one against the city that will not hear. The word is the slow work of war, and God decides whether it stands or falls.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the siege mound shows that human armies plan slowly and God answers quickly. Joab's mound is stopped by a wise word, and Sennacherib's is stopped by the angel of the LORD. I hold that no ramp built against God's people can stand when He says it will not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flour (as chipped off)
BiblicalUsage: Fine flour is the best of the wheat, ground smooth, and Sarah kneads it for the strangers at the door. The consecration offerings and the meal offerings are made of it, and the Nazirite brings cakes of it. The word is the offering of the best, given in the ordinary work of the kitchen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fine flour shows that God accepts the best of ordinary work, not only the grand gesture. Sarah's bread and the priest's offering are the same flour, and God takes both. I hold that the meal offering matters because it says a life of daily bread can be worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sophereth, a temple servant
BiblicalUsage: Sophereth is a servant of Solomon, named twice in the lists of the returning exiles. Her children return with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple, and her name is kept among the servants. Nothing more is told of her, and the return is her memorial.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sophereth matters because the servants of Solomon's house came home, and God counts the families who rebuild.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: So, an Egyptian king
BiblicalUsage: So is the king of Egypt to whom Hoshea sends messengers, looking for help against Assyria. The name appears once, and the alliance it names is the sin that brings the fall of Samaria. Egypt cannot save Israel, and the king's name is the proof.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe So shows that looking to Egypt for help is always a mistake, because the arm of flesh cannot save the people of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a session, i.e. company of persons (in close deliberation); by implication, intimacy, consultation, a secret
BiblicalUsage: A secret is the counsel of those who sit close together, and Jacob says his soul will not come into the secret of Simeon and Levi. Eliphaz asks Job if he has heard the secret of God, and the psalm says the secret of the LORD is with those who fear Him. Proverbs says the froward are an abomination, but His secret is with the righteous.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's secret is not hidden from His people; it is hidden for them, given to those who fear Him. The wicked have their own secret counsels, and they end in violence, but the secret of the LORD ends in friendship. My position is that intimacy with God is the reward of the fear of the LORD.
RelatedTopics: Friendship with Christ; Fear of the Lord; Wisdom
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sodi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Sodi is the father of Gaddiel, one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. His name appears once, in the list of the spies and their fathers. His son goes into the land and comes back with a report of fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sodi matters because the spies' fathers are named, and the fear that followed is traced to real families.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a termination}
BiblicalUsage: The end is the limit of a thing, and Nebuchadnezzar's tree grows until its height reaches to the end of the earth. Daniel tells the king the tree is him, and his dominion reaches to the end of the earth. Darius decrees that God is the living God whose kingdom will not be destroyed to the end, and the little horn's dominion is taken away at the end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the end in Daniel is always God's end, not man's. The tree grows to the end of the earth and is cut down, and the kingdoms of men end where God's kingdom begins. I hold that every earthly power has an end written into it, and God's kingdom has none.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a termination}
BiblicalUsage: The end is the limit of a thing, and Nebuchadnezzar's tree grows until its height reaches to the end of the earth. Daniel tells the king the tree is him, and his dominion reaches to the end of the earth. Definition: Sotai, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Sotai is one of the Nethinim, named twice in the lists of the servants who return from exile. His children come home with Zerubbabel to serve in the temple, and his name is kept among the temple servants. Nothing more is told of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sotai matters because the temple servants came home, and the work of God's house depends on people whose names are only in lists.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hut or lair
BiblicalUsage: A booth is a hut of branches, and Jacob builds booths for his cattle at Succoth and names the place for them. The feast of booths remembers the wilderness, when Israel lived in booths, and Uriah refuses to go home to his wife while the ark dwells in booths. The word is shelter that is temporary, and the feast makes the temporary holy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the booth teaches that all our shelter is temporary, and God means us to know it. Israel lived in booths so they would remember the wilderness, and Uriah stayed out while the ark dwelt in booths, while his king slept in sin. My position is that a life lived in booths is a life that trusts God for tomorrow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Sukkite, or inhabitant of some place near Egypt (i.e. hut-dwellers)
BiblicalUsage: A Sukkite is one of the peoples who come up with Shishak against Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year. The name appears once, in the list of the invading host. They are hut-dwellers, and they come against the city that has forsaken God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Sukkites matter because even a people named for huts is part of the judgment God sends on a faithless king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: booths of (the) daughters; brothels, i.e. idoalatrous tents for impure purpose
BiblicalUsage: The booths of the daughters are the idolatrous tents the Babylonians set up in Samaria, shrines for impure worship. The name appears once, in the list of the gods the settlers brought with them. The booths are the opposite of the feast of booths: a holy shelter turned into a brothel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the booths of the daughters show how a holy thing can be twisted into an unholy one, and the land is judged for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Succoth, the name of a place in Egypt and of three in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Succoth is the name of places in Egypt and in the land, and Jacob names the first one for the booths he builds there. Israel journeys from Rameses to Succoth on the night of the Exodus, and the name marks the first stage of the journey out. The place is named for shelter, and the shelter is the first thing a freed people needs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Succoth matters because the Exodus begins with a place to rest, and God gives His people shelter on the first night of freedom.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stair-case
BiblicalUsage: The ladder in Jacob's dream reaches from earth to heaven, and the angels of God ascend and descend on it. The word appears once, and it is the picture of the way between heaven and earth. Jacob wakes and says the LORD is in this place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ladder shows that heaven is not closed to earth, and God comes down to meet the man who is running away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Suach, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Suach is a son of Zophah in Asher's line, named once in the genealogy. His brothers are listed with him, and nothing more is told of his life. He is a name in the house of Asher, and the house is the point.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Suach is remembered because Asher's house is counted tribe by tribe, and no son is left out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a horse (as leaping); also a swallow (from its rapid flight)
BiblicalUsage: The horse is the strength of Egypt and the pride of kings, and Pharaoh's horses pursue Israel into the sea. The plague falls on the horses, and the song of Moses celebrates the horse and rider thrown into the sea. Joshua meets kings with horses and chariots as many as the sand, and the word is always a picture of power that cannot save.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the horse in Scripture is the test of trust: will you trust the chariot, or the God who throws it into the sea? Egypt's horses drowned, and Canaan's horses were hamstrung, because God fights for His people. My position is that every horse in the Bible asks the same question, and the right answer is always the LORD.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mare
BiblicalUsage: The mare is the picture the beloved is compared to, a mare among Pharaoh's chariots. The word appears once, in the first words of the lover to his beloved. The comparison is to beauty and strength together, in the harness of a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mare shows that love in the Song is strong and beautiful at once, and the lover is not embarrassed to say so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something swept away, i.e. filth
BiblicalUsage: Filth is what is swept away, and Isaiah says the dead bodies of the people will be as filth in the streets. The word appears once, in the judgment on a people who have refused God. The picture is of refuse, thrown out and left.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the filth in Isaiah is what sin makes of a people, and the judgment is that God leaves them to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Susi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Susi is the father of Gaddi, one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. His name appears once, in the list of the spies and their fathers. His son sees the land and brings back a report that frightens the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Susi matters because the spies' fathers are named, and the unbelief that follows is traced to real men.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hem in, i.e. bind
BiblicalUsage: To hem in is to bind or enclose, and the Song describes the beloved's navel as a round goblet that does not lack liquor, and her belly as a heap of wheat set about with lilies. The word appears once, in the praise of her beauty. The hemming is the picture of a thing made complete and enclosed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Song's praise is unembarrassed because God made the body good, and love may say so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hem in, i.e. bind
BiblicalUsage: To hem in is to bind or enclose, and the Song describes the beloved's navel as a round goblet that does not lack liquor, and her belly as a heap of wheat set about with lilies. The word appears once, in the praise of her beauty. The hemming is the picture of a thing made complete and enclosed.

Definition: an inclosure, i.e. cage (for an animal)
BiblicalUsage: The cage is where the lion is put, and Ezekiel says the nations took the young lion in chains and brought him to Babylon in a cage. The word appears once, in the lament for the princes of Israel. The cage is the end of a king who roared and devoured.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cage shows what happens to princes who devour their people: the nations cage them, and the roaring stops.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to smear over (with oil), i.e. anoint
BiblicalUsage: Anointing is the smearing of oil on the body, and the law says the olive will cast its fruit, so the anointing will do no good. Ruth washes and anoints herself before she goes to the threshing floor, and David anoints himself after his child dies. The captives are anointed by the men of Judah on their way home, and the word moves from the body to the burial and back to mercy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe anointing with oil is the Bible's picture of care: for the body, for the dead, and for the stranger on the road. Ruth anoints herself for a new life, David anoints himself to go on living, and the captives are anointed by their neighbours on their way home. I hold that oil on the skin is a small mercy, and small mercies are how God holds people together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bagpipe (with a double pipe)
BiblicalUsage: The bagpipe is one of the instruments that sound when Nebuchadnezzar's image is set up, and everyone must fall down and worship when they hear it. The herald lists it with the cornet, flute, harp, and psaltery, and the sound is the signal for idolatry. The word appears only in Daniel's account of the golden image.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bagpipe shows that idolatry always has music, and the music makes the bowing feel like a celebration. The three young men hear the same sound and do not bow, and their refusal is the sermon. I hold that the test of worship is not the music but the object, and no instrument can make a false god true.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to come to an end
BiblicalUsage: To come to an end is what happens to the kingdoms of men in Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the stone cut without hands will break them and bring them to an end. The same word describes Nebuchadnezzar driven from men, eating grass until his reason returns. The end comes to kingdoms and to kings alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's end is God's end, and every kingdom that sets itself against Him will come to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the Reed (Sea)
BiblicalUsage: The Reed Sea is named once in the opening of Deuteronomy, as the place where Moses speaks to Israel in the wilderness. The name marks the sea Israel crossed, and the place where the journey began. It is the boundary between Egypt and the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Reed Sea matters because it is the water God parted, and every retelling of the story starts from it.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to come to an end
BiblicalUsage: To come to an end is what happens to the kingdoms of men in Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the stone cut without hands will break them and bring them to an end. The same word describes Nebuchadnezzar driven from men, eating grass until his reason returns. The end comes to kingdoms and to kings alike.
