Definition: a battering-tower
BiblicalUsage: The battering tower is the engine of siege, built against the walls of Jerusalem and set up by the king of Babylon. Ezekiel pictures the ramps and the towers rising against the city, and Jeremiah records the siege that ended it. The tower is the slow, certain work of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tower warns the proud city: walls that are trusted instead of God will be battered down. The tower rises slowly and falls quickly, and the city that trusts its walls has trusted the wrong thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: threshing-time
BiblicalUsage: Threshing time is the season of harvest, when the grain is separated from the chaff and the labour of the year is gathered in. The law promises threshing that will reach to the vintage, and the vintage to the sowing time, if the people keep the covenant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe threshing time is the picture of God's harvest: the season when what was sown is finally separated and gathered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, pining; by analogy, fear
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Job's picture of the leviathan: his heart is as firm as a stone, and fear pines away before him. Pining is the fear that wastes the heart while it waits.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse pictures fear honestly: it does not strike once, it pines, and it wastes the strong.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pining
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, among the curses of the covenant: the Lord will give a trembling heart and failing of eyes and sorrow of mind, and the soul shall pine away. It is the slow wasting of a people who have turned away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows that disobedience wastes a people from the inside, long before any enemy arrives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: anxiety
BiblicalUsage: Anxiety is the care that eats the heart, and Scripture names it plainly. The prophets picture a land eating bread with carefulness and drinking water with astonishment, and the proverb says a word of anxiety in the heart makes it stoop, but a good word makes it glad. Anxiety is not a small thing; it bends the heart down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse in Proverbs is the prescription: a good word lifts what anxiety bends down, and the good word is God's. I hold that anxiety is not a sin to hide but a burden to bring, and the Lord who knows our cares has promised to carry them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: knowledge
BiblicalUsage: Knowledge in Scripture is not information but acquaintance, and the word gathers the knowledge that saves and the knowledge that accuses. Hannah sings that the Lord is a God of knowledge, Isaiah promises that the earth will be filled with it, and Job's friend claims to be perfect in it. The knowledge of God is the knowledge that matters.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe knowledge without the fear of God is only noise. The knowledge that saves is the knowledge of Him, and it begins where Hannah began: the Lord knows, and He weighs.
RelatedTopics: Knowledge of God; Wisdom; Fear of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably akin to G1161; a particle of emphasis or explicitness; now, then, etc.:--also, and, doubtless, now, therefore.
BiblicalUsage: The little word carries emphasis, and the New Testament uses it to press a point home. Paul writes that we are bought with a price, and the therefore is stronger for it; the Lord says the harvest is plentiful and the labourers are few, and the indeed sharpens the call. A small word, doing the work of a finger on the chest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe small words carry weight in Scripture: the therefore and the indeed are where the argument lands, and we should not skip them. The small word is the hinge, and the sentence turns on it more than we think.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Deuel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Deuel is the father of Eliasaph, prince of the tribe of Gad, named in the numbering, the offerings, and the march of the camp. His name appears where the tribes are counted and ordered for the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse honours the fathers behind the princes: the tribe is named by its father, and the father by his son.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle (adversative or continuative); but, and, etc.:--also, and, but, moreover, now (often unexpressed in English).
BiblicalUsage: This is the commonest little word in the Greek New Testament, the hinge on which sentences turn: and, but, moreover, now. It joins, it contrasts, it continues, and it appears thousands of times because every story needs it. Paul uses it to turn from argument to appeal, and the Gospels use it to move the narrative from one scene to the next.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word teaches us that Scripture is a story, not a list: the and and the but are where one thing leads to another, and the gospel itself turns on a but. The little word is the thread that holds the story together, and the story is the gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: knowledge
BiblicalUsage: Knowledge is the treasure Job's friends claim and the gift Elihu promises to lay out plainly. Job demands knowledge of his case, Elihu claims perfect knowledge, and the Lord answers from the whirlwind with the knowledge that humbles them all. The word gathers the debate about who really knows.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the book of Job ends the debate: the knowledge that matters is not the kind we argue about, but the kind that kneels when God speaks. The knowledge that kneels is the knowledge that saves, and the rest is only argument.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sacrifice
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the decree for the rebuilding of the temple: the height and the breadth of the house are given, and the sacrifice is to be offered there. A sacrifice is the cost of the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse ties worship to its cost: the house is built for the offering, and the offering is what makes it a house of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sacrifice
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the decree for the rebuilding of the temple: the height and the breadth of the house are given, and the sacrifice is to be offered there. A sacrifice is the cost of the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse ties worship to its cost: the house is built for the offering, and the offering is what makes it a house of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to stick to
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Daniel's picture of the kingdoms: the iron and the clay do not stick to one another, and the divided kingdom cannot hold. A mixture that will not cleave is the image of a world that cannot be joined.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse pictures every human empire: strong in part and brittle in part, and unable to hold together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: honey (from its stickiness); by analogy, syrup
KeyPassages: 1 Kings 14:3; Exodus 3:17; Judges 14:8; Song of Solomon 5:1; 2 Chronicles 31:5
BiblicalUsage: Honey is the sweetness of the promised land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and the gift that marks abundance. Jonathan tastes it and his eyes are enlightened, Samson finds it in the lion's carcass, and the beloved's lips drop as the honeycomb. The law commands the firstfruits of honey to be brought to the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe honey is the taste of the promise: God does not only feed His people, He feeds them sweetly, and the land He gives is good. I hold that the sweetness of His word is better still, sweeter than honey to the mouth.
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Judges; 1 Kings; 2 Chronicles; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cake of pressed figs
BiblicalUsage: The cake of figs is the food of the journey and the medicine of the king: Abigail carries two hundred of them to David's men, and Hezekiah's boil is healed with a lump of figs laid on it. It is the plain, pressed provision of ordinary life, and God uses it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fig cake is the gospel of ordinary provision: God feeds His people with what is at hand, and He heals with what is pressed and plain. The plain provision is the provision God uses, and the fig cake in the hand is worth more than the feast in the dream.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a joint; by implication, solder
BiblicalUsage: The word names the joint where the spear finds its way between the plates of armour, and the solder that holds metal together. Ahab is wounded at the joint of his harness, and the workman strengthens the solder of the idol. The joint is the weak place and the joining place both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the joint is a picture of the body: where we are joined we are strong, and where the joint fails the whole armour fails. The joint is where the body holds together, and the body that holds together is the body that stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pestilence
BiblicalUsage: Pestilence is the judgment that walks with sword and famine, and the word appears wherever God warns His people. David is offered three judgments and chooses the pestilence, the hand of the Lord rather than the hand of man. The psalm promises that the pestilence that walks in darkness will not come near the one who dwells in the secret place of the Most High.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pestilence teaches us to choose our judge: David chose the hand of the Lord because the Lord's hand is merciful, even in judgment. I hold that the shelter of the Most High is the only refuge when the pestilence walks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Debir, the name of an Amoritish king and of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Debir is a name that belongs to three places at once: an Amorite king who fought against Joshua, and two towns in the land. The king of Debir is named among the kings Joshua defeated, the town in the south is taken by the tribe of Judah, and the town in the east is a city of refuge on the border of Gad. One name, a king and two cities, all on the map of conquest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name reminds us that the conquest was a real campaign against real kings in real towns, and the Lord gave them all into Israel's hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the shrine or innermost part of the sanctuary
BiblicalUsage: The innermost part of the sanctuary is the holy of holies, where the ark rested beneath the wings of the cherubim. Solomon built the oracle within the temple, overlaid it with pure gold, and set the ark there, and the psalmist lifts his hands toward it in prayer. It is the place where God dwells between the cherubim, and no one enters but the high priest, once a year, with blood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the inner shrine is the heart of the temple and the heart of the gospel: the place where God meets man was once shut, and Christ has opened it. I hold that the veil is torn, and the way into the holiest is now open to all who come by His blood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Deborah, the name of two Hebrewesses
BiblicalUsage: Deborah is the name of two women: the nurse of Rebekah, buried under the oak at Bethel, and the prophetess who judged Israel under the palm tree. The prophetess summoned Barak, went with him to the battle, and sang the song of the victory over Sisera. The nurse's death is a grief; the judge's song is a triumph, and both are remembered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Deborah shows that God raises up whom He wills: a nurse who served faithfully and a prophetess who led a nation, and both are written down. My position is that faithfulness in the small place prepares a person for the great one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the bee (from its systematic instincts)
BiblicalUsage: The bee is the small, ordered worker whose sting and whose honey both appear in Scripture. The Amorites chased Israel as bees do, the Lord whistles for the fly and the bee of Assyria, and Samson finds honey in the lion's carcass where the bees have made their hive. The psalmist's enemies compass him about like bees, and are quenched as the fire of thorns.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bee is a picture of the ordered life: small, busy, and dangerous to disturb, and the honey it makes is the sweetness God puts in unlikely places. The bee works in order and stings in defence, and the life that is ordered is the life that bears honey.
RelatedTopics: Nature and Creation; Diligence; God's Provision
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to slink, i.e. (by implication) to fear, or (causatively) be formidable
BiblicalUsage: To fear, in the Aramaic of Daniel, is the dread that falls on kings and peoples before the God of heaven. Nebuchadnezzar's dream makes him afraid, Darius trembles when Daniel is thrown to the lions, and the beasts of the vision make Daniel himself shake. The word also names the formidable power that makes men afraid.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and the fear of man is its ruin: Daniel feared God and did not fear the lions, and the kings who feared men lost their kingdoms. The kings who feared men fell, and the man who feared God stood, and the lions knew the difference.
RelatedTopics: Fear of God; Courage; God's Power
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a push, i.e. (by implication) a fall
BiblicalUsage: The word appears twice, both times for the stumbling foot: the psalmist's feet slipping toward the grave, and the Lord keeping his feet from falling. A push is a small thing, and a fall is a great one.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the prayer of everyone who has felt the ground give way: keep my feet, Lord, for I cannot keep them myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a primary verb; to receive (in various applications, literally or figuratively):--accept, receive, take. Compare G2983.
BiblicalUsage: To receive is the heart of the gospel, and the word gathers the receiving of the message, the receiving of the offering, and the receiving of one another. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, Paul says, and the grace of God must not be received in vain. The Philippian gift is received as a sacrifice well pleasing to God, and the brother who was once unprofitable is to be received as a brother.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe receiving is the first act of faith: we do not take, we receive, and everything we have is a gift from the hand of God. The receiving is the whole of faith: the hand that is open is the hand that is filled.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dedan, the name of two Cushites and of their territory
BiblicalUsage: Dedan is the name of two Cushites and of the territory their people held, on the trading roads of Arabia. The merchants of Dedan trade in ivory and ebony and precious cloth, and the prophets warn them to flee from the sword. The territory is named with the nations that will fall in the day of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dedan shows that no trading nation is outside God's judgment: the caravans and the markets are His, and the merchants answer to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dedanites, the descendants or inhabitants of Dedan
BiblicalUsage: The Dedanites appear once, in Isaiah's burden upon Arabia: the travelling companies of Dedanim lodge in the forest, and the inhabitants bring water to the thirsty and bread to the fugitive. It is a word of shelter on the road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse honours the small kindness: water for the thirsty and bread for the fugitive is the hospitality God remembers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1189; a petition:--prayer, request, supplication.
BiblicalUsage: Prayer in the New Testament is petition, supplication, the asking of the heart laid before God. Paul prays night and day for the churches, the widow Anna serves God with fastings and prayers, and the church is told to continue in prayer and supplication for all saints. The prayer of a righteous man avails much, and the Lord's ears are open to the righteous.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe petition is the privilege of the child: we do not inform God, we ask Him, and He who hears in secret answers in the open. The asking is the child's right, and the Father who hears is the Father who answers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a flag
KeyPassages: Numbers 1:52; Numbers 2:17; Numbers 10:14; Song of Solomon 2:4
BiblicalUsage: The flag is the standard of the tribe, raised over the camp in the wilderness and carried before the host. Each tribe pitches by its own standard, and the armies march in order under their banners. The Song pictures the beloved's banner over her as love itself, the standard under which she stands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the standard is the sign of belonging: every tribe knew its banner, and every believer knows whose flag flies over them. The banner is the sign of whose we are, and the standard we march under is the name of the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: gold
BiblicalUsage: Gold is the metal of the image and the metal of the temple, and Daniel's book holds both. The head of gold is the glory of Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom, the golden image is the idolatry of the same king, and the vessels of gold are the plunder of the house of God. Ezra weighs the gold for the temple, and the wise men of the east offer it to the child.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that gold in Daniel's book is always a test: it can be the glory of a kingdom or the god of a king, and the difference is what it is given to. The gold that is given to God is gold that is safe, and the gold that is kept for itself is gold that will rust.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: 3rd person singular active present of G1210; also δέον; neuter active participle of the same; both used impersonally; it is (was, etc.) necessary (as binding):--behoved, be meet, must (needs), (be) need(-ful), ought, should.
BiblicalUsage: The little word means it must be, it is necessary, and the New Testament uses it wherever God's purpose presses on a life. Jesus says He must go to Jerusalem and suffer, a man must be born again, and the Son of man must be lifted up. The form itself is the impersonal of the verb to bind, and the manuscripts carry it under that verb's heading.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is the hinge of the gospel: what must be, God does, and what God must do, He does through Christ, because necessity in Scripture is never fate but the Father's purpose, and it always ends in redemption.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G1166; a specimen (as shown):--example.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Jude's warning: the cities of the plain are set forth as an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire. A specimen, shown for all to see.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the example is given so that we will not repeat it: Sodom is the warning written in fire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1164; to exhibit:--make a shew.
BiblicalUsage: To make a show of something is to expose it, and the word carries both a public display and a public shame. Christ spoiled principalities and powers, making a show of them openly and triumphing over them in the cross. Joseph, being a just man, was not willing to make Mary a public example, and chose to put her away privately.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cross is the great public show: what was meant to shame Christ became the shame of His enemies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of an obsolete primary of the same meaning; to show (literally or figuratively):--shew.
BiblicalUsage: To show is what Jesus does when He opens the future to His disciples and what the angel does when He shows John the holy city. The word survives in the manuscripts under the shorter verb form, and its three showings span the gospel: the suffering that must come, the sign the Jews demand, and the city that will come down from heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe showing is how God teaches: He does not only tell, He shows, and the showing makes the promise sure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1169; timidity:--fear.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Paul's charge to Timothy: God has not given us the spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind. Timidity is not from God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the antidote to every fearful ministry: the Spirit we received is not timidity, it is power.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1167; to be timid:--be afraid.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, on the night of the betrayal: let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. The timid heart is the heart the Lord steadies with His peace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the Lord's own answer to fear: His peace is the gift He leaves, and it is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from δεός (dread); timid, i.e. (by implication) faithless:--fearful.
BiblicalUsage: Fearful is the word for the timid, the faithless, the ones who shrink when the storm rises. The disciples are called fearful in the boat, and the fearful are named among those whose part is in the lake of fire. The word binds timidity to unbelief: the fearful are those who do not trust.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the storm still asks the same question: why are you fearful, O you of little faith? The answer is not to try harder, but to trust the One who is in the boat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same as G1171 (through the idea of forgetting the name as fearful, i.e. strange); so and so (when the person is not specified):--such a man.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, as a pronoun for a man whose name is left unsaid: such a man, in such a place, at such a time. It is the deliberate vagueness of a story that does not need the name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word reminds us that Scripture names what matters and leaves the rest unnamed, and the unnamed still belong to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of the same as G1169; terribly, i.e. excessively:--grievously, vehemently.
BiblicalUsage: The word means terribly, exceedingly, and it appears twice: the man who begs for his paralysed servant, grievously tormented, and the scribes and Pharisees who press Jesus vehemently, laying wait for Him. The adverb measures the pressure of suffering and of opposition.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows how honestly the Gospels speak of pain: grievously is not an exaggeration, it is the measure of a father's grief.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1173; to dine, i.e. take the principle (or evening) meal:--sup (X -er).
BiblicalUsage: To sup is to sit at the table for the evening meal, and the word gathers the suppers of the Gospels: the master who bids his servant to make ready and serve him, the Lord who sups with the one who opens the door, and the cup of the new testament in His blood. Supper is fellowship, and the Lord's Supper is the fellowship that remembers Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the table is where the Lord meets His people: He who was betrayed at supper still invites us to sup with Him. The supper is the fellowship that remains when the crowds have gone, and the Lord still sets the table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G1160; dinner, i.e. the chief meal (usually in the evening):--feast, supper.
BiblicalUsage: Supper is the chief meal, the evening feast, and the word gathers the great suppers of Scripture: the wedding supper of the king's son, the supper of the great God where the birds are called, and the Lord's own supper where the bread is broken. The feast is the picture of the kingdom, and the invitation is the gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the supper table is the picture of the kingdom: God sets a feast, the invitation goes out, and the blessed are those who sit down to eat. My position is that the Lord's Supper is the rehearsal of that feast, and we eat it looking forward.
RelatedTopics: Communion; Kingdom of God; Fellowship; Invitation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the compound of a derivative of the base of G1169 and G1142; more religious than others:--too superstitious.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Paul's address on the Areopagus: I perceive that in all things you are too superstitious, or more religious than others. The comparative form survives in the manuscripts under the plain adjective, and Paul turns their religiosity into his opening.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's tact is the model for witness: he begins where they are, even with their superstition, and leads them to the God they do not know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G1174; religion:--superstition.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the hearing before Festus: the Jews have certain questions against Paul, of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. Religion is the charge, and the resurrection is the answer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows the world's verdict on the faith: they call it superstition, and we call it the resurrection.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: this
BiblicalUsage: The word means this, and the Aramaic of Ezra uses it for the decree, the letter, and the record: this is the copy of the letter, this is the decree of the king. It is the finger pointing at the document.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows how the exiles kept their history: they wrote it down, they filed it, and the record stood. The record stands when the voices fade, and the decree that is written is the decree that is kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary number; ten:--(eight-)een, ten.
BiblicalUsage: Ten is the number of the commandments, the virgins, the lepers, and the days of testing, and the word gathers them all. Ten servants receive ten pounds, ten lepers are cleansed and one returns, and ten horns rise on the beast. Ten is the number of completeness in the counting of men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ten in Scripture is the number of the whole: the whole law on two tables, the whole church in ten virgins, and the whole debt in ten thousand talents. The number is complete because God counted it, and the counting is His, not ours.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1176 and G1417; two and ten, i.e. twelve:--twelve.
BiblicalUsage: Twelve is the number of the tribes and the apostles, and this spelling of it never stands in the Greek New Testament: every occurrence of twelve is written with the single word for a dozen, and this compound form is a word-list entry with no verse to its name. I say so plainly, because no verse may be invented for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gap is honest: a word that never occurs still belongs in the record, and the twelve it names are real enough without it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1176 and G4002; ten and five, i.e. fifteen:--fifteen.
BiblicalUsage: Fifteen is a small number with a great reach: the distance from Jerusalem to Bethany, the years added to Hezekiah's life, and the years Paul waited before he went up to Jerusalem to see Peter. Fifteen marks the space between the city and the grave, and between the conversion and the visit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fifteen is the measure of patience: the Lord gives Hezekiah fifteen years, and Paul gives the gospel fifteen years to grow. The fifteen years are the Lord's gift, and the gift is given to be used, not wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1176 and G4172; the ten-city region; the Decapolis, a district in Syria:--Decapolis.
BiblicalUsage: The Decapolis is the ten-city region beyond the Jordan, and the word gathers the crowds that followed Jesus from there and the demoniac who was sent to publish in Decapolis what the Lord had done for him. The cities are Gentile ground, and the gospel crosses the river to reach them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Decapolis is the proof that the gospel is for the other side of the river too: the man who was bound is sent home to tell it, and the cities listen. The cities across the river are not beyond the gospel, and the man who was sent home carried it there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a male, i.e. of sheep
BiblicalUsage: The word names the male of the flock, and it appears in the law of the offering: the ram for the burnt offering, the male lamb for the sacrifice, and the male of the sheep for the peace offering. A male without blemish is the standard of the offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the male without blemish points to the Lamb who was without blemish, and the offering that was only a shadow. The male without blemish is the picture of the One who was without blemish, and the shadow points to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G1182; a tenth, i.e. as a percentage or (technically) tithe:--tenth (part), tithe.
BiblicalUsage: The tenth is the tithe, the portion set apart for the Lord, and the word gathers the great tithing passages: Abraham gives the tenth of all to Melchizedek, the Levites receive the tenth of Israel, and the author of Hebrews shows that Levi himself paid tithes in Abraham. The tenth is the confession that all belongs to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tithe is the tenth that teaches the whole: the one who gives the tenth confesses that the nine-tenths are also His. The tenth is the confession, and the confession is that all of it belongs to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1176 and G5064; ten and four, i.e. fourteen:--fourteen.
BiblicalUsage: Fourteen is the number of the generations in Matthew's genealogy and of the years between Paul's visits to Jerusalem. Fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the exile, and fourteen from the exile to Christ: the number orders the history of redemption. Paul counts fourteen years and goes up again, with the gospel he preaches among the Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fourteen is the number that says God keeps count: the generations are ordered, the years are numbered, and the Christ comes on time. The generations are ordered because God orders them, and the Christ comes exactly on time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1181; to tithe, i.e. to give or take a tenth:--pay (receive) tithes.
BiblicalUsage: To tithe is to give the tenth, and the word appears twice in Hebrews, both times of Abraham and Melchizedek: he who received the tithes blessed him who had the promises, and Levi, who receives tithes, paid tithes in Abraham. The tithe is the lesser blessing the greater.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tithe honours the greater: Abraham gave to one greater than himself, and we give to the One who is greater still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ordinal from G1176; tenth:--tenth.
BiblicalUsage: Tenth is the ordinal, the tenth part and the tenth hour and the tenth foundation of the city. The tenth hour is when Andrew and John first abode with Jesus, the tenth part of the city falls in the earthquake, and the tenth foundation of the wall is the chrysoprasus. The tenth is the measure of the whole.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tenth hour is the hour worth remembering: the day Andrew first sat with Jesus is the day his life changed. The tenth hour is the hour the disciple remembers, and the remembering is the beginning of the following.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1209; approved; (figuratively) propitious:-- accepted(-table).
BiblicalUsage: Accepted is the word for the time and the offering that God receives: the acceptable year of the Lord, the sacrifice acceptable to God, and the man who is accepted with Him. Paul writes that now is the accepted time, and now is the day of salvation. The word gathers the welcome of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the acceptable time is now, and the acceptable offering is the life laid down in Christ. The accepted time is the time God has given, and the giving is the grace we must not waste.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {to flame (literally or figuratively)}
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days: His garment was white as snow, and the hair of His head like pure wool, and His throne was like the fiery flame, and His wheels as burning fire. A flame is the picture of the throne.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the flame is the holiness of God made visible: the throne burns, and the Ancient of Days sits in the fire.
RelatedTopics: God's Holiness; Visions; Majesty of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Delajah, the name of five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Delaiah is the name of five Israelites, and the word gathers them all: the priest of the fifth course, the son of Shemaiah who tried to stop Jeremiah, the companion of the return, and the men of the registers. One name, five men, all in the service of the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name honours the many who serve without a story: five Delaiahs, and the Lord knows them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G1388; to entrap, i.e. (figuratively) delude:--allure, beguile, entice.
BiblicalUsage: To allure is to entice with a bait, and the word gathers the seductions of the false teachers: they allure through the lusts of the flesh those who are barely escaping, and they promise liberty while they themselves are servants of corruption. The bait is always freedom, and the hook is always bondage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the allure is the oldest trick in the book: the serpent's promise, the teacher's flattery, and the world's offer all say the same thing, and the end is the same. The bait is always sweet and the hook is always hidden, and the wise man looks for the hook.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dripping
BiblicalUsage: The dripping is the picture of the contentious wife and the leaky roof: a continual dropping in a very rainy day, and a quarrelsome woman are alike. The proverb pairs them because both wear a house down, drop by drop.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the proverb is honest about the home: the drip that never stops is the quarrel that never ends, and both need mending.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something swinging, i.e. the valve of a door
BiblicalUsage: The door is the swinging valve that guards the house and opens to the guest, and the word gathers the doors of Scripture: the doors of the temple overlaid with gold, the doors of the city shut against the enemy, and the door of the house where the Levite's concubine lay. The door is the threshold between inside and out, and the Lord stands at it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the door is the picture of the heart: it swings on its hinges, it opens to the guest, and the Lord knocks at it still. The door swings both ways, and the heart that opens to the Lord is the heart He enters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pail or jar (for drawing water)
BiblicalUsage: The pail is the vessel for drawing water, and the word pictures the blessing of the people: their buckets run over with water, and their seed is in many waters. A small vessel, full to the brim, is the picture of abundance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pail is the measure of blessing: God does not give a cup, He gives a bucket, and it runs over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Delilah, a Philistine woman
BiblicalUsage: Delilah is the Philistine woman who loved Samson and sold him, and her name is the story of the fall of the strongest man in Israel. She pressed him daily with her words until his soul was vexed unto death, and he told her the secret of his strength. The Philistines bound him, put out his eyes, and made him grind in the prison house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Delilah is the warning about the slow press: she did not conquer Samson in a day, she wore him down word by word, and the strongest man fell to the smallest weapon. My position is plain: the secret of our strength is the Lord, and it must never be given away to please another.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1212; to make plain (by words):--declare, shew, signify.
BiblicalUsage: To declare is to make plain by words, and the word gathers the declaring of the gospel: the report brought to Paul, the witness of the prophets, and the declaration of the end from the beginning. The apostles declare what they have seen and heard, and the Lord declares what will be.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe declaring is the work of the witness: we do not invent the message, we make plain what God has shown. The declaring is the plain telling of what God has done, and the telling is the witness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; clear:--+ bewray, certain, evident, manifest.
BiblicalUsage: Manifest is the word for what is clear, evident, and impossible to miss: the righteousness of God is manifest, the works of the flesh are manifest, and the speech of the Galilaean betrays the disciple. What is manifest cannot be hidden, and the truth will out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe manifest is the word for the gospel's clarity: the righteousness of God is not hidden in a corner, it is revealed for all to see. The manifest is what cannot be hidden, and the truth that is manifest will judge us all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tear; figuratively, juice
BiblicalUsage: The tear appears once, in the law of the firstfruits: the first of your ripe fruits you shall bring to the house of the Lord. The tear is the juice of the grape, the first drop of the harvest, and it belongs to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the first tear of the harvest is the confession that the whole vintage is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to resemble
BiblicalUsage: To resemble is the word for likeness in Daniel's visions: the one like a son of man, the beast like a lion, and the form of the fourth like the Son of God. Resemblance is the language of the visions, where the heavenly is described by the earthly it is like.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe resemblance is how God speaks of heaven: He shows us what it is like, and the likeness is enough to make us worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quiet
BiblicalUsage: Stillness is the sound of the Lord passing by, and the word gathers the quiet places: the still small voice on the mountain, the silence of the deep before the storm is calmed, and the stillness of the sea when the wind ceases. The Lord is not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire, but in the still small voice that follows.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe stillness is where God is found: the wind and the fire pass by, and the voice that remains is the still one. The stillness after the storm is the Lord's own voice, and the voice that remains is the one to follow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably for G1216; Demas, a Christian:--Demas.
BiblicalUsage: Demas is the fellow labourer who loved this present world and forsook Paul in his last imprisonment. He is named with Luke and Mark in the letters of the earlier years, and in the last letter he is gone. The contrast is the warning: the faithful remain, and the one who loved the world departs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Demas is the saddest name in the letters: a man who worked beside Paul and left him, because the present world seemed better than the coming one. I hold that his story is written so that we will not follow it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1218 and G58; to be a people-gatherer, i.e. to address a public assembly:--make an oration.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the public address of Herod: he arrayed himself in royal apparel, sat on his throne, and made an oration to the people, who cried that it was the voice of a god. The speech is the pride of a king, and the angel strikes him down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the oration is the warning about the platform: the voice that takes God's glory is struck down in the hearing of the crowd.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: damask (as a fabric of Damascus)
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Amos's picture of the remnant: as the shepherd takes out of the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be taken out that dwell in Samaria. Damask is the fabric of the wealthy, named for the city that wove it, and the remnant is as small as a scrap of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a sober picture of the remnant: what is saved is as small as a piece of cloth, and it is saved by the Shepherd's hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Δημήτηρ (Ceres); Demetrius, the name of an Ephesian and of a Christian:--Demetrius.
BiblicalUsage: Demetrius is the name of two men: the silversmith of Ephesus who made silver shrines for Diana and stirred the riot against Paul, and the Christian of whom John writes that he has a good report of all men and of the truth itself. One name, a persecutor and a witness, and the contrast is the whole story.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Demetrius shows that a name is not a destiny: the silversmith fought the gospel for his trade, and the Christian lived it for the truth. My position is that the report of all men is worth having, and it is earned by a life, not bought with silver.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Demetrius, the Silversmith; Demetrius (3 John)
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1218 and G2041; a worker for the people, i.e. mechanic (spoken of the Creator):--maker.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the faith chapter: Abraham looked for a city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God. The maker is the workman of the city, the craftsman of the foundations that do not move.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the city is the hope of every pilgrim: the foundations are God's, and the builder is God Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quiet
BiblicalUsage: Quiet is the word for the stillness of the soul and the silence of the land: Hezekiah's prayer that he would go softly all his years, the watchmen who are never to hold their peace, and the psalmist's cry to God not to keep silence. Quiet can be peace or it can be the silence of a God who seems far away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe quiet is the test of trust: the watchman who will not be silent is the one who believes God hears, and the soul that is quiet before Him is the soul at rest. The quiet soul is the soul that trusts, and the trust is the rest that the world cannot give.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1210; the public (as bound together socially):--people.

Definition: the crimson-grub, but used only (in this connection) of the color from it, and cloths dyed therewith
BiblicalUsage: 1) worm, scarlet stuff, crimson; 1a) worm-the female 'coccus ilicis'; 1b) scarlet stuff, crimson, scarlet; 1b1) the dye made from the dried body of the female of the worm "coccus ilicis"; 2) worm, maggot; 2a) worm, grub; 2b) the worm "coccus ilicis"; ++++; When the female of the scarlet worm species was ready to give birth to her young, she would attach her body to the trunk of a tree, fixing herself so firmly and permanently that she would never leave again. The eggs deposited beneath her body were thus protected until the larvae were hatched and able to enter their own life cycle. As the mother died, the crimson fluid stained her body and the surrounding wood. From the dead bodies of such female scarlet worms, the commercial scarlet dyes of antiquity were extracted. What a picture this gives of Christ, dying on the tree, shedding His precious blood that He might "bring many sons unto glory" (Heb 2:10)! He died for us, that we might live through him! Ps 22:6 describes such a worm and gives us this picture of Christ. (cf. Isa 1:18) (from page 73, "Biblical Basis for Modern Science", 1985, Baker Book House, by Henry Morris)
